t.el remosillo@42.1,0.3:
If you ride north from Barbastro toward Graus, the Ésera river eventually forces its way through a ridge of limestone, and the result is the Congosto de Olvena, a short, deep gorge with the road squeezed between rock and water. Up on the cliffs around here are rock shelters with prehistoric paintings, and El Remosillo is one of the best known in this corner of Aragón, between Estadilla, Graus and Fonz.

The paintings at El Remosillo are of the schematic type, red figures reduced to their essentials, and the site has been studied for a long time because it shows layers of occupation. Archaeologists have also worked in the caves of the gorge on evidence of people living here over a very long span of prehistory. Like the other sites that make up the Mediterranean rock art inscription, it is small, protected and best appreciated with a bit of patience and context. The local interpretation of these sites is often organised through the nearby villages, so if you want to see the panels properly, check ahead.

The road through the gorge itself is a treat: short, rocky and dramatic, with overhanging walls and the river running green below. The old road still exists alongside newer sections, and the area is popular with climbers and cyclists, so keep your eyes open on the bends. North of the gorge you reach Graus, a lovely small town with an arcaded main square and painted façades, which works well as a lunch stop. From there the roads branch toward Benabarre, Campo and the Pyrenean valleys, with tight bends and steady climbs. South and west, the gentler roads through the Somontano wine country around Barbastro roll past vineyards and almond groves.

Graus, under ten kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and shops; Barbastro, about sixteen kilometres south, is the bigger town for anything more serious. The Somontano wines are well worth a bottle in the pannier for the evening, and Graus is known in Aragón for its sausages and for its old fairs. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer is hot, and the reservoir country around Barasona can be dazzling in the midday glare.
t.abric del mas dels ous@40.6,0.2:
Xert is the kind of village you pass through on the way to somewhere else and then wonder why you did not stop. It lies in the Baix Maestrat in northern Castellón, below a ridge of bare limestone, with the old village climbing the slope and a newer part down by the road. The shelter called the Abric del Mas dels Ous, the shelter of the farmhouse of the eggs, is out in the dry hills nearby, between Xert, Canet lo Roig and Rosell.

The Maestrat is one of the heartlands of Levantine rock art. Within a modest radius of here are some of the most important painted shelters in Spain, including the Valltorta gorge near Tírig with its museum, where the scenes of archers and hunted animals are among the most celebrated examples of the style. Smaller shelters like this one fill in the picture: the same small, energetic figures, the same reddish pigments, the same choice of overhangs looking out over valleys where game would have moved. Most are protected and some are only accessible with a guide.

The landscape is the point. This is dry, rugged country of almond and olive terraces built over centuries with dry-stone walls, abandoned masias, holm oak and kermes oak on the slopes, and the smell of thyme and rosemary on a warm day. The name Maestrat comes from the Maestre, the master of the military orders, Templars and then the Order of Montesa, who ruled here after the conquest.

The roads are excellent for a bike. The CV roads from Xert toward Morella climb steadily through the hills with long series of bends and good views, and the route west over the passes toward the interior is famous among local riders. Traffic is light except on summer weekends. Surfaces are generally good, though gravel and the odd crumbling edge appear on the smaller roads. Xert has a bar or two, but for fuel and a proper choice of food, plan around Sant Mateu, Vinaròs on the coast, or Ulldecona, about twenty-five kilometres away, which is the nearest larger town. Sant Mateu, close by, was once the capital of the Maestrat and has a lovely arcaded square.
t.prop de la cova pintada@40.8,0.3:
The Ports massif rises abruptly at the meeting point of Catalonia, Aragón and Valencia, a tangle of limestone peaks, deep gorges and pine forest that feels surprisingly wild given how close it is to the Ebro delta and the coast. Prop de la Cova Pintada, meaning near the painted cave, sits on its southern side, between Mas de Barberans, Valderrobres and the old city of Tortosa.

The painted shelters of this area belong to the eastern Spanish rock art tradition, small figures of hunters and animals in red and black, painted on rock walls by people who lived from the game in these mountains. Some of the panels around the Ports are well known and visited, others are small and obscure. The whole massif is a protected natural park, home to a thriving population of Iberian ibex that you may well spot on the crags.

The riding here is superb. From Mas de Barberans the road into the Ports climbs through pine and holm oak with tight, technical bends, and the routes connecting Roquetes, Alfara de Carles, Paüls and Horta de Sant Joan cross some of the most dramatic scenery in Catalonia. Horta de Sant Joan is famous because the young Picasso spent time there and later said it was where he learned everything he knew; there is a small centre dedicated to him. On the Aragonese side, Valderrobres has a gorgeous old town with a medieval bridge, castle and church grouped above the Matarraña river. Surfaces range from excellent to rough, and some mountain roads are narrow with sheer drops. Watch out for wild boar at dusk.

Tortosa, about sixteen kilometres away, is the main town with fuel, food and accommodation. It has a fine Gothic cathedral and the Suda castle above the Ebro, and its old quarter tells of Jewish, Muslim and Christian communities. Mas de Barberans is small, with a bar or two. The Ebro delta, a short ride east, is Spain's great rice-growing wetland, flat and full of birds. Spring and autumn are best: summer heat in the valleys is intense, and storms can build quickly over the peaks.
t.les coves@41.9,0.6:
The western edge of Catalonia, around Lleida, is fruit country. Irrigation canals bring water from the Pyrenean rivers to a broad, flat plain of orchards growing apples, pears and peaches, laid out in neat lines that stretch to the horizon. Les Coves lies in this area, close to the Aragonese border, between Alfarràs, Albelda and Algerri, where the valley of the Noguera Ribagorçana spills out of the hills and onto the plain.

The painted shelters of this part of Lleida province are lesser known than those of the Valencian mountains, but they are part of the same UNESCO inscription and reflect the same long story: hunting and later farming communities choosing rocky overhangs near water to make their images. Many shelters along the valleys north of here hold schematic and Levantine paintings. Visits to the more significant ones are often organised by local councils, so check in advance if you want to see anything beyond the setting.

The riding is gentle on the plain and much better as you head north. The roads around Alfarràs and Almenar are flat and straight, running past orchards and farm complexes with occasional tractors and fruit lorries. Head north toward Os de Balaguer, Camarasa or up the valley toward the Montsec range, and things change: the Montsec is a great limestone wall cut through by spectacular gorges, including Mont-rebei, and the roads climbing toward Àger and over the range are some of the best in Catalonia, with tight hairpins and huge views.

Alfarràs and Almacelles have the basics; Almacelles, about twenty-one kilometres away, is the larger town, and Lleida itself is less than an hour away, with its cathedral, La Seu Vella, dominating the city from a hill. Fruit stalls along the roads in summer sell peaches and nectarines by the box. Lleida's food speciality is snails, cooked a la llauna on a metal tray with garlic and aioli. In blossom season, usually in March, the whole plain turns pink and white, and it is one of the loveliest times to ride here.
The Tinença de Benifassà is one of the emptiest corners of the Valencian Community, a group of tiny stone villages scattered across rugged limestone mountains in the far north of Castellón, right where Valencia, Catalonia and Aragón meet. The Cova dels Rossegadors, also called the Cova del Polvorí, lies on the edge of this country near Rossell, with Mas de Barberans and Canet lo Roig the other nearby villages.

The cave holds painted figures in the Levantine style, part of the network of shelters protected by UNESCO along the eastern side of Spain. Its alternative name, the gunpowder cave, suggests later use, perhaps for storing explosives or as a refuge. As with most such sites, it is fragile and protected, and access to the paintings themselves is limited. The reward is understanding how these mountains were used by people over thousands of years, as hunting grounds, pastures and hiding places.

The Tinença is wonderful riding country. The road from La Sénia and Rossell climbs into the mountains toward the Cistercian monastery of Santa Maria de Benifassà, founded in the thirteenth century after the Christian conquest and still home to a community of nuns. From there, narrow roads wind between the villages of El Ballestar, La Pobla de Benifassà, Fredes and Coratxà, on twisting tarmac with dramatic views over gorges and forested slopes. Fredes, high in the mountains, is one of the remotest villages in the region, close to the point where the three regions meet. The roads are narrow and sometimes in poor condition, with loose gravel, and you are as likely to meet a herd of goats as another vehicle.

There is little in the way of services in the mountains. Rossell is a small town with a bar or two, and fuel can be found in La Sénia or in Ulldecona, about twenty-one kilometres away. Fill up before heading in and plan a loop. The area is known for its forests of black pine and beech, unusual this far south, and in autumn the colours are superb. Winter can bring snow to the higher villages, so check conditions before setting out.
t.la fenellosa@40.8,0.2:
People in Aragón like to call the Matarraña their Tuscany, and for once the comparison is not entirely marketing. It is a comarca of honey-coloured stone villages on hilltops, olive groves on terraces, almond trees and vineyards, with the limestone wall of the Ports de Beseit rising behind. La Fenellosa lies in this country, between Valderrobres, Fuentespalda and Mas de Barberans across the Catalan line, in the rough hills where the farmland gives way to the mountains.

The Matarraña has a notable concentration of rock art. Painted shelters with Levantine figures are scattered through the ravines of the river and its tributaries, and the comarca has done more than many to make them visible, with signposted paths and an interpretation network. Calaceite, to the north, adds another layer: the Iberian hill town of San Antonio, an excavated settlement with streets, houses and a cistern, which shows how people lived here two and a half thousand years ago. La Fenellosa itself is a quiet shelter in that long sequence, protected and best appreciated with patience.

Beceite, the village closest to the mountains, is the gateway to the Parrizal, a narrow gorge of the Matarraña river where a walkway lets you follow the water between sheer walls, sometimes barely a few metres apart. It is a popular walk, so in summer go early. The upper river has deep green pools, and people swim in them on hot days.

The roads here invite a slow ride. The A-231 and the smaller roads linking Valderrobres, Beceite, Fuentespalda, Peñarroya de Tastavins and Monroyo wind over hills with a steady stream of bends and constant views of the Ports. Peñarroya leads up toward the sanctuary of the Virgen de la Fuente, a lovely spot in the mountains. Surfaces are mostly decent, traffic sparse, but some routes are narrow, and the comarca is popular with cyclists.

Valderrobres has fuel and a range of restaurants; Tortosa is the nearest big town, about twenty-seven kilometres away. Matarraña olive oil is outstanding, and the local ham and cured meats are well worth tasting. Spring and autumn are best, when the hills are green and the light is soft.
t.cueva de revilla@42.6,0.2:
Revilla is one of the most spectacularly placed hamlets in the Spanish Pyrenees, perched on a ledge above the Garganta de Escuaín, a deep gorge cut into the limestone of the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park. It looks down into the canyon from a terrace of meadows, with the high peaks behind. The Cueva de Revilla is a cave in the cliffs near the hamlet, and the area between Bielsa, Plan and Boltaña is some of the wildest country in Aragón.

The Escuaín gorge is the least visited of the four great valleys of the national park, and that is a large part of its charm. Revilla and Escuaín, a neighbouring hamlet, were nearly abandoned in the twentieth century, and only a few houses are lived in today. The gorge is home to the lammergeier, or bearded vulture, a huge bird that feeds on bones, dropping them from a height to break them. There is an observation point for spotting them, and the sight of one gliding over the canyon is extraordinary. The cave itself is one of many in this limestone country, and caves in the area have yielded traces of prehistoric occupation.

Getting to Revilla is a ride in itself. The access road branches off the road up the Cinca valley toward Bielsa and climbs on a narrow, twisting, sometimes broken lane through the hamlets of Tella-Sin. It is single track in places, with steep drops and no barriers, so take it slowly. The main road up the Cinca, toward Bielsa and the tunnel into France, is a great ride in its own right, through the gorge of Las Devotas and along the river.

Bielsa, about six kilometres away, is the nearest village with services, including fuel. It has a few hotels and restaurants, and is known for its carnival with figures dressed in goat horns and skins. During the Spanish Civil War, Bielsa was the site of a famous episode, the Bolsa de Bielsa, when Republican troops held out in the valley before retreating into France in 1938.

The road is often closed by snow in winter, so check conditions. Late spring to autumn is best, when the meadows are green and the peaks still have snow.
t.pyrenees mont perdu@42.7,0.0:
Monte Perdido, the lost mountain, at 3,355 metres, is the highest limestone massif in Europe and the centrepiece of a cross-border World Heritage site shared by Spain and France. On the Spanish side, it gives its name to the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park, with deep canyons radiating out from the summit; on the French side, it looks down on the great cirques of Gavarnie and Troumouse. The point at these coordinates lies high in the massif, between Broto, Bielsa and Luz-Saint-Sauveur in France.

The landscape here is the result of glaciers carving through layers of limestone, leaving towering cliffs, waterfalls and terraced valleys. The Ordesa valley itself, with its sheer walls in shades of red and grey, beech and fir forest, and the cascades of the Arazas river, is one of the most beautiful in Europe. Marmots, chamois and griffon vultures are common, and the rare Pyrenean ibex lived here until its extinction in 2000. The UNESCO listing also recognises the pastoral culture of the mountains, with shepherds who moved flocks across the border for centuries.

No road reaches the mountain itself, of course, so this is about the rides around it. The road up the Ara valley from Broto to Torla is the gateway to Ordesa; in summer, access to the national park's parking is restricted and visitors use a shuttle bus from Torla. To the east, the road up the Cinca valley to Bielsa and through the tunnel into France is a classic, as is the road from Bielsa into the Pineta valley, which ends below the north face of Monte Perdido. On the French side, the roads to Gavarnie and the Cirque de Troumouse are spectacular. Mountain roads here are often narrow, and snow can close the higher passes well into spring.

Broto and Torla have fuel and plenty of restaurants; Sabiñánigo, about thirty-five kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. The local food includes lamb from the mountains, and the mountain hotels serve hearty stews. Late spring to early autumn is the time to ride here, with snow possible at any time on the high ground.
t.els secans@41.1,0.1:
The lower Matarraña, in the far east of Aragón, is a drier, emptier country than the green upper valley. Here, the river flows through low hills of sandstone and limestone, with olive groves, almond trees and cereal fields, and the villages stand on hilltops, built of golden stone. Mazaleón is one of them, a small village above the river, with Maella and Calaceite nearby. Els Secans, a name meaning the dry lands, is a shelter with prehistoric paintings in the hills just outside the village.

The rock art of the Matarraña and the Bajo Aragón is part of the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO, and the shelters here have some interesting figures of hunters and animals. The area is also rich in Iberian sites: the Iberians, who lived here before the Romans, built fortified towns on the hilltops, and the remains of several of them can be visited. Mazaleón has its own Iberian site, and Calaceite, nearby, has the excavated town of San Antonio. The region is a good place to understand how this landscape was settled over thousands of years.

Maella is a pleasant town with a castle and a museum dedicated to the sculptor Pablo Gargallo, who was born there in 1881 and became one of the key figures in modern sculpture, working with metal in Paris alongside Picasso. Calaceite, with its noble houses and arcaded square, is one of the most beautiful villages in Aragón.

The riding here is relaxed and quiet. The roads between Mazaleón, Maella, Calaceite and Nonaspe wind through the hills, with gentle bends and long views, and very little traffic. Further south, the roads toward Valderrobres and the Ports de Beseit are more mountainous. The surfaces are generally good, but watch out for gravel and agricultural vehicles. The cierzo wind can be strong.

Services are limited. Maella has fuel and shops, and Alcañiz, about twenty-one kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. Local food includes the olive oil of the Bajo Aragón, which has a designation of origin, lamb and cured meats. Spring, with almond blossom, and autumn are the best seasons.
t.the@41.2,1.2:
The truncated label on this point hides an interesting site: the coordinates fall at Centcelles, just outside the town of Constantí, where a Roman villa holds one of the most extraordinary late antique buildings in Spain. Inside a plain-looking farmhouse building is a domed hall from the fourth century, its cupola covered in mosaics of hunting scenes, biblical stories and figures that may represent the imperial family. Some scholars believe it was built as a mausoleum for Constans, son of Constantine the Great, who was killed in 350; others are not so sure, and the debate is part of the fun. The site belongs to the UNESCO listing for the Roman town of Tarraco.

Tarragona, the old Tarraco, capital of a huge Roman province, lies only a few kilometres away, with its amphitheatre by the sea, the circus vaults under the old town, the walls, and the Pont del Diable aqueduct in the hills to the north. Centcelles makes a quiet counterpoint to all that grandeur: you may well have the dome to yourself, with only birds outside and the distant hum of traffic.

The immediate landscape is not glamorous. The Camp de Tarragona plain around Constantí and La Pobla de Mafumet is a mix of hazelnut and olive groves, industrial estates, motorway junctions and the large petrochemical complex that dominates the skyline to the south. But the riding gets good fast once you head inland: the roads up into the Prades mountains, toward Alcover, Mont-ral and the Serra de la Mussara, climb through pine forest with tight hairpins and views back over the coast. Summers here are hot and humid, so morning or late afternoon riding is kinder, and the Mediterranean wind can kick up in the afternoons.

Constantí is a town of over five thousand with fuel, shops and simple bars where you can order a coffee and a bocadillo. For a proper lunch, Tarragona's Serrallo fishing quarter serves seafood and rice dishes by the harbour, while Reus, a short ride west, is the birthplace of Antoni Gaudí and the home of vermouth, which locals take as an aperitif before lunch with olives and anchovies.
t.roca roja@41.5,1.5:
Roca Roja, the red rock, is a fitting name for this corner of inland Catalonia, where sandstone and conglomerate cliffs glow rust-coloured in the evening light above pine forest and small terraced fields. The point lies in the hills between Querol and Mediona, where the comarques of Alt Camp, Alt Penedès and Anoia meet, a rugged, thinly populated upland that most people speed past on the motorway between Barcelona and Lleida without realising it exists. Rock shelters in this area belong to the scattered network of prehistoric art sites along Spain's Mediterranean side, though I cannot promise there is anything visible at the precise spot.

Querol is the centre of this little world, a tiny village below a ruined castle on a rocky spur, at the head of the valley of the Gaià river. Follow the Gaià downstream and you reach the Cistercian monastery of Santes Creus, one of the three great monasteries of the Cistercian route in Catalonia, founded in the twelfth century and the burial place of several kings of Aragon. It makes a fine destination for a ride, with its Gothic cloister and the calm of the monks' gardens.

The roads here are made for motorcycles: narrow, twisting, mostly well surfaced and almost empty on weekdays. The route from Querol through Pontils and down toward Santa Coloma de Queralt, or east toward Sant Joan de Mediona and the Penedès, climbs and falls through forest with hairpins and blind crests, so keep to your side of the road, as local drivers and cyclists often do not. In summer the heat can be oppressive and forest fire risk high; in winter morning frost lingers in the shaded valleys. Late spring and October are ideal.

There is little in the way of services around Querol, so plan accordingly. Igualada, about seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and is known for its leather-tanning history and a museum devoted to it. Sant Joan de Mediona and Santa Coloma de Queralt have bars and small shops, and the Penedès to the southeast offers wineries where you can taste cava, though of course you will save that for after parking the bike.
t.triumphal arch of bera@41.2,1.5:
For centuries traffic on the main coastal road of Catalonia drove straight through a Roman triumphal arch. The Arc de Berà stands on the line of the Via Augusta, the great Roman road from the Pyrenees to Cádiz, about twenty kilometres northeast of Tarragona, and until the road was diverted around it in the late twentieth century, cars and trucks passed under its single span. It was built at the end of the first century BC, and an inscription records that it was erected according to the will of Lucius Licinius Sura, a figure whose identity historians still discuss. It is part of the UNESCO listing for the Roman remains of Tarraco.

The arch is a simple, elegant structure of local stone, with fluted pilasters and a cornice, and it stands alone in a small park beside the N-340, with pine trees and the noise of traffic around it. It probably marked a boundary between the territories of two towns, and travellers on the Via Augusta would have passed through it on their way to and from Tarraco. Today it is a popular stop for photographs, and a short walk takes you along a preserved section of the Roman road nearby.

The N-340 is the old main road along this coast, and it is usually busy with local traffic, trucks avoiding the parallel toll motorway, and summer tourists, so riding here is more about getting somewhere than enjoying the curves. The coast itself is lined with resorts, campsites and holiday homes, especially around Roda de Barà, Creixell and Coma-ruga. Head inland, however, and you soon find quiet roads through vineyards and olive groves, leading toward the Penedès wine region and the hills of the Baix Gaià.

Roda de Barà and Torredembarra have fuel, supermarkets and plenty of beach restaurants serving paella, grilled fish and seafood. Coma-ruga is known for its long sandy beach and its spa, and Torredembarra has an old town with a castle and a lighthouse. If you want to combine the arch with other Roman sites, the Tarraco remains, the Centcelles mausoleum and the Pont del Diable aqueduct are all within a short ride. In summer, avoid the coast road on weekend afternoons, when traffic can be heavy.
t.cova dels segarulls@41.3,1.7:
The vineyards of the Penedès roll out in every direction from Vilafranca, and the Cova dels Segarulls lies among them, a few kilometres outside the town in the low hills toward the coastal range. It is one of the scattered rock-art and prehistoric sites of eastern Spain, and although I cannot tell you exactly what it holds, the setting tells you plenty: these sheltered limestone outcrops above fertile land have attracted people for a very long time, from the first farmers to the Iberians, Romans and the monks who later planted vines here.

Vilafranca del Penedès is the capital of this wine region, a lively town of almost forty thousand people. It is famous for its castells, the human towers that teams of castellers build to dizzying heights during festivals, especially at the Festa Major at the end of August, when the town's teams compete in the Plaça de Sant Jaume. The Vinseum, the museum of wine cultures of Catalonia, explains the history of wine in the region. The town has a beautiful Gothic basilica, Santa Maria, and a modernist market.

The Penedès is the home of cava, the Catalan sparkling wine, made mainly around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, a short ride north, where the big houses like Codorníu and Freixenet have their cellars, some in buildings by modernist architects. The countryside is a patchwork of vineyards, farmhouses and small villages, with the jagged silhouette of Montserrat on the horizon. The riding is gentle, with quiet roads winding through the vineyards and over low hills; the road south over the Garraf massif to Sitges and the coast is more dramatic, with tight bends and sea views.

Vilafranca has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. Local dishes include xató, a salad with salt cod and a romesco-like sauce, and seasonal calçots, grilled spring onions dipped in sauce, served in late winter at outdoor feasts called calçotades. Many wineries offer tours and tastings, but if you are riding, enjoy the views and buy a bottle for later. The vineyards are most beautiful in autumn, when the leaves turn red and gold after the harvest, and in spring, when the new shoots appear.
t.pintures rupestres d alfes@41.5,0.7:
South of Lleida the irrigated orchards give way abruptly to dry, open steppe, and the little village of Alfés sits on the edge of that change. The Pintures Rupestres d'Alfés are rock paintings in a small sandstone shelter near the village, schematic designs in red pigment, mostly abstract lines, dots and simplified figures, that belong to the later, more symbolic phase of prehistoric art in eastern Spain, and they are included in the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean Basin rock art. They are modest to look at, but there is something powerful about seeing marks left by people thousands of years ago in such an open, wind-swept place.

The area around Alfés is one of the last remnants of the Catalan steppe, the Secans de Lleida, a protected area of dry cereal fields, scrub and gypsum hills that is home to rare birds like the little bustard, the stone curlew and the pin-tailed sandgrouse, which birdwatchers come from far away to see. In spring, the fields are green and full of birdsong; in summer, they turn golden and the heat shimmers over the land. An old military airfield nearby, built during the Spanish Civil War, is a reminder of the battles that raged along the Segre river in 1938.

The riding here is about wide horizons rather than curves. Roads are flat or gently rolling, mostly straight, with little traffic apart from farm vehicles. The wind can be strong and gusty, especially the cierzo from the northwest, so be prepared for crosswinds. To the south, the roads climb into the Les Garrigues hills, with olive groves and stone villages, and further on into the Serra de Prades and the Priorat, with excellent twisty roads and world-class wine.

Lleida, about eleven kilometres away, is a city of about 140,000 people, with all services. Its old cathedral, the Seu Vella, stands on a hill above the city, a striking Romanesque-Gothic building with a tall bell tower and a beautiful cloister, and the view from the top over the plain of the Segre is worth the climb. Lleida is famous for its snails, cooked a la llauna on a metal tray, and celebrated with a huge festival, the Aplec del Caragol, in May.
t.abric de la tenalla@40.7,0.2:
The Tinença de Benifassà is one of the wildest corners of the Valencian region, a cluster of tiny villages in the mountains where Valencia, Catalonia and Aragon meet, and the Abric de la Tenalla lies on its southeastern edge, near Rosell. It is one of the many rock shelters in this area with prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, and the nearby Serra de Godall and the Ulldecona shelters to the east are among the most important sites in Catalonia. The landscape is dramatic: limestone cliffs, deep gorges, pine and holm oak forests, and abandoned terraces where shepherds once grazed their flocks.

The Tinença takes its name from the Cistercian monastery of Santa Maria de Benifassà, founded in the thirteenth century after the Christian conquest, which still stands in a remote valley and is occupied by an order of Carthusian nuns. The villages of the Tinença, such as Fredes, El Boixar and Castell de Cabres, are among the highest and smallest in the region, and many have been almost abandoned, though some are coming back to life with rural tourism.

The riding in the Tinença is fantastic for those who enjoy narrow, twisty mountain roads with no traffic. The road from Rosell to La Sénia and up to the Tinença villages climbs through forests and gorges, with tight hairpins, steep gradients and spectacular views. The Ulldecona reservoir, surrounded by pine forest, is a beautiful spot for a break. Surfaces can be rough, with gravel and rockfalls, and there are few services, so plan carefully. Weather in the mountains is changeable, with cold winters and fog, and summers warm but cooler than the coast.

Ulldecona, about twenty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town with more than five thousand people and all services, and La Sénia, a furniture-making town, is closer and also has fuel. In the villages, simple restaurants serve mountain food: grilled lamb and rabbit, wild mushroom dishes in autumn, and cured meats. The coast, with the Ebro delta and its rice fields and lagoons, is about an hour away, offering a complete change of scenery.
t.albi ii balma dels punts@41.5,0.9:
L'Albi is a small village on a hill in Les Garrigues, the dry, olive-covered district southeast of Lleida, and its name appears in the archaeological record thanks to rock shelters in the area, including the Balma dels Punts, the shelter of the dots. The name suggests schematic paintings in the form of dots and lines, typical of the later phase of prehistoric art in the region, and the site is part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The shelters are small and fragile, and some can only be visited with a guide, so check with the town hall or a local interpretation centre before heading out.

Les Garrigues is olive oil country. The Arbequina variety, named after the nearby village of Arbeca, produces a fruity, delicate oil that is one of the most prized in Spain, and the landscape is dominated by olive groves, almond trees and dry-stone huts called cabanes de volta, built by farmers as shelters. The villages are built of golden stone, with churches, castles and arcaded squares, and the rhythm of life follows the seasons of the olive harvest, which takes place from November to January.

The riding here is quiet and relaxed. The roads wind through the olive groves and over low hills, with little traffic and wide views. To the south, the Serra de la Llena and the Prades mountains offer more challenging roads, with forests, climbs and hairpins, and the Cistercian monastery of Poblet, one of the most important in Spain and the burial place of the kings of Aragon, is about twenty kilometres away. Summers are hot and dry, winters cold, with fog in the plains; spring and autumn are the best seasons, with green fields and mild temperatures.

Services in the Garrigues villages are limited, so fill up in Mollerussa, Les Borges Blanques or Lleida. Vinaixa and Arbeca have small shops and bars. Local food is simple and delicious: bread rubbed with tomato and drizzled with olive oil, grilled meats, snails and the famous olive oil soup. Many olive oil cooperatives offer tastings and sell oil directly, and a bottle of fresh Arbequina is a wonderful souvenir, if you have space in your luggage.
t.abric de gallicant@41.3,1.0:
Alforja is a village on the southern edge of the Prades mountains, where the plain of the Camp de Tarragona meets the steep slopes of the Serra de l'Argentera and the Serra de la Mussara. The Abric de Gallicant lies in the hills near Alforja, Vilaplana and Ulldemolins, and it is one of the many prehistoric shelters in these mountains that form part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The name means rooster's song, a poetic touch typical of Catalan place names. The paintings in this area are generally schematic, with simple figures and geometric shapes, and many shelters are protected by fences.

The Prades mountains are a beautiful, rugged range, with red sandstone and limestone cliffs, pine and holm oak forests, and small stone villages. The area is popular with climbers, especially around Siurana, a tiny village perched on a cliff above a reservoir, which is one of the most famous climbing destinations in Europe. Legend says that the last Moorish queen of Siurana jumped from the cliff on horseback rather than surrender to the Christians, and you can see the queen's leap from the village.

For riders, the Prades mountains are a playground. The road from Alforja over the Coll d'Alforja to Porrera and into the Priorat wine region is a classic, with tight bends, steep climbs and views over vineyards and mountains. The roads to Siurana, Cornudella de Montsant and Prades, the red village built of reddish stone, are also excellent. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, cyclists and occasional livestock. Summers can be very hot, and the area is at risk of forest fires; spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Alforja has a few shops and bars, but for fuel and more services, head to Riudoms, Reus or Cornudella. The Priorat is famous for its powerful red wines, grown on steep slopes of black slate called llicorella, and many wineries offer tastings, though you will have to save the wine for after the ride. Local food includes grilled lamb, calçots in season and the hazelnuts and almonds that grow on the plain. Reus, about twenty kilometres away, is a vibrant town with modernist architecture.
t.valmayor iv@41.3,0.2:
Where the Ebro, the Segre and the Cinca meet in eastern Aragon, a vast reservoir stretches for dozens of kilometres between bare, ochre hills. The locals call it the Mar de Aragón, the Sea of Aragon, and it was created in the 1960s when the Mequinenza dam flooded the valley. The old town of Mequinenza went under the water too, and its people were moved to a new town built above, a story told in moving detail in the local museums and in the novels of Jesús Moncada, who grew up there.

In the hills around, sheltered under rock overhangs, are the paintings of Valmayor IV and its neighbours, part of the Levantine rock art inscribed by UNESCO as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The figures are small, fragile and often fenced off, and the shelters are not always easy to find without directions, so ask at the tourist offices in Mequinenza or Caspe before setting out on foot.

This is a dry, open country, half desert, with gypsum and limestone hills, thyme and esparto grass, almond and olive groves where there is enough water, and very few people. The light is sharp and the summer heat can be brutal. The reservoir has made the area famous among anglers from all over Europe, who come for the enormous wels catfish that grow here, some of them longer than a person.

The riding is open and fast, with long sightlines across the hills and few cars. Roads follow the edge of the reservoir and cross the hills in long, flowing curves, with occasional tight sections where they drop to the water. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel washed onto the road after storms and for the strong winds that sweep across the plateau. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; in July and August ride early and rest through the afternoon, as the locals do.

Caspe, about eighteen kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, shops and restaurants; it is also famous in Spanish history as the place where a dispute over the crown of Aragon was settled in 1412. Mequinenza has services too. A long lunch in either town, followed by a swim or a walk along the water, is the right rhythm here.
t.balma d en roc@41.0,0.8:
Inland from the Costa Daurada, the Serra de Llaberia rises abruptly above the coastal plain, a jagged wall of limestone separating the sea from the valley of the Ebro. The rock shelter of Balma d'En Roc lies in this rough country, part of the Levantine rock art inscribed by UNESCO, and like most of its kind it is small, fragile and best visited with local guidance. The nearest villages are scattered: Ginestar on the Ebro, El Perelló on the coastal side, and Mont-roig del Camp to the north-east.

The landscape is the star. The mountains are covered in pine, holm oak and dense Mediterranean scrub, broken by cliffs and gorges, and from the higher roads you can see down to the sea on one side and across the Ebro valley to the hills of the Terra Alta on the other. Eagles and vultures ride the thermals above the ridges. In summer the air smells of pine resin and dry herbs, and the risk of forest fires is high, so be careful with anything that might spark.

History runs deep here. The Ebro valley just to the west was the scene of the longest and bloodiest battle of the Spanish Civil War in 1938, and the area around Gandesa and Corbera d'Ebre still has trenches, memorials and the ruins of the old village of Corbera, left as a reminder. The Priorat wine region, with its steep terraces of slate and powerful red wines, lies a short ride north.

The roads around the Serra de Llaberia are a fine mix of twisty mountain passes and quiet back lanes. Climbs through the hills from the coast to the Ebro valley have tight hairpins, steep gradients and great views, and traffic is light away from the main routes. Watch for gravel and for cyclists, who love these climbs as much as motorcyclists do. Summer brings heat and holiday traffic on the coast; spring and autumn are perfect.

For fuel and supplies, Mont-roig del Camp, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, and the coast has plenty of stations. Smaller villages may have only a bar or a shop. Try a plate of calçots in late winter, the grilled spring onions dipped in romesco sauce, or simply local olive oil drizzled on bread with a glass of Priorat wine.
t.chateau de puilaurens@42.8,2.3:
Perched on a rocky spur above a forest of firs and beeches, at around seven hundred metres, the castle of Puilaurens looks like something drawn by a child who loves castles: battlements, towers, walls following every edge of the rock. It is one of the so-called Cathar castles of the Languedoc, a group of fortresses linked to the crusade launched against the Cathar heretics in the thirteenth century. After the region came under French control, the castle was rebuilt as a royal fortress guarding the frontier with the Kingdom of Aragon, which lay just to the south until the seventeenth century. The climb up from the car park is steep but short, and the views from the top over the Fenouillèdes and the Pyrenean foothills are superb.

Like many old castles, Puilaurens has a ghost: a White Lady said to wander the walls, linked by legend to a medieval princess who once stayed here.

The area around is wild and beautiful. To the north, the D117 runs between Quillan and Axat through the Défilé de Pierre-Lys, a narrow gorge with cliffs towering above the road and the river rushing below. To the east, the Gorges de Galamus are a classic: a narrow road carved into the cliff face, with a sheer drop to the river, a hermitage clinging to the rock and only room for one vehicle in places. It can be very busy in summer, and traffic restrictions may apply, so check before you go. Further east still, the castles of Peyrepertuse and Quéribus perch on even more dramatic ridges, each worth a visit.

The riding here is among the best in southern France. Roads twist through gorges, climb over passes and wind through forests and vineyards, with constant changes of scenery. Surfaces are generally good, but gravel, fallen rocks and narrow sections demand attention, and summer brings camper vans and tourists. Spring and autumn are perfect, with mild temperatures and fewer crowds; winter can bring snow higher up.

Quillan, about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a cassoulet, the rich bean stew of the Languedoc, or local charcuterie with a glass of Corbières or Fitou red wine, and finish with a coffee overlooking the river Aude.
t.cabra feixet@40.9,0.6:
El Perelló is a hill village on the old coast road between Tarragona and Tortosa, and it is famous for honey. Bees have been kept on these scrubby limestone slopes for centuries, feeding on rosemary, thyme and wild flowers, and every winter the village holds a honey fair that draws visitors from across Catalonia. In the hills around, sheltered under an overhang, is the rock art of Cabra Feixet, part of the Levantine paintings of eastern Spain inscribed together by UNESCO. The figures are small and faded, and the site is best visited with a guide or after asking at the village; please do not touch the rock.

The landscape is dry Mediterranean country: terraces of olive and carob trees, almond groves, pines and garrigue, with ravines dropping towards the sea. From the higher ground you can see the Ebro Delta spreading out to the south, a vast, flat triangle of rice paddies, lagoons and beaches pushing into the Mediterranean, one of the most important wetlands in the western Mediterranean. Flamingos, herons and countless ducks gather there, especially in winter, and the rice fields change colour with the seasons, flooded and silver in spring, green in summer, golden at harvest.

Tortosa, on the Ebro a short ride inland, is a city with a long and layered history: Roman, Moorish, Jewish and Christian. Its Gothic cathedral, the Suda castle on the hill above, now a parador, and its Renaissance colleges tell of centuries as a frontier and trading city on the river.

The riding varies. The old coast road is busy with trucks, but the minor roads through the hills between El Perelló, Rasquera and the Ebro valley are quiet and twisty, with fine views and good surfaces. Heading down into the delta changes the mood completely: flat, straight roads between rice fields, with big skies and birds everywhere. Watch for slow agricultural vehicles, and for strong winds, both the mestral from the north-west and the sea breezes, which can be gusty. Summer is hot and humid on the coast; spring and autumn are lovely.

Tortosa, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel and everything else, and El Perelló has basic services. Buy a jar of local honey, then head to the delta for a rice dish or a plate of mussels and oysters farmed in its bays.
t.balma de les ovelles@42.3,0.8:
The Balma de les Ovelles, the Sheep's Shelter, lies in the high country where Catalonia meets Aragon, between the valleys of the Noguera Ribagorçana and the Noguera Pallaresa. This is the southern edge of the Pyrenees, a land of limestone ridges, deep gorges, reservoirs and scattered villages, many of them half empty. Rock shelters like this one, used by shepherds and their flocks for thousands of years, are found throughout the region, and some hold traces of prehistoric painting or occupation. The name tells you what it was most recently used for, and the landscape around still carries the sound of sheep bells.

To the north, up the valley, lies the Vall de Boí, whose Romanesque churches, with their tall bell towers and painted interiors, are a World Heritage site; the churches of Santa Eulàlia at Erill la Vall and Sant Feliu at Barruera are among them, and in Taüll the church of Sant Climent has a famous painted apse, now reproduced on site with light projections. To the south, the Montsec range is cut by the Congost de Mont-rebei, a spectacular gorge where a walkway is carved into the cliff above the river, one of the most dramatic walks in Spain. Near Tremp and Isona, the rocks are full of dinosaur remains, including eggs and footprints, and a museum displays them.

The riding is superb and varied. The main road up the Noguera Ribagorçana valley follows the river past reservoirs and through gorges, with tunnels and cliffs, towards the Vielha tunnel and the Val d'Aran. Smaller roads climb over passes between valleys, narrow and twisty, with little traffic and huge views of the mountains. Surfaces are generally good on main roads, more variable on minor ones, and rockfalls are possible after storms. Winter brings snow at altitude, and some higher roads close; summer can be hot in the valleys and stormy in the afternoons.

Fuel needs planning. The nearest larger town listed is Tremp, about nineteen kilometres away, and El Pont de Suert is another option up the valley. Smaller villages may have only a bar or none at all. Try the hearty mountain food of the Pyrenees: trinxat, a cabbage and potato cake with bacon, local lamb, and sausages called xolís, washed down with a strong coffee before heading on.
t.cueva de mas del abogat@41.0,0.2:
Calaceite is the kind of village that makes you slow down without being asked: honey-coloured stone, arcaded squares, a big baroque church and grand old houses with carved doorways, all perched on a ridge in the Matarraña, the corner of Teruel where Aragón meets Catalonia and Valencia. A few kilometres from it lies the Cueva de Mas del Abogat, one of the painted rock shelters that belong to the UNESCO listing of prehistoric art in the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula. As with its sisters across eastern Spain, the paintings are small and often hard to read; the setting is what you take away.

People have lived on these hills for a very long time. Just outside Calaceite is the Iberian settlement of San Antonio, a hilltop town from the centuries before the Romans, with foundations of houses and walls you can walk among. Later came Muslim rule, then the Christian repopulation, then centuries of olive oil, wine and wheat. Today the area is often called the Tuscany of Aragón, a nickname that fits the rolling olive groves, almond trees and stone farmhouses, and many Catalan and foreign visitors have restored old houses here.

The riding is relaxed and very rewarding. Roads between Calaceite, Valdeltormo, Mazaleón and Valderrobres wind gently through farmland and over low ridges, with a few properly tight stretches where the land breaks into ravines. Traffic is light, apart from the occasional farm vehicle. The Ports de Beseit massif to the south offers more dramatic climbs if you want them. Spring blossom and autumn harvest are lovely; summer is hot and dry, with the cicadas drowning out the engine.

For services, think ahead. Calaceite has bars and places to eat, but the reliable choice for fuel and everything else is Alcañiz, about twenty-seven kilometres away, a town of sixteen thousand with a castle of the Order of Calatrava looking down on it. Bikers know Alcañiz for another reason: the MotorLand Aragón circuit just outside town, which hosts major motorcycle racing. Try the local olive oil, which is excellent, the cured ham from Teruel and, if you are lucky, a peach from Calanda in late summer.
t.centelles abric i@40.4,0.0:
Albocàsser and Catí are two quiet stone towns in the inland hills of Castellón, and between them, in a rocky ravine, the Centelles shelters hold some of the prehistoric paintings that make this corner of Spain a capital of Levantine rock art. The style is distinctive: small human figures, often archers, painted in red with long legs and dynamic poses, hunting deer, ibex and boar, sometimes in groups, sometimes in battle. The sites are part of the UNESCO listing of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Nearby, the Valltorta gorge, near Tírig, holds some of the most famous examples, and its museum explains the art and the people who made it.

Catí is a beautiful medieval town, with a Gothic church and fine stone houses built by wealthy wool merchants. The surrounding countryside was once famous for its cheese and sheep. Nearby is the spring of l'Avellà, where a small spa has been taking the waters since the nineteenth century, and a sanctuary stands above it. Albocàsser, in a fertile valley, is known for its almonds and olive oil.

The riding here is splendid, if you like empty roads and wild scenery. The roads that link the villages climb and descend through limestone hills, past almond terraces and pine woods, with countless curves and very little traffic. Some sections are narrow and the surface is uneven, so take care, especially after rain, when gravel can be washed onto the road. The weather is Mediterranean but with mountain influence: hot, dry summers, cool winters, and sudden storms in spring and autumn.

The nearest town of five thousand or more is Alcalà de Xivert, twenty-three kilometres away on the coastal plain, with fuel and supermarkets. The inland villages have bars and small restaurants, but services are limited and opening hours can be erratic, especially in the off-season. Fill up before heading into the hills. Try local dishes such as olla de la Plana, a hearty stew, or cured meats and cheeses from the mountains. If you are lucky, you may find homemade cakes made with almonds and honey.
t.la vall de la coma@41.5,0.9:
The Garrigues is the dry heart of Lleida province, a land of terraced hills, stone walls and endless olive groves, and La Vall de la Coma is one of its quiet valleys, in the municipality of L'Albi. In a few rock shelters here, prehistoric people painted small figures in red, part of the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean basin that is recognized as a World Heritage Site. The paintings are fragile and modest in size, and access is usually organized through local guides or interpretation centres, so plan ahead rather than expecting to wander in.

The landscape around is shaped by centuries of farming in a dry climate. Almond trees blossom pale pink in late winter, and the olive groves produce one of the most famous oils in Spain. The Arbequina olive takes its name from the village of Arbeca, just a few kilometres to the north, and the Garrigues olive oil appellation is renowned for its fruity, green flavour. Dotted across the fields are dry-stone huts, the barraques, built by farmers as shelters and tool stores, some of them remarkably elegant domed structures.

The riding in the Garrigues is a pleasant surprise. Small roads wind between villages through terraced hillsides, with good visibility and very little traffic, and the surface is generally fine. It can be hot in summer, often above thirty-five degrees, so mornings and evenings are best. In spring the green of the young cereals and the white of the almond blossom make the landscape particularly lovely, and in autumn the olive harvest brings tractors and activity to the villages.

For fuel and supplies, head to Les Borges Blanques, the county capital, or to Juneda; Mollerussa, on the plain to the north, is larger. The villages have small bars where you can get a coffee and a sandwich, and many have cooperative mills where you can buy oil directly. L'Albi itself has a castle and a small old town. A good plan is to combine the visit with a meal in Les Borges Blanques and a slow ride through the olive groves, stopping wherever the view opens up across the hills. In the evening the light on the stone walls and silver-green leaves has a warmth that is hard to describe.
t.cova de vallmajor@41.2,1.5:
Inland from the Costa Daurada, behind the beach towns of El Vendrell and Calafell, the land rises into the low hills of the Baix Penedès, a landscape of vineyards, almond and olive groves, pine woods and small villages. The Cova de Vallmajor, near Albinyana and Bonastre, is a rock shelter in these hills with prehistoric paintings, part of the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean that is recognised as a World Heritage Site. The paintings are faint and the shelter is protected, so visits are usually by arrangement.

The Penedès is wine country, famous above all for cava, the Catalan sparkling wine, whose capital is Sant Sadurní d'Anoia to the north. The Baix Penedès produces still wines too, and many cellars offer tastings. El Vendrell, five kilometres away, was the birthplace of the cellist Pau Casals, and his house on the beach at Sant Salvador is now a museum. A few kilometres west, at Roda de Barà, the Roman triumphal arch of Berà stands beside the old Via Augusta, a reminder that this coast was part of the Roman province around Tarraco.

The riding in the hills behind the coast is pleasant and quiet. Small roads wind through the vineyards and over the hills, with views to the sea, and traffic is light compared with the busy coastal roads. Further inland, the mountains of the Serra de Montmell and the Alt Camp offer more winding roads. Summer is hot and the coast is crowded, so spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and the colours of the vineyards changing.

El Vendrell, a town of thirty-five thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Bonastre and Albinyana are small villages with a bar or two. The local cuisine includes calçots in late winter, grilled spring onions dipped in romesco sauce, a Catalan tradition celebrated in large outdoor feasts, and xató, a salad with salt cod and a romesco-like sauce, typical of this part of the coast. A glass of local wine after the riding is done is well deserved. The light in the hills in the late afternoon, falling across the vines, is beautiful.
t.arles@43.7,4.6:
Arles is where the Rhône splits in two and the Camargue begins, and for more than two thousand years it has been a city of power, art and sun. The Romans made it one of the great cities of Gaul, building an amphitheatre that still hosts events, a theatre, baths and an underground gallery, the cryptoportiques, and the Roman and Romanesque monuments of Arles are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Romanesque church of Saint-Trophime, with its carved portal and cloister, is one of the finest in Provence.

Vincent van Gogh lived in Arles in 1888 and 1889, and painted some of his most famous works here, including the Café Terrace at Night, The Yellow House and Starry Night over the Rhône. He cut off part of his ear here after a quarrel with Paul Gauguin, and was treated at the hospital, whose courtyard garden he painted, now the Espace Van Gogh. The Fondation Vincent van Gogh shows exhibitions linked to his work, and the LUMA tower, designed by Frank Gehry, has added a striking modern landmark.

The riding around Arles is varied. To the south, the Camargue is a flat land of marshes, lagoons and rice fields, with white horses, black bulls and pink flamingos, and the roads to Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer and the beaches are straight and windy, with the mistral blowing hard from the north. To the north-east, the Alpilles, a range of limestone hills, have winding roads through olive groves and pine forests, past the village of Les Baux-de-Provence. Summer is hot and crowded, and the mosquitoes in the Camargue can be fierce.

Arles, a city of fifty thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and its old centre is a pleasure to walk. Fourques and Fontvieille, nearby, are smaller villages. Provençal food is rich and aromatic: bouillabaisse, tapenade, and the local specialties of the Camargue, such as red rice, gardianne de taureau, a bull stew, and saucisson d'Arles. The Saturday market, along the boulevards, is one of the largest in Provence. In the evening, the light over the Rhône, the same light that inspired Van Gogh, is magical.
t.cova del cogullo@42.0,1.0:
Between the plains of Lleida and the first serious mountains of the Pyrenees there is a band of country that most people cross without noticing, and it is a mistake. The Cova del Cogulló lies here, in the hills of the Noguera between Artesa de Segre and the Montsec, a long limestone wall that rises abruptly from the farmland. Rock shelters in these hills carry prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean rock art tradition that runs all along eastern Spain, and the region's churches add a medieval layer, small Romanesque buildings in nearly every village.

Artesa de Segre is a small town on the river Segre, with a few thousand people and the essentials. North of it, the land wrinkles into dry hills of oak and pine before slamming into the Montsec, which is cut by the dramatic gorges of the Noguera Pallaresa and the Noguera Ribagorçana. The Àger valley behind the range has become famous for its dark skies, with an astronomical park and observatory taking advantage of the lack of light pollution. Vultures and eagles ride the thermals along the cliffs, and the air in spring smells of rosemary and broom.

For riding, the area is superb and quiet. Roads climbing toward the Montsec and over its passes offer sequences of corners on clean, grippy surfaces with almost no traffic, and the views back across the plain toward the distant Pyrenean peaks are huge. The run toward Tremp passes reservoirs of improbable turquoise. Expect strong sun in summer, frost and occasional snow on high bends in winter, and plenty of cyclists and climbers at weekends. Some of the minor lanes to the shelters are narrow, steep and patched; take your time.

Fuel is available in Artesa de Segre and Ponts; beyond that, villages are small, so plan ahead before heading into the Montsec. Tremp, the main town of the Pallars Jussà, is about twenty kilometres away and has everything. Catalan country cooking is generous: grilled meats, snails in season, mountain sausages and coca bread, washed down with water if you are riding. Give the shelters the respect they deserve, keep to the paths, and finish the day on a high road above the Segre, watching the plains turn pink and the Montsec go dark against the sky.
t.the maison carree of nimes@43.8,4.4:
Most Roman temples survive as a jumble of columns and a lot of imagination. The Maison Carrée in Nîmes is the exception: a complete temple, standing on its podium with its roof and columns intact, two thousand years after it was built for the grandsons of Augustus. It owes its survival to being constantly reused, as a meeting hall, a stable, a church and a museum. Thomas Jefferson admired it so much that he based the Virginia State Capitol on it, and in 2023 UNESCO finally listed it in its own right.

Nîmes is a city of about one hundred and fifty thousand in the south of France, at the foot of the garrigue hills between the Cévennes and the Camargue. The Romans called it Nemausus, and it was one of the great cities of Gaul. The arena is the best preserved in France and still hosts bullfights and concerts during the ferias, when the city fills with music, crowds and smoke from grills. Opposite the temple stands the Carré d'Art, a glass and steel building by Norman Foster, a deliberately modern conversation with the old stones. And the word denim, for those wearing it under their riding gear, comes from serge de Nîmes.

Riding into the centre is honest work: traffic, one-way systems, pedestrian zones and limited parking. Better to park on the edge of the old town and walk. Once out of the city, though, the riding becomes very good. The garrigue to the north is criss-crossed with small roads through vineyards and scrubland, and further north the Cévennes offer some of the most entertaining mountain roads in France. To the south, the flat Camargue is all wind, horses and flamingos. Summer is hot and the mistral can blow hard down the Rhône valley, so take care on exposed roads.

Fuel, food and all services are easy to find in Nîmes. The local cuisine reflects its Provençal and Languedoc roots: brandade de morue, a creamy salt cod purée, is the city's signature dish, along with olives from the Gard and wines from the Costières de Nîmes. A coffee on the square facing the temple, watching the evening light turn the stone gold, is a good way to end the day. Look closely at the carved capitals and frieze: Roman craftsmen made them, and they are still sharp.
t.pont du gard@43.9,4.5:
Built without mortar, three tiers of arches carry a water channel across the gorge of the Gardon nearly fifty metres above the river, and the stones still fit together as if they had been placed last week. The Pont du Gard was one section of an aqueduct some fifty kilometres long that brought spring water from near Uzès to Roman Nîmes in the first century, with a total drop of only a few metres over the whole distance. It is a masterpiece of surveying as much as building, and it has stood through floods that have destroyed far younger bridges.

The setting is the lower valley of the Gardon, where the river leaves its gorges and runs between limestone banks shaded by holm oaks and pines. The villages of Vers-Pont-du-Gard, Castillon-du-Gard and Remoulins are small, sun-baked and quiet away from the main roads. In summer the river below the bridge becomes a swimming spot, with people diving from the rocks and canoeists paddling down from Collias, and the water is cool and clear. The smell of the garrigue, thyme, rosemary and hot pine, hangs over everything.

Riding here is about the approach. The roads from Uzès and the hills of the garrigue wind through vineyards and olive groves with good surfaces and an easy rhythm. The Gardon gorge upstream is wild and beautiful, and the small roads around Collias and Sanilhac are worth exploring. The site itself has managed parking with a fee, a museum and paths along both banks, so plan to walk a little. In summer, come early to avoid the heat and the coaches; in spring and autumn, the light is softer and the crowds thinner. The mistral can make the approach roads gusty.

Remoulins has fuel and shops; for a bigger choice, Nîmes or Avignon are both within easy reach. Uzès, upstream, is one of the most beautiful small towns in the south, with a Saturday market and a ducal castle, and it makes a lovely detour for lunch. Bring water and a hat if you plan to walk, and take time to look at the stones themselves: the Roman builders left marks, numbers and even projecting blocks used to support the scaffolding. They knew it would last, but they probably did not imagine motorcycles parked nearby.
t.decorated cave of pont d arc@44.4,4.4:
In December 1994, three cavers felt a draught coming from a pile of rocks above the Ardèche gorge, dug their way in and found themselves in a cave that nobody had entered for thousands of years. On the walls were lions, rhinoceroses, mammoths, horses and bears, drawn with a mastery that changed what we thought we knew about early art. The paintings of the Chauvet cave, named after one of the trio, Jean-Marie Chauvet, are around thirty-six thousand years old, roughly twice the age of Lascaux. The original cave is sealed to protect it, but a full-scale replica, the Grotte Chauvet 2, opened nearby in 2015.

The cave lies close to the Pont d'Arc, a natural limestone arch over the Ardèche river near Vallon-Pont-d'Arc. Downstream, the river carves the Gorges de l'Ardèche, one of the most spectacular canyons in France, with cliffs up to three hundred metres high. The Gorges road runs along the rim with viewpoints over the river and its meanders, a gift for riders. Canoeists paddle down the gorge in summer, and the river below the arch is a popular swimming spot.

The riding is superb, with a warning. The Gorges road, from Vallon-Pont-d'Arc to Saint-Martin-d'Ardèche, is twisty, narrow and full of views, but in July and August it is clogged with camper vans, cars and coaches. Spring and autumn are much better, with clear air and empty bends. Surfaces are generally good, but gravel collects in corners, and the heat can be intense. The plateaus north and west of the gorge offer quieter roads through oak woods, vineyards and lavender fields, with villages of honey-coloured stone.

Vallon-Pont-d'Arc has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Ruoms and Barjac are close by. The local food is southern and simple: chestnuts are a regional speciality, along with goat's cheese, charcuterie and wines from the Ardèche. For the replica cave, book in advance in summer; visits are guided and timed. If you can, ride the Gorges road early in the morning, when the cliffs glow and the river is still quiet, and then visit the cave in the afternoon, when the heat sends everyone else to the water.
t.crypt at the colonia guell@41.4,2.0:
Few people ride out of Barcelona expecting to find Gaudí in a mill village, but that is exactly what waits at Santa Coloma de Cervelló, a short hop up the Llobregat from Sant Boi. The Colònia Güell was a textile colony founded by the industrialist Eusebi Güell, who moved his cotton works out of the city in the 1890s and built housing, a school, shops and a theatre for the workers around the factory. He asked his friend Antoni Gaudí for a church. Gaudí spent about ten years on the design and its foundations, and when money and the Güell family's enthusiasm ran out around 1914, only the lower level had been finished. That crypt is what you come to see.

It is a strange, wonderful room. The columns lean like tired men, some of them rough basalt, some brick; the vaults are ribbed with brick in patterns that look improvised and are anything but. Gaudí worked out the forces with a hanging model of strings and little bags of shot, then turned the shape upside down, and you can feel that logic in the way the whole thing seems to grow rather than stand. Many ideas later used at the Sagrada Família were tested here first, which is why the crypt is part of the Gaudí World Heritage listing. The pews and the coloured glass, shaped like butterfly wings when the shutters open, are his too.

The colony itself rewards a slow walk. The red-brick workers' houses, the modernista villas of the managers and the old factory halls along the river make a tidy little town, quiet on weekdays and lively when the bar terraces fill on Sunday. Coffee and a sandwich are easy to find, and Santa Coloma and Sant Boi both have petrol stations on the way in or out.

As for the riding, be realistic: the approach is suburban, a knot of roundabouts, the B-23 and the old N-340 corridor, with industrial estates and plenty of vans. The reward comes once you head west or north. The hills of Collserola and the Ordal range are close, and the climb towards Cervelló and Corbera de Llobregat turns into proper twisting tarmac through pines and vineyards within twenty minutes. Early morning is best, before the heat and the traffic, and the light through the crypt windows is softest then anyway. Start or finish here and you get a hit of genius bookending a day of curves.
t.britus il@41.3,1.1:
The name on the map is obscure, and honestly I could not tell you what a rider should expect to find at the exact pin. What matters is the country around it, which is some of the finest in inland Catalonia. You are in the Conca de Barberà, the basin of the Francolí river, a few kilometres from the walled town of Montblanc and the village of Alcover, with the wooded wall of the Serra de Prades rising to the west. The area is dotted with prehistoric rock shelters, part of the great arc of Mediterranean rock art that runs down eastern Spain, and many of the site names along these rides are exactly that: a ledge of sandstone or limestone where hunters painted deer and archers thousands of years ago.

Montblanc deserves an hour. Its medieval walls survive for much of their circuit, the gates still funnel traffic, and local legend puts Saint George's fight with the dragon right outside them, which the town celebrates every April with gusto. A little further west, near Vimbodí, the Cistercian monastery of Poblet holds the tombs of the kings of Aragon and is still home to monks. Wine is everywhere here; the Conca de Barberà grows Trepat and the base wines for cava, and old stone cooperative wineries in the villages, some built in a modernista style that people call wine cathedrals, are worth a look even from the saddle.

The roads are the reason to come. The C-14 climbs from Valls over the Coll de Lilla in a run of smooth, well-cambered bends before dropping into the basin, and the minor roads into the Prades mountains, towards Prades village and the red sandstone at Siurana, are narrow, twisting and wonderfully empty midweek. Watch for gravel on the inside of hairpins after rain and for cyclists, who love these climbs as much as we do. Summer afternoons get very hot down in the basin, so ride the high ground at midday and the valleys in the morning.

Montblanc has fuel, cafés and bakeries; Alcover is smaller but has the basics. Grab water before heading into the hills, because villages up there are tiny and often shut in the afternoon. If you have time, a short walk among the pines near any of the painted shelters, with the smell of resin and thyme in the air, is a fine way to break the ride.
t.chateau de peyrepertuse@42.9,2.6:
You see it long before you understand it. From the road below Duilhac, Peyrepertuse looks like part of the mountain: a grey ridge of limestone with walls grown along its spine, so long and thin that people compare it to a stone ship. Up close it is two castles in one. The lower fortress on the eastern end is older, and at the western summit stands the keep of Sant Jordi, added by the French crown after Louis IX took control of the Corbières in the mid-thirteenth century. The site sits around 800 metres up, and the climb from the car park is short but steep, on a rocky path that is no fun in stiff motorcycle boots, so bring trainers if you can.

These fortresses are usually sold as Cathar castles, and the Cathars did shelter in this country during the Albigensian Crusade, but what you see is largely royal French work, built to guard the border with Aragon. When the Treaty of the Pyrenees moved the frontier south in 1659, places like this lost their purpose and slowly emptied. Standing on the walls you can see why they mattered: the Fenouillèdes to the south, Quéribus on its own crag, and on clear days the Mediterranean and the snowy bulk of the Canigou.

The riding nearby is outstanding. The classic approach is from Saint-Paul-de-Fenouillet through the Gorges de Galamus, a road cut into the cliff face above a deep, narrow canyon; it is single-lane in places, with a stone parapet and oncoming cars, and in summer there are often traffic controls. Take it slowly and enjoy the drop. Beyond, the D14 through Cubières and Duilhac winds through scrub, vines and rock, and the run east towards Cucugnan and Quéribus is a joy of short straights and tight bends.

The wind deserves respect. The tramontane comes down hard from the northwest and can push a bike around on the ridges, and the castle walls get properly blustery. Go early in summer before the heat and the coaches arrive; late afternoon light on the stone is lovely too. Fuel is the thing to plan: Saint-Paul-de-Fenouillet is the nearest town with pumps, otherwise Estagel or Ille-sur-Têt. Duilhac has a café or two, and the local reds, Corbières and the sweet wines of Maury, are for the evening, not the ride.
t.val de caballe i@41.3,0.2:
Here the Ebro stops being a river and becomes a lake. Behind the great dams at Mequinenza and Riba-roja, the water backs up for kilometres into the dry hills of eastern Aragon, and locals call the reservoir the Mar de Aragón, the sea of Aragon. Val de Caballé is a gully in the hills south of the water, between Mequinenza, Nonaspe and Fabara, part of a scatter of prehistoric rock shelters in this corner where Aragon, Catalonia and the Matarranya meet.

The landscape is stark and beautiful in its own way: terraces of olives and almonds, wheat fields, low cliffs of pale sandstone, and the occasional ruined farmhouse. It feels remote even though it is not far from busier roads. Mequinenza has an extraordinary story. The old town sat at the confluence of the Ebro and the Segre and was largely flooded when the reservoir filled in the 1960s and 70s; residents were moved to a new town built nearby. There is a museum dedicated to the old village and another to the coal mines that once employed much of the population. The reservoir is now famous among anglers for its giant wels catfish, introduced decades ago, and you will see fishing camps along the shores.

Fabara, a few kilometres south, has a well-preserved Roman funerary monument, the mausoleum of Lucius Aemilius Lupus, a small temple-like tomb standing in a field. It is a lovely, slightly surreal stop.

The riding is mostly open and flowing. The roads that link Mequinenza, Fayón, Nonaspe and Caspe follow the contours of the hills and the reservoir, with long views and a mix of fast bends and tighter sections as they drop into side valleys. Traffic is light, though you will meet the odd truck heading to a farm or quarry. Wind can be strong and gusty, especially the cierzo from the northwest, and summer heat here is serious. Spring and autumn are ideal.

For fuel, Mequinenza and Caspe are the safe bets; smaller villages may not have pumps. Mequinenza has bars and restaurants, many catering to visiting anglers. Carry water, because between villages there is little shade and fewer people, and the hills can feel very empty in the heat of the afternoon.
t.chateau d aguilar@42.9,2.7:
Aguilar is the castle people overlook, and that is its best feature. While coaches crawl up to Peyrepertuse and Quéribus, this one sits quietly on a low hill above vineyards just outside Tuchan, at the eastern edge of the Corbières, with a squat keep inside a hexagonal outer wall studded with small round towers. It is a modest fortress compared with its famous siblings, but you can walk around it in peace and the views over vines towards Mont Tauch are lovely, especially in the evening.

Like the other so-called Cathar castles of the region, Aguilar's history runs from local lords drawn into the Albigensian Crusade in the early thirteenth century to French royal control. Afterwards it was strengthened as part of the defensive line facing the kingdom of Aragon just to the south, and it fell into decline once the border moved after 1659. The outer wall with its corner towers is the most distinctive part, a solid example of thirteenth-century military architecture.

This is serious wine country. Tuchan lies at the heart of the Fitou appellation, one of the oldest in the Languedoc, and the slopes around the castle are covered with vines, garrigue and stone terraces. In late summer you will see harvest machines and tractors on the roads and smell crushed grapes in the villages. A tasting in Tuchan is a fine end to a day of riding, once the key is out of the ignition.

The roads here are wonderful. The D611 between Tuchan and the coast near Fitou winds through low hills and gorges, while the roads west towards Padern, Cucugnan and the Galamus gorge become tighter and more dramatic. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, with stone walls and ditches close to the edge. The tramontane wind can be ferocious, often gusting strongly enough to push the bike sideways on exposed ridges.

Tuchan is a decent-sized village with a café, a bakery and basic shops; you may find fuel, but Estagel, Salses-le-Château or Rivesaltes are safer options. The castle path is short but rough, and summer afternoons can be fiercely hot with little shade, so go early or late. Aguilar is a fine spot to start or finish a loop of the Corbières castles, quieter and gentler than the giants to the west.
t.abric de la serra de la mussara@41.2,1.0:
Climb out of Reus on a clear morning and the Serra de la Mussara rises ahead like a wall, a limestone escarpment that holds up the edge of the Prades plateau and drops steeply to the plain of the Camp de Tarragona. The rock shelters along this cliff line, close to the village of Vilaplana, are part of the prehistoric painted landscape of eastern Spain. The best reason to stop, though, is the view: on a good day you look straight down over hazelnut orchards and olive groves to Reus, Tarragona and the sea.

The road up is the T-704 from Vilaplana, and it is a beauty. It climbs in a ladder of tight hairpins and short straights cut into the face of the escarpment, with stone walls and the occasional sheer drop. The surface is mostly good, but the hairpins collect gravel and the weekend brings cyclists and walkers in numbers. At the top the road crosses a high, wooded plateau towards the abandoned village of La Mussara and then on to Prades or down towards Mont-ral and Capafonts, with excellent tarmac and very little traffic midweek.

La Mussara itself is a ruin now, a church and a handful of broken houses on the edge of the cliff. It was abandoned during the twentieth century, and the combination of the empty buildings and the fog that often swallows the plateau has fed a whole industry of ghost stories and tales of people losing their way, some of which you will hear repeated in local bars with a straight face. In reality it is a peaceful, windswept place with remarkable views, and walkers use it as a starting point for routes along the cliff edge.

The plain below is famous for hazelnuts; the Reus area grows a protected variety, and you will see orchards everywhere around Vilaplana and Alforja. Reus is also the birthplace of Antoni Gaudí, and the town has a small centre dedicated to his work.

Vilaplana is a small village with a bar or two, but fuel means dropping back to Reus or the larger towns on the plain. Carry a layer even in summer; the plateau is several hundred metres higher than the coast and the temperature drops noticeably, and fog can roll in quickly in spring and autumn, turning a pleasant ride into a careful crawl.
t.la pedra de les orenetes@41.6,2.3:
