La Pedra de les Orenetes, the Swallows' Stone, is a granite boulder in the hills above La Roca del Vallès, and its surface is covered with small carved hollows and other marks left by people in prehistory. Nobody knows exactly what they meant; such engraved rocks are found across Catalonia, and theories range from ritual offerings to maps of the stars. The rock sits among cork oaks and pines in the Serralada Litoral, the coastal range that separates the Vallès plain from the sea, and the walk to reach it is short and pleasant, through scented forest with views over the plain.

The hills around La Roca are full of prehistoric remains, including dolmens and the Cova de Vallmajor, a cave used in prehistoric times. The area is a popular place for walkers and cyclists from Barcelona, who come to escape the city at weekends. La Roca itself has a small old centre with a castle, though most visitors know it for the big designer outlet village on the edge of town.

The Vallès is an industrial and suburban region, with towns, factories and motorways, but it has a special place in the hearts of motorcyclists. Just a few kilometres south, at Montmeló, lies the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, home of the Catalan MotoGP and the Spanish Formula One Grand Prix. On race weekends the whole area fills with fans, and the roads are packed. Granollers, the nearest large town, is a lively place with a market and a historic centre.

The riding nearby is excellent. To the north rises the Montseny massif, a natural park and biosphere reserve with beech and holm oak forests, and the roads that climb from the Vallès to the villages of Montseny and Viladrau and over the Coll de Sant Marçal are a joy, with endless bends, good surfaces and views. They are very popular with riders and cyclists at weekends, so take care. Closer at hand, the roads over the coastal range towards the Maresme and the sea are also good, with tight bends and views of the Mediterranean.

La Roca and Granollers have fuel, shops and restaurants. Try botifarra amb mongetes, sausage with white beans, or a plate of calçots in season, grilled spring onions dipped in romesco sauce. The weather is Mediterranean, with hot summers and mild winters.
t.chateau de queribus@42.8,2.6:
Quéribus clings to the top of a limestone pinnacle like a crown, so improbably perched that it is hard to believe people ever built it, let alone held it under siege. It is often described as the last Cathar stronghold: when Montségur fell in 1244, the remaining Cathar refugees and their supporters found shelter here, and the castle held out until 1255, when it finally surrendered to the forces of the French king. It then became a royal fortress guarding the border with Aragon, until the frontier moved south in 1659 and its usefulness ended.

The climb from the car park is steep but short, with steps cut into the rock, and the wind at the top can be ferocious; the tramontane can make it hard to stand on the walls. The highlight inside is the great hall of the keep, a Gothic chamber with a single central pillar from which the ribbed vault spreads like the branches of a palm tree. It is a surprisingly elegant space in such a harsh place. The views from the top stretch over the Corbières, the Fenouillèdes, the plain of Roussillon and the sea, and on a clear day the snowy summit of the Canigou dominates the south.

Below the castle, the village of Cucugnan is famous in France thanks to Alphonse Daudet, who retold a local tale about its priest, who frightened his flock into virtue with a sermon describing heaven empty of Cucugnanais. There is a small theatre in the village that tells the story, and a windmill on the hill that still grinds flour.

The riding is magnificent. The road from Maury climbs over the Grau de Maury, a pass just below the castle, with tight hairpins and views over the vineyards of the Agly valley. On the other side, the road descends to Cucugnan and continues towards Peyrepertuse and the Galamus gorge, through rocky, scrub-covered hills. Surfaces are generally good, traffic is light outside summer, and the scenery is spectacular. Watch for gravel on the bends and the wind on exposed sections.

Saint-Paul-de-Fenouillet and Estagel have fuel and shops; Cucugnan and Maury have restaurants and cafés. Try the sweet wines of Maury, rich and nutty, and the local Corbières reds. Summer is hot; spring and autumn are perfect.
t.corral de la gascona@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar is one of the most dramatic villages in Spain: a cluster of ochre houses piled on a rocky spur above the canyon of the Vero river, crowned by a castle and a collegiate church built on the site of a Moorish fortress. It lies at the southern edge of the Sierra de Guara, a limestone range in Aragon cut by deep canyons, and the area is famous across Europe for canyoning, with people abseiling, jumping and swimming through the narrow gorges in summer. The Corral de la Gascona is one of the rock-art sites in the Vero canyon and its surroundings, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The Vero canyon holds an extraordinary concentration of rock art, from different periods, including Levantine and schematic paintings. A cultural park protects the sites and the landscape, and guided visits to some of the shelters, such as Mallata and Chimiachas, can be arranged from Alquézar. A walk along the river, with its footbridges and walkways over the gorge, is a lovely way to see the canyon even without a guide.

The region around is the Somontano, the foothills of the Pyrenees, known for its wines, produced from vineyards on the gentle slopes south of the mountains. Barbastro, the main town, has a cathedral and a wine museum, and many wineries in the area offer tastings. Olive groves and almond orchards cover the hills, and in early spring the almond blossom is beautiful.

The riding is excellent. The roads around Alquézar and into the Sierra de Guara are narrow and winding, with tight bends and views of canyons, cliffs and villages. To the north, the roads climb into the Pyrenees, towards the Ordesa National Park and the Aragonese valleys, some of the best riding in Spain. Surfaces vary, and you will meet cyclists, campers and tractors. In summer, Alquézar is busy with canyoning groups, and parking can be difficult.

Alquézar has restaurants, bars and accommodation, but fuel is more reliable in Barbastro, a short ride south. Try ternasco de Aragón, roast lamb, or migas, fried breadcrumbs with sausage and grapes. Summers are hot and dry, winters cold. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding and walking.
t.camino de la cova plana ii@41.4,0.4:
Three rivers come together near Mequinenza: the Ebro, flowing in from the west, and the Segre and Cinca, arriving together from the Pyrenees to the north. The meeting point, now swallowed by the reservoirs behind the dams, has always been a strategic place, and the much-restored castle on the hill above the town has watched over it for centuries. The Camino de la Cova Plana is a track in the hills east of town, towards the Catalan border, and the site recorded here is one of the many prehistoric rock shelters scattered across this dry, rugged landscape.

The country is stark and empty, with low hills of pale sandstone and gypsum, scrub, terraces of almond and olive trees, and the vast blue sheet of the reservoir. It feels remote, though the fertile plain of Lleida is only a short ride away. Downstream, the Ebro continues through the Riba-roja reservoir towards Flix and the Catalan interior.

To the north, along the Segre, the landscape changes dramatically. Around Seròs, Aitona and Alcarràs, the irrigated fields are covered with fruit trees: peaches, nectarines, apples and pears. In late winter and early spring, usually in March, the orchards around Aitona burst into blossom, turning the valley pink and white, and the village organises visits and festivities to celebrate it. It is a beautiful sight, and well worth a detour if you are here at the right time.

The riding is open and flowing. The roads along the reservoirs and through the hills have long views and a mix of fast bends and tighter sections, with very little traffic. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel, agricultural vehicles and the occasional truck from the quarries and farms. The wind, especially the cierzo from the northwest, can be strong and gusty, and in summer the heat is intense, with little shade.

Mequinenza has fuel, shops and restaurants, many catering to the anglers who come for the reservoir's giant catfish. Seròs and Fayón have basic services. Carry water, and avoid riding in the heat of the afternoon in summer. Try local fruit in season, and coca de recapte, a flatbread topped with roasted vegetables, a specialty of the Lleida region.
t.abric de les llibreres@40.7,0.5:
The Montsià range rises abruptly from the coastal plain at the southern tip of Catalonia, a long, rocky ridge of limestone that separates the Ebro delta from the inland valleys. Around its foot lie the villages of Santa Bàrbara, Masdenverge and Ulldecona, surrounded by olive groves, some of them with ancient trees hundreds of years old, their trunks twisted into extraordinary shapes. The Abric de les Llibreres is one of the prehistoric rock shelters in this area, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The most important rock art site nearby is at the Abrics de l'Ermita, near Ulldecona, in the Serra de Godall, where a group of shelters contains hundreds of painted figures, including hunting scenes with archers and deer. An interpretation centre explains the art and arranges guided visits.

The olive groves of the Montsià and the neighbouring Baix Maestrat contain some of the oldest olive trees in the world, and some are believed to have been planted in Roman times. The Farga de l'Arion, near Ulldecona, is one of the most famous. The oil produced here is excellent.

To the east lies the Ebro delta, a vast, flat wetland of rice paddies, lagoons, beaches and reed beds, home to flamingos, herons and countless other birds. The delta is a natural park, and the roads that cross it, between the rice fields and canals, are flat and straight, with wide skies and a sense of space. Sunsets over the paddies are spectacular.

The riding is varied. To the west, the mountains of Els Ports offer some of the best riding in Catalonia, with winding roads through pine forests and limestone cliffs, up to Mont Caro, the highest peak in the area, and through villages such as Horta de Sant Joan, where Picasso spent time as a young man. Closer at hand, the roads around the Montsià are pleasant, with gentle bends through olive groves. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light, but watch for agricultural vehicles and cyclists.

Santa Bàrbara has basic services; Ulldecona and Amposta have fuel, shops and restaurants. Try rice dishes from the delta, such as arròs negre, black rice with squid ink, or local olive oil on bread. Summer is hot and humid; spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.the@41.1,1.4:
Just inland from the beach at Altafulla, on the Costa Daurada north of Tarragona, the remains of a grand Roman villa look out over the Mediterranean. This is the Villa dels Munts, one of the finest Roman country houses in Catalonia, built in the first and second centuries AD, with baths, gardens, mosaics and painted walls. It is thought to have belonged to an important citizen of Tarraco, the Roman capital of the province of Hispania Tarraconensis, and it is part of the World Heritage inscription of the Archaeological Ensemble of Tarraco, inscribed in 2000. The villa's setting, on a gentle slope above the sea, makes it easy to see why a wealthy Roman would choose it for a retreat.

Altafulla itself is a charming small town, with a medieval old quarter on a hill crowned by a castle, and a seafront of old fishermen's houses, known as the Botigues de Mar. The nearby castle of Tamarit stands right on the beach on a rocky headland, a romantic sight. Tarragona, about ten kilometres away, has a wealth of Roman remains, including an amphitheatre by the sea, the circus, the forum and the walls, as well as a beautiful medieval cathedral.

The riding here is mostly coastal and suburban, with busy roads and plenty of traffic in summer. The N-340, which follows the route of the Roman Via Augusta along the coast, is heavily used, but inland roads offer better riding. Head north into the hills of the Alt Camp and the Baix Penedès, and the roads wind through vineyards, olive groves and small villages, with curves and gentle climbs. The Prades mountains, further inland, offer some excellent riding, with steep, twisting roads through pine forests. Summer heat can be intense, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Altafulla has cafés, restaurants and shops, and Torredembarra, about two and a half kilometres away, has fuel and more services. The local food is Catalan, with seafood, rice dishes, and the calçots, grilled spring onions with romesco sauce, a winter speciality of the region. Visit the villa, walk down to the beach and Tamarit castle, and then explore Altafulla's old town. It is a lovely stretch of coast, with history at every turn.
t.britus i@41.3,1.1:
Between Montblanc and Vimbodí, in the Conca de Barberà, the land rises toward the Prades mountains and the Serra de la Llena, and in the sandstone and limestone outcrops of these hills, prehistoric hunters left paintings in rock shelters. Britus I is one of these sites, with figures painted in the distinctive style of Levantine rock art, which shows scenes of hunting, gathering and daily life with lively human and animal figures. The rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula was inscribed by UNESCO in 1998, covering hundreds of sites from Catalonia to Andalusia. Many are small and fragile, and access is often restricted to protect them.

The Conca de Barberà is a region of vineyards, almond orchards and medieval towns. Montblanc, a short ride to the east, is surrounded by an impressive circuit of medieval walls, and claims to be the place where Saint George, the patron saint of Catalonia, slew the dragon. Every April, the town celebrates with a medieval festival. The great Cistercian monastery of Poblet, a UNESCO site and the burial place of the kings of Aragon, lies a few kilometres to the west, near Vimbodí, with its massive walls and peaceful cloisters.

The riding here is very good. The roads through the Conca de Barberà wind through vineyards and hills, with good surfaces and light traffic. The climb into the Prades mountains, toward the village of Prades or over the Coll de Lilla toward Valls, offers tight bends, steep gradients and views over the plain. The roads around Poblet and up toward the forests of the Serra de Prades are particularly enjoyable. Summer heat is intense, and spring and autumn are the best times to ride, when the vineyards are green or golden.

Montblanc, about seven kilometres away, has petrol, places to eat and shops, and the villages nearby have smaller options. The local wines are excellent, including the Trepat red grape, a regional variety used for rosé cava. Visit Poblet, walk the walls of Montblanc, and if the rock shelter is open or a guided visit is available, look closely at the paintings. They are small, faint and precious, a direct link to people who lived here thousands of years ago.
t.abric de can castellvi@41.3,1.7:
The Penedès is wine country, and the landscape around Vilafranca del Penedès is a patchwork of vineyards rolling away toward the Montserrat massif in the north and the limestone hills of the Garraf in the south. Abric de Can Castellví is a small rock shelter in this landscape, one of the many sites of Levantine and schematic rock art scattered across Catalonia and included in the UNESCO serial site of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. Like many such sites, it is modest in appearance, a hollow in the rock where faint painted figures have survived thousands of years, and access is often limited to protect the art.

Vilafranca is the capital of the Penedès, a lively town with a medieval core, a fine Gothic basilica, and the wine museum, Vinseum, which tells the story of winemaking in the region. The town is also famous for its castellers, the teams who build human towers several storeys high, a tradition inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. The Festa Major at the end of August, when the castellers perform in the main square, is spectacular. Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, just to the north, is the capital of cava, the Catalan sparkling wine, with dozens of cellars open for visits.

The riding around Vilafranca is enjoyable, with quiet roads winding through the vineyards and hills, good surfaces and light traffic on weekdays. The roads south through the Garraf massif toward Sitges and the coast are particularly good, with tight bends, steep climbs and views of the sea. North toward Montserrat, the roads climb dramatically to the mountain monastery, with hairpins and stunning views of the strange rock formations. Weekend traffic around Barcelona can be heavy, and summer heat is intense.

Vilafranca, about four kilometres away, is a town of nearly forty thousand people with pumps, coffee, proper meals and shops. Try local dishes such as xató, a salad of endive, salt cod and anchovies with a romesco-like sauce, and of course a glass of local wine or cava, but only when the riding is done. Visit the Vinseum, stroll the old town, and take a quiet ride through the vineyards. The rock shelter is a reminder that people have been living in this landscape for thousands of years.
t.abrigo del plano del pulido@41.1,0.0:
South of Caspe, the lower Aragón country is a dry, sculpted landscape of ochre hills, flat-topped mesas and gullies cut into soft sandstone, with almond and olive groves clinging to the valley floors. In these sandstone outcrops, prehistoric people found shelter and left paintings, and the Abrigo del Plano del Pulido is one of the rock shelters of the area included in the World Heritage site of the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The painted figures, in the reddish tones of Levantine art, are small and faded, and as at most of these sites, access is controlled and visits may need to be arranged in advance.

Caspe has a special place in Spanish history. In 1412, the Compromise of Caspe was agreed here, when delegates from Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia chose Ferdinand of Antequera as king of Aragon after the old royal line died out, a peaceful solution to a succession crisis that shaped the future of the Iberian kingdoms. The town sits beside the Mar de Aragón, the long reservoir formed by damming the Ebro at Mequinenza, which is famous among anglers for its giant catfish. To the south, the Matarraña region, sometimes called the Tuscany of Aragon, has medieval villages, olive groves and dramatic rock formations.

For riders, there is one name in the area that needs no introduction: Alcañiz, about thirteen kilometres to the south, is home to the MotorLand Aragón circuit, which hosts MotoGP and draws motorcyclists from all over Europe. The roads around it are equally tempting: long, empty stretches across the steppe, winding climbs through the hills of the Matarraña toward Valderrobres, and twisty roads along the reservoir. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light, and the views wide. Summer heat is fierce, and the cierzo, a strong, cold northwest wind, can blow hard across the open country.

Caspe, about ten kilometres away, is a town of roughly eight thousand people with fuel and a choice of places to eat, and Alcañiz has more. Local food includes Aragonese lamb, ternasco, roasted with potatoes, and the excellent olive oil of the Bajo Aragón, along with peaches from Calanda, a protected variety. Plan your visit to the shelter if possible, then ride the roads around the reservoir and into the hills. It is a dry, sunlit land, and on a motorcycle it feels wide open.
t.abric de masets@40.7,0.5:
The Montsià range rises like a wall behind the Ebro delta in southern Catalonia, a ridge of grey limestone with steep slopes and rocky crags, and in a shelter on its flanks, near Santa Bàrbara and Masdenverge, the Abric de Masets holds traces of prehistoric paintings. It is part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The paintings here are faded and fragmentary, but the site is a reminder that people have lived and hunted in this landscape for thousands of years.

Nearby, at Ulldecona, the sanctuary of the Ermita de la Pietat has some of the most important rock art in Catalonia, with dozens of shelters and many painted figures. Guided visits can be arranged, and the paintings there are better preserved.

Below the mountains lies the Ebro delta, one of the largest wetlands in the western Mediterranean, a flat world of rice paddies, lagoons, beaches and reed beds. Flamingos, herons and many other birds live here, and the rice grown in the delta is used in some of Spain's best paellas. Amposta, seven kilometres away, is the delta's main town, and its suspension bridge across the Ebro, built in the early twentieth century, is a local landmark.

The riding is varied. The roads across the delta are flat and straight, with wide views and strong winds. The roads into the Montsià and the hills behind are winding and steep, with views over the delta and the sea. To the west, the Ports de Beseit massif offers serious mountain riding, with tight curves and dramatic scenery. Traffic is light outside summer, when the coast fills with visitors.

Amposta has the fuel stations, the bike shop and the supermarkets. In the delta everything comes back to rice and the sea: arròs negre, black rice with squid ink, paella, and fish from the sea. A sunset over the delta, with flamingos in the lagoons and the mountains glowing behind, is unforgettable.
t.abric del barranc de sant jaume@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza had to move. In the 1960s and 1970s, two dams built on the Ebro created a huge reservoir known as the Mar de Aragón, and the old town at the meeting of the Ebro and the Segre was abandoned and largely demolished, its people resettled in a new town above. The story is told in the town's museums and in the novels of Jesús Moncada, who grew up in the old Mequinenza. In a ravine nearby, the Abric del Barranc de Sant Jaume holds prehistoric paintings, part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The landscape around Mequinenza is dry and dramatic, with eroded hills, gypsum cliffs and the great expanse of the reservoir. The water attracts anglers from all over Europe, drawn by the giant catfish, the wels, which were introduced into the Ebro and can grow to enormous sizes. The banks are lined with fishing camps and boats.

The riding here is a mix of open, straight roads across the plateau and winding routes along the rivers. The road from Mequinenza to Fraga follows the Segre valley, and the roads south towards the Matarraña and the Ports de Beseit offer more mountains. Summers are very hot, often over forty degrees, and the wind can be strong. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride.

Fraga, thirteen kilometres away on the Cinca, is the place for fuel, a workshop or a proper meal. Its old town climbs a hillside above the river, and it is famous for its figs, dried and sold across Spain, with a fig fair every autumn. Out on the plains, irrigation from the rivers has turned the dry land into orchards of peaches, apricots and cherries, and in early summer roadside stalls sell fruit by the box.

Mequinenza's museums tell the story of the drowned town and of the lignite mines that once employed much of the population, with a recreated mine gallery you can walk through. After that, a dip where the rivers meet, or a cold drink on a terrace above the water watching the anglers wait for their monster, is about the right speed for a summer afternoon in a place that regularly sees forty degrees.
Where the Segre comes down from the Pyrenees towards the plains of Lleida, it squeezes through a gap at Oliana, held back by a dam and a reservoir that fills the valley above. On the slopes nearby, Roc del Rumbau, also called the Roca dels Moros, the Moors' rock, is a shelter with prehistoric paintings, one of the Catalan sites of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The name is a common one in Catalonia and Spain: local people often attributed anything ancient and mysterious to the Moors.

This is the pre-Pyrenees, a land of limestone ridges, deep gorges and pine-covered hills, with the high peaks visible to the north on clear days. The Segre valley has been a route between the Pyrenees and the plains for thousands of years, and the villages along it have Romanesque churches, castles and old stone houses.

Coll de Nargó, eleven kilometres upstream, has a beautiful Romanesque church, Sant Climent, with a tall bell tower, and the hills around the village are known for fossil dinosaur eggs, found in large numbers in the rocks of the area. A small museum explains the finds. Further north, the road passes through the gorge of Tresponts and reaches La Seu d'Urgell, with its cathedral, and Andorra.

The riding is excellent. The C-14 follows the Segre valley, with curves, tunnels and views of the reservoir and the mountains. Side roads climb into the hills, with tight bends, steep gradients and little traffic. The roads towards Solsona and the Cardener valley, and over the Coll de Bóixols towards Tremp, are among the best in Catalonia. Watch for cyclists, rockfalls and occasional ice in winter.

Oliana, three kilometres away, has a filling station and a couple of shops, and Solsona, twenty-two kilometres away, is a historic town with a cathedral and an old quarter. Up here the kitchen turns mountain: trinxat, a fried cake of cabbage and potato, and the cured meats and cheeses of the Pyrenees. A coffee in a village square, with the mountains around you, is a pleasant break from the curves.
t.calcaes del mata@40.4,0.1:
Ares del Maestrat sits on a crag so steep that the village seems glued to the rock, and below it, in the Gasulla gorge, the Cingle de la Mola Remigia holds some of the most famous Levantine paintings in Spain, scenes of archers, hunters and even an execution. Calçaes del Matà is a shelter in the same broad landscape near Albocàsser, and with the Gasulla and Valltorta sites it belongs to the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. The shelters here are reached on foot, and guided visits can be booked through the local museums.

This part of the Maestrat is a high, rugged plateau with deep ravines, limestone cliffs and pine forests, crossed by drystone walls and dotted with old farmhouses. Villages like Albocàsser, Catí and Ares were once rich from the wool trade, and their churches, town halls and mansions reflect that prosperity. Catí, in particular, has a beautiful Gothic town hall and old houses of wool merchants.

The landscape changes with the seasons: green in spring, golden in summer, and sometimes white with snow in winter. Almond trees blossom in February and March, and the forests smell of pine and herbs. The sky is often clear, with sharp light and long views.

The riding is among the best in the region, with quiet roads, endless curves and dramatic views. The road from Albocàsser to Ares and on to Morella, the great walled town of the Maestrat, is a classic, and the roads down to the coast offer fast, flowing descents. Traffic is light, and surfaces are generally good. Watch for livestock, cyclists and occasional gravel.

Albocàsser has basic services, and Alcalà de Xivert, sixteen kilometres away near the coast, has fuel and more. Lamb, rabbit and, in winter, black truffles dug in the oak woods fill the menus. A meal in Morella, with its castle above and walls around, is a good end to a day in the mountains.
t.cova del cingle@41.0,0.7:
The Ebro still has rope ferries. At Miravet, a flat boat attached to a cable across the river carries cars, bikes and walkers from bank to bank, driven only by the current and the skill of the ferryman, as such ferries have done for centuries. Above the village, on a rocky hill, stands one of the great Templar castles of Catalonia, a stern stone fortress that controlled the river. Nearby, among the hills of the Ribera d'Ebre near Ginestar and Rasquera, the Cova del Cingle is a rock shelter with prehistoric paintings, part of the World Heritage Site of Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin.

The Ribera d'Ebre is a land of orchards, olive groves and vineyards along the river, with dry hills and mountains on either side. In 1938 it was the scene of the Battle of the Ebro, the longest and bloodiest battle of the Spanish Civil War, when the Republican army crossed the river in a last great offensive and was eventually pushed back. The ruins of the old village of Corbera d'Ebre, destroyed in the fighting and left as a memorial, and the trenches and memorials in the Serra de Pàndols tell the story.

The landscape is dramatic, with the river winding through gorges and plains, and the mountains of the Serra de Cardó and the Ports rising to the south. Summers are hot, and the valley can be very warm. Spring and autumn are pleasant, with green fields and blossoming trees.

The riding is a mix of river roads and mountain routes. The road along the Ebro, through Miravet, Benissanet and Móra d'Ebre, is scenic, and the roads into the hills are steep and winding. The Serra de Cardó and the roads towards the Priorat wine region offer excellent curves and views. Traffic is light, but watch for slow farm vehicles and cyclists.

Móra d'Ebre, the market town of the valley, is where to refuel and eat, and Mont-roig del Camp, twenty-three kilometres away, is the nearest larger place on the coast side. The olive oil is superb, and the dark, strong wines of the Terra Alta and Priorat grow on the hills around you. A crossing on the Miravet ferry, with the castle above and the river flowing beneath, costs a few coins and feels like stepping back two hundred years.
t.mas d en josep abric l@40.4,0.1:
If the rock art of eastern Spain has a capital, it is the Valltorta gorge in the Maestrat of Castellón, and the Mas d'en Josep shelter is one of its classic sites. The paintings here belong to the Levantine style, small, lively scenes of hunters with bows, running figures and animals in motion, drawn with an energy that still feels modern. One famous panel from this area shows a deer hunt; others depict archers in mid-stride. The shelters of the Valltorta are part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, and the museum at Tírig, near the gorge, is the place to start: it explains the art, shows reproductions, and organises guided visits to the shelters, which are fenced and protected.

The landscape is high limestone plateau and dry gorge, crossed with dry-stone walls, old farmhouses called masos, and terraces of almond and olive trees. Albocàsser, the nearest village of any size, has a little over a thousand people and an old town of stone houses. Catí, to the north, is one of the loveliest villages in the Maestrat, with Gothic mansions built by wool merchants in its prosperous centuries.

The riding is superb if you like empty roads. The CV-15 and the smaller roads across the plateau link Albocàsser, Tírig, Coves de Vinromà and Catí with long bends, short straights and constant views over wide country. Traffic is minimal, but watch for farm vehicles and loose gravel at junctions. Winter can bring ice in the high villages, and the wind across the plateau can be strong. Spring, when the almond trees flower and the fields go green, is the most beautiful time.

Wool, sheep and cheese shaped this region for centuries, and Catí still produces a well-known cheese. Restaurants serve mountain cooking: lamb, game, slow-cooked stews and the olleta, a thick soup of beans, rice and pork that keeps riders going on cold days.

Plan fuel carefully. The villages are small and stations scarce; Alcalà de Xivert, down near the coast and the AP-7, is the nearest larger town, and Sant Mateu or Vinaròs are other options. Fill up before you head inland, carry water, and leave enough time at the museum. The gorge rewards those who slow down, which is a hard lesson for some of us.
t.caidas del salbimec@41.0,0.1:
The Matarraña, or Matarranya as most locals call it, is the corner of Aragón that feels Catalan, Valencian and Aragonese at once, and it has quietly become one of the most rewarding regions in Spain to explore on two wheels. The shelter known as Caídas del Salbimec lies in the hills between Valdeltormo, Mazaleón and Calaceite, one of the many prehistoric art sites along the eastern edge of the peninsula that are protected together by UNESCO. The paintings are modest, and access may involve a rough track and a walk, but the setting is typical of the region: a sandstone outcrop above olive groves and almond terraces, with the river cutting below.

Calaceite, a few kilometres away, is the village to see. Its main square is surrounded by stone mansions and arcades, and there is an Iberian settlement on a hill nearby, San Antonio, where the pre-Roman people of the area built a walled town. Further south, Valderrobres has a Gothic bridge over the Matarraña river leading straight through a gate into the old town, with a castle and church above it. It is one of the most photographed views in Aragón, and it deserves it.

The roads are a joy. Small, well-maintained and almost empty outside weekends, they wander between Calaceite, Cretas, Valderrobres and Beceite through rolling country that turns rugged towards the Els Ports massif in the south. Corners come one after another without ever becoming frantic, and the surface is mostly good. A little further west, near Alcañiz, the Motorland circuit hosts MotoGP, and on race weekends the whole area fills with bikes of every kind.

This is olive oil country first and foremost; the Bajo Aragón oil has its own protected designation, made mainly from the Empeltre variety, mild and golden. Peaches from nearby Calanda are bagged on the tree to protect them, and are famous across Spain. Ham, lamb and robust red wines complete a menu that suits a hungry rider.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The villages are small, Calaceite among them, and stations are thinly spread. Alcañiz, about twenty kilometres away, is the reliable choice, and Valderrobres has a station too. Summer heat is fierce in the valleys, while spring and autumn are glorious, with the rivers running and the hills green.
t.chateau de montsegur@42.9,1.8:
The castle of Montségur sits on a steep limestone peak, the pog, at about twelve hundred metres above the valleys of the Ariège, and even from the road below it looks impossible. In the thirteenth century it was the last great refuge of the Cathars, the dualist Christians condemned as heretics by the Church and crushed by the Albigensian Crusade. In 1243 a royal army laid siege to the summit, and after ten months the defenders surrendered in March 1244. Those who refused to renounce their faith, more than two hundred people, were burned at the foot of the mountain, in a place still called the Field of the Burned. A simple stone memorial stands there today.

The ruins you climb to are actually later, rebuilt as a royal fortress after the siege, but the atmosphere is powerful. The path up is steep, rocky and slippery when wet; allow an hour for the round trip and wear decent footwear rather than riding boots if you can. From the top, the view sweeps across the Pyrenean foothills and on clear days to the high peaks to the south.

The roads around here are wonderful. The D9 climbs from Lavelanet through Montferrier and then winds up towards the village of Montségur, below the castle, with tight bends and steep gradients. From there it continues towards the Col de la Croix des Morts and the Gorges de la Frau, a narrow limestone gorge, or descends towards Bélesta. Near Bélesta, the Fontaine de Fontestorbes is an intermittent spring that rises and falls on a rhythm during dry periods, a natural curiosity well worth a stop.

The surrounding area, often called the Pays Cathare, is full of other castles of the same era, perched on improbable summits: Puivert, Peyrepertuse and Quéribus among them. Riding between them is one of the great motorcycle tours of southern France, through forests, gorges and vineyards with very little traffic outside summer.

Lavelanet, the nearest town, was once a centre of textile production and is now quieter; it has fuel, supermarkets and cafés. The village of Montségur has a small museum and a few places to eat. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; in winter, the high roads can be closed by snow and the castle path can be icy.
t.arc de triomphe@44.1,4.8:
Orange is a Provençal town of thirty thousand on the edge of the Rhône plain, and it has two of the finest Roman monuments in Europe. The first is the triumphal arch, standing on the old Via Agrippa at the northern entrance to the town, built in the time of Augustus and later dedicated to Tiberius. It is covered in carved reliefs of battles, naval trophies and captured Gauls, celebrating the victories of the legions, and despite two thousand years of wind and traffic, the carvings remain impressive. The second is the Roman theatre, with its stage wall still standing intact, more than a hundred metres long and over thirty high. Louis XIV is said to have called it the finest wall in his kingdom. In summer, the theatre hosts the Chorégies, an opera festival with performances under the stars. Both monuments were listed by UNESCO in 1981.

The town's name has a curious history. In the Middle Ages, Orange was an independent principality, and through inheritance it passed to the House of Nassau, which became the House of Orange-Nassau, the royal family of the Netherlands. The Dutch colour orange and the name of Orange in South Africa and America all trace back to this small town in Provence.

The riding around Orange is excellent. To the south, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, among its vineyards strewn with round stones, is a short ride away. To the east, the Dentelles de Montmirail, a jagged limestone ridge, and the villages of Gigondas, Vacqueyras and Séguret offer winding roads through vineyards. Further on, Mont Ventoux rises to over nineteen hundred metres, with a famous road to its bare summit. Beware of the mistral, the cold north wind that funnels down the Rhône valley, sometimes blowing hard for days; it can push a motorcycle across the road and makes exposed stretches tricky.

Summer is hot and crowded, especially in July during the festival season. Spring, with the vineyards greening and the poppies in the fields, and autumn, during the grape harvest, are the best times to visit.

Orange has fuel, garages and plenty of cafés and restaurants, especially around the theatre. Try the local wines, but save them for the evening, and look out for the Provençal markets that fill the squares on certain mornings.
t.historic fortified city of carcassonne@4:
Carcassonne is the fortress that every child draws when asked for a castle: a double ring of walls with about fifty towers, pointed slate roofs, a drawbridge and a keep, rising from a hilltop above the river Aude. The medieval city, known as La Cité, is the largest walled town in Europe still standing, and much of what you see was heavily restored in the nineteenth century by the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, whose steep roofs on the towers are more northern French than local. The result is spectacular if debatable, and UNESCO listed the site in 1997.

The place has a past of great drama. In 1209 a crusading army, sent by the pope against the Cathars, a dissenting Christian movement in southern France, besieged and took the city, and its lord Raymond-Roger Trencavel died in captivity. Carcassonne then became a royal frontier fortress, facing Aragon, and the walls were strengthened. Later it lost its military value and was nearly demolished before the restoration saved it. Nearby are Cathar castles perched on cliffs, such as Peyrepertuse and Quéribus, which make a splendid day's ride.

The riding in the area is excellent. From Carcassonne, roads lead west along the Canal du Midi, a UNESCO-listed waterway lined with plane trees, and east and south into the Corbières hills, where the roads twist through vineyards, scrub and limestone gorges. Surfaces are generally good, with some rough patches, and traffic is light outside July and August, when tourism peaks. The wind, called the Cers or Tramontane depending on direction, can be strong. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool evenings, and the scent of wild thyme and rosemary on the hills.

Carcassonne has fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, both in the lower town and on the approach roads, and the Cité itself is crowded in summer. The local speciality is cassoulet, a slow-cooked stew of white beans, sausage, pork and duck, rich enough to need an afternoon's rest. Park outside the walls, since the cobbled streets are steep and crowded, and plan to arrive early or late in the day to escape the tour groups.
t.madriu perafita claror valley@42.5,1.6:
Andorra is famous for shopping and ski lifts, which makes the Madriu-Perafita-Claror valley a surprise. A glacial valley that runs up into the mountains from the edge of the capital's built-up area, it is a landscape of granite peaks, lakes, pastures and stone shepherd huts, almost untouched by roads. UNESCO listed it in 2004 as a cultural landscape because it shows, in one place, how people have lived in the high Pyrenees for thousands of years, with pastoral farming, iron forges and mountain paths shaping the land together.

The valley is closed to motor vehicles, so this is a place for the walker, not the rider. You park at the entrance near Les Escaldes and Engolasters and go in on foot, passing through woods of pine and fir and up into meadows where cattle and horses graze in summer. The old iron forges used charcoal from the forests, and some stone huts and terraces survive from the centuries when communities moved their flocks up each summer. The high lakes, which are cold and clear, lie beneath peaks of nearly three thousand metres.

The riding in Andorra is, nevertheless, famous. The main road from the French border climbs to the Port d'Envalira, at about 2,400 metres the highest paved pass in the Pyrenees, then drops in long bends to Encamp and Andorra la Vella, and the road toward Spain follows the Valira river down. Surfaces are generally good, though patched, and weather can change very fast, with snow possible even in early summer and fog clouding the pass. The best months are June to September, and winter riding is for the experienced. Traffic is thick in the capital and at the borders, where customs checks may cause delays.

Fuel in Andorra is cheaper than in France or Spain, because of low taxes, so many riders fill up here, and Encamp, Escaldes and Andorra la Vella all have plenty of stations. The Mont-Louis citadel, across the border in France and also on the UNESCO list as one of Vauban's fortresses, is a worthwhile detour. Eat a hearty plate of trinxat, a dish of potato, cabbage and bacon, and wear warm clothing even in July, because the weather up high can turn cold at once.
t.cova del taller@40.9,0.8:
South of Tortosa the Ebro river slows down and spreads into one of the great wetlands of the western Mediterranean, but a few kilometres inland the country is hilly and dry, with limestone outcrops and terraced olives. Cova del Taller sits somewhere in this landscape of the Baix Ebre, near El Perelló and L'Ampolla, and is one of the shelters that carry prehistoric paintings in Catalonia. I cannot tell you what is painted there, and the site is probably not marked in any big way, so treat it as a quiet corner of the region rather than a certain spectacle.

The region itself has plenty to offer. The Ebro delta, a flat triangle of rice paddies, lagoons and sandbars built by silt from the river, shelters flamingos, herons and many other waterbirds, and in autumn the paddies turn gold before the harvest. Not far inland, around Gandesa, the Battle of the Ebro in 1938 was the longest and bloodiest of the Spanish Civil War, and its trenches, shelters and memorials are open to visitors. Olive oil from the hills here is among the best in Catalonia.

Riding is varied and often delightful. The coastal road past L'Ampolla is flat and fast, with views of the sea and delta, while the roads inland wind through olive terraces, pine woods and small villages, with enough bends and gradients to keep a rider alert. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light outside summer weekends. The wind, especially the cold, dry mestral from the northwest, can be strong, and in summer the heat is intense. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the light is clear and the fields are fresh.

El Perelló, about ten kilometres away, has small shops and a station or two, and Mont-roig del Camp, the bigger town in the neighbourhood, has more services, though it is a good distance off. For dinner, look for arròs negre, rice cooked with squid ink, or a plate of the Ebro's eels and shellfish, and wash it down with local white wine. Carry water for any walk, and ask the locals about access, since farmland often surrounds the shelters.
t.eglesia de santa maria de l assumpcio@42:
Valleys in the high Pyrenees of Catalonia and Aragon are full of small Romanesque churches, and the area around the Alta Ribagorça is among the richest. They were built in the eleventh and twelfth centuries by craftsmen working in what is called the Lombard style, with plain stone walls, round arches and tall, slender bell towers decorated with blind arcades, and they stand in villages that often have only a few houses. A group of them in the nearby Vall de Boí is on the UNESCO list, and this church is part of the same family of buildings, though I cannot describe its interior with confidence.

What makes these churches memorable is their setting. They sit above narrow valleys of pasture, beech and fir, with snow-covered peaks behind, and the bell towers seem to echo the sharp peaks. The wall paintings that once covered the interiors were removed in the twentieth century for safekeeping, and many are in the National Art Museum of Catalonia in Barcelona, where the Christ in Majesty from Taüll is a masterpiece. Copies in the churches give an idea of how colourful the interiors were.

Reaching this area on a motorcycle means serious mountain roads. From the Vall d'Aran, the road through the long Vielha tunnel, more than five kilometres, leads south, and the roads of the Ribagorça twist through gorges and past reservoirs, with tight bends, short tunnels and views of high rock walls. Surfaces are usually good but can be damaged by frost and rockfall, and fog and rain are not unusual. Traffic is light outside July and August. The best months are June to September, when the passes are clear, and October for the autumn colours.

The villages are small and have very little fuel, so plan carefully: Vielha, about twenty-nine kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, and Benasque and Castejón de Sos lie on the other side. Meals in the mountains are hearty, with stews, grilled lamb and mountain cheese, and sweet chestnut desserts in autumn. Churches are often locked outside opening hours, so ask in the village for the key or check the visiting times, and carry warm clothes, because the temperature falls quickly after sundown.
t.val de mamet i@41.3,0.1:
The Ebro river cuts through Aragon in a wide, dry valley, and where it meets its tributaries the Segre and Cinca around Mequinenza it was dammed in the twentieth century to make long, narrow lakes among bare hills. Val de Mamet is a dry side valley in this country, with a shelter that holds prehistoric paintings. The surroundings are arid and open, with low limestone cliffs, thyme and rosemary scrub, and scattered pines and almonds, and the silence is broken mostly by the wind and the occasional hawk.

Mequinenza has an unusual story. The old town stood by the river for centuries, a coal-mining place whose lignite fuelled boats and industry, and in the 1960s the building of the Mequinenza dam flooded the lower town, forcing the population to move to a new town on higher ground. Remains of the old town lie beneath the lake, and a popular claim is that the reservoir's huge catfish, introduced decades ago, grow to the size of a man. Nearby Caspe is famous in Spanish history for the Compromise of Caspe in 1412, when delegates met to decide the succession to the throne of Aragon.

Fabara, close by, has a beautiful Roman mausoleum, a small tower-tomb from the second century AD, standing in a field beside a road. The landscape draws bird-watchers, and the paths along the water attract anglers from across Europe. The silence of the countryside, the smell of herbs and the broad horizons make it a good place for a rider who likes space.

Roads are quiet and wide, with long straights, a few bends and occasional gravel patches, and surfaces are mostly good, though minor tracks to shelters are rough. The wind can be fierce, and the summer sun is merciless, so ride early and carry water. Fuel stations are found at Caspe, about seventeen kilometres away, and Mequinenza has a few. Eat local lamb, or a plate of freshly fried river fish, with peaches from Aragon in summer, and plan your fuel carefully, since the villages are small and far apart.
t.la roca dels moros@41.5,0.7:
El Cogul is a village of a few dozen houses in Les Garrigues, the low, stony plateau of western Catalonia where the whole landscape seems to be one big olive grove. Just outside it, a wall of rock above a small valley holds one of the most important prehistoric paintings in the country. The shelter is known as the Roca dels Moros, the Moors' Rock, which is simply the Catalan habit of attributing anything old and mysterious to the Moors, and it was brought to scientific attention in the early twentieth century by a local priest.

The famous scene shows a group of small women in long skirts, apparently dancing around a tiny naked man, painted in dark red and black. It is one of the few Levantine compositions that people instantly read as ritual, and visitors argue happily about what is going on. Centuries later, in Roman times, someone scratched inscriptions in Latin and Iberian script on the same wall, which suggests the shelter was treated as a holy place for a very long time. The art belongs to the group of Levantine sites that UNESCO lists, and there is a small interpretation centre in the village.

Les Garrigues is the home of the Arbequina olive, a small, fruity variety that produces much of the oil Catalans pour on their bread. The terraced fields are bordered by dry-stone walls, and the harvest in late autumn brings out whole families with nets and sticks. Almond trees bloom in February, and the plateau is a quilt of silver green and rust brown, with distant views to the Pyrenees on clear days.

For riding, the roads between the villages are straight, narrow and quiet, climbing and dropping gently across the plateau, and the pace is easy. Surfaces vary from fresh asphalt to rough patches, and tractors and delivery trucks are the main traffic. Summer heat is heavy, and winter mornings can be foggy and cold. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Take the time to roll slowly through the villages, where old men sit outside the bar and dogs sleep in the road.

Lleida, about eighteen kilometres away, has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and Juneda, nearer, is also large enough for the essentials. Try the local olive oil on a slice of toasted bread with tomato, or a plate of snails cooked with herbs, a Lleida favourite.
t.muriecho e1@42.2,0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is the first big step of the Pyrenean foothills, a tumbled mass of limestone that has been cut into canyons so deep and narrow that people come from all over Europe to descend them with ropes. Muriecho is a tiny place on the southern fringe of the range, in the Somontano, the land at the foot of the mountain, and E1 is one numbered shelter of several recorded around it. The paintings belong to the Mediterranean-arc rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and this region of Huesca has some of the best examples in Aragon. I cannot say what E1 holds, but the surrounding country gives you plenty.

Alquézar, five kilometres away, is the place to head for. It is a village of under four hundred people on a rock above the Vero river, crowned by a collegiate church that began as a fortress, and its streets of pale stone tilt down to a gorge where metal walkways hang above the green water. Park below, since the village is steep and cobbled. In the evening, when the day trippers leave, the place is unbelievably quiet, and swifts scream around the walls.

The riding is first class. From Barbastro the road to Alquézar and further to the canyons weaves through olive groves and almond terraces, with bends of every radius and a dramatic view of the Guara ridge. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends, when canyoners and climbers fill the lay-bys. In spring, the almond blossom is a fine sight, and in autumn the oak and box turn rusty. Summer afternoons are very hot, so start early.

Fuel comes from Barbastro, twenty kilometres away, a cheerful market town of seventeen thousand with a cathedral and the headquarters of the Somontano wine region. The villages themselves are too small to rely on. In the high cliffs above, griffon vultures circle all day, and the bearded vulture, the lammergeier, nests in the area, so keep an eye on the sky. For lunch, ask for a plate of local ternasco, the young Aragonese lamb, or a bowl of migas, and try a glass of Somontano red or the dry white from the cooler slopes.
t.abric de can ximet@41.3,1.7:
The Penedès is a broad, gently rolling basin between the coastal ranges and the Montserrat massif, and it is one of the great wine regions of Catalonia. Vilafranca del Penedès, its capital, is a lively town with a Gothic church, a wine museum and a passion for castells, the human towers that teams of men, women and children build in the main square on feast days. UNESCO added the castells to its list of intangible heritage in 2010. Can Ximet is a farm name on the fringe of this landscape, and the shelter nearby is a modest rock overhang associated with prehistoric art. I do not know enough about it to describe the paintings, but the area is dense with archaeology.

For a rider the Penedès is a pleasant, easy landscape, with vineyards in neat rows, small lanes through the fields, and the odd stone farmhouse with a tower. The roads vary from smooth to patched. Weekend traffic includes cyclists and cars heading for wine tastings, so go early. In autumn, after the grape harvest, the vines turn yellow and red and the air has a faint smell of fermentation. In spring the fields are green and the wind from the sea is mild.

This is also the home of cava. Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, just to the north, is the centre of Spanish sparkling wine, with huge cellars and long tours. A tasting is hard to combine with a motorbike, so ask for a non-alcoholic option or save it for the evening. Vilafranca is large enough to supply fuel, food and workshops. It is a town of thirty-eight thousand, and the old town is easy to wander on foot.

If you want more twisting roads, head south and west into the Garraf massif, a rugged limestone upland with scrub and caves, and a quick route down to the coast at Sitges. Barcelona is around fifty kilometres to the north-east, and the afternoon ride from there is a classic. The early evening light on the vine rows is the best sight of the day.
t.roca de marta@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza lies where the Segre river meets the Ebro, and the town you see today is not the one that stood here before the 1960s. When a dam was built downstream on the Ebro, the old town was flooded by the reservoir, known as the Mar de Aragón, and its people moved to a new settlement on higher ground. The old castle still sits above the water, and the reservoir stretches in long fingers between bare, ochre hills. It is a landscape both beautiful and a little melancholy, and the lake is famous among anglers for enormous catfish. Roca de Marta is a rock shelter in the dry hills nearby, another of the sites of Mediterranean-arc rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, though I cannot describe what the walls carry.

The riding is dry, open and a little bleak, in the way that Aragon can be. Roads here cut across steppe-like plateaus of rosemary and thyme, then drop to the reservoir shore with views over flat blue water and cliffs that glow orange at sunset. The surface is generally fine, with long gentle bends and little traffic. Wind is a regular companion, and in summer the heat comes up the valley like an oven door. Spring and autumn are better, when the air is clear.

Mequinenza has about two and a half thousand people, with fuel, a few bars and a small museum on the history of the coal mines, since the area was a lignite-mining district for generations. The town's fish restaurants serve river catfish and other Ebro fish, if you are curious. Fraga, seventeen kilometres away, is bigger, and has fuel, supermarkets and a good range of services, and it sits on the road toward Lleida and Zaragoza.

Fayón, across the water, has a similar story, with a new town and an old church tower sticking out of the reservoir in dry years. There is a certain charm in a landscape that has been so thoroughly reshaped, where the water hides a village and the hills lean over it. Park near the shore, walk down to the edge, and listen. If a fisherman is there, ask about the fish. It is probably an enormous one.
t.cova de les calobres@40.9,0.7:
The Ebro is near its end here. South of Tortosa the river spreads into a flat delta of rice fields, lagoons and sand spits, and the coast of the Baix Ebre curves out into the sea. The Cova de les Calobres, the Cave of the Snakes, is a shelter inland from El Perelló, in the dry limestone hills of the Serra de Cardó. The rock paintings of this area belong to the Mediterranean-arc group that UNESCO listed in 1998, and the nearby shelters have given their names to the ride titles. I cannot tell you what survives in Calobres, but the sites in this part of Catalonia are typically small, red and tucked under overhangs.

This is easy and gentle riding. The roads around El Perelló run between olive groves, carob trees and low hills, with the sea sparkling in the distance. The coast road is busy in summer, and the old N-340 has a lot of trucks, but small roads inland are quiet. If you want a longer loop, the Via Verde, an old railway line turned into a path, runs through the area, and the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit mountains to the west offer real hairpins and rock scenery. A strong wind from the north-west called the mestral blows down the valley often and can push a bike around on exposed stretches.

El Perelló has nearly three thousand people, and L'Ampolla has a similar number, so fuel and food are easy to find, though the larger town of Tortosa, fifteen kilometres away, has a better choice. Tortosa has a cathedral, a castle above the river, and a long history as a frontier city. On the coast, the delta is famous for rice, eels and the pink flamingos that gather in its lagoons, and a plate of rice with seafood is the obvious order.

Go in spring or autumn, when the air is mild and the delta is busy with migrating birds. In summer the coast is crowded and hot, and in winter the north wind is cold. Take a few moments at a viewpoint over the water and let the wind blow over you.
t.roman theatre and its surroundings and t:
Orange has one of the best Roman theatres still standing anywhere, and what makes it special is the stage wall. It is a tall, plain facade, thirty-seven metres high and more than a hundred metres long, which in most other theatres has fallen or been taken apart for stone. Here it survives, and Louis XIV is supposed to have called it the finest wall in his kingdom. The theatre was built in the first century, under Augustus or soon after, and a statue of the emperor still stands in the central niche. The nearby triumphal arch, on the edge of town, is also Roman and also in good shape. UNESCO listed the theatre and arch together in 1981.

The theatre is still used for performances. Every summer the Chorégies d'Orange, an opera festival that dates from the nineteenth century, fills the seats at night, and the acoustics, helped by the old wall, are remarkable. The town itself is a pleasant small Provençal place, with plane trees, cafes and a market, and the name Orange has nothing to do with the fruit. It comes from an old Celtic or Roman name, and the princes of Orange, the house that later gave the Dutch royal family its name, took their title from this town.

The riding in the area is a pleasure. The Rhône valley is flat and busy, but turn east and you reach the vineyards of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, about ten kilometres away, and the limestone teeth of the Dentelles de Montmirail, where the roads curl between vines and olive trees. Further on, Mont Ventoux rises to 1,912 metres, and the climb to its bare summit is one of the classic rides in France. The mistral, the cold north wind that blows down the valley, can be fierce, and gusts will push a bike sideways. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while midsummer afternoons are very hot.

Orange has thirty thousand people, so fuel and food are simple. Many local cafes serve lunch under the plane trees. Order a glass of Côtes du Rhône with lunch if you are not riding, or a coffee if you are. Aim for early morning at the theatre, because the stone gets hot and the light flattens.
t.ningbo sanjiangkou@29.9,121.6:
Ningbo is where three rivers meet, the Yao, the Fenghua and the Yong, and Sanjiangkou, the three rivers' mouth, is the heart of the old city. For more than a thousand years, Ningbo was one of the great ports of China, a place from which silk, porcelain and tea went to Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia, and where the monks and merchants of those countries landed. It was also the southern end of the Grand Canal, which connected it to Hangzhou and the north, and so it was a meeting point of river, canal and sea. Today, Ningbo-Zhoushan is the busiest cargo port in the world by tonnage, and the old waterfront is a neat, modern riverfront park.

Some of the old city survives. The Tianyi Pavilion, a library founded in the sixteenth century, is the oldest private library in China, and its quiet gardens, with ponds and rockeries, are a pleasant retreat. The old Bund area on the river has a historic church, and small museums that tell the story of the maritime trade. The cuisine is a pleasure for seafood lovers, with the yellow croaker, crabs and eels prominent, and the local dessert, tangyuan, glutinous rice balls filled with black sesame paste, is famous across China.

A hundred and fifty kilometres to the north-west lies Hangzhou and the West Lake, a cultural landscape of lakes, causeways, pagodas and hills that has inspired poets and painters for a thousand years and was listed by UNESCO in 2011. The Hangzhou Bay Bridge, about thirty-six kilometres long, links Ningbo to the Shanghai side across the muddy waters of the bay. The surrounding plain is flat and crowded, with canals, rice fields and factories.

Riding in this part of China is, for foreigners, extremely difficult, since most are not allowed to ride their own bikes or to rent them freely, so trains and taxis are the practical choice. Fuel and services are everywhere in the city, which has about three and a half million people in the urban area. Spring is mild and rainy, summer is hot and humid with typhoons possible in late summer, and autumn is the best season.
t.camino de la cova plana l@41.4,0.4:
Where the Segre and the Cinca rivers meet the Ebro, the land opens out into a dry, tawny basin that feels far from the sea. Mequinenza sits at the heart of it, a small town of about 2,500 people that has a story unlike any other on the Ebro. The old town was flooded in the 1960s when the Ribarroja dam created the Mar de Aragón, a huge reservoir, and the inhabitants were moved to a new town built higher up. The writer Jesús Moncada, born here, wrote about the vanished town in his novel Camino de sirga, and the loss still colours the way people talk about the place.

The countryside around is steppe-like, with pale clay hills, juniper and thyme, a few almond and olive groves, and long views over the water. This region of the lower Cinca and the Ebro, on the border between Aragon and Catalonia, holds shelters with rock paintings, small and often hard to find, part of the Levantine art that UNESCO listed in 1998. Treat the area as a place for walkers who have good local guidance, and ask in Mequinenza or Fraga about access, since many sites are protected and not marked on maps.

The riding is easy and wide open. Roads are generally good, with long straight stretches and bends where they cross ridges or follow the river valleys. The wind can be strong, and in summer the heat is extreme, so ride early and carry water. Autumn, when the light is soft and the temperature is mild, is a pleasure. The reservoir is a popular spot for anglers, and the enormous catfish that live in the Ebro attract fishermen from around Europe.

Fraga, a town of about 14,000 people 18 km away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and is the better place to stock up, as services in Mequinenza are limited. The area is known for its fruit, and for the local peaches and olive oil, and a plate of grilled lamb or a rice dish with rabbit is a typical lunch. Mequinenza also has a coal-mining history, with a museum devoted to it, and the black seam of the old mine tells another part of the story.
t.monderes@41.9,0.6:
The plain of Lleida is one of the great orchards of Spain, a flat, fertile basin of peach, pear and apple trees, irrigated by canals drawn from the Segre. Alfarràs, Algerri and Almenar are villages in this agricultural world, set among fields and ditches on the edge of Catalonia, where the green plain begins to rise towards the dry hills of the Montsec to the north. In spring the orchards bloom in pink and white, and in late summer the fruit lorries crowd the roads. It is not dramatic scenery, but it is a landscape built by water, and the canals, including the long Canal d'Urgell and the canal of Aragon and Catalonia, are the reason it exists.

The hills on the northern margin of the plain hold shelters with prehistoric paintings. The best known in the region is at Cogul, in the Garrigues, where a rock shelter called the Roca dels Moros has a painted scene of women in bell-shaped skirts dancing around a small male figure, one of the most celebrated images of Levantine rock art, which UNESCO listed in 1998. The shelter has a small interpretation centre, and visits are usually guided, so check opening times before heading out. Other shelters in the area are small and fragile, and many are closed to the public.

The riding in this part of Catalonia is gentle. Roads run in straight lines across the plain, past irrigation channels and fruit farms, and then rise into the hills with gentle curves and views over the plain. The wind can be strong, and summer afternoons are very hot. Spring blossom is spectacular, and autumn light is warm and golden. Be careful near the farm entrances, where tractors and trailers pull out onto the road.

Fuel and food are best found in the larger towns, such as Almacelles, about 20 km away, or Balaguer and Lleida, and small villages may have little. A plate of grilled lamb with allioli, snails cooked in a rich sauce, which Lleida is famous for, or fresh fruit from a roadside stand are the local pleasures. The olive oil of Les Garrigues, made from the small arbequina olive, is considered among the best in Spain, and a bottle makes a good souvenir.
t.abrics de l apotecari@41.2,1.3:
The coast south of Barcelona has been a corridor since the Romans, and the Via Augusta, the main road from Rome to Hispania, ran along it. At Roda de Berà, a few kilometres down the coast, a freestanding triumphal arch from that road still stands, the Arc de Berà, and the Roman city of Tarraco, now Tarragona, is a short ride away with its amphitheatre above the sea, its circus and walls, all listed by UNESCO. So the hills behind Torredembarra and Altafulla sit in a landscape that already carries a lot of history, even before you get to the much older layers of paint on the rocks.

The hills hold small rock shelters, the Abrics de l'Apotecari, and the name suggests an apothecary's cabinet, though I would not guess at the story behind it. Shelters of this kind belong to the wider tradition of Mediterranean rock art on the Iberian Peninsula, listed by UNESCO in 1998. Access to such places is often restricted to protect the paintings, so contact the local museum or tourist office before going, and expect to walk on rough paths. Do not touch or mark the walls.

The seaside towns are the pleasant part. Altafulla has a walled medieval village on a hill with a castle, white houses and narrow lanes, and below it a wide, sandy beach. The Roman villa of Els Munts, with its mosaics and baths, lies close by and belongs to the Tarraco World Heritage group. Torredembarra, with about 15,000 people six kilometres away, is the larger town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a good beach promenade, and it is the sensible place to fill the tank.

The riding is easy rather than exciting. The old N-340 runs close to the coast and is busy in summer, while the inland roads climb into small hills of pine and carob with gentle bends and good views of the sea. Spring and autumn are lovely, with warm days and fewer visitors, and the Mediterranean is warm enough for swimming into October. Try a plate of calçots in late winter, spring onions grilled over fire and dipped in romesco sauce, and a glass of cava from the Penedès, which lies just inland.
t.c3 western migjorn area@40.0,4.0:
Menorca has more prehistoric monuments per square kilometre than almost anywhere in Europe, and the south-west of the island is a good place to see why. The people who lived here in the Bronze and Iron Ages built talayots, round towers of stacked stones, and taules, T-shaped stone altars, and navetas, burial chambers shaped like upturned boats, in a culture that lasted for over a thousand years. In 2023 UNESCO added the Talayotic Culture of Minorca to its list, and the western Migjorn area, the south-west of the island, is one of the zones included.

The Migjorn, the southern coast, is a landscape of limestone and ravines. The island's flat, dry plateau is cut by deep, narrow gorges, the barrancs, which run down to the sea and end in small coves with white sand and turquoise water. Cala Galdana, with its curved bay, is the most famous of them, and the Algendar ravine behind it is green and shady. Stone walls divide the fields, in a pattern that has changed little for centuries, and wild olive, pine and juniper cover the land. The whole island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and much of the coast is protected.

Riding in Menorca is a gentle pleasure. The main road, the Me-1, runs along the spine of the island from Maó to Ciutadella, and small roads branch off toward the coast, with gentle curves, stone walls and farmhouses. Speed limits are low and enforced, and in summer the roads fill with tourists in hire cars and scooters, so early morning is best. The tramontana, a strong north wind, can blow hard in winter and spring. The old Camí de Cavalls, a path round the coast, is for walkers and bikes, not motor vehicles.

Ferreries, with about 4,400 people, and Es Mercadal are the closest towns for fuel, shops and food, and Alaior, larger, is 12 km away. Menorca is known for its cheese, Mahón, for the gin that the British introduced in the eighteenth century, and for caldereta de langosta, a lobster stew. Alaior makes ice cream and shoes, and the island has long made footwear and costume jewellery. A swim in a quiet cove, after seeing a talayot in the olive groves, is a fine combination.
t.antona i@41.9,1.0:
In the Pre-Pyrenees of Lleida, the plain of Urgell ends and the land starts folding into dry, golden hills. Artesa de Segre, Camarasa and Cubells are small places along the edge of this country, where the Segre river and the Noguera Pallaresa bring water down from the mountains, and where reservoirs and gorges give the landscape its character. The Camarasa dam, built in the early twentieth century on the Noguera Pallaresa, is a big wall of concrete holding back a long, green-blue lake in a narrow valley.

North of here the Montsec range rises as a wall of pale limestone. The Congost de Mont-rebei, a gorge cut by the Noguera Ribagorçana, is one of the sights of Catalonia, with cliffs over a hundred metres high on both sides of a narrow green channel. A path is cut into the rock and walkers cross it above the water. The country is wild, with griffon vultures soaring over the crags and, at night, some of the clearest skies in Spain, a feature that has made the Montsec a centre for astronomy.

Rock shelters in these hills belong to the same tradition as the better-known paintings at Cogul and elsewhere, part of the UNESCO listing of 1998. They are small, fragile and mostly not signed, so do not go searching on your own. The Cova del Cogulló, famous for its dancing women, is within reach and is the place to see what the painters of this region achieved. Be respectful of local rules and guide arrangements.

The riding is a pleasure. Roads from Artesa through Camarasa and up toward the Montsec offer bends, climbs and gorges, with views over blue water and pale cliffs, and few other vehicles. Surfaces are mostly good, though some narrow roads have rough patches. Summers are hot and winters cold, with fog in the valleys. Agramunt, 14 km from here and with just over 5,000 people, has fuel and shops, and it is famous for its turrón, a nougat made with almonds and honey, which has a protected name. Try a piece with a coffee before you ride on.
t.sierra de los rincones i@41.4,0.2:
Aragon and Catalonia meet along the Segre and Ebro here, and the map is full of names that mean corners and nooks. The Sierra de los Rincones is a low range of dry, rocky hills above the confluence of the Segre, Cinca and Ebro rivers, with scrub of juniper, thyme and pine and a lot of bare ground, in a region that gets less than 400 millimetres of rain a year. The great reservoir of Mequinenza, the Mar de Aragón, lies to the south, and from the high ground the view takes in water, hills and a haze of dust. The Ebro here is more than a river, it is a reservoir, with the valley flooded and the old towns beneath the water.

Mequinenza was a mining town, which surprises people. The lignite seams under the hills were worked for coal, and the town's life revolved around the mines and the barges on the river. The coal has gone, and the mines are closed, but a museum recalls the work. The steppe birds are the quiet bonus, with larks, sandgrouse and the occasional bustard in the open scrub, and the sky here is huge.

Rock shelters in these hills belong to the family of Levantine paintings that UNESCO listed in 1998, with small red figures that may be thousands of years old. They are fragile and mostly unmarked, so ask in Fraga or Mequinenza for guidance and keep to any rules about access. A visit is more rewarding with a local guide than alone.

The riding is hot and dry, with roads running along the ridges and through the valleys with gentle curves, and you will be surprised how few cars you meet. Summers are scorching, so ride early, and winters can be cold and foggy. Fraga, with about 14,000 people 16 km away, is the nearest place with fuel, supermarkets and rooms. The local peaches and olive oil are good, and the reservoir attracts fishermen who come for the huge catfish. A coffee on the plaza in Fraga makes a good break.
t.malfora i@42.2,0.0:
The Sierra de Guara is where the Pyrenean foothills turn to stone. Limestone ridges, deep canyons and rocky crags form a country that is famous among canyoners, and the Vero river runs through the middle in a gorge of pale, polished rock. Alquézar, a village of only about 300 people, perches on a rocky spur over the river, with a collegiate church and a castle on top, and its narrow lanes are among the most photographed in Aragon. It was once a Moorish stronghold, and in the eleventh century it fell to the Christian king Sancho Ramírez, an event that marks the early Reconquista in this region.

The shelters of the Vero and Mascún valleys hold rock art, which surprises people so far from the Mediterranean coast. The Mascún gorge, with its huge rock walls, hides small overhangs where red paintings have survived, listed by UNESCO in 1998 together with the rest of the Mediterranean Basin rock art. As always, the sites are fragile, many are closed, and access is by arrangement. The Alquézar tourist office is a good place to ask.

Riding here is very good indeed. Roads from Barbastro wind into the hills with tight bends, some sharp climbs and long views of the Pyrenees to the north, and the surface is generally good, though the narrower roads have patches. The area is popular with walkers, climbers and canyoners in summer, and the road to Alquézar can be busy at weekends. Winters are cold, with snow on the higher parts, and summers can be very hot. Spring, with green slopes and flowers, and autumn are best.

Barbastro, about 21 km from here, is the nearest town of any size, with about 17,000 people, fuel stations, shops and hotels, and it is also the centre of the Somontano wine region, where local reds and whites have won a name. Alquézar has several restaurants, and local dishes include ternasco, roast lamb, and migas, and the olive oil from the area is excellent. Book ahead in high season, and be ready for crowds in the village at midday.
t.palacio guell@41.4,2.2:
Antoni Gaudí was in his thirties when Eusebi Güell asked him to build a town house just off the Ramblas, and he gave his patron a palace that looks plain on the street and wild inside. The Palau Güell, built between 1886 and 1890 for the industrialist who became Gaudí's greatest supporter, stands in the Raval, a narrow street in what was then a respectable neighbourhood and is now one of the most multicultural districts of Barcelona. The front has two huge parabolic arches of wrought iron, with a pattern of whiplash lines in the gates, and the interior has a central hall that rises through the building to a dome pierced with small holes, so that on a sunny day the ceiling is spotted with starry light.

The roof is the part that people remember. A forest of chimneys covered in broken ceramic and glass tiles, each different in shape, stands against the sky, and it is the first sign of the later Gaudí who would build the Casa Batlló and the Sagrada Família. The palace is part of the UNESCO listing of Gaudí's works in Barcelona, from 1984 and extended in 2005, and it has been restored and is open to visitors. Check the opening days and book ahead for busy periods.

Riding in this part of Barcelona is a challenge.
