The streets are narrow, many are pedestrian, the traffic is dense and parking is limited, though motorcycles are a common sight in the city and there are designated bays. Be careful of pickpockets in the crowded Ramblas area, and leave nothing on the bike. A better way is to leave the bike in a secure garage and walk. The nearby harbour and the Montjuïc hill offer pleasant riding and good views over the city.

Fuel stations are around the edges of the city, and the Ronda del Litoral ring road is the usual way to reach them. Food is a pleasure: a plate of jamón and bread rubbed with tomato, a coffee at a café on the Ramblas, or a longer meal at one of the old restaurants in the Raval. The Boqueria market, close by, is full of colour and smells, with fruit stalls, seafood and cured meats. Early morning is a good time for the palace and the market.
t.cova del pi@41.0,0.7:
The Ebro takes a long turn through southern Catalonia before it reaches the sea, and in this stretch it flows wide and slow between orchards and dry hills, past old towns on rocky promontories. Miravet, with fewer than eight hundred people, is the most dramatic, a cluster of ochre houses stacked up below a Templar castle built in the twelfth century, with the river curving below. The castle was one of the main strongholds of the Knights Templar in the region, and in 1308, when the order was suppressed, its defenders held out for a time against the king's army. A small flat barge, the barca de Miravet, has long carried people across the river on a cable, and the crossing is a neat way to see the village from the water.

The country around is Terres de l'Ebre, a land of olive groves, almonds, carob and the odd vineyard, with the dry limestone range of the Serra de Cavalls to the west. Ginestar and Rasquera are small villages with farms and a quiet bar, and the pace of life is slow. Cova del Pi, the cave of the pine, belongs to the shelters of this region, and in the wider area there are painted shelters of the Levantine tradition, listed by UNESCO in 1998. As with all rock art, sites are fragile and access must be arranged locally.

The riding here is gentle and varied. Roads follow the river on both banks, with long straights and the odd bend, and rise into the hills with views over the water. Traffic is light, and the wind, the cierzo or the garbi, can be strong. Summers are very hot, and the best seasons are spring and autumn. A ride down the right bank to Tortosa passes orange groves and old villages. Take care at the ferry ramp, which can be slippery.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The nearest town of any size in the data is Mont-roig del Camp, about 23 km away, and the bigger towns of Tortosa and Móra d'Ebre are the usual places to stock up. Local food includes rice dishes from the delta, grilled snails, and olive oil of high quality, as well as grilled artichokes in spring. A small glass of local wine under the castle walls is a pleasant way to wait for the evening light.
t.la saltadora abric xiv@40.4,0.1:
La Saltadora is a ravine and a rock shelter in the dry hill country of the Alt Maestrat, in the north of Castellón province, about six kilometres from Albocàsser. The name means the jumper, the leaper, and the shelter is one of dozens that carry paintings in the Levantine style: small red figures of people and animals, often archers and hunters, painted on the limestone walls by people who lived here long before the Romans. Together with other sites across Spain's eastern side, these paintings are protected as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, a UNESCO listing from 1998. I cannot tell you which figure sits where on this particular wall, and many of the images are faded, so go expecting to look carefully rather than to be dazzled.

The setting does most of the work. This is a country of ravines cut into pale limestone, with dry-stone terraces holding almonds and olives, scrubby holm oak, rosemary and thyme, and the smell of resin in the sun. Albocàsser, a village of about fourteen hundred people, is the closest place, with Les Coves de Vinromà and Catí not much farther. Catí is known for its goat's cheese, and the Maestrat as a whole was once the domain of the Templars and later the Order of Montesa, which explains the number of fortified hilltops.

The roads leading in are narrow, twisting and sometimes rough. Corners come tight and often blind, and surfaces are patched, with gravel at the edges. Traffic is almost nothing, which is a blessing, but the cattle and tractors around Albocàsser appear without warning. The best time is spring, when almond blossom fades into green, or autumn; summers are hot and dry.

Do not count on fuel in the small villages. Fill the tank before leaving the coast, in Alcalà de Xivert or a bigger place, and carry water. The last stretch to the shelter is usually on foot, so wear boots you can walk in.
t.la saltadora abric xiii@40.4,0.1:
Albocàsser belongs to a stretch of upland that history keeps passing through. The Maestrat, the Master's country, takes its name from the military orders that ran it after the Christian conquest of the thirteenth century, first the Templars and then, after their suppression, the new Order of Montesa. Fortified hilltops like Culla and Cervera dot the horizon, and the villages are built tight and defensive, with stone houses and old arcades. At this shelter, in the ravine known as La Saltadora, you are reaching back much further than that, to the people who painted red hunters on the rock.

These are Levantine paintings, listed with others across eastern Spain as UNESCO World Heritage. They are typically small figures, often a few centimetres tall, and sometimes lively: archers in motion, animals running, groups apparently in step. Time and weather have faded most of them. I cannot tell you which image is on which wall here, so take a torch and patience, and look for the colour of old brick against paler stone.

The landscape in between is a surprise to many riders who expect the Mediterranean to be all beaches. This is a high plateau cut by ravines, with almond and olive terraces, patches of pine and oak, and fields of cereals that turn gold in June. In the distance, rows of wind turbines sit along the ridges, which gives the Maestrat a slightly modern, windswept look. The wind is real, and it can make a bike twitchy on open crests.

The roads are narrow, twisty and almost empty, with decent surfaces on the main links and rougher ones in between. Distances look short on a map but take time. Albocàsser has about fourteen hundred people and a few bars, while Les Coves de Vinromà, a little larger, is the safer bet for supplies. For a big fuel stop, plan on Alcalà de Xivert or one of the towns nearer the coast. If you are here in spring, the almond blossom is long gone, but the smell of wild herbs is at its best, and the air is wonderfully clear.
t.cingle de l ermita abric iv@40.4,0.1:
Cingle means a band of cliff in Valencian, and the Cingle de l'Ermità is exactly that: a rim of pale limestone above a ravine in the dry highlands around Albocàsser, with a hermitage somewhere in its name and its history. The shelter here, Abric IV, is one of a cluster along the cliff, painted in the Levantine style that UNESCO protects as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. These were made by hunting peoples who used the overhangs as a canvas, and the paintings are small and mostly red. I cannot tell you which figure is on which wall, so go as someone prepared to look for a long time.

Cliffs like this are good places for wildlife. Griffon vultures are common in the Maestrat and ride the thermals along the rim in the middle of the day, and you may spot smaller raptors, ravens and, if you are lucky, a Spanish ibex higher in the hills. The cliff itself is warm to the touch in the afternoon sun, and the ground below is scented with thyme, rosemary and juniper. In late spring wild flowers fill the gaps in the rock.

The nearest village is Albocàsser, under six kilometres away and with fewer than fourteen hundred people. Catí, a little farther, has its Gothic stone houses and a long reputation for goat's cheese, and you should try some if a shop is open. Les Coves de Vinromà is the bigger place nearby, and Alcalà de Xivert, in the plain, is where I would aim for a proper fuel stop and a large meal.

The ride in is narrow and quiet. Bends are tight, sometimes blind, with patchy surfaces and loose gravel where tractors cross. In the middle of the day, the heat reflects off the limestone, so ride early or late, and bring water. Spring and autumn are lovely, with clear air and long views toward the sea on good days. Mist can fill the ravines in winter and make the road greasy for the first hours.
t.abric d ermites vii@40.6,0.5:
Ulldecona is a country town of about six thousand people in the far south of Catalonia, close to the border with Valencia, with a long reputation for olive oil, and the rock shelters in the hills above it, known as the Abrics de l'Ermita after the hermitage of La Pietat on the slopes, are among the most rewarding painted sites in the region. Abric d'Ermites VII is one of the series, and carries Levantine painting like its neighbours, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Iberian Mediterranean basin. The other shelters in the group are more famous, but this one rewards a patient eye.

The setting is the Serra de Godall, a low range of limestone ridges and pine forests between the plain of the Ebro delta to the east and the highlands of the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit to the south and west. The ridge views are among the best in the area, taking in olive groves in the valley, the sea beyond, and in clear weather the distant hump of the Ports. A pleasant mix of rosemary, thyme and wild lavender grows underfoot, and the air smells of resin on warm afternoons.

This is good riding country. From Ulldecona, quiet roads climb in easy bends through olive terraces and pine woods, with enough elevation to give open views and enough corners to keep you busy. Surfaces are generally decent, with a few rough patches after rain, and there is little traffic. Take care on blind corners, where farm vehicles can appear. Spring and autumn are best, and midday heat in summer is considerable.

Fuel and food are easy in Ulldecona itself, and Alcanar, on the coast, with more than ten thousand people, is another good option. Santa Bárbara, a small town to the north, also has the basics. Try the local olive oil, the small, delicate arbequina variety that is typical of Catalonia, either in a shop or as part of a lunch, and drink a lot of water before you head up to the shelters.
t.covetes del puntal abric v@40.4,0.1:
Albocàsser is a small town in the dry highlands of the Alt Maestrat, and the Covetes del Puntal, the Little Caves of the Peak, lie about six kilometres from it in the ravines of the same name. Abric V is one of at least five painted shelters that bear the name, and they all belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Nobody will hand you a leaflet explaining what is on this wall, so allow yourself to enjoy the not-knowing, and the walk.

The ravines here have a particular character. The limestone is pale and smooth, and the ground is covered by pine, juniper, holm oak and a thick undergrowth of rosemary and rockrose. In spring, flowers cover the slopes in yellow and purple, and in early summer the air is full of the buzzing of bees, which is fitting, given that honey-gathering is one of the oldest activities depicted in Spanish rock art. Dry-stone walls, field huts and old threshing floors dot the countryside, evidence of centuries of farming.

The roads to the area are narrow and winding, and many are lightly surfaced, with gravel patches and the occasional pothole. Corners tend to be blind and tight. Navigation can be tricky, since signs are sparse and phone signal may drop. A gentle pace is the right one, partly because you will want to look around, and partly because a farm vehicle or flock of sheep may appear around any bend.

Fuel is not available in the small villages, so fill up in Alcalà de Xivert on the plain, or in one of the larger towns near the coast, before heading inland. Albocàsser itself has a few bars where you can get coffee and a bocadillo, and Les Coves de Vinromà, about nine kilometres away, has more services. Take plenty of water, sun cream and a hat, particularly in summer.
t.vallbufandes i@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza sits where three rivers meet. The Segre and the Cinca flow into the Ebro here, and the town has lived by them for centuries, first as a river port and a fortress with a Gothic castle, then as a coal-mining town, with lignite dug from the hills and shipped by barge. In the 1960s, the Ebro was dammed downstream and a huge reservoir, now known as the Mar de Aragón, flooded the valley and swallowed much of the old town. Its people moved to a new town above the water, and the old streets lie under it. It is a poignant story, and locals have not forgotten it.

Vallbufandes lies about a kilometre and a half from the town, and its shelter is a painted site of the Levantine tradition, protected with other rock art of eastern Spain by UNESCO. As elsewhere, the paintings are small and fragile, so take care and keep to paths.

The landscape is surprising: a semi-desert of pale hills, dry gullies, and thyme-scented scrub, with the blue-green reservoir like an inland sea in between. Fishermen come from all over Europe for the catfish, which grow to huge sizes in these waters, and the town is known as a fishing destination. In summer it is very hot and dry, and the wind can be strong, particularly in the afternoon.

For riders, the area has an unusual charm. The roads around Mequinenza wind through the arid hills with good views over the water, and the nearby stretches along the reservoir have enough bends to make them fun. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light, though lorries use the main roads. The border between Aragón and Catalonia is close, and you may cross it without noticing.

Mequinenza has around two and a half thousand people, with fuel and food, including some excellent local fish dishes, and Fraga, about sixteen kilometres away, is a bigger town of more than fourteen thousand, with every service. Fill up in either before heading into the hills.
t.mas d en salvador abric v@40.4,0.0:
In the Maestrat, shelters are named after whoever owned the nearest farm, and Mas d'en Salvador is an example: a mas is a farmstead, and Salvador was presumably the man who worked this patch of land at some point. Abric V is one in a numbered series of painted rock shelters in the ravine near the farm, about five kilometres from Albocàsser, carrying the small red figures of the Levantine tradition that UNESCO lists among the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Such shelters have no grand frontage, just a lip of rock, a dry floor and a good view down the ravine.

The farmsteads tell their own story. For centuries, this high country lived on sheep, almonds, olives and grain, and shepherds moved their flocks along ancient drove roads between summer pastures in the hills and winter grazing near the coast. Many masos stand empty now, their stone walls crumbling and their threshing floors overgrown with thyme, but the dry-stone terraces climbing every slope are still there, a remarkable piece of human labour. Walking among them, it is easy to appreciate how little water this land offers and how hard people worked to keep what they had.

Getting here is a quiet pleasure. The lanes around Albocàsser are narrow and twisty, with surfaces that range from decent to broken, and they carry hardly any traffic. Corners are often blind. You are more likely to meet a flock of sheep than a car, and a dog will sometimes run out of a farm gate. Take it slowly, and keep your speed low on gravel. Early morning is the best time, with cool air and low light on the limestone.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people and is the only place close by, so top up the tank before you arrive. Les Coves de Vinromà and Catí are bigger options a short ride away, while Alcalà de Xivert, on the coastal plain, is the safest place for a full tank and a proper meal. Carry water and wear solid shoes for the last stretch.
t.mas del gran@41.3,1.1:
Montblanc is a walled medieval town in the Conca de Barberà, a broad basin of vineyards in inland Catalonia, and it is one of the best-looking small towns in the country. According to local legend, it is where Saint George killed the dragon, which is why Catalonia's patron saint is honoured here with a medieval week every year. The ramparts, with their towers and gates, are largely intact, and walking the streets inside is a pleasure. A few kilometres away, in the hills near Vimbodí, the Cistercian monastery of Poblet, a royal pantheon and one of the great monasteries of Europe, is on the World Heritage list and well worth a visit.

Mas del Gran and the Vall de la Coma lie in the broken country between Montblanc and Alcover, about seven kilometres from the former. The rock-art shelters here belong to the same family as the Levantine paintings farther south, protected by UNESCO. Some of the images are faint, so give your eyes time to adjust. A Roman connection in the ride, the old walls of Tarragona, reminds you that this was a Roman province long before the Middle Ages.

The landscape is a patchwork of vines, almond and olive groves, scrubby oak and pine, and the soft grey hills of the Serra de Prades and Serra de Miramar. Wine is the local business, the Conca de Barberà being a well-known zone for white varieties and for the cava industry, and the smell of fermenting grapes in autumn is one of the pleasures of the place. In May, poppies fill the field margins.

The riding is delightful. Roads between Montblanc, Alcover and the monastery wind through gentle hills, with comfortable bends, well-kept tarmac and not much traffic outside peak holiday times. In autumn the leaves of the vineyards turn red and gold. At weekends, cyclists enjoy these roads too, so keep an eye out. Wind is moderate, and the weather is generally mild, though summer afternoons can be baking.

Montblanc has about six and a half thousand people and all the services you need, including fuel and restaurants serving substantial Catalan food. Alcover, with just over four thousand, is another good option.
t.mas d en salvador abric iii@40.4,0.0:
Catí is the town people mention when they talk about goat's cheese in this part of Castellón, a small, handsome place of stone houses and arcades in the high Maestrat, and the shelter at Mas d'en Salvador, Abric III, lies about nine kilometres away to the south-west of it, near Albocàsser. It is one of a group of Levantine painted rock shelters in the same ravine, part of the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the series number is the only label it has. Do not expect signs or a ticket office.

The cheese is made from the milk of goats that graze on the same hillsides: herbs, scrub and scrawny oak. It is fresh and slightly tangy, often eaten young and sometimes cured, and it is the sort of thing you should buy from a farm shop or a market stall if you see one open. The village also has a Gothic town hall and a church with a fine bell tower, and the old centre is worth a half hour on foot, with narrow lanes and carved stone doorways.

The surrounding country is poor and beautiful, with pale limestone, dry terraces and ravines carved by the occasional storm. In winter it can be bitterly cold at this height, with frost and the odd snowfall, and in summer the heat is dry and intense. The best times for riding are spring and autumn, when the light is soft, the air clear and the hillsides green or golden.

The roads are narrow, winding and lightly used. Bends come in clusters, with short straights in between, and the surfaces are patchy, with gravel and the odd rough stretch where a ravine has washed across. Distances look short on the map, but progress is slow, which is a good reason to plan a long lunch in Catí. Catí itself has fewer than nine hundred people, so I would not count on fuel there. Les Coves de Vinromà and Albocàsser are small, too, and Alcalà de Xivert, on the plain, is the sensible place to fill up before the climb.
t.covetes del puntal abric iv@40.4,0.1:
Anyone who rides the roads around Albocàsser and Catí finds that they are among the best in the Castellón highlands: quiet, twisty and rarely used by anything bigger than a tractor. The Covetes del Puntal shelters lie about six kilometres from Albocàsser, in a ravine that holds at least five painted overhangs, and Abric IV is one of them. The paintings are in the Levantine style, small and red, and belong to the UNESCO-listed rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. A handsome museum devoted to this art stands in the village of Tírig, not far to the north, in the Valltorta ravine, and it helps put what you see into context.

Valltorta and its sister ravine Gasulla are among the best places in Spain to see Levantine art, and the Covetes del Puntal are part of the same tradition. The scenes you can find in the district include hunters with bows, deer and wild goats, and sometimes small, lively groups of people. They remind you that the land here was good hunting country, and that people have lived in these ravines for at least ten thousand years.

For the rider, the road is the thing. From Albocàsser, the CV roads climb through almond terraces and pine, with bends tight enough to make you work and wide enough to give you time to look at the views. Surfaces are patched, with gravel in the corners, and in a few places the tarmac is narrow enough that you must slow for oncoming vehicles. The wind is the main hazard on exposed crests, and it can blow across the plateau with real force. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and midday in summer is hot.

Fuel is a question to settle before the climb. Albocàsser has about fourteen hundred people, and Les Coves de Vinromà, with nearly nineteen hundred, may have a station, but Alcalà de Xivert is the safer choice. Bring water, a hat and sturdy shoes, and allow time for the walk to the shelter.
t.cingle de l ermita abric ii@40.4,0.1:
Valencian and Catalan have a way of naming places that is worth a moment. A cingle is a cliff band, an abric is a rock shelter, a racó is a corner or nook, a mas is a farmstead, a molí a mill, a font a spring. Put them together and you can read the landscape from the map: the Cingle de l'Ermità is the cliff of the hermit's chapel, and Abric II is the second of several shelters along it. It lies about six kilometres from Albocàsser, in the Alt Maestrat, and carries painted figures in the Levantine style that UNESCO protects with the rest of the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula.

The hermitage itself is a clue to the area's later history. Many of the Maestrat's high places were claimed by small chapels and hermitages, where a hermit lived and looked after the shrine, and where the neighbouring villages held a pilgrimage and picnic on a feast day. They are often at the foot of a cliff, beside a spring, and it is not by chance that the prehistoric painters chose such places too. The same cliffs and the same water have attracted people for ten thousand years.

Getting here is simple but slow. The lanes from Albocàsser are narrow, winding and sometimes rough, with plenty of blind bends, and they carry hardly any traffic. Gravel and loose stone gather in the corners, and in a few places the surface is patched with cement. Take it gently, ride in the morning when the light is clear, and expect to share the road with the odd farmer. Summer is hot, and the rock holds the heat into the evening, while winter can bring frost and fog to the ravines.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred inhabitants and a couple of bars, and Catí and Les Coves de Vinromà are not much bigger. The sensible place for fuel and a meal is Alcalà de Xivert, on the plain, about nineteen kilometres away. Bring water, sun protection and a map or downloaded route, since mobile coverage in the ravines can be patchy.
t.abric d ermites v@40.6,0.5:
The Hospitallers once held Ulldecona, the knightly order that grew out of a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem and ended up with castles all over southern Catalonia. The town still has the look of a fortified place, with a tall church, narrow lanes and the remains of a castle on the hill, and the shelter at Abric d'Ermites V lies about four and a half kilometres from it, on the slopes of the Serra de Godall, where a hermitage stands among the pines. The paintings in the Abrics de l'Ermita belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Neighbouring sites are known as Valmayor and La Fenellosa, and they appear on the same rides.

What I like about this corner of Catalonia is the nearness of the sea. From the ridge above the shelters, on a clear day, you can see the Ebro delta spread out like a map, its rice fields shining, and the long pale line of the coast beyond. The delta is one of the best birdwatching places in the Mediterranean, with flamingos, herons and thousands of waders, and the rice paddies are the base of the local cooking, including the famous rice dishes cooked with seafood and the local eels.

The riding here is a gentle mix of valley and ridge. The roads climb from Ulldecona through olive terraces and pine woods in easy bends, with open views to the south and the mountains of the Ports. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light outside August, when the coast fills with holidaymakers. The wind, called the Mestral in Catalan, blows hard from the north-west and can be a nuisance on exposed sections.

Ulldecona has more than six thousand people and all the services you need, from fuel to a decent lunch. Alcanar, a bigger town on the coast, with over ten thousand people, offers more options, and Santa Bárbara is a handy small stop on the way. Bring water for the walk to the shelter, as there is little shade on the final path, and wear boots.
t.muriecho l@42.2,0.1:
The Somontano, the land at the foot of the mountains, is the soft belt of the Huesca province, where the high Pyrenees give way to rolling hills of vines, almonds and olives, and the Sierra de Guara rises like a wall to the north. Muriecho is a hamlet in that country, and the shelter that carries its name, Muriecho L, lies about five kilometres from Alquézar. It holds painting in the Levantine style, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it with El Remosillo and Mascún V, other shelters in the canyons of the Guara.

The Guara is superb wildlife country. It is one of the best places in Spain for vultures, and griffon vultures drift over the canyons in numbers, often at eye level from the road, along with rarer species such as the bearded vulture, the lammergeier, reintroduced to the Pyrenees. The limestone is cut into sheer gorges by the Vero, the Alcanadre and their tributaries, and the walls are warm and golden in the late afternoon.

For riders, the combination of valley and mountain is excellent. Roads from Barbastro climb through vineyards and olive groves into the foothills, with long, easy bends that tighten as they enter the canyons, and views that open without warning over a gorge. Surfaces are generally good, but narrow, and some of the minor roads are patched with gravel or rough in places. Traffic is light, though weekend canyoners and walkers can crowd the car parks in summer. The best times are spring, with green hills and clear air, and early autumn, when the vines turn red.

Alquézar, with just over three hundred people, is a popular tourist village and has bars and a couple of small shops, but the nearest sizeable town is Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, with nearly seventeen thousand people and fuel in plenty. Barbastro is also the capital of the Somontano wine region, and a glass of the local red or a plate of ternasco, the regional lamb, is a good reward for a day in the saddle. Bring water, since the hills are dry and hot in summer.
t.vinamala i@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar is the village everyone photographs in the Sierra de Guara, a cluster of golden-stone houses on a rocky spur above the Vero river, crowned by a collegiate church that began life as a castle. The Muslim rulers of Barbastro built a fortress here, and in the eleventh century, King Sancho Ramírez of Aragón captured it and turned it into a base for the reconquest of the plain below. The church that now stands on the site, with its Romanesque and later Gothic features, preserves some of the old walls, and the view from the terrace across the canyon is worth the climb.

The shelter at Viñamala I lies about four and a half kilometres from the village, in the same country, and carries painting of the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Another painted site on the ride, the Cueva de los Moros, takes its name from the Moors, a label that Spanish folk memory often attaches to anything old and mysterious. The paintings are far older than any Moor, of course, by several thousand years.

Below the village, the Vero river runs through a spectacular canyon, with a path of wooden walkways bolted to the cliffs, which is a popular walk. Swimming pools in the gorge are cold and bright green, and in summer, canyoners and families fill them. The surrounding hills are grey with holm oak and scrub, and honey from the area, flavoured with rosemary and thyme, is sold in the village shops.

Riding to Alquézar from Barbastro is a pleasure, a road of easy curves through olive groves and low hills, then a few tighter bends as it approaches the canyon. Tarmac is good, but narrow, and weekend traffic of cars and cyclists can slow you. Aim to arrive early, to find parking and beat the crowds. In summer the heat is fierce.

Alquézar has about three hundred people and no reliable fuel, so tank up in Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, which has a good range of shops and cafes. The village has several restaurants with terraces, where you can try the local lamb and the Somontano wines.
t.cova gran del puntal@40.4,0.1:
A cova gran is a big cave, and in the limestone of the Alt Maestrat that is an easy thing to find. This whole upland is karst, pale rock that rain has been dissolving for millions of years, leaving ravines, sinkholes, springs that vanish underground and a good number of overhangs deep enough to sleep under. The Cova Gran del Puntal sits about six kilometres from Albocàsser in the ravine that the rides call the Barranco Hondo, the deep one, and it belongs to the family of Levantine rock-art shelters that UNESCO has listed across eastern Spain. Paintings of this kind sit in shallow recesses rather than in the dark depths of a cave, so do not expect Altamira. Expect a modest rock wall, a lot of faded red, and a very good view down the gully.

Caves in this country are not just prehistoric. Shepherds have sheltered in them for centuries, kept goats in them, and in lean times hidden grain in them. Some have walls of stacked stone built across the mouth, turning a hollow into a pen. You can sometimes see where soot has blackened the ceiling. In the evening, swifts and bats use the same cracks, and the air smells of warm stone and wild herbs.

Reaching the area on a motorbike is a matter of patience. The lanes out of Albocàsser are narrow and sinuous, twisting between almond and olive terraces, with short climbs and drops, blind corners, and a patched surface that often carries gravel. The rewards are the views across the ravine and the near-total lack of traffic. A walking path leads the final stretch, and in dry weather it is easy enough, though loose stones demand some care.

Albocàsser has under fourteen hundred people and is the nearest settlement, with Les Coves de Vinromà and Catí a short way beyond. None of them is large enough for me to promise fuel at a convenient hour, so fill the tank at Alcalà de Xivert, down on the coastal plain, before climbing. Late spring and early autumn bring the best weather, clear and mild. In midsummer the stone throws back the heat, and a cave mouth in the shade is the best place to be at noon.
t.mas d en salvador abric iv@40.4,0.0:
If you want to understand what the ground cover is like in the hills behind Albocàsser, crouch down and smell it. Thyme is the loudest note, then rosemary, then something resinous from the juniper and the pines, with a dry mineral edge from the sun-baked limestone. In late April and May this country is a rock garden: rockrose with its crinkled white and pink flowers, yellow broom, wild lavender, tiny orchids in the shadier folds, and the grey-green sprawl of kermes oak, whose spiny leaves nobody enjoys brushing against. Abric IV at Mas d'en Salvador sits in the middle of all this, about five kilometres from the village, one in a numbered series of rock shelters that carry Levantine paintings of the kind UNESCO protects across eastern Spain.

The paintings themselves are modest, small red figures that have faded with time, and the people who made them knew this vegetation intimately. They gathered plants, hunted what ate them and followed the water. I find it helpful to think of the shelter less as a gallery than as a kitchen table, a dry, sunny place with a view in which a family could spend a day.

The ride suits that thought. Lanes lead out of Albocàsser between dry-stone walls, rising and dropping through small folds in the land, with surfaces that go from newly laid to cracked and gravelly within a kilometre. Bends are tight and often blind. Because the ground is open, you can see a long way, and if you stop and switch off the engine, you can hear sheep bells and, at dusk, the endless trill of crickets. Farm tracks branch off in every direction, and phone signal can fade, so a downloaded map is wise.

The nearest village, Albocàsser, has fewer than fourteen hundred inhabitants and I would not rely on a petrol pump. Catí and Les Coves de Vinromà are also small. Alcalà de Xivert, near the coast, is a town of more than six thousand and the dependable place to fill up. Wear long trousers for the walk if you can, because the scrub scratches, and in warm months keep an eye out for the odd snake sunning itself on the path.
t.bco de la plana i@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza sits where the Segre and the Cinca join the Ebro, and the Barranco de la Plana, a dry gully less than a kilometre from the town, is one of the painted shelters scattered through the hills above them. The ride that includes it also touches Roca Roja, the Red Rock, and another shelter of the Abrics d'Ermites group far to the south, which shows how far these rock-art routes range. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO along with the rest of the Mediterranean rock art of Spain, and in this semi-arid corner of Aragón, where there is little to shelter a painted wall from the weather, what survives is a small miracle.

The land around has been rewritten twice in living memory. First came coal: lignite was mined in the hills around Mequinenza, and for decades it was loaded on barges and floated down the Ebro. Then came the dam at Ribarroja, in the 1960s, whose reservoir drowned the old town and forced its families uphill into a new one. The town's best-known writer, Jesús Moncada, made that lost world the subject of his novels, and if you want to feel what the place was like, his name is the one to look for in a bookshop. The reservoir, the Mar de Aragón, now fills the valley with a long ribbon of blue-green water, an odd and rather beautiful sight in a landscape of pale rock and thyme.

Fish are the draw for many visitors, and the catfish of the Ebro are famous among anglers. For riders, the draw is the road. It twists above the water, with long sightlines and few cars, and it passes through a country that looks more like North Africa than the green Spain of postcards. The tarmac is good, and the bends are well cambered. Wind is common, especially in the afternoon, and the sun is strong enough to make a visor tint a good idea in every season but winter.

Mequinenza has about two and a half thousand people and enough services for fuel and a meal. Fraga, about sixteen kilometres away, is bigger, with more than fourteen thousand people, and has everything. Seròs and Fayón, on the Catalan and Aragonese sides of the border, are small but useful for a coffee and a rest on the way.
t.la saltadora abric xii@40.4,0.1:
Weather is the thing nobody mentions about the Maestrat, and it matters. At seven hundred metres or more above sea level, the plateau around Albocàsser has a climate quite unlike the coast thirty kilometres away. Summers are hot and dry, though evenings cool quickly. Winters can be properly cold, with frost, fog in the ravines and the occasional snowfall, and Penyagolosa, to the north-west, is often white. In spring, sea air pushes inland and brings low cloud, and the whole upland can vanish into mist for a morning. The best riding months are late April, May, and then September and October, when the air is clear.

La Saltadora is a ravine about six kilometres from Albocàsser, and Abric XII is one of the numbered painted shelters there. Its paintings belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride includes another shelter at the Arenal de la Fonseca. The people who made these pictures lived through the great climate swings at the end of the last ice age, and the warming that followed, and you can easily imagine the hunters watching the weather as carefully as any modern farmer.

When fog or rain settles in, the roads here become more serious. Limestone dust turns to slick paste, gravel gathers in corners, and the narrow lanes through the terraces offer little room for error. In dry weather they are delightful, but consider a day with low cloud a day for the coast road. Wind is a regular factor, and on exposed crests it can blow hard enough to move a bike.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people and no promise of fuel, so fill up at Alcalà de Xivert, a town of about six thousand six hundred on the plain, before you climb. Les Coves de Vinromà, a little larger than Albocàsser, may help in an emergency. Bring a rain jacket even in sunshine, and a warm layer in spring and autumn, when the temperature at altitude can drop quickly after sunset.
t.mas d en josep abric li@40.4,0.1:
Rock art is easy to walk past. The paintings in the Maestrat shelters are small, usually a hand's breadth to a forearm's length, painted in a red that has faded to the colour of dried blood or brick, and often covered by a film of mineral crust or a scatter of lichen. The trick is to stop, let your eyes adjust, and look slowly, not for pictures but for shapes: a line that is too regular for a crack, a blob that has a head and legs, a slender figure with a bow. Raking light helps, so mid-morning or late afternoon is better than noon, and a torch held at a low angle can reveal what the sun hides. At Mas d'en Josep, Abric II, about six kilometres from Albocàsser, that patience is the whole game.

The shelter is one of a numbered group, part of the Levantine rock art that UNESCO has protected as a single World Heritage listing across eastern Spain. Another site on the same ride, the Arenal de la Fonseca, has a name that sounds like a beach, and in a way it is: arenal means sandy ground, and the pale sandstone ledges do crumble into grit. Never touch the paintings or wet them to make them clearer. It has been done, and it does damage.

The country around is a lovely mixture of terraced slopes and ravines. Almond and olive trees stand in rows on stone steps built by farmers over centuries, and between them grow thyme, rosemary and tufts of grass. In spring, poppies and yellow daisies fill the margins, and in autumn, the carob trees drop their long, dark pods. Sheep graze in the open spaces, with a dog and a shepherd somewhere near.

The lanes to the shelter are narrow and quiet. Bends are tight, and the surface changes from decent asphalt to rough patches in a few hundred metres. Gravel is common. On a motorbike, a relaxed pace is the right one, and you will have time to enjoy the view across the ravines. Fuel is not available in the villages, so fill up at Alcalà de Xivert, about sixteen kilometres away, or at one of the towns on the coast. Albocàsser itself has a couple of bars, and Les Coves de Vinromà has a few more services.
t.abric d ermites iv o cova fosca@40.6,0.5:
The Sénia is a modest river, but it matters: it marks the boundary between Catalonia and the Valencian Community along the south of Tarragona province, and it runs close to Ulldecona, the town about four and a half kilometres from this shelter. People on both banks speak Catalan, or the Valencian variety of it, and the old territory of the Sénia, with its olive groves and stone farmhouses, feels like one place with a line drawn through it. Abric d'Ermites IV, which the rides also call the Cova Fosca, the Dark Cave, is one of the painted shelters of the Abrics de l'Ermita, on the slopes of the Serra de Godall. The paintings belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. A neighbouring site on the ride is the Roca dels Moros, the Moors' Rock, a name used in several places for old painted walls.

It is a good example of how a place can be strange and ordinary at once. The hillside is a mix of olive terraces, pine woods and low scrub, with a small hermitage among the trees, and from the shelter you can see the plain stretching towards the sea. The painted figures, small and faded, are remnants of hunters who may have had just that view while waiting for deer.

The roads in this corner are a pleasure to ride. From Ulldecona, they curl up into the hills through olive groves in bends of every size, and the surfaces are generally good, with the odd patch of loose stone. Traffic is light apart from August. The Mestral, a cold dry north-westerly, can blow hard through the valleys, and in winter makes the hills feel bleak.

Ulldecona has more than six thousand people and the services that go with it: fuel, bakeries and bars. Alcanar, a coastal town of more than ten thousand, is another option, as is Santa Bárbara, a smaller place to the north. The coast, with its beaches, is only a short ride away if you want a swim after your walk. Carry water and wear sturdy shoes for the final ascent, because the path is stony and exposed to the sun.
t.abric d ermites ii@40.6,0.5:
The Sénia country has some of the oldest olive trees in Europe. Around Ulldecona and the neighbouring villages, a few specimens are said to be a thousand years old or more, with trunks twisted into great, hollow knots and crowns that still bear fruit. Nobody can say exactly how old, since olive wood rots from the middle, but the trees are a proud local asset, and visitors are sometimes taken to see them. The shelter at Abric d'Ermites II lies on the slopes of the Serra de Godall, about four kilometres from Ulldecona, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. A second site on the ride, Valmayor V, adds a taste of the wider district.

The oil from these groves is excellent, golden and slightly peppery, made mostly from the small arbequina olive. You can buy it at local cooperatives and farm shops, and it makes a heavy but worthwhile souvenir. Locals eat it with bread and salt for breakfast, and drizzle it on everything else. Almonds, carobs and figs grow among the olives, and the whole slope smells of resin and warm earth.

It makes sense that the painters chose this area. The valley has water, game and sheltered ledges, and the slope faces south, catching the winter sun. The shelter is a modest hollow in the rock, with a view over the olive terraces and the plain, and it would have made a fine lookout.

The roads from Ulldecona climb in easy bends through olive groves, then through pine woods to the hermitage, and they are some of the pleasantest in the area, with decent tarmac and not much traffic. Take care in autumn, when harvest vehicles and fallen leaves can make corners slippery. The Mestral wind, from the north-west, blows strongly in winter, and in summer the heat is intense by midday, so go early.

Ulldecona, with more than six thousand people, has everything you need, including fuel. Alcanar, on the coast, is bigger, and Santa Bárbara, to the north, is smaller but adequate. Bring water for the walk, because the last stretch is open and sunny, and consider a cap.
t.la saltadora abric vi@40.4,0.1:
Peníscola is a rock that sticks out into the Mediterranean about twenty kilometres from here, topped by a Templar castle, and it is the one place on this stretch of coast that every visitor knows. The castle later gave refuge to Pedro de Luna, Pope Benedict XIII, who refused to give up the papacy after the Western Schism and lived out his years here, earning the nickname Papa Luna. His coat of arms and the story of his stubbornness are all over the town, which is now a busy summer resort. The shelter at La Saltadora, Abric VI, is a world away from that. It lies in the dry hills above Albocàsser, about six and a half kilometres from the village, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with another site, the Racó de Nando.

That contrast makes a good day. In the morning you can ride the quiet lanes through the ravines, walk to a shelter, and eat bread and cheese on a rock, and by evening you can be on the seafront at Peníscola, eating a plate of rice with fish and watching the castle floodlit. It is only forty kilometres or so, but it feels like moving between centuries.

The hills have a harsh, dry beauty. Limestone terraces of almond and olive, pale cliffs, thyme and rosemary, and the occasional wild fig growing from a crack. Late spring is lovely, and so is autumn, while midsummer heat is intense and the rock radiates it into the evening.

The lanes out of Albocàsser are narrow, twisty and patchy, with tight bends and gravel, and traffic is hardly a factor. A slow pace pays off here. At weekends, you may meet cyclists, and in spring and autumn, hunters' vehicles. Albocàsser itself has fewer than fourteen hundred people and no promise of fuel. Alcalà de Xivert, about sixteen kilometres away, is the town to rely on, with over six thousand people and several stations. Carry water, and wear shoes you can walk in over rough ground.
t.les aparets i@41.9,1.0:
Artesa de Segre lies in the broad valley where the Noguera Pallaresa comes out of the Pre-Pyrenees, a market town of about three and a half thousand people with the long wall of the Montsec range blocking the northern horizon. The country is the Catalan interior in its most characteristic form, with wheat and barley on the flats, almond and olive on the lower slopes, and pine and oak where the hills become steep. Les Aparets, about five kilometres out, is one of the rock shelters of the region, and the rides tie it with the Cova dels Vilars, sometimes spelled Vilasos, and the Cova del Cogulló. These belong to the cluster of Levantine painted sites that reach into Catalonia, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. Further west in the same province lies the famous Roca dels Moros at El Cogul, with its scene of dancing women, which gives you a sense of how widespread the tradition once was.

It is a country of dramatic water engineering. A little way downstream, at Camarasa, a dam across the Noguera Pallaresa, built early in the twentieth century, holds back a long reservoir of deep green water in a narrow gorge, and the road beside it is one of the prettiest short rides in Lleida province. The old villages of the district, with names like Cubells, cling to hilltops, their church towers visible for miles.

The riding is relaxed. Quiet roads cross the valley in long, easy bends and climb the lower slopes with views over fields and the grey wall of the Montsec. Surfaces are generally good, with some rough patches on the minor lanes. In summer, the heat is intense and the afternoons are very still, so early morning is best. Winter brings thick fog to the valley, and ice on the higher roads.

Artesa de Segre has fuel and food, and Agramunt, about sixteen kilometres away, is bigger, with over five thousand people, and famous across Catalonia for torró, the nougat of almonds and honey that is made and sold in its shops. It is a fine place to buy something to take home. Cubells and Camarasa are small, so do not rely on them for a pump.
t.l arc@40.4,0.1:
L'Arc means the arch, and it is one of those place names that makes you look up. In the limestone of the Maestrat, weathering has worked on the rock for millions of years, carving ledges, hollows, pinnacles and now and then a natural arch or bridge where a thin wall has been eaten through. I cannot promise what this one looks like, but the name suggests a landmark that local people noticed and kept. The shelter lies about six kilometres from Albocàsser, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with the Arenal de la Fonseca, a sandy ledge where the rock crumbles to grit.

The limestone is the key to the place. It was laid down on the floor of an ancient sea, and if you look closely at the rock, you can sometimes find fossil shells, small spirals and fragments of coral. Rain then dissolved it, slowly, creating the ravines and caves that run through the country. Water is rare on the surface, but it moves underground and comes out in springs, which is why the old farms and villages are located where they are.

The roads around Albocàsser suit anyone who likes empty lanes. They are narrow, twisty and lightly surfaced, rising and dropping between almond and olive terraces, with views across the ravines to the pale hills beyond. Bends are tight, and gravel gathers at the edges. Mid-morning, when the sun is high enough to light the rock but the heat has not yet built, is the best moment, and spring and autumn the best seasons.

Fuel needs a plan. Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people, and neither Catí nor Les Coves de Vinromà is large enough to promise a pump. Alcalà de Xivert, on the plain, about eighteen kilometres away, is the town to rely on, with over six thousand people. Benassal and Culla, to the west, are small villages with a bar or two. Bring water, sun protection and a hat.
t.covetes del puntal abric i@40.4,0.1:
Food in the Maestrat is mountain food: filling, simple and made with whatever the land gives. Lamb and kid from the local flocks, roasted or stewed with potatoes and herbs, take the place of fish. Cured sausages, ham and cecina, dried and salted meat, hang in the farm shops. Olive oil, bread, almonds, cheese from Catí, and honey fill the larder, and in the colder months, you can find thick stews and bean dishes made with pork. Wine is local, strong and unpretentious. If you ride here, plan to eat well and slowly, and do not be in a hurry.

The Covetes del Puntal, the Little Caves of the Peak, are about six kilometres from Albocàsser, and Abric I is the first of a numbered series of painted shelters in the ravine. They belong to the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links this site with the Arenal de la Fonseca. After the walk, an appetite is guaranteed.

The country is dry and beautiful, a plateau of pale limestone with terraces of almond and olive, ravines full of pine and scrub, and the smell of thyme everywhere. The silence is notable. Outside the villages, the only sounds are birdsong, the wind, and the occasional sheep bell.

The roads are slow, twisty and quiet. Bends are tight, surfaces vary, and gravel is common, so a moderate pace is the sensible one. You will not need to worry about traffic, though you may meet a tractor or a flock of sheep on a blind corner. In summer, the heat is intense by midday, and in winter, there may be frost and fog in the ravines.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred inhabitants and a bar or two, and Catí is about the same. Les Coves de Vinromà is a bit larger. None is guaranteed to have fuel, so fill up in Alcalà de Xivert, a town of over six thousand people, before climbing. Bring water, and pick up bread and cheese for a picnic.
t.abric d ermites ix@40.6,0.5:
At the southern edge of Catalonia, the mountains known as the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit rise from the plain like a wall, and they are among the wildest in the region. Rocky ridges, deep gorges and thick pine forest cover them, and they are the home of the Spanish ibex, a wild goat with long curved horns, which was nearly wiped out in the twentieth century and has made a comeback here. A lucky rider may see one on a crag. The shelter at Abric d'Ermites IX is on the lower slopes of the nearby Serra de Godall, about four and a half kilometres from Ulldecona, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with Valmayor V.

The painters would have known the same goats, or their ancestors, and the shelter may have been a hunter's lookout. From the rock, the view stretches across olive groves to the plain, and on a clear day to the glint of the sea. The air is scented with rosemary, thyme and pine, and cicadas fill the afternoon with sound.

The ride in is a good one. From Ulldecona, a narrow road climbs through olive terraces and pine woods in easy bends, with views opening at every turn. The surface is generally decent, though gravel and leaves gather at the edges, and traffic is light. A short walk from the road leads to the shelter, and the path is stony, so sturdy shoes are a good idea. The wind, the Mestral, can blow hard, and the heat in summer is substantial.

Ulldecona has over six thousand people and everything you need, including fuel. Santa Bárbara, with about three and a half thousand, and Masdenverge, with just over a thousand, are smaller but useful for a coffee. Alcanar, with more than ten thousand, is the big town nearby. Bring plenty of water, and wear a hat in the sun.
t.covetes del puntal abric iii@40.4,0.1:
The name Levantine art is slightly misleading, because the style is not found on the coast. It takes its name from the Spanish Levante, the Mediterranean side of the peninsula, but the painted shelters sit inland, in the ravines and sierras of the interior, in an arc running from the Pyrenean foothills of Lleida down through Aragón, the Maestrat, Albacete and Murcia, to the mountains of Almería. Hundreds of sites are known, and every few years someone finds another. The people who painted them were hunter-gatherers and early farmers, and the style, with its small, lively, red or black human figures and animals, is quite different from the great bison of the Ice Age caves in the north.

The Covetes del Puntal, the Little Caves of the Peak, lie in the ravines about six kilometres from Albocàsser, and Abric III is one of a numbered series. It belongs to the group protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride ties it to Racó de Nando, Nando's Corner, a site named for a local man. Dating the paintings is still argued over, and nobody can say for certain when each was made, but the span runs over several thousand years.

For the visitor, the practical matters are modest. The last stretch is on foot, along a path that may be steep and loose, and shade is scarce. A hat, sturdy shoes, water and some patience are all you need. In spring, the slopes are rich with flowers, and in autumn the light is clear and gold. Summer is hot, and the middle of the day is best avoided.

The lanes out of Albocàsser are narrow and quiet, with bends that tighten without warning and a surface that varies from fresh tarmac to broken edges. Take it slowly. You will probably be alone, and the silence is memorable.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people and the only certain thing is a coffee. For fuel, fill up at Alcalà de Xivert, on the coastal plain, before heading inland. Les Coves de Vinromà and Catí are small, but have bars and a few shops. Carry water in all seasons.
t.cueva de regacens@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar takes its name from the Arabic for the fortress, al-qasr, and the name fits: a hill of honey-coloured rock above the Vero, crowned by a castle and a church, with a tangle of arcaded lanes tumbling down below. The Cueva de Regacens lies about eight hundred metres from the village, a shelter in the limestone that carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. It is one of the closest sites to a village of any on these rides, which makes it an easy and pleasant walk, though the paintings are small and faded.

The village sits on the edge of the Sierra de Guara natural park, a wild limestone range that rises behind it, cut by canyons. Olive trees surround the village, and the local oil, golden and fruity, is sold in the shops. Almond groves, vines and box hedges fill the foothills, and the air smells of wild herbs. Griffon vultures glide over the rim of the gorge, and in the evening, swifts scream around the church tower.

The collegiate church, built on the site of the Muslim fortress after the Christian conquest in the late eleventh century, was rebuilt over centuries, and the Romanesque cloister is a beautiful, quiet space. The lanes below are narrow and steep, paved with stone and lined with houses that lean against each other. It is a lovely place to walk, and early morning or late afternoon, when the tour buses are gone, is best.

The ride from Barbastro is a delight, climbing gently through vineyards and olive groves and then twisting into the gorge. Surfaces are good, but the road is narrow, and traffic can be heavy at weekends in summer, with coaches and canyoners' vans. Park at the entrance to the village, since the lanes are closed to most traffic.

Alquézar has only about three hundred people, so fuel is at Barbastro, about seventeen kilometres away, a town of nearly seventeen thousand with plenty of stations and good restaurants. Salas Altas, to the south, is tiny. Bring water for the walk, since summer heat in the gorge can be intense.
t.abric d ermites v exterior@40.6,0.5:
The Montsià is a small, rocky massif that rises abruptly above the Ebro delta, the last real mountain before the river dissolves into rice paddies and lagoons, and the hills around Ulldecona are its northern neighbours. From their ridges you can look across the flat delta to the sea, a view that changes from silver in the morning to gold in the evening. Abric d'Ermites V exterior lies about four and a half kilometres from Ulldecona, on the slopes of the Serra de Godall, and carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain. The ride links it with Valcomuna, a site name that sounds like a village meeting place.

The word exterior in the title marks a painted panel on an open rock face rather than in a deep recess, which means the paintings have had to survive the weather. It is a good reminder of how fragile this heritage is. Rain, sun, lichen and the occasional vandal all take their toll, and the figures have faded over thousands of years. Look, photograph if allowed, and leave nothing.

The country has a gentle Mediterranean beauty: olive terraces, carob trees, scrub of rosemary and thyme, and woods of Aleppo pine. In spring, the ground is bright with flowers, and in autumn, farmers bring in the olives, with nets spread under the trees. The delta itself, a short ride away, is a paradise for birdwatchers, with flamingos, herons and many other species, and for anyone who enjoys a plate of rice cooked with seafood.

The roads from Ulldecona are a pleasant mix of straight and twisty, with easy bends through the olive groves and a few tighter ones as they climb. Surfaces are generally good, with the odd rough patch. Traffic is light except in August. The Mestral, the strong north-westerly, can be a nuisance, especially on exposed ridges.

Ulldecona, with more than six thousand people, has all the services you need, including fuel. Alcanar, a bigger coastal town of over ten thousand, and Santa Bárbara, a smaller one, are alternatives. Bring water for the walk.
t.eglesia de sant climent@42.5,0.8:
The Vall de Boí is a deep valley in the Catalan Pyrenees, and its tiny villages hold a remarkable collection of Romanesque churches from the early twelfth century, tall, plain and beautifully proportioned, with slender bell towers. UNESCO listed nine of them in 2000, and Sant Climent de Taüll is the finest. The church, with its six-storey Lombard-style tower, stands on a slope above the village, and its interior was once decorated with a great painting of Christ in Majesty, the Pantocrator, in strong red, blue and ochre. The original apse painting was removed in the early twentieth century and now hangs in the National Art Museum of Catalonia in Barcelona, while a faithful copy fills the church. The building was consecrated in 1123.

The valley itself is a landscape of steep green slopes and stone villages with slate roofs, below the high peaks of the Aigüestortes National Park, a place of granite, lakes and torrents. The air is clear and smells of pine and cut hay, and in autumn the larches turn gold.

For riders, the ride up the valley from the main road is a pleasure. It follows the Noguera de Tor, winding up through the villages with a mix of tight bends and easy curves, and a good surface. Take care in winter, when snow and ice are common, and the weather can turn quickly at any season. Traffic can be heavy in July and August, with coaches and campers, so aim to arrive early. Parking is available at the village edges, and the church is a short walk.

Taüll is small, and the nearest places with certain fuel are El Pont de Suert, on the main road to the south, or Vielha, a mountain town of over five thousand people on the far side of the Vielha tunnel, about twenty-one kilometres away. Sort, with just over two thousand people, is another option. Bring a warm layer even in summer, as the evenings are cool.
t.mas d en salvador abric ii@40.4,0.0:
Dusk is the best time on these lanes, and also the time to be careful. As the heat leaves the plateau around Albocàsser, the animals come out: rabbits darting across the tarmac, red-legged partridges whirring from the verge, and in the half-light, the occasional wild boar crossing from one bit of scrub to another. Foxes trot along the road edge, and owls hunt from the walls. A bike at dusk needs a slow pace and sharp eyes. The reward is the colour: the limestone goes from white to gold to rose, the sky turns violet, and the scent of thyme rises from the warm ground.

Mas d'en Salvador, Abric II, is about five kilometres from the village, and its painted shelter, in the Levantine tradition protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, is best visited in daylight, of course. The ride links it with the Cueva de Mas del Abogat, which suggests that a lawyer, an abogado, once owned or farmed the land. Both sites are small and have no facilities.

If you are in this country late in the day, the lights of the villages show far across the valleys, and the dark is real. There is very little light pollution, and the stars come out thick. Take a torch, and tell someone where you are going. Phone signal drops out in the ravines, so a downloaded map is wise, and a thin jacket is useful for the evening chill, even in summer.

The roads are narrow, winding and quiet, with gravel and patchy tarmac, and many corners are blind. Aim to be back on the main road before full dark, since farm tracks branch off at unexpected places and there is little signposting. In winter, ice and fog can form quickly on the plateau.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people and may not have fuel on hand. Alcalà de Xivert, about nineteen kilometres away, is the reliable place for a tank and a meal. Catí and Les Coves de Vinromà are smaller and quieter.
t.cingle de l ermita abric i@40.4,0.1:
In 2018, UNESCO added the art of dry stone walling to its list of the intangible heritage of humanity, a joint listing by Spain and several other countries. Anyone who has ridden the lanes around Albocàsser will understand why. Every slope is stepped with terraces, every field is edged with a wall, and the walls, built without a speck of mortar, have stood for centuries. Small huts with corbelled roofs, called barraques in Valencian, shelter farmers from sun and rain. It is a vast, unsigned work of art, made by thousands of people over hundreds of years, and the hillsides would wash away without it.

The Cingle de l'Ermità, the cliff of the hermitage, rises above the ravine about six kilometres from the village. Abric I, the first of a numbered series, carries painting in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it to the Abric de la Tenalla. The painters used the same rock that the farmers later used for their walls, and the cliff face is a source of the stone.

Look closely at a wall, and you will see how it is made. The large stones form the base and face, smaller ones fill the gaps, and the top is capped with flat slabs. Lizards sun themselves in the crevices, and snails cling to the shady side. Almond and olive trees grow on the terraces, and wild thyme and rosemary seed themselves in the cracks.

The lanes through the terraces are narrow and twisting, with tight bends and a patchwork surface. Gravel gathers at the edges, and walls sometimes rise right to the edge of the road, which makes blind corners worse. A gentle pace suits the setting, and you will see more.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people, and fuel is best taken at Alcalà de Xivert, nineteen kilometres away. Catí, smaller, has a good cheese shop, and Les Coves de Vinromà has a few more services. Carry water.
t.la saltadora abric ix@40.4,0.1:
The first Levantine paintings were found by chance, in the first years of the twentieth century, by shepherds, hunters and local amateurs who noticed red marks on a rock wall and told someone who might care. Archaeologists were sceptical at first. Some thought the figures too lively and natural to be prehistoric, and the debate went on for decades, with the French scholar Henri Breuil, who had studied the great painted caves of the north, playing a leading role in making the case for their antiquity. Today, the paintings are accepted as the work of hunter-gatherer and early farming peoples, and the argument has moved to the question of exactly when.

La Saltadora, a ravine about six and a half kilometres from Albocàsser, holds a number of these painted shelters, and Abric IX is one of them. It carries paintings in the Levantine tradition, protected by UNESCO as part of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin in Spain, and the ride links it with the Racó de Nando. The pictures are small, and many are faded, but they reward the patient eye.

It is worth remembering that each shelter was first found by someone on foot, and that the best way to see them is the same. The paths are rough, the signs few, and the sense of finding the place yourself is part of the pleasure. Take your time, go quietly, and look at the whole landscape, not just the wall, because the choice of site was part of the meaning.

The lanes from Albocàsser are narrow, twisty and patchy, with tight bends and gravel. Traffic is almost nil, though you may meet a farmer on a tractor. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and mild temperatures. Summer is hot and dry, and winter can bring frost and fog.

Albocàsser has fewer than fourteen hundred people and no guarantee of fuel, so fill up at Alcalà de Xivert, about sixteen kilometres away. Les Coves de Vinromà and Catí have bars and a few shops. Carry water and wear sturdy shoes.
t.abric d ermites iiia@40.6,0.5:
Ulldecona sits at the southern edge of Catalonia, in the Montsià district, where the Ebro delta flattens out to the east and the Serra de Godall rises in a blunt wall behind the town. The Abric d'Ermites IIIa is one of a group of rock shelters in the hills here, painted in the Levantine style and part of the UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Mediterranean basin. The paintings are red, simple and old, showing hunters and animals, and the group in this range is well regarded for the quality of the figures that survive.

The shelters are reached on foot, and the sites are managed locally. There is a visitors' route and an interpretation point in the area, but opening times and booking arrangements change, so check before you set off. In the meantime the Serra de Godall is a reward on its own, with rocky ridges, pine, rosemary and the sort of limestone that holds heat all afternoon.

Getting in is not difficult. The roads between Ulldecona and the hills are narrow, lightly used and lined with olive terraces. Olives are the money crop here, and the oil from the Terres de l'Ebre has a protected name. Expect gentle climbs, a few tight bends near the sanctuary and the sort of surface that has seen too many farm tractors. Ulldecona has around six thousand people, with fuel, a bakery and bars where a small coffee is the standard opener. The village of Santa Bàrbara, a little to the south, is smaller but handy.

The season matters. In July and August the heat is serious and the Mistral can swing across the delta in winter, making the coastal roads cold and blustery. Spring is the sweet spot, with wildflowers in the scrub and cool mornings. In autumn, when the olive harvest begins, the roads fill with small trucks and the smell of crushed fruit drifts from the mills. A half-day here, with a walk and a lunch of rice and seafood from the delta, is a very good way to spend a weekend.
t.abric d ermites viii@40.6,0.5:
There is a lot of rock in the hills behind Ulldecona, and a lot of shelter in it. Abric d'Ermites VIII is another of the painted overhangs in the same range as its neighbours, a short stretch of cliff where people thousands of years ago left red figures of animals and hunters on the stone. It belongs to the Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO, a style found along Spain's eastern side from Catalonia down to Andalusia, and it is a close neighbour of other numbered shelters here.

Do not set your watch by the coordinates. They point to the area and not to a signpost, and the shelter is a walk from where you leave the bike. Spend a few minutes studying the surrounding rock before you go looking, because the paintings are small and the overhangs are many.

What makes the afternoon worthwhile is the country. This is the edge of the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit mountains, where Catalonia meets Valencia and Aragon, a rugged range with some of the best twisty roads in the region. Wild goats live up in the rocks, and eagles ride the thermals above the ridges. The tarmac in the foothills is narrow but mostly well kept, with a succession of bends that suit a middle gear and a patient hand. In the valleys below, almond and olive trees stand in rows on stone terraces that have been farmed since Roman times and probably earlier.

Fuel in Ulldecona, about six thousand people, is easy. Santa Bàrbara, to the south, has fewer services but is on the way. If you are planning a longer day, remember that the villages up in the mountains tend to close early, and some have no pump at all. Fill up before you leave the plain.

Late April and May are the best months, when the hillsides are green and flowers crowd the verges. September is also a good bet, with warm days and crisp mornings. In the middle of winter, the high ground can ice over, and the coast road catches the wind off the sea. A flask of something hot and a windproof layer will do more than any amount of kit.
t.cingle de l ermita abric iii@40.4,0.1:
The Maestrat is a high, empty, wrinkled country in the north of Castellón province, and Cingle de l'Ermità is a cliff in the heart of it. A cingle is a rock band, a stratum of limestone that outcrops along a hillside like a belt. The shelter here, listed as Abric III, is one of a handful on this cliff, and carries Levantine paintings in the red pigment that gives the style its look. The nearest villages are small. Albocàsser has about fourteen hundred people, Catí under nine hundred, and neither is the place for anything beyond a coffee and a bottle of water.

Catí is famous in the region for its goat's cheese, which has a protected name, and the cheese shops on the main street are a good reason to stop. The route up to the shelter is on foot and the cliffs are impressive in the right light, with ochre and grey walls above a dry streambed.

Alcalà de Xivert, with a little over six thousand people, is the larger town that has fuel. It lies down towards the coast, near the Serra d'Irta, a rough natural park of coastal mountains. If your ride leaves it late, fill up there before heading for the interior, since pumps in the Maestrat are rare and distances are longer than the map suggests.

The roads are the real draw. From Albocàsser and Catí the tarmac climbs and drops through terraced olive groves and holm oak, with more corners per kilometre than a rider can count. Surfaces are variable, good on the main roads and rough where winter water has found a way in. Traffic is almost absent midweek. The wind is a factor on exposed ridges, and fog can sit in the valleys on cold mornings.

Spring and autumn are the seasons to come. The Maestrat's history, from the Knights Templar and then the order of Montesa who ran this country in the Middle Ages to the Carlist wars of the nineteenth century, is written in the stone farmhouses and fortified villages. It is a place where a half-day detour turns into a whole day easily.
t.eglesia de santa maria@42.5,0.9:
Taüll is a mountain village at roughly fifteen hundred metres in the Vall de Boí, one of the high Pyrenean valleys in Catalonia, and the church of Santa Maria is one of nine Romanesque churches here that UNESCO lists together. It was consecrated in the early twelfth century, and its square tower rises beside a plain stone nave in the way that many valley churches do, with Lombard bands along the walls. Inside, the apse paintings that made the valley famous are, in the main, copies: the originals were moved in the 1920s to the museum in Barcelona. The reproductions, projected and painted in place, give you the sense of the original even so.

The road in is part of the pleasure. From Vielha, with five thousand people and the only reliable fuel for a long way, you pass through the long Vielha tunnel and drop over the other side towards El Pont de Suert, then turn up into the valley. The final climb to Taüll is steep and tight, with hairpins up through fir and meadow, and the village arrives at the end of a last steep rise. It is quiet outside the ski season, and parking is limited, so take it slowly.

The valley sits next to the Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park, the only national park in Catalonia, a landscape of granite peaks, glacial lakes and streams. Even without hiking, the setting is dramatic, with snow on the summits well into early summer. The village has a few cafes and bars and the kind of stone houses with slate roofs that suit the weather.

Come between late May and October for the best chance of dry roads. The valley can be cold, and snow arrives early and leaves late, which means the upper road is not for winter riding. If you are staying the night, the cold clear air and the astonishing stars are a fair reward for the hours in the saddle.
t.eglesia de sant joan de boi@42.5,0.8:
Boí is the lowest and quietest of the Romanesque villages in this Pyrenean valley, and its church of Sant Joan stands among old stone houses a little above the road. It is one of the nine churches in the Vall de Boí listed by UNESCO, and unlike the better-known Taüll it has a quieter, more domestic feel. The nave is plain, the tower is square and slim, and a porch along the side gives the building the look of a country chapel rather than a monument. Painted decoration survives inside, including scenes on the walls, though much of what you see is a careful reproduction while the original fragments are kept in museums in Barcelona and Lleida.

The valley road is the thing to enjoy. From Vielha, the main town of the Val d'Aran with a little over five thousand people, you ride through the long tunnel and out onto the southern side of the range, then follow the Noguera de Tor river down to the junction at Barruera. The last section into Boí is narrow, slowly climbing, with a few blind bends and occasional shreds of gravel from spring rock falls. The scenery tightens up as you go, with steep meadows, fir woods and, behind the village, a wall of granite peaks marking the edge of the national park of Aigüestortes.

Fuel is the practical issue. There is nothing in Boí itself and little in the neighbouring villages, so fill the tank at Vielha or at El Pont de Suert, which sits lower down at the valley mouth. Cafes in the valley tend to cater to walkers and skiers, and they open early and close early.

The valley is cold and often wet in winter and early spring, and snow can linger in the upper section. The best riding months run from June to October, with September offering clear light and a hint of autumn colour in the beech and birch. Thunderstorms build over the peaks on hot afternoons in July, so plan to be down in the valley before they break.
t.la saltadora abric vii@40.4,0.1:
La Saltadora is a painted shelter in the wild hills of the Castellón interior, near Albocàsser, in a landscape of ravines and stone terraces. It carries the number VII in the series of shelters in the area, and its paintings belong to the Levantine tradition: hunters, archers and animals, painted in red a very long time ago and now protected as part of the UNESCO listing of the rock art of the Mediterranean basin. The name, meaning the jumper, suggests a leaping figure, a deer or a goat, but you will have to judge for yourself once you are standing in front of it.

Do not expect to ride straight up to the shelter. The approach is on foot and the site is a protected one, so respect the paths and any fencing. A short walk in the quiet of the ravine, with pines creaking overhead and cicadas in the heat, is already a good reason to be here.

Albocàsser, with fourteen hundred inhabitants, is the nearest village, and Cuevas de Vinromà, a bit larger at nearly two thousand, lies to the south. Neither is a refuelling stop. Alcalà de Xivert, with around six and a half thousand people, is the place to count on for a petrol station, and it is about sixteen kilometres away as the crow flies, rather more by road.
