Plan accordingly.

The roads here are ideal for a day in the country. They run between orchards of almond and olive, over low passes, and along the sides of dry valleys where limestone cliffs stand like fortress walls. The corners are mostly open and flowing, with a few tighter ones near the villages, and you should expect gravel and the odd goat. The Maestrat is not busy, and a Tuesday morning in April will leave you with whole kilometres to yourself.

The heat of high summer is hard on riders and walkers, so aim for spring or autumn. Autumn brings a gentle sun and the first mushrooms in the woods.
t.bco de campells i@41.4,0.3:
The Ebro runs a long way to reach the sea, and at Mequinenza it was blocked, drowned and then reborn as a reservoir. Bco. de Campells, the ravine that shares the shelter's name, lies in the dry hills near this town in the Aragonese Bajo Cinca, where the Segre, the Cinca and the Ebro all come together in the same area. The shelter is one of the painted rock sites of the Mediterranean basin, with red figures in the Levantine style, and the setting is the sort of arid, sun-baked limestone country that gives the paintings their lasting quality.

Mequinenza has an unusual story. Coal was mined here for generations, and the town was largely rebuilt in the 1960s when the Ribarroja dam flooded the old centre. The new streets sit above the water, and the castle still looks down on the confluence of the rivers. The reservoir, now known as the Sea of Aragon, is famous with anglers who come for the giant catfish, and it has made the town a minor destination for water sports.

For the ride, the roads that wind between Mequinenza, Fraga and the small villages of the area are among the quieter in Aragon. Expect long, gentle curves along the reservoir, then climbs into scrubby hills of rosemary, juniper and pine, with occasional dust on the tarmac. Fraga, with over fourteen thousand people, is the big town for fuel, food and a bed. Mequinenza and Serós are smaller, but you can usually find coffee and a bocadillo in the bars along the main street. In summer the heat in this part of Aragon is extreme, and the wind can be strong across the open plateaus.

Spring brings green wheat and red poppies, autumn gives lovely light over the reservoir, and winter is cold but dry. Avoid midday in summer.

The shelter itself is reached on foot, and as with all rock art sites it is best to ask locally about access. The bike will be quite happy sitting at the roadside for an hour.
t.coves del civil o ribasals abric i@40.4,:
Coves del Civil, also known as Ribasals, is one of the great concentrations of Levantine rock art in the Valltorta gorge area of Castellón province, and the number I beside its name marks the first shelter in the series. The Valltorta, a deep dry ravine running through limestone near the village of Tírig, was one of the first places where scholars recognised that this painting tradition existed, and a museum in Tírig tells how the paintings came to light. The paintings show archers, hunting scenes and animals, with a vividness that surprises anyone who expects scratchy marks on a wall.

The access to the shelters is regulated. The museum in Tírig is the place to start, and guided visits take you into the ravine, so be ready to ask what is open and when, since arrangements change from season to season. The coordinates here lead to the general area of the ravine, not to a car park at the door.

The ride is a delight. From Albocàsser, with about fourteen hundred people, or from Catí, the roads wind through the Maestrat, an upland of olive, almond, holm oak and terraced slopes dotted with abandoned farmhouses. The bends come thick and steady, with few straights, and the tarmac is mostly good with occasional poor stretches. In the villages the streets tighten abruptly, so keep an eye out for parked cars and delivery vans. Alcalà de Xivert, about nineteen kilometres away, is the town to rely on for fuel and a full meal.

In summer the heat is fierce and the air in the ravine is still. Spring and autumn are much better, and in October there are mushrooms under the pines and a smell of damp earth after rain. Early mornings can be foggy on the valley floor, and the light on the cliffs in the late afternoon is warm and golden.

Wear boots rather than motorcycle shoes if you plan to walk, because the paths are stony.
t.cova de rull@40.4,0.1:
Cova de Rull sits in the same dry country as its neighbours in the northern Valencian interior, in the hills around Albocàsser, and it carries a different feeling from the great ravine galleries. A cova is a cave, and this one is a modest opening in the rock with painted figures that belong to the Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO. Archers, animals and signs are rendered in the red pigment that the style is known for, and what survives gives a hint of how many more once decorated the cliffs of this region.

You will not find a ticket office. The shelter is on a hillside, reached on foot, and the exact route depends on local guidance and the current state of the paths. Take the coordinates as a guide to the area and not a destination.

Riding to this part of Castellón is a pleasure for anyone who likes quiet, winding roads. The surface is mostly good, the bends are frequent but not savage, and the gradients are gentle enough that you can enjoy the views of limestone cliffs and small villages tucked into folds of the hills. In spring the verges are full of wild orchids and rosemary flowers, and in autumn the hunters' trucks are about early in the morning, so ride carefully near the field edges. Albocàsser and Catí are the two nearest villages, both small, with a bar or two. Alcalà de Xivert, a larger town at about eighteen kilometres, has fuel and supermarkets.

Weather in the Maestrat is changeable. The mountains behind the coast catch moisture in winter and the temperature can drop fast, so a layer in the top box is sensible. In summer the heat is dry and relentless, and the rock face can burn bare skin. Late April and early October are the best times, with soft light and few other visitors.

If you have time, add a stop in Catí for the goat's cheese and a long lunch.
t.abric d ermites iiib@40.6,0.5:
The ridge behind Ulldecona has a name for each of its overhangs. Abric d'Ermites IIIb is a neighbour of the IIIa shelter, a twin in the numbering and a few paces away in the rock, and its paintings tell the same story in a slightly different voice. The red figures belong to the Levantine tradition, and the group in this part of Catalonia is part of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean basin art.

I would not try to find it without help. The shelters in the Serra de Godall are small, tucked behind rocks and scrub, and the local interpretation of the area is the best way to learn where they are and how to see them without harming them. Ask in Ulldecona, where people take pride in what lies on their doorstep.

The town itself has about six thousand inhabitants and is a good place for a break. There is a castle on a hill, an old centre of narrow streets and a church that dominates the main square. Fuel is easy to find, and the bars along the main road serve robust food: rice dishes, grilled meat, local olives and strong coffee. Santa Bàrbara, a smaller town to the south, sits on the road to the coast and has a few services too.

The ride between the town and the hills is a good one, if slow. The roads are narrow and winding, with olive groves on both sides and the occasional old stone farmhouse. In the foothills the road rises through pine and rosemary, with sudden views of the plain and the sea beyond. A short distance to the east, the Ebro delta, one of the great wetlands of the Mediterranean, is flat and full of birds, and a sharp contrast to the rugged ground behind.

Weather is generally kind, but the cold wind that sometimes blows down from the north in winter can be harsh. Spring is the best time, with flowers in the grass and thin white clouds. Midsummer is very hot, and the stone of the shelters warms up quickly.
t.covetes del puntal abric ii@40.4,0.1:
A shelter called Covetes del Puntal sits in the limestone country of the northern Valencian interior, in the hills between Albocàsser and Cuevas de Vinromà. A coveta is a little cave, and this one is the second shelter, Abric II, in a series of painted sites. Its paintings are in the Levantine style, with the small red figures that make the art of the region so recognisable, and they are part of the UNESCO listing for the rock art of the Mediterranean basin.

Cuevas de Vinromà, with just under two thousand people, takes its name from the caves around it, and sits on the road that links the coast with the interior. The town has a handful of bars and a quiet main street, and the land around is a patchwork of almond, olive and carob. The Serra d'Irta, a coastal range of wild hills, lies to the east, and the Desert de les Palmes rises farther south, giving the area a grand backdrop.

For fuel and a proper meal, make for Alcalà de Xivert, about sixteen kilometres away, with a little over six thousand people. The old town has a castle on a hill, and the beaches at Alcossebre, nearby, are quiet outside the summer.

The roads are a joy. They link tiny villages across high ground, with a lot of bends and sudden dips into dry riverbeds. The surfaces are mostly good, and the traffic is light, apart from the occasional tractor. If you ride in spring the verges are full of flowers, and the smell of wild fennel and rosemary is strong. In autumn, the almond harvest brings men with nets and ladders into the groves. Fog sometimes settles on the high plateau at dawn, and when it lifts the views are extraordinary.

Summer is hot and bright, so keep to the early and late hours. The shelter is reached on foot, and the sites are protected, so ask locally about access and take water.
t.episcopal city of albi@43.9,2.1:
Albi is built of brick, which is unusual in the south of France, and the colour changes through the day, from salmon in the morning to a deep red at dusk. The great cathedral of Sainte-Cécile dominates the old town, and from a distance it looks more like a fortress than a church, with a massive tower and walls that have no windows at the bottom. It was begun in the late thirteenth century, soon after the crusade against the Cathars had been won, and its builders wanted the faithful, and the heretics, to see where power lay. Inside, the painted vault and a huge fresco of the Last Judgement are astonishing. The whole episcopal city, with the old bridge and the bishop's palace, was listed by UNESCO in 2010.

The palace, called the Berbie, now houses a museum devoted to Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was born in Albi and left his entire studio output to his home town. The collection is the largest in the world, and the garden below the palace overlooks the Tarn river.

For a rider, the setting is lovely. The Tarn flows below the town, spanned by an old bridge that dates from the eleventh century, and the roads along the river run through vineyards towards Gaillac, a wine town with an old tradition. In the other direction, the roads climb into a rolling country of fields and woods, with villages perched on cliffs, like Cordes-sur-Ciel. Corners are gentle and the surfaces are generally good, making it an easy area for a day of leisurely riding. Traffic builds up in the town in the evenings and on market days.

Albi has over fifty thousand inhabitants, so fuel, hotels and parking are not a problem. A cassoulet is the local dish, though it is more suited to winter than to a warm afternoon, and the pink garlic of Lautrec is a regional product worth buying. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with warm light and quieter roads. In July and August the heat can be fierce, and the town's brick walls give it back long after sunset.
t.the causses and the cevennes@44.2,3.5:
Most visitors to the Cévennes come for the gorges, but the real character of this country lies on top of them. The causses are high limestone plateaus, treeless and wind-scoured, where sheep have grazed for millennia and the horizon runs on for fifty kilometres. Cut deep into them are the gorges of the Tarn and the Jonte, with their cliffs and caves, and to the east the Cévennes mountains rise in ridges of schist and chestnut forest. The whole area is listed by UNESCO as a cultural landscape of Mediterranean agriculture and pastoralism, and much of it falls within the Cévennes National Park, set up in 1970.

Meyrueis, with a little over a thousand inhabitants, lies in a green cleft at the meeting of the Jonte and the Béthuzon. It is a pleasant base, with cafes in the square and fuel, if not much more. Florac is the other nearby town, with just under two thousand people, on the edge of the Tarn gorge. Mende, the biggest town in the area at nearly fifteen thousand, lies a good thirty kilometres away and is the better bet for a bigger shop or garage.

The roads are some of the best in France. The Corniche des Cévennes follows a ridge high above the valleys, with views for miles and a long sequence of bends. Along the gorges the road narrows, with overhanging rock, tunnels and pull-outs that suit a short stop. On the plateaus, the bends are wide and the straights long, and the wind can be strong. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for loose gravel and sheep. In summer the gorges are busy with kayakers and sightseers, and the most popular sections are slow.

Griffon vultures, reintroduced in the 1970s, are common over the gorges and are easy to watch from the roadside. The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson walked through here in 1878 with a donkey called Modestine, and the trail he followed is now a popular long-distance path.

Spring and autumn are best. Summer is hot on the plateaus but pleasant in the gorges, and winter brings snow and ice to the high ground, which can close roads without warning.
t.sivil@42.2,0.0:
Sivil is one of those names you will not find on a signpost, and that is rather the point. It belongs to the dry, folded country of the Somontano in northern Aragon, where the last foothills of the Pyrenees run out into the Ebro basin. The labels attached to it speak of a Moorish cave and a tobacco cave, which tells you the real subject: shelters in the limestone where people painted animals and hunters thousands of years ago, part of the Mediterranean rock art that UNESCO lists as a single family of sites. I would not promise you a spot to park beside any particular overhang, and most of these shelters are guarded by their own fragility, so treat the coordinates as a doorway into the area rather than a door.

The area itself is the reward. The Sierra de Guara rises just north, cut by the Vero and its tributaries into gorges that canyoneers come from all over Europe to descend. Alquézar, the nearest village at under nine kilometres, sits on a rock above the river with a collegiate church tucked inside the walls of an old Moorish fortress, and it is the sort of place where you will want to leave the bike at the edge and walk the stepped lanes. Barbastro, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the real town here, with some seventeen thousand people, fuel at any hour you will need it, and the cathedral and wine houses that give the Somontano its name.

On two wheels this is quiet, broken country. The roads are narrow and tarmac is patchy once you leave the main routes, with tight bends between almond and olive terraces and sudden dry-stone walls. Gravel washes onto the road after storms, so go gently on the descents. Summer is hot enough to make midday riding a chore; spring and early autumn, when the stone glows orange in late light, are far better. Look up as you ride, because griffon vultures ride the thermals over the gorges and you will often see a dozen at once.

For food, think of the local reds and whites, which have a respectable reputation, and of the grilled lamb and borage-and-potato dishes that Aragonese kitchens do well. Water is easy to find in the villages, but carry some between them. Fill the tank in Barbastro before you wander in, since the hamlets around Sivil are small and the next station can be a long way.
t.ainsa@42.4,0.1:
Aínsa sits on a hilltop above the meeting of two Pyrenean rivers, the Cinca and the Ara, and the old village on top is one of those places where the medieval layout has simply been left to get on with itself. You enter through a gate into a great sloping square of rough cobbles surrounded by stone arcades, with a castle and a Romanesque church on the high side and views out over the valley. It was once the capital of the little Kingdom of Sobrarbe, whose rulers, according to legend, rallied here against the Moors, and the town still stages a spectacular festival recalling that story every few years.

Today it is a small place, with a couple of thousand residents, and the arcaded square is filled with restaurants, craft shops and terraces in summer. Local food is hearty mountain Aragonese: grilled lamb, cured ham, mushrooms, and cheese, with the strong red wines of Somontano close by. The castle houses a museum of local history, and the church bell tower makes a good viewpoint. In the evening, when the day-trippers drift away, the square has an easy, lamp-lit calm.

The surrounding landscape is spectacular. To the north rise the high Pyrenees, including the Monte Perdido massif and the canyons of Ordesa, one of Spain's oldest national parks. To the south the land drops away into dry, folded hills and reservoirs with the unlikely turquoise of Mediano. Griffon vultures circle on the thermals and, with luck, the bearded vulture too, the bone-eating bird with a metre-and-a-half wingspan that makes the Pyrenees its stronghold. The sky here is often clear and the light is hard and bright.

For a motorcyclist, the road is the N-260, the Eje Pirenaico, a long east-west route that follows the grain of the mountains and crosses a series of passes and gorges. It is a twisting, demanding road, with plenty of hairpins and rock walls, and the surface is variable, with patches of gravel and occasional rockfall, so concentrate. Summer afternoons can be hot, and thunderstorms are possible in the mountains. Aínsa has the usual services for a small town, including fuel and shops, but supplies thin out in the valleys beyond, so top up here. Boltaña, a few kilometres south, has a few more services.
t.barcelona@41.4,2.2:
Start with the grid. Barcelona's Eixample, the nineteenth-century extension designed by Ildefons Cerdà, is a field of identical square blocks with the corners cut off, so that every junction becomes a small octagonal plaza. It was meant to be egalitarian and airy, and for a rider it is wonderfully legible: you can always work out where you are, and the wide avenues let a motorcycle breathe. The city also has more motorbikes and scooters than almost any other in Europe, so drivers are used to them and parking for two wheels is routine rather than a fight.

Gaudí's buildings are scattered among the blocks, with the Sagrada Família still under construction after more than a century, and the Casa Batlló and La Pedrera on the Passeig de Gràcia. Beyond them the old Gothic quarter holds the Roman foundations of the city, and Montjuïc, the hill over the harbour, gives you a view across the container ships to the sea. The traffic is dense, so take your time, watch for tram tracks and wet paint on pedestrian crossings, which are slick when it rains.

Getting out is the real skill. The Ronda de Dalt and Ronda Litoral are fast ring roads that can jam badly at rush hour, and it is best to leave before eight in the morning or after ten. Once through, the hills of Collserola, the large natural park behind the city, offer twisting roads and long views. Further out the Montseny and the Garraf coast give proper riding, with hairpins, cork oak and the smell of pine and dry herbs.

Fuel is everywhere. Eat late: the city does lunch at two and dinner at nine or ten. For a quick coffee stop, any neighbourhood bar will do, with a cortado and a small pastry at a counter. The ride that starts here heads for a prehistoric rock shelter inland, a good reminder that this coast was inhabited long before the Romans arrived.
t.pyrenees n 260 weekend photo pull off@41:
The pin falls on the coast south-west of Barcelona, between Cunit and Cubelles, on the sandy shore that marks the beginning of the Costa Daurada, and the Pyrenees named on the ride are a long way off to the north. Here the sea is warm and shallow, the beaches are wide and the railway line runs along the sand, so trains flash past between your bike and the water. Cunit and Cubelles are family seaside towns, a bit scruffy and a lot friendlier than the resorts to the south, and the old fishing quarters keep their small grids of whitewashed houses a couple of streets behind the promenade.

The land behind is the Penedès, a country of low hills, vines and stone farmhouses, and it is the home of cava, the Catalan sparkling wine. Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, in the hills about twenty-five kilometres inland, is its capital, and the first bottles of cava made in the traditional method are credited to Josep Raventós, who produced them in 1872. Cellars there still welcome visitors for tastings. North-east, the limestone Garraf massif drops steeply to the sea in a wild, scrubby landscape of dwarf palms and rosemary, with a dramatic coastal road, the C-31, climbing in tight curves above the water toward Sitges and Barcelona.

The riding choices are good. The old coastal road, the N-340, is often slow and busy with trucks and local traffic, while the toll motorway, the C-32, runs fast and direct and is expensive in summer. A better option is to turn inland on the side roads that wind through the vineyards between small villages, where the corners are gentle, the surface is decent and the views over the vine rows to Montserrat's serrated skyline are excellent. Summer afternoons can be fiercely hot, so start early, and the road is often busy with beach traffic at weekends.

Cunit, a town of about twelve thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and Cubelles is only a few kilometres away with more of the same. Vilanova i la Geltrú, just up the coast, is a larger town with a good fishing port and a famous seafood market. Try a plate of fideuà, the noodle cousin of paella, with a glass of cold local white wine, preferably on a terrace with a sea breeze, and finish with a coffee.
t.priorat vineyard curves@42.0,2.0:
The coordinates fall in the Lluçanès, a quiet plateau of farmland and low oak woods north of Vic and east of Berga, near the villages of Olost and Oristà, and it is a world away from the terraced slate hills of Priorat. This is the green, rolling heart of inland Catalonia, a landscape of masies, the big stone farmhouses with their barns and walled yards, scattered between fields of barley, pasture and patches of woodland. The land is gentle but constantly moving, and the roads rise and fall along ridges, with the dark line of the Pyrenees and the pale, jagged wall of the Cadí range on the northern horizon.

The Lluçanès was long a poor, remote area, and its people lived from livestock and pigs. That heritage survives in the food: this is cured meat country, with butifarra sausages, fuet, llonganissa and the excellent cured hams of nearby Vic, and in a village restaurant you can expect a plate of grilled sausage and white beans, or a stew of pork and mushrooms in autumn. Romanesque chapels, with their simple stone arches and slender bell towers, stand in the fields and village centres. Berga, the nearest big town, is the site of the Patum, a festival at Corpus Christi that was recognised by UNESCO in 2005, in which giants, devils and dragons dance through the streets amid fire and gunpowder.

The riding is good rather than famous. The roads here are narrow and quiet, with gentle bends over the rolling hills, long views and little traffic, and the surface is generally sound, though it can be patched and sandy at the edges. Tractors and cyclists are the main hazards, and mist often fills the hollows on autumn mornings, which can leave damp tarmac for hours. Winter nights bring frost, and snow occasionally falls on the plateau. Spring is lovely, with green barley and red poppies, and autumn brings the smell of woodsmoke and fallen leaves.

There are few services in the villages, though most have a bar and a small shop that open for mornings and early evenings. Fuel is available in Prats de Lluçanès and in Berga, which has about seventeen thousand people and fuller services, and in Vic, a bit further south. Carry cash for small bars, and if you can, take lunch at a village restaurant, because the portions are generous and the prices honest. Layers are wise in the morning, since the plateau is cooler than the coast.
t.costa brava and tossa de mar@41.4,1.6:
The pin sits in the hills of the Alt Penedès, near Mediona and Sant Joan de Mediona, which is a long way from the sea at Tossa, and it is a country of vines, almond trees and pine woods in the folds of the Catalan pre-coastal range. The land is dry, aromatic and sunbaked, with red-brown soil, pale limestone and the scent of rosemary and thyme, and the villages are old stone clusters on low hills, many with a ruined castle above. Mediona's castle, on a ridge above the valley, has been a landmark since the Middle Ages, and the small reservoir of Foix, a short distance to the south, brings a touch of blue to the landscape.

The wine here is the draw. The Penedès has been a wine region for two thousand years, and cava, the sparkling wine, is made in many of the cellars around, while the still whites from the local varieties, Xarel·lo, Macabeo and Parellada, are crisp and fruity. A short distance north, Capellades, a town of just over five thousand people, has a more unusual speciality, paper. Its mills, powered by the Anoia river, were making handmade paper from the eighteenth century, and the old Molí Paperer is now a museum where you can see paper being made by hand. Montserrat, the great serrated mountain with its Benedictine monastery, rises to the north-east, visible from many of the ridges.

The riding is a pleasant mix of quiet country lanes and mountain curves. Roads wind between vineyards and through pine forests, with gentle bends, short steep climbs and long views, and there is little traffic during the week. The surface is generally good, but sandy patches and gravel are common where tractors have crossed, and in autumn, harvest vehicles can appear around any corner. The summer heat is intense, so aim for early starts and an afternoon rest. Spring is green and cool, and autumn is warm, with golden vine leaves.

There is fuel at Capellades and in the larger towns along the main roads, such as Igualada to the north, though the small villages rarely have pumps, so plan your fills. Many villages have a bar that serves a cheap, filling menu del día at lunchtime, with a starter, main course, dessert and wine, and a siesta follows. Barcelona is about an hour away, so it is also a good place for a half-day escape from the city, with the sea breeze as a reward in the evening.
t.tibidabo dawn short loop photo pull off@:
The coordinates lie in the Congost valley, near the villages of Aiguafreda and Figaró, about fifty kilometres north-east of Barcelona, and this is not Tibidabo at all but a very different Catalonia. It is the green, wooded foothills of the Montseny massif, which was declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 1978. The valley of the Congost river is narrow and steep-sided, with beech and holm oak forests on the slopes and small stone villages along the water, and the climate is cooler and damper than the coast. In the mornings, mist lingers in the valley and the whole place smells of wet leaves and woodsmoke.

Figaró-Montmany is the village at the heart of it, a dignified place with an old railway station, a few old industrial buildings and a lively Sunday market. A little to the north, in a gorge cut by the Riera de Tenes, stands the hermitage of Sant Miquel del Fai, a sanctuary built into a cliff face, with a waterfall dropping some twenty metres beside it, and a series of caves and a pool. The monastery was founded in the early Middle Ages, and the setting is wonderfully dramatic. Montseny itself rises behind, with the highest summit, Turó de l'Home, reaching 1,706 metres, and a mountain road, the BV-5114, goes to Santa Fe, a high plateau of beechwood and mountain pastures.

The riding here is excellent and underrated. The old road along the Congost winds in gentle, tree-shaded curves, and the climbs into the Montseny are tight and steep, with hairpins, damp patches and falling leaves. Traffic is low on weekdays, but at weekends the roads fill with cyclists and day-trippers from Barcelona, so take care on blind corners. The main practical advice is to ride early, to catch the soft morning light and avoid the crowds, and to dress in layers, since mist and cool air are common even in summer.

There is fuel in nearby Centelles, a town of about six and a half thousand people, and larger towns like Granollers and Vic have everything else. The village bars serve strong coffee and tortilla, and at lunch, local restaurants offer rabbit, mushroom dishes and the fat white sausages that Catalans love. Autumn is a wonderful time, with the beechwoods gold and orange and chestnuts roasting in villages.
t.pyrenees n 260@41.5,2.5:
The Maresme is the strip of coast that runs north-east from Barcelona, and the pin falls in the hills above it, inland from Mataró. The sea is a few kilometres away, with its flat line of beach towns along the old coastal road, while here the ground rises into the Serralada de Marina, a ridge covered in pine and holm oak, with villas and vineyards scattered on its slopes. The label points to the Pyrenees and the N-260, the long road along the foot of the mountains, so this is the sea-level ending to a ride that spent its days in the high country.

Mataró, the biggest town nearby, has more than a hundred thousand people and a place in railway history. In 1848 the first railway on the Spanish peninsula opened between Barcelona and Mataró, and the line still runs along the shore. The town has a handsome old centre, a market, and a long beach promenade. Smaller towns such as Vilassar de Mar and Sant Andreu de Llavaneres are quieter, with whitewashed houses and a Catalan seaside charm. Further inland, the region around Alella produces wine, and the vineyards on the slopes behind the coast have been tended for centuries.

The roads through the hills are good for an evening ride. Narrow lanes climb through the forest with tight bends and views over the Mediterranean, and in the early evening the light turns the sea gold. Surfaces are mostly smooth, though cyclists use these roads in large numbers, particularly at weekends. Summer heat can be fierce, and fires are a risk in dry years, so heed warnings. Spring and autumn are more pleasant.

Fuel, food and rooms are plentiful along the coast, with Mataró offering everything. Local tapas and a plate of grilled sardines with a glass of cold white wine are the perfect way to end the day. Traffic on the coastal road, and on the motorway to Barcelona, can be heavy at rush hour.
t.costa brava@41.5,2.4:
A few minutes from the sea but already in the hills, Argentona and Cabrils are two of the pleasantest places on the Maresme. They lie in the folds of the Serralada Litoral, a low ridge of pine and cork oak behind the coast north-east of Barcelona, and their stone houses, old farmhouses and modernist villas speak of a time when wealthy Barcelona families built their summer homes here. The hills catch cooler air than the city, and the smell of pine resin hangs in the warm afternoons.

The Maresme has long been Barcelona's market garden, and the sunny slopes grow flowers, strawberries and vegetables, sold across the region. Argentona, a town of about twelve thousand, has a compact old centre with a church, a fountain and a few cafes, and Cabrils is smaller and quieter. A little further on, tiny Òrrius has barely three hundred people. All of them are good places to stop for a coffee and a pastry in the shade, and the ride between them is a gentle tour of narrow roads and small bridges.

The label talks of the Costa Brava and Tossa de Mar, about fifty kilometres to the north, where the road clings to cliffs above clear coves, and the old walled town of Tossa stands on a headland, with towers and ramparts dating from the twelfth century. After a long day along that coast, this finish in the hills is a calm one. Roads here run in smooth curves among woods and vineyards, with hairpins on the climbs and fast stretches along the ridges. Surfaces are generally good, though cyclists are numerous and gravel sometimes washes onto the bends after storms.

Fuel and food are no trouble. Argentona has stations and a handful of restaurants serving Catalan dishes such as grilled meat with calçots in season and rice with seafood. Mataró is a few minutes away if you need a mechanic. The best seasons are spring and autumn. In summer, forest fires are possible and some tracks may be closed.
t.montseny natural park@41.1,2.5:
On a map, this pin sits well out in the Mediterranean, about thirty kilometres off the Barcelona coast, which makes it a pretend fuel stop and a good moment to talk about where you actually fill up before heading for the Montseny. The massif itself rises inland to the north, about fifty kilometres from the city, and it is the highest ground in its part of Catalonia.

Montseny is a Natural Park and a UNESCO biosphere reserve, recognised in 1978, and it is unusual because it sits so close to the sea yet has three distinct climates stacked up its slopes. Cork oak and holm oak cover the lower sides, then come chestnut and beech forests, and on the highest ridges, Turó de l'Home and Les Agudes, both around seventeen hundred metres, there are heather moors and stretches of grass that see snow in winter. The beech woods in autumn go gold and copper, and are one of the best sights in the region.

For the rider, the sensible fuel stops are in the towns on the approach, such as Granollers, Sant Celoni and Arbúcies, where petrol stations are plentiful. Inside the park, villages like Santa Fe and Montseny are small and the pumps are few, so arrive with a full tank. Roads here are twisting, narrow and often shaded, with moss and damp patches on the north-facing bends, so approach each corner with a little extra care, particularly in the morning.

The massif collects cloud. Humid air from the sea rises and condenses on the slopes, so a bright morning in Barcelona can become a wet, foggy afternoon on the ridge. Pack a rain layer even if the sky looks clear at the coast, and keep a warm mid-layer, because the temperature can be ten degrees lower than at sea level. Weekend traffic includes walkers, cyclists and Barcelona day-trippers, so mornings and weekdays are quieter.

A good habit before leaving the coast is a proper breakfast, with coffee and a bocadillo, and an eye on the weather. The mountain rewards a patient rider with silence, cool air and the smell of wet leaves.
The coordinates here fall in the sea southwest of Barcelona, so there is no mountain under this pin. The label promises a high point for the Montseny ride, and it is easy enough to find the real thing a good way to the north, where the massif lifts to the Turó de l'Home at about seventeen hundred metres and the nearby Les Agudes.

Few visitors realise how much of a mountain Montseny is. It is not part of the Pyrenees but of the Catalan Coastal Range, an older, rounder set of hills of granite and slate, and it rises abruptly out of the plain. On a clear winter day the view from the top reaches over the sea toward Mallorca, so locals say, and across to the snowy Pyrenees in the other direction, although you need good air for either. A road reaches the village of Santa Fe, high up among the beeches, where there is a small reservoir and good walking, and from there a track continues toward the summits, with restrictions on traffic that you should obey.

The riding on the approaches is a pleasure. Roads such as the one from Fogars de Montclús or from Sant Celoni wind through chestnut and beech woods, with bend after bend, a steady gradient and just enough width. The tarmac tends to be reasonable, though shaded sections hold damp and leaf litter in autumn. Cyclists are common, particularly at weekends, and a few of the bends tighten more than they first appear.

The area has stories. The massif has long been a refuge, and the dense woods have served as hiding places in several wars. Stone farmhouses, called masies, dot the valleys, and old hermitages and shrines lie along the paths. In the villages around the base, you can buy local sausage, honey and chestnuts in season, and there is a long tradition of mountain cooking with game and mushrooms.

In practice, bring a full tank, a rain layer and a flask of something hot. The weather can turn without warning, and a mountain this close to the sea likes to make its own cloud.
t.montseny natural park scenic road@41.1,1:
Cunit and Cubelles, a pair of seaside towns of twelve and fourteen thousand people, lie some seventeen kilometres from this spot on the coast southwest of Barcelona. Between the two sits the hinge of the Penedès and the Tarragona coast, a flat, bright, sandy country with long beaches, a railway line running along the sand, and vineyards in the hills behind.

This is not a mountain road, and it does not pretend to be. It is a coastal run, a mix of the main road along the shore and the lanes that run inland through orchards and vines. The corners are gentle, the surface is usually good, and the view is of a calm blue sea on one side and rows of vines on the other. It is a relaxed stretch for the end of a long day, or the start of one.

A short distance away is El Vendrell, the birthplace of the cellist Pau Casals in 1876. He is remembered as both a great musician and a symbol of Catalan resistance, and a museum devoted to him stands on the beach at Sant Salvador, in the house where he lived. Casals left Spain after the Civil War and spent his later years in exile, and his performance of the Catalan folk tune El cant dels ocells became a kind of anthem.

For a rider, the pleasures are simple. The beach towns are full of cafes and seafood restaurants, and a grilled fish with a cold drink in the shade is hard to beat in summer. In July and August the coast is crowded and the road slow, and the sun heats the tarmac, so wear ventilated gear and drink plenty of water. In spring and autumn the same stretch is calm, light and warm without being hot.

Fuel is easy. Both Cunit and Cubelles have petrol stations, and the larger town of Vilanova i la Geltrú is a short ride east. If you have time, the dramatic Garraf cliffs further along the coast are worth a look, with the old railway built in the nineteenth century to carry passengers and wine.
t.montseny natural park@42.1,2.7:
Les Planes d'Hostoles, with about eighteen hundred people, and Camós, with about six hundred, sit within ten kilometres, and the larger town of Banyoles lies eleven kilometres off. This is the quiet country between Girona and Olot, where the plain of the Pla de l'Estany meets the first wooded hills of the Garrotxa. It is green, folded and much less visited than the Costa Brava a short distance east.

Banyoles is built around the biggest natural lake in Catalonia, a long, clear body of water with a promenade around it and a rowing course that served at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona. Locals swim and fish in the lake, and the old town has a handsome arcaded square. A little farther west, the Garrotxa volcanic zone preserves dozens of extinct cones, forest of beech and oak growing in the craters, and the famous fageda d'en Jordà, a beech wood that grows on a lava flow and became a favourite of Catalan poets and painters.

The food in this region is rooted in the land, and it is the reason for the stop. Expect grilled meat over embers, mushrooms in autumn, local cured sausage called fuet, and thick stews, with a plate of cold meats and tomato bread at the start of any meal. The menu del dia, a fixed-price lunch served on weekdays, is typically excellent value, with a first course, a second and dessert, and a drink included.

The roads here are enjoyable without being demanding. They follow river valleys and cross low ridges, with bends that tighten and ease in a rhythm, and the surface is generally good. Farm traffic is common, as are cyclists on summer weekends. Heat is rarely an issue in the hills, and the shade of the oaks keeps the road cool.

Fuel is easiest in Banyoles, which has several stations and supermarkets. In the smaller villages, a pump can close for the siesta, and few stay open late. Eat at the Spanish hour, after two, and you will find kitchens in full swing and tables full of locals.
t.tibidabo@41.2,1.9:
Castelldefels is where Barcelona's beaches run out and the mountains begin. The town sits on a long flat stretch of sand south-west of the city, with the Garraf massif rising steeply behind it, a rough block of limestone, scrub and pine that tumbles into the sea. A hilltop castle, first recorded in the eleventh century, overlooks the town, and the coast road, the C-31, runs along the shore toward Sitges through tunnels and above cliffs.

The label points to Tibidabo, the mountain behind Barcelona on the other side of the city, about twenty kilometres to the north-east, topped by a church and an old amusement park with a Ferris wheel and views across the whole city. The ride has crossed the whole of Barcelona, from that summit to the south-west, so this is the end of a long loop. The riding in the Garraf is the sort that suits a dawn start, with tight bends, steep climbs and wide views over the Mediterranean, and the Garraf Natural Park has gravel tracks and winding lanes through scrub that smells of thyme and rosemary.

The surrounding towns are practical rather than pretty. Gavà, with about forty-six thousand people, is a working town with a long beach and a mining museum, and nearby are archaeological sites from the Neolithic, when people dug galleries for a green mineral called variscite. Begues, higher up in the hills, is a small village with a more rural air, and a good place for a coffee. In summer, heat is intense, and in dry years fire danger can close some tracks.

Fuel, food and rooms are no trouble in Castelldefels, which has more than sixty thousand people, and beach restaurants serve rice with seafood and grilled fish. Weekend traffic on the coast road can be heavy, particularly on summer evenings, when everyone heads home from the beach. The best months are April to June and September to October, when the air is warm and the crowds thinner.
t.norseman@-32.2,121.8:
Norseman is the end of the line, or the start of it, depending on which way you are going. It sits at the western end of the Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor, a gold town in the dry woodlands of Western Australia, and for anyone arriving from Eucla it is where the long emptiness finally breaks into trees and a proper main street. The name comes from a horse: the prospector Laurie Sinclair's horse, Norseman, supposedly scratched up a gold nugget in 1894 and the rush that followed made a town. The town has since honoured the animal with a statue and has a row of camel sculptures made from scrap on the main street, which is the sort of civic humour you get after a thousand kilometres of straight road.

The ride in is long and mostly dead straight. Between Caiguna and Balladonia is a stretch of about ninety miles with no bend at all, one of the longest straight sections of road in Australia, and it will test concentration more than skill. The advice from locals is simple: take breaks, drink water, avoid riding at dawn and dusk when kangaroos, emus and wedge-tailed eagles feeding on roadkill are most active, and watch for road trains, which are enormous and not in a mood to move over. Crosswinds can be fierce, and the temperature swings between baking afternoons and cold desert nights.

Landscape-wise, the Nullarbor's name comes from the Latin for no trees, and the treeless limestone plain gives way somewhere before Norseman to salmon gum and mallee woodland, with salt lakes shimmering to the south. Skylab famously dropped debris around Balladonia in 1979, and you will see a mention of it in the roadhouse there.

Practical matters are straightforward in this country but unforgiving if ignored. Fuel is sold at roadhouses spaced a couple of hundred kilometres apart and also in Norseman, which has the full range of services, so fill whenever you can and carry reserve if your tank is small. Accommodation in town is basic and fills up with grey nomads in the cooler months, so book ahead in winter. Behind the town, the Mount Norseman lookout shows the lakes and mine workings spread out below, a good place for sunset.
t.sarlat la caneda@44.9,1.2:
Sarlat is built of honey-coloured limestone, and when the evening sun hits it, the whole medieval town glows as if lit from inside. It lies in the Périgord Noir, a region of walnut groves, oak woods and steep green valleys in the Dordogne, and its centre is one of the best-preserved in France, a maze of lanes, courtyards and stone staircases that escaped the demolition fever of the nineteenth century. Pointed turrets, carved doorways and tall slate roofs crowd every street, and filmmakers have used it so often that locals barely look up when a camera crew appears. The writer Étienne de La Boétie, the close friend of Montaigne, was born here in 1530.

Food is the other main attraction. This is the land of foie gras, duck confit, walnuts and truffles, and the Saturday morning market, spilling through the old centre, is a theatre of baskets, cheeses and cured sausages that has been going for centuries. There is also a strange stone tower on the hill above the cathedral, the Lanterne des Morts, built in the twelfth century and thought to be a funerary beacon, though nobody can say exactly what for. Sit in a square in the evening with a glass of Bergerac and you will see why people stay longer than they planned.

For motorcyclists, Sarlat is a friendly start to the Dordogne valley route. The centre is largely pedestrianised, so park in one of the car parks on the edge, where bikes are usually tolerated, and walk in. A town of eleven thousand has fuel stations on the ring road, bakeries that open early and enough cafés to make leaving hard. Heading south, the road drops toward the river and runs through villages of ochre stone, past the cliff-hugging castles of Beynac and Castelnaud and the bastide village of Domme on its high rock. The corners are gentle, the surface mostly smooth, and the views across the valley are long and green.

Summer is busy, with caravans and coaches on the narrow roads, so aim for early morning or late afternoon, and spring and autumn are far better. In October, the oaks go bronze, mist lies in the valley and the smell of woodsmoke and walnuts hangs in the air. It is a good time to be hungry.
t.florac@44.3,3.6:
Florac sits where several small rivers and several landscapes meet, at the foot of the great limestone plateaus of the Causses and the schist ridges of the Cévennes. A small town of nearly two thousand people, it is the headquarters of the Cévennes National Park, which occupies the old château, and it has a cheerful, unfussy air, with plane trees along the main street and a spring that gushes out of the rock just above town. The Tarnon river runs through, and the Tarn, a little way north, starts its journey toward the famous gorges.

This is Protestant country with a hard history. In the early eighteenth century, the Camisards, Calvinist peasants of the Cévennes, rose against the king's attempt to suppress their religion and fought a guerrilla war in these hills for years, and the memory of that resistance is part of local identity. The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson walked through Florac in 1878 with a donkey called Modestine, and his account of the journey, Travels with a Donkey, made the area known to the English-speaking world. The hillsides are covered with sweet chestnut trees, once the staple food of the region, and the landscape is a quilt of terraces and old stone farms.

For a rider, Florac is a very good place to start the Corniche des Cévennes, a high road that runs along a ridge for miles with views over a sea of wooded hills, and it is considered one of the finest drives in southern France. The road climbs from town in a series of tight bends, then follows the crest with gentler curves, though the surface can be patchy and the road is narrow, with steep drops on one side. Mist can fill the valleys in the morning, and the weather changes quickly. Florac has fuel, but supplies are limited, so it is wise to top up before leaving, and the larger town of Mende, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the next sure stop.

The best months are May, June and September, when the days are warm and the roads quiet. Summer brings crowds to the Tarn gorges, but the ridge roads stay peaceful. Buy a chestnut cake or a jar of chestnut cream in town, and keep it for the evening.
t.saint jean du gard@44.1,3.9:
On a day in early October 1878, Robert Louis Stevenson ended his walk through the Cévennes at Saint-Jean-du-Gard, and sold his donkey. The Scottish writer, then twenty-seven, had spent twelve days crossing the mountains with a stubborn grey animal called Modestine, and he recorded the adventure in Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes, one of the first books about hiking for pleasure. The route he followed is now a long-distance path, the GR70, the Chemin de Stevenson, and walkers with sticks and rucksacks are a common sight in the town.

Saint-Jean-du-Gard sits at the foot of the Cévennes, where the Gardon river runs out of the mountains in a deep, green valley. It is a town of about three thousand, with a fine seventeenth-century humpback bridge, the Pont Vieux, narrow streets and a long tradition of silk, which was once the main industry. The mulberry trees that fed the silkworms still grow in the hills, and a museum of the Cévennes valleys recounts the story. A little steam train runs from Anduze, a tourist line along the river, which is a pleasure to watch go by.

The town is also the start of the Corniche des Cévennes, the road that climbs along the ridge toward Florac. The road was built after the Camisard revolt, a Protestant uprising in the early eighteenth century, when the authorities wanted to move troops through the mountains quickly, and it clings to the side of the hills with a series of bends and views over deep valleys. The surface is good, the bends are rhythmic and the traffic is light, and the ridge, covered in chestnut and pine, gives a sense of space.

The chestnut was the staple of the mountain villages, its flour used for bread and porridge, and a good deal of the landscape is shaped by the terraces built to grow it. In autumn, the woods are filled with collectors, and a plate of roast chestnuts or a chestnut cake is a taste of the region. The weather can change fast, and storms in the Cévennes are dramatic, with sudden floods in the rivers.

Saint-Jean-du-Gard has fuel, and a number of cafes and restaurants, and is the natural place to stop before the climb. Anduze and Alès are the bigger towns for any further supplies.
t.monts d ardeche roads@44.8,4.5:
The Monts d'Ardèche are not tall, but they are steep, and that is what makes them interesting. Around the valley of the Eyrieux, between Saint-Sauveur-de-Montagut, Le Cheylard and Privas, the land is a tangle of narrow ridges and deep, wooded gorges, falling from the high plateau toward the Rhône. Chestnut woods cover most of the slopes, and on the lower ground the old terraces, built by hand to hold soil on the hillsides, still step down in grey stone walls, many of them abandoned and overgrown.

The roads here are the pleasure. They follow the ridges and the river sides in a long run of tight bends, with hairpins where they have to climb and drop and a lot of blind corners that reward a measured speed. The surface varies from smooth to patchy, with gravel on the corners after rain or after a wash of chestnut leaves, so scan ahead. There is little traffic outside the summer holidays, and in the early morning the valley can be filled with mist while the ridges stand clear above it.

Chestnut is the key to the culture of the place. For centuries the tree provided flour, food for animals and timber, and the Ardèche's chestnut is still protected as a regional product, celebrated in markets and festivals in autumn. The Eyrieux valley is also known for its fruit, especially peaches, cherries and apricots, which ripen in the warm, sheltered lower reaches, so that in spring the blossom is a strong reason to ride the valley floor. Silk was once a major industry, too, and traces of old mills and mulberry trees remain.

Fuel is the thing to plan with care. Saint-Sauveur-de-Montagut and Le Cheylard are small towns with basic services and a pump or two, but they close early and on Sundays, and hamlets between them have nothing. Privas, about fifteen kilometres away, is the bigger option, and the main roads to the east are better supplied. Carry water in summer, since the valley can be very hot and still, and expect phone signal to vanish in the deepest folds.
t.vallon pont d arc canyon@44.4,4.4:
The first sight of the Pont d'Arc is the sort of thing that makes you stop without being asked. A single arch of pale limestone, about sixty metres wide, spans the Ardèche river like a doorway cut by water, with the river running through and canoes drifting in the shade. It is a natural bridge, shaped over a very long time as the river found a shortcut through a narrow meander, and the little town of Vallon-Pont-d'Arc sits close beside it, full of campsites, bakeries and shops that sell kayaks and ice cream in about equal numbers.

The riding along the gorges is the main event. The road above the canyon, the Route des Gorges, runs for about thirty kilometres along the rim with a string of belvederes, each looking down onto the river through cliffs hundreds of metres high. Corners are open but numerous, the surface is generally good, and the views are among the best in southern France. The weakness is the traffic: in July and August the road can crawl, with camper vans, canoe shuttles and tourist cars filling the lay-bys, so go early or late, or choose a shoulder-season day.

Nearby, hidden in a limestone cliff, is the Chauvet cave, found in 1994 and containing some of the oldest known paintings in the world, more than thirty thousand years old. The cave itself is closed to the public to protect it, but a full-scale replica, the Caverne du Pont d'Arc, opened in 2015 and is a remarkable visit if you have the time. It adds a deep human layer to a landscape that already feels ancient.

Vallon has about two and a half thousand residents and the services you would expect of a busy holiday town, including fuel in the area, though prices are higher than in the larger centres. Bourg-Saint-Andéol, about twenty kilometres away, is bigger if you need more choice. Wear light layers in summer, because the gorge holds heat, and keep water in the panniers, as there are long stretches of the canyon road with no shops at all.
t.ardeche swim window@44.4,4.4:
Sometimes the best reason to stop is simply that it is hot. The Ardèche river just downstream of Vallon-Pont-d'Arc is a broad, shallow, clear stretch of water over pale stones, with small gravel beaches along the banks, and in summer it is the natural place to cool off. The label says swim window, and that is accurate: for an hour in the middle of the day, the heat of the gorge makes the river feel like a gift, and riders in boots and jackets quickly start thinking about paddling.

A few cautions are worth stating. The water is cold at first and the current is mild in normal conditions but changes with rainfall; the Ardèche is known for sudden rises after autumn storms in the Cévennes, which can turn a calm river into a dangerous one within hours. In summer, canoeists and kayakers fill the water, so keep clear of their line. Secure your kit before you go in, because a heap of helmet, jacket and bag on a beach is an obvious target, and ideally have someone stay with the bikes or leave your valuables locked away.

The landscape here is Mediterranean in feel, with holm oaks, scrub and the sharp smell of thyme and cistus on hot days. Cicadas make a constant noise, and the limestone walls change colour from white to gold as the light shifts. In the evenings the canoe traffic stops and the river is still, with swifts and martins feeding over the water. This is the time of day when the place feels most like itself.

The town is a minute away, so food and drink are easy: bakeries, small supermarkets, cafés with shade and, for the evening, simple restaurants serving local dishes. Ruoms, a short ride north, is the next sizeable village. If you need more fuel than a small station can provide, Bourg-Saint-Andéol is the larger town to the east. Take your time, because the riding home through the gorge is better with a cool head.
t.south lake tahoe@38.9,-120.0:
Lake Tahoe sits at 6,225 feet, which makes it one of the highest large lakes in the country, and the water is so clear that on a calm day you can see objects more than sixty feet down. It is also very deep, about 1,645 feet at its deepest, making it the second deepest lake in the United States after Crater Lake. The basin formed as the Sierra Nevada rose along fault lines and glaciers later carved the valleys, and the Washoe people spent their summers on its shores for thousands of years, long before Europeans arrived. Their name for the lake, Da ow a ga, means edge of the lake.

South Lake Tahoe is the busy end of that shoreline. It is a resort town, with a ski area, casinos across the state line in Nevada, beach clubs, motels and restaurants, and the main road through town, US 50, is thick with traffic in summer and during winter weekends. For a rider, the pleasure lies in getting out of town. Heading north on the Nevada side, the highway runs along the shore past Zephyr Cove and up to Spooner Summit, and then the road turns onto State Route 28 along the east shore, with granite boulders, pine woods and long views of the lake.

The west shore has Emerald Bay, a deep blue inlet with a small island and a castle-like house on the shore, probably the most photographed spot on the lake. That road, State Route 89, is narrow and winding, and can be very busy, so start early. In 2021, the Caldor Fire burned the Sierra to the south-west, and the road over Echo Summit, on US 50, was affected for some time. Smoke can also affect air quality in late summer, so check conditions.

South Lake Tahoe has around 21,000 people and every service you might need: fuel stations, food, bike shops and plenty of hotels. A dip in the lake in July is cold but exhilarating, and the evening light on the water is memorable. June and September are the best months, with warm days and fewer crowds. Winter brings snow, chain controls and ice.
t.incline village@39.2,-120.0:
Incline Village sits on the north-east shore of Lake Tahoe, on the Nevada side, a community of about 8,800 people with some of the most expensive lake-view houses in the country, though from the road the mood is quiet pine woods and low buildings. It is the sort of place where a casual cafe has a view of blue water, and where the boulders on the nearby beaches are so large and smooth that they seem to have been placed by a sculptor.

The ride along State Route 28, the east shore, is the star here. South of town the road hugs the lake, running past Sand Harbor, a state park with rock-strewn coves and clear green water, and each summer a Shakespeare festival is staged on its beach. Beyond that the road passes Spooner Summit and Cave Rock, a volcanic outcrop that is sacred to the Washoe, with a short tunnel cut through it. The curves are gentle, the surface is good, and the views of snow-capped peaks across the lake are lovely, though speed limits are low and tourists stop often. Cyclists share the road, so patience helps.

The Ponderosa Ranch, a theme park built around the set of the television Western Bonanza, once stood above the town, but it closed in 2004, and the land has been turned over to housing. Higher up, the Mount Rose Highway, State Route 431, climbs from the lake to nearly nine thousand feet before dropping to Reno, with long grades and fine views of the basin. The road can be icy or closed in winter, so check conditions.

Incline Village offers fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Kings Beach, a few miles west on the California border, has more modest restaurants. The lake is cold enough that a swim takes courage, but a picnic on a sunny rock is a lovely way to spend an afternoon. Early summer, with snow still on the peaks, and September, with quiet beaches, are the best times to be here. In winter, ski areas are close, and roads may need chains.
t.yangmingshan@25.2,121.6:
Yangmingshan rises just north of Taipei, a volcanic massif that fills the skyline and cools the air by several degrees. The park, a national park since 1985, takes in the Tatun volcano group, an old cluster of cones that has been quiet for a long time, though fumaroles, sulphur vents and hot springs still show the fire beneath. The highest peak, Qixing Mountain, stands at around 1,120 metres, and is the high point of the Taipei basin. The air smells faintly of sulphur at the vents, which is a surprise to those who thought they had left the city.

The mountain used to be called Caoshan, and was renamed in the 1950s by Chiang Kai-shek, after the Ming dynasty philosopher Wang Yangming. It became a retreat for officials and a weekend escape for the city, and today it is one of Taipei's best-loved outdoor places. In February and March, cherry blossoms line the paths, followed by calla lilies in spring and the silver grass of Mount Qixing in autumn. Hot springs are everywhere, and nearby Beitou is the traditional place to soak after a ride.

For a motorcyclist, Yangmingshan has some of the best roads close to a big Asian city. Yangjin Highway climbs from the city or from the coast in loops and hairpins through forest and open grassland, with views down toward Taipei and, to the north, the sea. The roads can be busy on weekends, with scooters, cyclists and tour buses, and the surface is generally good, if slippery in the drizzle that often drapes the mountain. In winter, the north-east monsoon brings mist and light rain, and visibility can drop quickly, so a clear dry day is a gift. Early mornings in spring and autumn are the best times, when the traffic is light and the air is washed.

Taipei is only fourteen kilometres away, so fuel, food and everything else are easy, with convenience stores on almost every corner and night markets that stay open late. On the mountain itself, there are a few small restaurants and tea houses by the roadside, and parking spots at the main visitor areas fill early on holidays. Keelung, on the north coast, is famous for its harbour night market and its seafood, and makes a natural next stop for hungry riders.

Wear something warm: the top can be much cooler and wetter than the city below.
t.yosemite west@37.7,-119.8:
Yosemite's western approach follows the Merced River as it falls out of the Sierra Nevada, and this gate is where the foothills end and the granite begins. For about an hour from Mariposa, Highway 140 climbs through a canyon of oak and pine, with the river rushing white and green beside the road, until the walls tighten and you pass through the Arch Rock entrance, where a huge boulder leans over the pavement as if it were a doorway. Beyond it the Valley opens, and the first sight of El Capitan and the Half Dome is one of the great moments of any American road trip.

The history of the place is as much about people as about stone. The Ahwahneechee lived in the valley for centuries, and gold miners poured into the foothills in 1849, soon followed by tourists. In 1864 President Lincoln signed an act that gave the valley to California as a public trust, a precursor of the national parks, and John Muir, the naturalist who walked here in the 1860s and 1870s, argued passionately for its protection. The photographs of Ansel Adams carried the image of the valley across the world.

For a rider, the road is a pleasure, with a narrow, twisting surface that follows the river through shade and sun, with plenty of corners but also heavy traffic in summer, including large recreational vehicles and slow tour buses. Rockfalls and construction have closed parts of the road at times, so check the park website before you go, and note that reservations or entry permits may be required in busy seasons. Mornings are best, before the heat and the crowds build up. Tioga Pass, on the east side, closes with snow from late autumn to late spring.

Fuel is not available at the gate, and the valley floor has only limited services, so fill the tank in Mariposa, about thirty kilometres from the entrance. Pack water, as the sun is strong and the air dry. Spring brings the waterfalls at their fullest, usually from April to June, while autumn brings quiet roads and golden light.
t.mariposa food@37.5,-120.0:
Mariposa is the Gold Rush town at the foot of the road to Yosemite, and it wears the history lightly. It sits in the Sierra foothills, in country of oak, grass and rocky ridges that turn gold in summer, along Highway 49, the road named for the forty-niners who flooded into California after gold turned up in 1848. The little town has a main street of wooden verandas, a few antique stores and restaurants, and a courthouse built in 1854 that is said to be the oldest in continuous use west of the Mississippi.

Mariposa has a larger place in history than its size suggests. John C. Frémont, the explorer and later presidential candidate, bought a large estate here in 1847, and found gold on it. Later, Mariposa was a gateway for those who first visited Yosemite Valley in the 1850s, and the state's mining museum, set up in the town, holds an impressive collection of minerals and gold specimens, including some enormous crystals. The surrounding hills are honeycombed with old mines and diggings.

The road to Yosemite, Highway 140, runs through the Merced River canyon, a twisting ride between steep slopes, with the river rushing beside you. It is a fine road, well surfaced and fun, though it carries heavy summer traffic, and rockfalls have closed it from time to time. Further up, the road enters the park at Arch Rock, with granite walls rising on both sides. It is wise to start early, especially in summer, when the park entrance can have long queues, and in winter, when snow can close the high roads and chains may be required.

Summer in the foothills is hot, often well over thirty-five degrees Celsius, so the air feels like a hairdryer on a bike, but the high country is cooler. The best times are spring, when the hills are green and the wildflowers are out, and autumn. Fire season can bring smoke and road closures, and it has to be taken seriously.

Mariposa is a proper town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a number of restaurants and cafes, and it is the last place with real choice before the park. Midpines, a few kilometres up the road, has a few services. Fill up here, buy water and snacks, and make use of the stop before you head into the mountains.
t.etang de vaccares@43.5,4.6:
The Étang de Vaccarès is the heart of the Camargue, a shallow, brackish lagoon of roughly sixty-five square kilometres, which makes it the largest in the Rhône delta. It is not the sort of lake you swim in. It is a wide sheet of pewter-grey water, ringed by reedbeds, salt flats and tamarisk, with the sky as the main feature. The water is so shallow that most of it is only a metre or two deep, and it is a nature reserve of international importance, a refuge for thousands of birds, including greater flamingos, herons, ibises and avocets.

Riding here is a flat, open experience, and it feels more like being at sea than on land. The roads that approach the lagoon, such as the D36B and the D570 from Arles, run dead straight across the delta between rice fields, marsh and pasture, with white horses and black bulls grazing at the verge, tended by gardians, the Camargue cowboys, on horseback. The tarmac is narrow and often patched, with no hard shoulder, and the main hazard is the wind. The mistral, a cold, dry wind from the north, can blow for days and will push a bike sideways, and in summer the mosquitoes are ferocious. Spring and autumn are the best times, with softer light, migrating birds and fewer insects.

The Camargue is a living landscape, made by the Rhône and the sea, and by centuries of human management. The salt pans, the rice fields and the ranches all shape the pattern. The park is run as a regional nature reserve, and you will find signed paths and small observation points where you can stop and look through binoculars. Walking is easy, with flat ground, but you should stay on the marked routes and keep clear of the horses and bulls. The light is the real gift: wide skies, low horizons and colours that change by the minute, especially at dawn and dusk.

Services are thin around the lagoon. A few farm restaurants and village cafés serve local dishes such as gardiane, a stew of bull meat in red wine, with Camargue rice, and are well worth trying if you find one open.
t.salin de giraud@43.4,4.7:
Salin-de-Giraud is a company village at the southern tip of the Camargue, built around salt, and the salt shapes the whole place. All around it, the flat land is cut into vast evaporation ponds, shallow basins where seawater is let in and left to the sun and wind. In summer the water turns pink and then almost red, a result of tiny algae and bacteria that thrive in the salty brine, and big white mounds of salt, the camelles, rise like miniature glaciers beside the pans. The effect, in clear light, is surreal, as though someone has dyed the landscape.

The village itself grew up in the nineteenth century with the salt works and, later, a large chemical plant, and its streets of neat workers' housing still show the planned layout of a company town. Today the Salins du Midi still harvests salt here, including the fleur de sel, the fine crust from the surface of the pans that cooks prize. Birdlife is rich, and flamingos feed in the shallows in their hundreds, standing on one leg and looking affronted by the world.

The ride is flat, open and straight. From Arles or from the Vaccarès, the road runs across the delta through rice fields and salt marsh, with the pans appearing on both sides, and the main variable is the wind. The mistral can make the final approach hard work, so brace the bike and lean into it. The surface is generally fine but narrow, and lorries from the salt works share the road. Summer is hot and glaring, and the midges are not kind, so spring and early autumn are the better seasons. The best light is early morning and evening, when the pans reflect the sky and flamingos glow pink.

From Salin-de-Giraud you can head to the wild beaches of the coast, such as Beauduc and Piémanson, where the track runs across dunes to long empty sand, and in summer informal camper camps spread along the shore. To cross the Rhône, there is a small ferry, the bac de Barcarin, that carries cars and bikes across the Grand Rhône towards Port-Saint-Louis-du-Rhône. There is a fare, and the crossing takes just a few minutes.

For practical needs, the village has a bakery, a café or two and shops. Port-Saint-Louis, about eight kilometres across the river, has supermarkets and fuel, which is the safer place to fill up. Bring water and sun protection.
t.saintes maries de la mer@43.5,4.4:
The Camargue is the great wet delta of the Rhône, a flat, wide, shimmering land of lagoons, reed beds and salt pans, and Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer is its small, strange capital. The village sits on the edge of the sea, with a fortified church, Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer, that dominates the skyline like a stone ship, built in the twelfth century with thick walls and a roof designed for defence against pirate raids. Legend says that Mary Jacobe and Mary Salome, followers of Christ, fled Palestine in a boat without sails and landed here, accompanied by their servant Sarah, and the village is named in their honour.

Every year on 24 and 25 May, thousands of Roma travel from across Europe to honour Sarah, known as Sara la Kali, the black Sara, who is their patron saint. The statue of Sara is carried down to the sea in a procession of horses, riders and singing crowds, and it is a very moving event, though crowded. At other times, the village is quiet and seaside, with white houses, narrow streets, a small bullring and a beach.

The land around is full of wildlife and character. Pink flamingos wade in the shallows of the lagoons in their thousands, white horses graze in the marshes, and black bulls are raised for the Provençal bullfights, in which the bull is not killed. The gardians, the Camargue cowboys, still ride in the saddles and wear hats and jackets of a traditional cut. Rice fields, salt pans and rows of reeds stretch to the horizon, and the light has a clear, pale quality that painters have loved, Van Gogh among them, who painted the boats here in 1888.

For motorcyclists, the road is flat, straight and scenic in an unspectacular way, with long views, big skies and the occasional flock of birds. The wind, particularly the mistral, can be strong, pushing the bike sideways, and mosquitoes are fierce from late spring until autumn, so bring repellent. There are fuel pumps in the village, but the crowds at the height of summer make a fuel stop slow, so the sensible option is to fill the tank at Arles or Aigues-Mortes. A plate of local bull stew, gardianne, with Camargue rice, makes a good supper.
t.lourdes@43.1,0.0:
Lourdes is a town built around a miracle, and everything in it, from the souvenir shops to the shape of the streets, follows from that. In February 1858, a fourteen-year-old miller's daughter named Bernadette Soubirous reported seeing a lady in a grotto by the river Gave de Pau, an apparition she saw eighteen times in that year. The Church eventually accepted it, and the grotto became one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world. Some three million pilgrims come each year, including many sick and disabled people, and the vast sanctuary has basilicas, processions and a candlelit procession in the evening that is moving whatever your beliefs.

Besides the shrine, Lourdes has a fortress on a rock, a lively old quarter and a funicular up the Pic du Jer, a limestone hill with a view over the plain to the Pyrenees. The town has about sixteen thousand residents but more hotel rooms than almost any other French town outside Paris, so beds are never scarce. Fuel, shops, bike mechanics and restaurants are easy to find. The atmosphere changes between the sanctuary, which is solemn and ordered, and the nearby streets, which are cheerfully commercial.

The Pyrenees begin close to the town, and the ride east from here is a tour of the great Tour de France climbs. The Col du Tourmalet, at 2,115 metres the highest road pass in the French Pyrenees, is a short way south, reached through Luz-Saint-Sauveur, and the Aubisque and Soulor passes lie to the west. The roads climb in long, steady bends through meadow and forest to bare, windswept summits, and cyclists in team colours labour up them in summer, so patience is needed. The surface is good, though patchy near the tops, and some passes close from November to May.

Weather in the mountains is changeable, with warm sun in the valley and fog, wind and rain at the top, so carry waterproofs and a warm layer. Livestock, including sheep, cows and horses, graze the high pastures and wander across the road, usually at corners. In the evenings, the air in the valleys smells of woodsmoke and cut grass. Fill the tank in Lourdes before you leave, because the mountain villages have few pumps, and enjoy a good breakfast before the climb.
t.col du tourmalet@42.9,0.1:
At 2,115 metres, the Tourmalet is the highest paved pass in the French Pyrenees, and it has a reputation to match. The name is said to mean something like bad detour in the local Occitan, and the Tour de France has used it since 1910, when the riders on their heavy single-gear bikes were so exhausted that one of them, Octave Lapize, is reported to have shouted at the organisers that they were murderers. A century on, it remains one of the most iconic climbs in cycling, and on any summer day you will share the road with riders in lycra suffering for the photo at the summit.

The pass links Sainte-Marie-de-Campan, on the Bigorre side, with Barèges and Luz-Saint-Sauveur on the western side. From the east, the road climbs through green meadows and past the ski station of La Mongie, then onto bare, high slopes where the trees give out and the sky seems to open. The gradients are steady, the bends are long and wide with a few hairpins near the top, and the surface is generally good. From the west, the road is narrower, steeper and more twisty, passing through Barèges before the final haul. Both sides are a joy on a bike, with the road clear and the views huge.

Do not underestimate the weather. At this altitude, cloud, wind and sudden cold can arrive within minutes, even in summer, and fog on the summit is common. The pass is closed in winter by snow, usually from around November until late spring, and may open and close with the weather, so check before heading out. Early and late in the day are the quietest times. At the summit, a famous bronze statue of a cyclist, the Géant du Tourmalet, marks the highest point, and a couple of cafés and souvenir stalls sell warm drinks and snacks.

The nearby Pic du Midi de Bigorre, a high observatory reached by cable car from La Mongie, is one of the great sites for astronomy, with very clear skies. Wildlife on the slopes includes marmots, which whistle at intruders, and griffon vultures cruise on the thermals.

Fill up in Bagnères-de-Bigorre on the east side, or Luz-Saint-Sauveur on the west, before you start, and bring a warm layer, since even a summer descent can be cold.
t.col d aspin@42.9,0.3:
After the severity of the Tourmalet, the Col d'Aspin is a gentler thing, a broad, grassy pass at 1,489 metres that feels more like a high meadow than an alpine crossing. The road, the D918, links the valley of Campan near Sainte-Marie-de-Campan with the Arreau side, and the climb through forest and open pasture is smooth and rhythmic, with wide bends, good visibility and a surface that is usually better than anything else in the area. It is a road for flowing riding, and a favourite with both motorcyclists and cyclists for that reason.

The Aspin often appears in the Tour de France alongside the bigger passes, and you will see fading painted names of riders on the tarmac, left by fans in the summer months. At the top, the ground opens into rolling pasture where cattle, sheep and sometimes semi-wild horses graze freely, wandering across the road with no regard for traffic.
