Watch for them, especially on blind corners, and give the animals plenty of room. A few cafés and stalls at the summit sell cheese and cold drinks in season.

The scenery is gentle but vast. From the summit you can look across to the peaks of the central Pyrenees, with the long ridge line fading into the haze, and on a clear day the high Néouvielle massif stands out, a granite landscape of lakes. Early morning brings the best light and the quietest roads, with a sense of space that is hard to beat. In July and August the road becomes busy, and the pass can close in winter with snow, so late spring to early autumn is the usual season. Mist on the northern slopes can be dense, so slow down if the visibility drops.

The pass is a natural link in a chain: ride the Tourmalet, then drop to Sainte-Marie-de-Campan, climb the Aspin, and continue to Arreau and the Peyresourde, and you have one of the great days in the Pyrenees.

For fuel and food, the nearest large town is Bagnères-de-Bigorre, about twenty kilometres from the pass, and Arreau, on the other side, has shops, cafés and basic services. There is no pump at the summit, so make sure the tank is full. Local cheeses, particularly those made from sheep's milk, are good to try if you find a farm stall open, and they travel well in a pannier.
t.col de peyresourde@42.8,0.5:
The Col de Peyresourde sits at 1,569 metres on the border between the Hautes-Pyrénées and the Haute-Garonne, and it is one of those passes that you cross without much ceremony but remember for the road. The D618 goes up from the Louron valley on one side and drops to Bagnères-de-Luchon on the other, and in between it is a ribbon of well-surfaced bends through grassy slopes, with wide views toward the high Pyrenean peaks. It is not a hard climb, but the setting is fine, and there is a modest ski station, Peyragudes, near the summit.

The south side, toward Luchon, is the more interesting. The road descends in a series of fast, open curves, passing through the village of Garin and following the green valley down toward the spa town. The surface is generally good and the gradient moderate, making it an enjoyable descent when the traffic is light. In summer, you will often share the road with cyclists, who know the pass well from the Tour de France, and with caravans, so patience is useful. Cattle graze the high pastures and may stray onto the road, particularly near the top.

Weather rules the mountain. Fog can drift in without warning, wind blows across the open crest, and temperatures at the top can be a good deal cooler than in the valleys. In winter the pass is open more often than some of its neighbours, but snow and ice are possible, so check before you set off. Late spring and early autumn offer the best combination of clear air and quiet roads. In the evening, the light on the peaks to the south is warm, and the temperature drops quickly.

The Pyrenees here are a rich area for wildlife and traditional pastoralism. Pastures at the top are grazed by cows and sheep in summer, in a system of transhumance that goes back centuries, and griffon vultures soar on the thermals above the slopes. Look for marmots near the rocks.

Services are limited at the pass itself, though a small café and a ski-station building can be open in season. For fuel, the nearest sure source is Bagnères-de-Luchon, about ten kilometres down the south side, or Arreau on the north. Vielha, across the border in the Spanish Val d'Aran, is the nearest larger town, but the border is a longer ride, so plan your fill-up on this side.
t.bagneres de luchon@42.8,0.6:
Luchon is a spa town built by the Belle Époque on the back of hot sulphurous water, and it still has the grand, slightly faded air of a place that once hosted the fashionable world. Its thermal springs were used by the Romans and revived in the eighteenth century, when an intendant named d'Étigny laid out the long, tree-lined avenue, the Allées d'Étigny, that still forms the town's backbone. Today the avenue is lined with cafés, shops and old hotels with wrought-iron balconies, and the baths still operate, though they are mostly for visitors rather than kings.

The town sits in a wide, green valley where several smaller valleys meet, ringed by high peaks, and it is the natural base for exploring the central Pyrenees. In summer it is a hiking and cycling centre, and the Tour de France has used it as a stage town many times. In winter, the Superbagnères ski station above it takes over, reached by a steep, winding road that starts in the town itself. For a motorcyclist, the roads out of Luchon in every direction are enticing: the Peyresourde to the north-west, the Col de Portillon to the Spanish border, the Col de Menté to the north-east, and the road to the Hospice de France, which runs up into wild country.

The climate is mild by Pyrenean standards, though afternoon storms can build over the mountains in summer, and the town sees plenty of rain. The best seasons for riding are late spring, summer and early autumn, with September often the finest month, clear, calm and quiet. In winter, snow closes some of the higher roads, so check conditions.

As the biggest town for a long way, Luchon is where a rider can find what they need: fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, a good choice of restaurants and plenty of places to stay. The local cuisine is hearty mountain food, with duck, cassoulet, garbure, a thick cabbage and meat soup, and local cheeses. A coffee on the Allées d'Étigny, in the shade of the plane trees, is a better introduction than any guidebook. From here the Spanish border is about ten kilometres away, over the Col du Portillon, and the Val d'Aran town of Vielha lies beyond.
t.saint girons@43.0,1.1:
Saint-Girons is the market town of the Couserans, a green, little-visited corner of the French Pyrenees in the Ariège, and it has the quiet self-sufficiency of a place that has always been on the way to somewhere else. The Salat river runs through the middle, with old houses along its banks and a bridge from which you can see the mountains rising to the south. On Saturday mornings the market fills the main square and the surrounding streets with cheese, honey, cured meat and vegetables, and it is a good place to stock up for a picnic. About seven thousand people live here, so there is fuel, there are supermarkets and the other services of a real town.

A couple of kilometres up the river is Saint-Lizier, an older and smaller town on a hill, with a Romanesque cathedral and a cloister of the twelfth century, and a very old pilgrimage route runs through it. The town is classed as one of the most beautiful villages in France and is part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino de Santiago routes in France. A visit takes an hour and rewards you with a quiet courtyard and a view.

The Pyrenees Cols Route finishes here after a long run of passes, and the last ones are the quieter ones. The Col de la Core, at about 1,400 metres, has a long, open approach from the south, through forest and then meadow, with a road that is narrow and winding, and the Col de Portet d'Aspet, a little lower, has a famous place at a bend on the descent, where a memorial marks the spot where the Italian cyclist Fabio Casartelli died in the 1995 Tour de France. Many riders stop for a moment there. The roads of the Couserans are quiet, wooded and scenic, with few tourists.

This is bear country: brown bears, reintroduced to the Pyrenees in the 1990s from Slovenia, live in the mountains above, though you are unlikely to see one. The local Bethmale cheese, a soft, mild cow's milk cheese, is made in the valley of the same name, and a plate of it with local bread is the right lunch. The weather is mild and humid, with the Atlantic influence bringing rain, and fog can cling to the passes, so ride with care. After the high peaks, the town is a gentle landing.
t.beynac@44.8,1.1:
Across the Dordogne from Beynac stands another castle, Castelnaud, and for much of the Hundred Years War the two stared at each other like rival boxers: Beynac held by the French, Castelnaud by the English, with a river valley between them and frequent raids in both directions. Beynac's fortress sits on the edge of a limestone cliff about a hundred and fifty metres above the water, with the village tumbling down the slope beneath it in tiers of honey-coloured stone. Richard the Lionheart is said to have held the castle in the twelfth century, which fits the local habit of attaching the biggest names to the oldest stones.

The village is small and steep, with narrow lanes, cobbles and an ever-present view of the river below. It earns its place among the most beautiful villages in France, and in summer it fills with visitors. A walk up to the castle is a stiff climb, and the reward is the view from the ramparts across the valley, with canoes drifting on the green water, walnut groves and fields of maize and the rooftops of Castelnaud on the far side. The interior has been restored and furnished, so you can see how a fortress was actually lived in.

Riding the Dordogne here is a pleasure at moderate speed. The D703 follows the river along the foot of the cliffs, with gentle bends, good surface and constant glimpses of water and rock, and the traffic, in summer, is steady and slow. If you want to enjoy the road, ride early or late, or visit in May, June or September, when the light is soft and the roads quieter. In July and August, expect queues at the pinch points and a parking squeeze in the village, and leave the bike below and walk up. After heavy rain the river can flood the low-lying road, and the cliffs sometimes drop rocks.

This is the Périgord Noir, a land of walnut oil, truffles, duck and foie gras, strawberries in season, and a strong local liking for lunch. Cafés and restaurants are plentiful in the village, though prices reflect the view. Fuel is best found in Sarlat-la-Canéda, about eight kilometres away, a lovely medieval town with supermarkets and stations. Smaller villages along the river have bakeries and a few shops, but for a full tank, plan to stop in a larger town.
t.la roque gageac@44.8,1.2:
La Roque-Gageac is a village with a problem that most places would envy: it has no room. A single street of ochre houses runs along the foot of a limestone cliff, with the Dordogne on the other side, and everything else is piled up the rock above, with gardens, steps and old stone staircases clinging to the face. The cliff leans slightly outwards, which gives the whole place a precarious look, and there have been rockfalls in the past that have damaged houses. Even so, the people have stayed for centuries, and the village is among the most photographed on the river.

The setting also produces a microclimate. The cliff faces south and traps the sun, and shelters the street from the colder winds, so the temperature is noticeably milder than elsewhere in the valley. Palms, fig trees, bananas and bamboo grow in gardens, and a small exotic garden near the top holds more tropical plants than you would expect in the Dordogne. On a warm day the rock radiates heat, and the village smells of stone, river and lime blossom.

For centuries the river was the main road, and the flat-bottomed wooden boats called gabarres carried wine, salt, timber and barrels along the Dordogne. Today replicas of them take tourists for gentle trips from the village quay, looking up at the cliffs and the castles on the skyline, and it is a pleasant way to understand how the valley was used. You can also see traces of troglodyte dwellings in the rock, caves that were once homes and fortresses.

The ride along the D703 here is straightforward and pretty, with the river on one side and the cliff on the other, and the road is narrow and busy in high season. There is little room to pass, and the village street is tight, with parked cars and walkers filling the carriageway. Park outside if possible and walk in. The best light is in the late afternoon, when the sun lights up the cliff, and the best seasons are late spring and early autumn. In winter, the village is quiet, and some restaurants close.

Cafés and restaurants line the riverside, and a long lunch of duck or walnut cake in the sun is the proper response. For fuel, Sarlat-la-Canéda, about eight kilometres away, is the main source, and the smaller towns of Cénac and Domme have limited services. Fill up before you set off along the river.
t.domme@44.8,1.2:
Domme is a fortified town on a cliff, laid out as a bastide in 1281 by Philip the Bold, the king of France, who needed a stronghold against the English in the Dordogne. The plan is as tidy as a chessboard: straight streets, a central square and three great gates in the walls. The bastide stands on a limestone spur some hundred and fifty metres above the river, and the walk to the edge, along the Belvédère de la Barre, gives one of the greatest panoramas of the valley, with the Dordogne winding below through fields and woods and the castles of Castelnaud and Beynac on the horizon.

One of its stranger stories is told in the Porte des Tours, the main gateway, where graffiti scratched into the stone walls inside are said to have been left by Templar knights imprisoned there in 1307, after the order was suppressed by the French crown. Historians quibble over details, but the carved signs and crosses give the room an unmistakable atmosphere. Under the market hall, a stair leads down into caves of stalactites and stalagmites that were used as shelters during the wars, and the cool, dripping darkness is a relief on a hot day.

The road up to Domme from the river, a steep climb with a handful of tight bends, makes for a short, lively ride after the gentle valley roads. From the top, the D46 and the minor roads that wander around the plateau are quiet and rolling, passing walnut orchards, fields and stone farmhouses. In high season, the town is crowded and the narrow lanes are full of walkers, so park at the edge and go on foot. Summer is hot and busy, spring and autumn pleasant and quiet, and the town's walnut market and shops sell the local specialities, from walnut cake and oil to duck and truffles.

The valley below is the Périgord Noir, named for its dark oaks, and its mix of cliffs, forests and river meadows is the reason the region is so beloved. In the late afternoon, the light on the stone turns golden, and the evening is the best time to walk the ramparts.

Domme has a few cafés, restaurants and shops. For fuel, the nearest sure option is Sarlat-la-Canéda, about ten kilometres to the north, which has several stations and supermarkets. Smaller villages in the valley may have a pump, but check before relying on them.
t.rocamadour@44.8,1.6:
Rocamadour is built on a cliff, and it should not work. The medieval village clings to the side of a limestone gorge above the Alzou river, with houses, chapels and stairways stacked one above another against the rock face, up to a castle at the top, and the whole thing looks like it is about to slide into the valley. It has been a pilgrimage site since the twelfth century, when the miraculous Black Virgin, a small wooden statue, and the relics of a hermit called Saint Amadour drew pilgrims from across Europe, among them kings and queens. Pilgrims used to climb the great staircase of two hundred and sixteen steps on their knees, and some still do.

At the top, the chapels hold the Black Virgin, as well as a sword said to be Roland's, the paladin of Charlemagne, stuck in the cliff. The village has been restored, and its lanes are lined with shops selling walnut products, honey and the local cheese, the Rocamadour, a tiny goat's cheese, round and creamy, with an appellation of its own. A lift takes you up from the lower village to the sanctuary if the steps seem too many. A good view comes from the castle path, with the whole gorge opening below.

The surrounding country is the Causse de Gramat, a dry limestone plateau of oak scrub, stone walls and sheep, with underground rivers and caves, including the Gouffre de Padirac, a vast chasm with a river and boat trip underground, a few kilometres away. The plateau is quiet, empty and beautiful in its own way, with stone barns and small farms. The nearest towns are Gramat, eight kilometres off, with fuel and shops, and Gourdon, twenty kilometres. The Dordogne valley lies just to the north, with its castles and rich farmland.

The ride to Rocamadour follows the Dordogne for a long way, with the river looping between cliffs, castles and pretty villages, and the roads are gentle and winding, with a few narrow places. Summer is crowded here, and the village gets very busy at midday, so go early or late, and be careful on the steep hairpin approach. Park below and walk up. After a long ride, a plate of confit de canard, a glass of Cahors wine and a walnut tart is hard to better.
t.col des faisses@44.2,3.7:
The high Cévennes do not look like the south of France that most visitors imagine. This is a land of schist and granite ridges folded one behind the other, cloaked in chestnut woods and heather, with deep valleys where the villages cling to terraces held up by dry-stone walls. The Col des Faisses, at a little over a thousand metres, is a quiet saddle in this world, a place where the road tops a ridge and the forest opens to a view of blue hills fading into distance. It is far from any large town, and that is much of its charm.

The Cévennes have a history of resistance. In the early eighteenth century, Protestant peasants known as Camisards rose against Louis XIV's persecution, and fought a guerrilla war in these hills from 1702 to 1710, hiding in caves and forest and ambushing royal troops. A hundred and sixty years later, in 1878, the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson walked through the region with a donkey called Modestine and wrote Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes, which put the area on the map for English-speaking visitors. Parts of his route are now a long-distance trail, the GR70.

The riding is slow, intimate and rewarding. The roads in this part of the Cévennes are narrow, with plenty of tight bends and blind corners, and the surface is often patchy, with loose gravel on the edges and the occasional rockfall. Traffic is light, especially outside July and August, and you can ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle. Weather can change quickly. Autumn storms, called épisodes cévenols, bring heavy rain, and in winter the high roads can ice over or close. Spring and early autumn are the best times, with the chestnut leaves turning gold in October.

The sweet chestnut was once the staple food of the region, the bread tree of the poor, and the old terraces and drying sheds can still be seen. Nearby Mont Aigoual, at 1,567 metres, has a weather observatory that has been in operation since the late nineteenth century, and the whole region is protected as a national park and part of a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, the Causses and Cévennes.

Services are thin on the ground. Florac, about fourteen kilometres away, has fuel, cafés and shops, and Alès, a larger town, is about thirty kilometres further. Fill up before you head into the hills, carry water, and expect to take longer than the map suggests.
t.anduze@44.1,4.0:
Anduze is the gate of the Cévennes, a town on the Gardon river where the flat vineyards of Languedoc end and the schist mountains begin. The main entry is under the Tour de l'Horloge, a clock tower of the fourteenth century that stands at the edge of the old town, and the streets inside are narrow, shaded and full of small shops. The town is also known for the Anduze vase, a large, glazed, urn-shaped pot that became fashionable in the seventeenth century and decorated the gardens of Versailles. Potters still make them in workshops around the town, and you can visit and watch them being thrown.

The history of the area is intertwined with Protestantism. The Cévennes were a stronghold of the Huguenots, and when the French crown tried to suppress them after 1685, the mountain people rose in the Camisard revolt in the early eighteenth century, fighting a guerrilla war in the forests and hills. The memory of the struggle is still strong, and a museum in the town tells the story. Just outside Anduze, the Bambouseraie, a garden planted in the nineteenth century with giant bamboo and other exotic trees, is a strange and lovely sight in the middle of France, and a steam train runs through the valley to Saint-Jean-du-Gard.

The riding in the Cévennes is a pleasure, with the Corniche des Cévennes, the D9, running along a ridge between Saint-Jean-du-Gard and Florac with views over a sea of ridges and valleys. The road is narrow and winding, cut into the hillside, with bends and drops. The surface is mostly good, but gravel and fallen branches can appear after storms. In summer it is hot, with the sun beating on the road, while in spring and autumn the colour of the chestnut woods is a delight. The sweet onion of the Cévennes and the chestnut, in every form, are the local foods.

Anduze has about thirty-three hundred people, with fuel, bakeries and cafés, though the larger stations are at Saint-Christol-lès-Alès, about eight kilometres away. The Gardon is a pleasant place for a swim in summer, and its clear pools lie below the old stone bridge, though it can rise suddenly in storms, with flash floods in autumn. Be careful in the rainy season, because the cévenol storms can be violent. Order a plate of charcuterie and a glass of local wine at a café in the square, and watch the village go about its day.
t.cave rock@39.0,-119.9:
Cave Rock is a lump of volcanic rock on the Nevada shore of Lake Tahoe, and US 50 goes straight through it. Two tunnels bore through the stone, the older from 1931 and a second added in the 1950s, and when you ride through you are literally passing through a mountain that has been sacred to the Washoe people for thousands of years. The Washoe consider it a place of power and healing, and rock climbing was banned there after a long legal fight. Visitors are asked to treat the site with respect, and the park around the base has a boat ramp and picnic area.

The lake is the star. Tahoe is among the deepest in the world, at about 500 metres, and one of the clearest, so the water close to shore shifts from turquoise to deep blue, with granite boulders glowing under the surface. It sits at about 1,900 metres, ringed by Sierra peaks that hold snow well into early summer. The lake is cold all year, even in August, and in winter the surrounding mountains are a skiing region.

The riding here is a pleasure. The east shore road, along US 50 and then SR 28, runs close to the water, with views over the lake, long, flowing curves and short climbs through pine and juniper, and the road surface is generally excellent. Traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends and in summer, and the speed limit is low through the tunnels and near the beaches. Watch for pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers who brake without warning when the view opens up. Early morning is quiet and bright, and in autumn the aspens add colour. Winter brings snow and chain controls on the passes beyond.

Fuel and food are easy. South Lake Tahoe, about thirteen kilometres south in California, is a proper town with everything, and Stateline, just over the border, has casinos and restaurants. Kingsbury and Zephyr Cove also have services. The parking at Cave Rock is small and fills in summer, but is free for short stops. The altitude can make you breathless if you climb on foot, and the sun is stronger than you expect, so bring sunscreen. At sunset the lake turns gold and pink, and the whole scene feels very still.
t.sand harbor@39.2,-119.9:
Sand Harbor is where Lake Tahoe shows off. A cluster of smooth granite boulders sits in water so clear that it looks like glass, with pale sand coves between them, and the colour of the lake runs from bright aqua in the shallows to deep blue just beyond. The setting is a Nevada state park on the east shore, and in high summer it is among the busiest beaches on the lake, with the car park often full by mid-morning. Come early or late, and it is very different.

The ride along the east shore is part of the draw. State Route 28 runs north from Incline Village, hugging the shore with long, easy curves, gentle climbs and wide views across the lake to the snowy Sierra ridges. It is not a technical road, and the speed limit is low, but the combination of pines, granite and water makes it feel unusually pretty. Heavy summer traffic and the occasional jam mean patience is needed. The best time is early morning in June or September, or at sunset, when the light turns the lake pink. Winter can bring snow, ice and closures.

There is also a cultural side. The Lake Tahoe Shakespeare Festival is held at Sand Harbor in summer, with outdoor performances on a stage set among the rocks and the lake as a backdrop, which sounds improbable until you see it. The nearby Thunderbird Lodge, a stone mansion built in the 1930s by the eccentric millionaire George Whittell, shows another side of the shore's history, and the surrounding hills were once heavily logged to feed the silver mines of Virginia City. The lake itself is cold, deep and clear, and swimming is bracing even in August.

Sand Harbor has a day-use fee, and parking can be full on summer weekends, so plan accordingly. Incline Village, about seven kilometres away, is a small resort town with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Kings Beach, on the California side, is another option. Boat rentals and a seasonal snack bar are available at the park, but bring your own water. Wear sunscreen, remember that the altitude intensifies the sun, and take care on the rocks, which are slippery when wet.
t.lake alpine@38.5,-120.0:
Lake Alpine is a high, clear reservoir in the Sierra Nevada, about 2,200 metres above sea level, and it sits like a cupped hand among granite and lodgepole pine. Highway 4 runs along its edge, and for a few months of the year it is a delightful stop: a lodge with a deck, a small boat ramp, and a view down the water to bare rock. It is the sort of place where you take your helmet off, buy a cold drink, and for a few minutes forget that the road beyond is a serious one.

The ride up from the west, from Arnold and Bear Valley, is gentle at first, with sweeping bends through tall conifers, but the road beyond the lake gets narrower, steeper and rougher. It is the western approach to the Ebbetts Pass Scenic Byway, which crosses the Sierra at nearly 2,700 metres, and the sections east of here are among the toughest paved ones in California. The lake is a good place to prepare: top up with water, tighten your luggage and check your brakes. The surface up to Alpine is generally good, with the occasional frost heave, and traffic is light.

The climate shapes everything. Winter snow is deep, and Highway 4 is closed east of the Bear Valley area from late autumn until spring, usually until at least May, and sometimes into June. In summer the days are warm and bright and the nights cold, and afternoon thunderstorms drift over the crest. The lake is fed by snowmelt and is cold enough to take your breath away if you wade in. Spring flowers appear late and in a rush, and in autumn the aspens turn gold along the creek.

The surrounding region was gold country on the western slope and silver on the eastern side, and the old wagon routes across the mountains were rough and slow. Today the main business is recreation: fishing, camping, hiking the Pacific Crest Trail section nearby, and in winter cross-country skiing around Bear Valley.

Fuel is not available at the lake. Arnold, about forty kilometres back, has petrol and supermarkets, and so does Murphys further west, while Bear Valley village has a few small shops. On the east side, Markleeville and Gardnerville have fuel. Fill up in Arnold, carry some food, and enjoy the lake before the climb.
t.ebbetts pass@38.5,-119.8:
Ebbetts Pass is one of the narrowest, steepest and least-visited paved passes in the Sierra Nevada, and for that reason it is a favourite with riders who like their mountains a bit raw. It tops out at 2,663 metres, on Highway 4 between the western foothills and the eastern desert, and the road that climbs it is a patchwork of single-lane sections, tight hairpins, steep gradients and rough surfaces. It was named for Major John Ebbetts, who explored the route in the 1850s hoping to find a place for a railway, and the railway never came, which is why the road is the way it is.

The east side is the steeper and the more dramatic. The road clings to the mountainside, with grades that reach well over ten percent in places, and the lanes are so narrow that oncoming cars can feel like a negotiation. There are stretches with no centre line, no guard rail, and long drops, and the road passes the high, bare ridges of the Carson-Iceberg country and the emerald water of the Kinney Reservoirs. Take it slowly, stay well to the right on the blind bends, and use engine braking on the descent. Caravans and trailers are discouraged, and for good reason.

The pass is open only in summer, usually from late May or June until the first big snows, and storms can bring ice or snow at any time of the year. Summer is warm during the day and cool at night, and afternoon thunderstorms are possible. The high country is full of granite, wildflower meadows and small lakes, and Pacific Crest Trail hikers cross the road nearby, so watch for them. The summit itself is a quiet saddle, with a sign and a view over snow patches into the next valley.

There is nothing at the pass. Fuel and food are in Markleeville to the east, a tiny county seat with a few cafes and a famous cycling event, or at Gardnerville in the Carson Valley, which is bigger. On the west side, Arnold is the last good place. Keep a close eye on your fuel gauge, because distances are long, and carry water. If you can, choose a weekday and an early start, so you meet few other vehicles and have the light behind you in the afternoon.
t.markleeville@38.7,-119.8:
Markleeville is the seat of Alpine County, which has fewer residents than any other county in California, and the town feels like a mountain hamlet that has never been in a hurry. A few hundred people live along the East Fork of the Carson River, with a courthouse, a small museum, a general store, two or three cafes and the rest hidden in pine and aspen. At around fifty-five hundred feet, in the eastern Sierra, the air is clear and cool, and the sound of the river runs through the village.

The place was created by the mining boom of the 1860s, when silver was found in the nearby hills, and the town was named after Jacob Marklee, an early settler. The boom was short, and by the 1880s most of the miners had moved on, leaving ghost camps and shafts in the woods. Today, the main business is recreation, with hiking, fishing, skiing in winter, and the hot springs of Grover Hot Springs State Park, a few miles to the west, where a pool fed by natural springs sits in a meadow below high peaks and is open all year.

Cyclists know the town for the Death Ride, a one-day event held each July in which thousands of cyclists climb five mountain passes in a single day. In the same way, motorcyclists enjoy the passes, because the roads are lightly trafficked and demanding. From the west, the ride over Ebbetts Pass descends in a sequence of tight bends along the river, and here the road widens, becomes smoother and sweeps into the valley. Monitor Pass, to the north, is another wonderful road, with big sagebrush views toward Nevada.

Supplies are limited, so bring a full tank. The town has a small station, but the larger town of Gardnerville is about twenty-two kilometres to the east in Nevada, and has everything you need. Weather can change quickly, with summer storms, cold nights and snow in the cooler months, so pack extra layers. Late September is a lovely time, when the aspens along the creek turn gold and the crowds are gone. At night, the sky is dark and clear, and the Milky Way is often visible.
t.dardanelle@38.3,-119.8:
Dardanelle is a bend in the Stanislaus River and a name on the map, and it is the last place of any size before Highway 108 starts to climb in earnest. The name comes from the Dardanelles, a long line of dark volcanic cliffs on the ridge above, which early travellers thought resembled the straits of the same name in Turkey. The cliffs are the remains of mudflows from ancient volcanoes, and they give the upper canyon a rugged, castellated look that you notice as soon as the trees open up.

At about 1,700 metres, this is a mountain community of cabins, a small resort and campgrounds by the river, in a forest of pine and fir with cold, clean water running through it. The air smells of resin and wet stone. For riders it is a natural pause on the way up, a place to adjust layers, since the temperature drops steadily as you climb, and to look at what you are about to do. Highway 108 beyond here is a proper mountain road, with narrower lanes, steeper grades and tight switchbacks, culminating in Sonora Pass at nearly 3,000 metres.

The road along the Stanislaus is lovely. It follows the river upstream from Strawberry in a series of rolling curves, with the water close at hand and big granite outcrops above, and the traffic is generally thin outside holiday weekends. Spring snowmelt makes the river loud, and in autumn the aspens colour the roadside. The road is closed by snow in winter, usually from about November until May or June, so check the conditions before you set out. Summer thunderstorms are common in the afternoon.

The region was Miwok country long before gold diggers arrived in the 1840s, and later the mountain roads were pushed over the Sierra by miners and ranchers heading east to the Nevada silver towns. The route over Sonora Pass was a wagon road in the 1860s, and it has never really lost its rough edges.

Dardanelle has a small store and seasonal services, but they are limited, and you should not assume there is fuel. Sonora, the big town on the foothills side, and Twain Harte have petrol stations, and Pinecrest is another stop nearby. Fill up before you start the climb, carry water and warm clothes, and check your brakes. On the east side, Bridgeport is the next fuel, some eighty kilometres away by road, which is a long gap if you are running low.
t.sonora pass@38.3,-119.6:
Say Sonora Pass to a Californian rider and watch for the pause. At 2,933 metres it is the second highest road over the Sierra Nevada, after Tioga, and it has a reputation for its gradients: the stretches on the eastern side are rated at around twenty-six percent, which is the sort of number that makes you check your clutch cable. Lanes are narrow, guard rails are rare and the edges are dramatic. It is not the place to try your first mountain pass, but it is a wonderful one to graduate to.

The western approach climbs in long, steady sweeps from the Stanislaus canyon, through fir forest and then into open granite country with big volcanic cliffs hanging above. Near the top the trees thin, the air chills and the road squeezes through a gap between two pale ridges. The summit is a simple saddle with a sign, a gravel pull-out and a view that looks like the end of the world. On the eastern side the road drops in a series of tight hairpins and steep descents toward the Walker River, with the Great Basin spreading below like a map. Trailers longer than about twenty-five feet are banned, and no one with a caravan should be tempted to try.

The pass takes its name from the Mexican miners from Sonora who flooded into the foothills during the Gold Rush, and gave their name to the foothill town on the western side. A wagon road crossed the summit in the 1860s, linking the gold camps with the Nevada silver towns. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road close to the top, and walkers often camp in the meadows nearby. A little further down the east side, the Marine Corps runs a mountain warfare training centre, which accounts for the occasional convoy and the sound of helicopters.

The road is open only in summer, typically from late May or June until the first snow in October or November, and there is almost nothing along it. Bridgeport, about 36 kilometres from the summit on the Nevada side, is the nearest real settlement, with fuel, a courthouse and a couple of places to eat, and Sonora is the large town on the western side. Check fuel before leaving either, carry layers, and start early, since afternoon thunderstorms are routine. The best light comes late in the day, as the sun drops behind the crest and the eastern slopes turn gold.
t.bridgeport@38.3,-119.2:
Bridgeport is a small, sun-baked county seat in the eastern Sierra, at the edge of a high valley of sagebrush and meadow, ringed by snow-capped peaks. Fewer than six hundred people live here, at an elevation of about sixty-five hundred feet, and the main street along Highway 395 is a short row of cafes, motels, a store and a stately white courthouse. That courthouse, built in 1880 in a Victorian style with a cupola, is one of the oldest in California still in use, and gives the town a quiet dignity.

The valley's history is tied to mining and ranching. In the 1860s, the gold and silver strikes at Bodie, about thirteen miles to the north-east, drew thousands to the high desert, and Bridgeport became a supply town for the camps. Bodie is now a ghost town in a state of arrested decay, with the buildings left as they were when the mine closed, and is a state historic park. The road to it is partly unpaved, and the town is a long, strange step into the past.

For those arriving from Sonora Pass, the descent into the east side is a revelation. The road drops from the forested west slope into a dry, open landscape of sagebrush, rock and big skies, and the temperature rises sharply. Highway 395 follows the valley, with the Sierra crest on the west and the Nevada desert on the east, and runs smooth and fast, with long straights and gentle bends. Wind can be strong, and weather changes quickly, with the odd summer thunderstorm and snow in winter.

Bridgeport has fuel and basic services, plus a few places to eat, and the nearby Bridgeport Reservoir is a favourite for fishing. Hot springs scattered through the area, including Travertine Hot Springs just south of town, are good for a soak after a day on the road. The scenery is at its best in autumn, when aspens glow along the creeks and the air is crisp. In the evening, the light on the mountains is warm, and the town goes quiet early.
t.fresno@36.7,-119.8:
Fresno is the biggest city of California's Central Valley, a flat, sunburnt metropolis of over half a million people surrounded by some of the most productive farmland in the world. Raisins, almonds, grapes, figs, peaches and oranges all come from this valley, and the city was once the raisin capital of the world, a distinction it still takes some pride in. In summer it can be brutally hot, with temperatures above forty degrees Celsius for days at a time, while in winter, a thick ground fog known as tule fog sometimes hangs over the roads for days.

The city has a layered history. Basque, Armenian, Portuguese, Hmong, Punjabi and Mexican communities have all left a mark, and you can taste it in the restaurants, from Armenian bakeries to taquerias and Basque dinners. The Tower District, with its old art deco theatre, is the lively quarter, and the Forestiere Underground Gardens, a maze of tunnels and sunken orchards dug by an Italian immigrant, Baldassare Forestiere, to escape the summer heat, is a strange and delightful curiosity.

The ride begins on Highway 180, the Kings Canyon Scenic Byway, which leaves the flat farmland and quickly rises into the Sierra foothills, passing orange groves, then oak woodland and finally pine and fir forest. The road climbs in broad bends, with the temperature dropping steadily, until it reaches Grant Grove, home of the General Grant Tree, one of the largest living things on Earth. Beyond it, the road dips into the deep canyon of the Kings River, one of the deepest in North America. It is about fifty miles from Fresno to the park gate and beyond, so allow plenty of time.

Fill the tank in Fresno, as supplies are limited above the foothills, and take plenty of water, especially in summer, when the valley is a furnace. Start early to beat the heat, and the haze that often hangs over the valley. In spring, the orchards bloom pink and white, and the foothills are green. Autumn is clear and pleasant, and the high country is at its most beautiful. Be prepared for a big change in temperature as you climb, and bring a jacket.
t.grant grove@36.7,-119.0:
The first big tree you meet here is a surprise because it looks like a building. The General Grant Tree, in the grove that bears its name, is about 270 feet tall and nearly 30 feet across at the base, and by volume it is the second largest tree on Earth, after the General Sherman a few miles south. It is somewhere around 1,700 years old. President Coolidge named it the Nation's Christmas Tree in 1926, and it was later declared a national shrine to those who died in war, and each December a ceremony is held at its foot. It stands in a quiet loop of giant sequoias and fallen logs, a short walk from the visitor centre.

Highway 180, the Kings Canyon Scenic Byway, takes you up from Fresno through orange groves and oak foothills, then climbs into the conifers and through the entrance of Kings Canyon National Park. The upper part of the road is a pleasant, winding ascent through pine and fir, and in the grove itself the road narrows and the speed limit drops. This is not a technical ride, but the bends are good, the surface is decent and the air smells of cedar. Mornings are best, before the tourist buses arrive, and in spring and autumn the temperatures are comfortable.

The grove was protected in 1890, making General Grant National Park one of the earliest in the country, before it was absorbed into Kings Canyon in 1940. The preservation of these trees owes much to a campaign by local residents and conservationists who feared that logging companies would cut them down, and indeed, many of the neighbouring sequoias were felled in the 1880s, and stumps still dot the area. Look for the Big Stump basin near the entrance, a graveyard of huge stumps that shows what happened. Sequoias have thick, fire-resistant bark and rely on fire to open their cones, so the park uses prescribed burns to keep the forest healthy.

Grant Grove Village has a visitor centre, a lodge, a restaurant and a small market. Fuel is a more difficult matter, since there is none at the grove, and services inside the park are limited, so fill up before you leave the foothills. Squaw Valley and Dunlap, near the road to the mountains, have petrol, and Fresno has all the rest. A park entry fee applies. Snow is common in winter, and chains may be required, so check before you go.
t.kings canyon overlook@36.8,-118.7:
Highway 180 east of Grant Grove does something rare: it goes down. After the sequoias and the climb through the high forest, the road begins to descend into the canyon of the Kings River, and at a series of overlooks above the gorge you can see how steep the descent will be. The canyon is among the deepest in North America, plunging from ridge crests over three thousand metres to a valley floor less than half that height, and the walls are cliffs of granite, streaked with water stains and dotted with pines.

The road down is an engineering effort, shelved into the canyon wall with tight bends, guard walls and a drop beside you. It is a joy to ride, as the bends are wide enough and the surface is good, but the exposure is real and the descent is long, so use engine braking and keep to your side. The views change at every corner, from the white spray of waterfalls in spring to the glinting river at the bottom. At the end, the road reaches Cedar Grove, a quiet valley with meadows and a campground, and finally stops at a place called Road's End, where the trails begin. In the early morning, mist fills the valley and the light spills slowly down the cliffs.

The glaciers that carved the canyon are long gone, but their work is visible in the polished granite, the U-shaped sections and the hanging valleys. John Muir visited and compared the place with Yosemite, and some people prefer this one precisely because it is quieter. Black bears live in the area and are used to people, which means campers must store food carefully. Mule deer graze along the road in the evening.

The road beyond Grant Grove is closed in winter, generally from about November to April, because of snow and rockfall, so check conditions. In summer it is hot in the bottom of the canyon and the temperature difference between rim and floor can be thirty degrees. The small store and restaurant at Cedar Grove open seasonally, but I would not rely on them for petrol. Fill up in the foothills before you start, and carry water. If you are returning the same way, remember the climb back is steady and demands a bit more throttle.
t.cedar grove@36.8,-118.7:
Cedar Grove is at the bottom of Kings Canyon, a deep, glacier-carved trench in the Sierra Nevada that John Muir compared to Yosemite, and it feels like the end of the world in the best sense. The road runs out a few miles beyond, at a place called Road's End, where the Kings River rolls past and trails lead into some of the wildest country in the lower forty-eight. The valley floor is at about forty-six hundred feet, framed by granite walls that rise thousands of feet, and the air smells of pine and river water.

The canyon walls are among the highest in North America, with the rim rising far above the floor, and the combination of scale and quiet is humbling. Zumwalt Meadow, a green lawn along the river beneath a sheer granite cliff, makes a lovely short walk, and Roaring River Falls, close to the road, throws up spray in early summer. Black bears wander the valley, and it is important to keep food locked away. The Kings River, fed by snowmelt, is cold and fast.

The road in is the highlight. Highway 180 descends from Grant Grove into the canyon in a long sequence of curves, with sweeping views of the river far below and the high peaks beyond. The surface is generally good, but the road is narrow in places, there are steep drop-offs, and rock falls can occur. Because of heavy snow, the road is closed in winter, usually from November until April or May, and the facilities at Cedar Grove operate only in the warmer months. Check conditions before you go.

Services here are seasonal and limited, with a small store, a lodge and a campground, and I would not count on fuel, so fill the tank in Fresno or on the way up. It is a long way to anywhere else, and mobile coverage is poor. Be prepared for summer heat on the valley floor, with cool nights, and carry water. Late September and early October are a lovely time, with cool air, golden light and fewer visitors. Take it easy on the road, since wildlife and cyclists are about.
t.yosemite valley@37.7,-119.5:
Yosemite Valley is a mile-wide trench cut into the granite of the Sierra Nevada, with walls that rise three thousand feet or more from the flat, meadow-covered floor, and it is as astonishing in person as in any photograph. El Capitan, a sheer, blank face, stands on the north side, Half Dome, a sliced dome of granite, towers at the head, and waterfalls drop from the rim, most dramatically Yosemite Falls, which falls nearly twenty-five hundred feet in three stages. The Merced River winds through the meadows below.

Glaciers carved the valley's U-shape during the ice ages, working on a landscape of granite that had been uplifted and cracked. The Ahwahneechee people lived here for generations before settlers arrived, and they were driven out by a militia in 1851. In 1864, President Lincoln signed a grant that protected the valley, an early step in the national park idea, and John Muir, who came in 1868, argued for protection of the surrounding high country. Ansel Adams spent a lifetime photographing it, and his pictures helped to define the American idea of wilderness.

Tioga Road leaves the western end of the park at Crane Flat and climbs eastward over the Sierra, and in summer riders often start at the valley and take the road to the high country. The valley itself is slow, with heavy traffic, one-way loops, low speed limits and crowds of visitors, so expect delays, and in busy seasons the park has needed advance reservations for entry, so look at the park website before you set out. Parking is tight, but motorcycles can often squeeze into small spaces.

The valley has restaurants, a grocery store and lodging, but it is crowded and busy at weekends. Waterfalls are at their best in May and June, when snowmelt feeds them, and often dry up by late summer. Black bears are active, so lock food away. Spring and autumn, with fewer visitors and crisp air, are the best times, and early morning light on the cliffs is wonderful.
t.olmsted point@37.8,-119.5:
Olmsted Point is where you finally see the back of Half Dome, and it is a shock. From the valley floor, Half Dome is a sheer-faced icon; from here, several miles away, it is a smooth, rounded profile, set at the far end of the long granite trench of Tenaya Canyon. The overlook is on the Tioga Road, a wide, flat shelf of pale glacier-polished granite, and in front of you the rock rolls off in great bare slabs toward the canyon, with giant boulders sitting about on it like dropped marbles.

These are glacial erratics, rocks carried by ice and left stranded when the glaciers melted. The Tuolumne glacier that once filled this country was thousands of feet thick, and it scoured the granite smooth, leaving scratches and polish that are still visible. The landscape is almost lunar, with scattered, wind-bent pines and tufts of grass in the cracks. The viewpoint is named for Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who designed Central Park, and his son of the same name, who both took an interest in Yosemite's protection.

The road here, Highway 120, is the Tioga Road, built in the 1880s as a mining track, then rebuilt as a proper highway in the twentieth century. It is a long and graceful ride, with sweeping bends through red fir and lodgepole forest, then open stretches along granite domes. The surface is excellent, the traffic can be heavy in summer, and the speed limit is low. Oncoming tour buses are a fact of life. The road is open only in summer, usually from late May or June until the first big snow, and can close abruptly in autumn. At about 2,400 metres the air is crisp, and nights are cold.

Fuel is available at Crane Flat, to the west, and at Tuolumne Meadows, to the east, in summer, though both can run short on busy days, and Lee Vining, beyond the pass, has more. Park entry is paid at the gate, and in some seasons a reservation is needed. Bring a layer even on a hot day, because the wind on the granite can bite, and walk carefully on the polished rock, which is slippery when wet. The best light is in the late afternoon.
t.tenaya lake@37.8,-119.5:
Tenaya Lake lies right beside the Tioga Road at about 2,500 metres, a long, bright, glacier-carved basin ringed by polished granite domes, and it is one of the few places in Yosemite where you can park, walk thirty steps and be sitting on a beach with a mountain view. The water is startlingly clear and cold, and on a still morning the domes and pines are reflected in it so perfectly that it is hard to tell which way up the picture goes. A fine sandy beach sits at the eastern end and a smaller one at the west, and in summer people swim, if briefly.

The lake was named for Chief Tenaya, the leader of the Ahwahneechee people who lived in Yosemite Valley, whom the Mariposa Battalion pursued here in 1851. The story of the first non-native visit to Yosemite is a dark one, and the Ahwahneechee were driven out. Whatever the details, this was Ahwahneechee ground, and it is worth remembering when you arrive.

The ride is among the best in the Sierra. The Tioga Road runs along the north shore in gentle curves, past big domes and boulders, with the water flashing through the trees. The road is smooth and the views are great, and though the speed limit is low, the ride feels like a sort of floating. Weather can change fast, and afternoon thunderstorms are possible, so early starts are better. At this height the nights are cold even in August, and ice can form on the lake margins in September. In winter the road is closed, and the lake freezes and disappears under snow.

Parking at the lake can be crowded in summer, and the shoulder fills with cars. Tuolumne Meadows, about ten kilometres east, has a seasonal store, a grill and a fuel station, and Crane Flat to the west has another. Bring water, a hat and sunscreen, because the sun at 2,500 metres burns fast, and stay away from the slippery granite near the water.
t.tuolumne meadows@37.9,-119.4:
Tuolumne Meadows is the largest subalpine meadow in the Sierra Nevada, a wide, grassy bowl at about 2,600 metres along the Tuolumne River, ringed by granite domes and peaks. In the early morning the grass is silver with frost even in summer, and mist hangs on the river, and the sun comes up over Lembert Dome and the long, bare ridge of Cathedral Peak. It is a favourite with climbers, walkers and photographers, and the car parks and campgrounds are busy from July to September.

John Muir came here in the 1860s and 1870s and wrote about the meadows and domes with great enthusiasm, and in 1889, he and Robert Underwood Johnson sat in this meadow and planned the campaign to make Yosemite a national park. It was established the following year, and the meadows are a good reason why. The river is clear and fast, carving its way through granite, with pools and cascades that make good places for a break. Marmots whistle on the rocks, and deer graze at dusk, and you may see a black bear if you are not careful about your food.

The Tioga Road passes through the meadows on the way to the pass, and the ride is a gentle, rolling affair. The road is level here, running beside the river, with the domes on the left and wide views to the south, and it is a good moment to relax after the climbs from the west. The surface is good, and the speed limit is low, with cyclists and walkers crossing at the visitor centre. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, with lightning on the domes, so aim to be gone by early afternoon if the sky looks dark. Mosquitoes in July can be fierce.

Tuolumne has a grill, a store and a gas station, all seasonal and usually busy, a visitor centre, a campground and a high sierra camp, but supplies can run short, so plan ahead. Yosemite Valley is about 24 kilometres away in a straight line, but a long way by road, and the nearest town of any size, Mammoth Lakes, is beyond the pass. Park entry is by fee, and the road closes with winter snow. Fill up when you can, and bring warm layers.
t.tioga pass@37.9,-119.3:
Tioga Pass is the highest highway pass in California, at 3,031 metres, and it is the eastern gate to Yosemite. A small park sign, a ranger kiosk and a stony meadow mark the top, with snowbanks lingering into July and the peaks of the Sierra crest rising to either side. It feels like the edge of something, and it is: on the east side the road drops about 3,000 feet in a dozen miles to the high desert of Mono Lake and the Great Basin, a change of climate and scenery as abrupt as any in North America.

The road down the eastern side is a classic. Tioga Road becomes Highway 120 and plunges through Lee Vining Canyon in a series of tight bends and hairpins, with steep walls, big drops and the blue of Ellery Lake flashing below. Further down, the whole eastern plain opens, with Mono Lake, a vast, salty, alkaline lake dotted with strange tufa towers, spread like a mirror. The road is narrow in places, the surface is good, and the traffic is heavy at weekends. Riders love it for the climb, the change in scenery and the sense of arrival. It is also very cold at the top, even in August, and thunderstorms and sleet can arrive without warning.

The road was first built in the 1880s to reach a silver mine, and then bought by Stephen Mather, the first director of the National Park Service, who paid to have it made public in 1915. The route is closed by snow from about November until late May or June, and its opening is a minor local event. Check conditions before you set out, and be prepared to turn around.

There are no services at the pass itself, other than a small, seasonal resort with a cafe just below the summit on the east side, a favourite for pie and coffee. Fuel is available at Lee Vining, about twenty kilometres east, and Tuolumne Meadows, farther west, in season. Mammoth Lakes, about 38 kilometres away, has everything. Fill up in Lee Vining before riding west, carry layers and enjoy the thin, bright air. The park charges an entrance fee, and the altitude can leave you breathless.
t.lee vining@38.0,-119.1:
Lee Vining is a tiny town on the eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, at the foot of Tioga Pass and the edge of Mono Lake, and it is the eastern gateway to Yosemite. At nearly seven thousand feet, with a few hundred residents, it has a main street along Highway 395 of cafes, motels, gas stations and a store, a mountain town with a desert view. The air is dry and sharp, and the light, bright and clear, is the kind that makes the mountains look cut out of paper.

Mono Lake, just below the town, is one of the oldest lakes in North America, at least seven hundred and sixty thousand years old, and it has no outlet, so the salts and minerals carried by the streams have built up over time, making the water salty and alkaline. Calcium-rich springs bubbling up beneath the surface have built tufa towers, strange, pale pinnacles that were exposed when the lake level dropped. Brine shrimp and alkali flies feed millions of migratory birds, and thousands of California gulls nest on the islands.

The lake has a political history too. In 1941, Los Angeles began diverting the streams that fed it to supply the city's water, and the level dropped by forty-five feet, exposing the tufa and threatening the birds. A citizens' campaign, which began in the late 1970s, took the city to court, and in 1994 the state ordered the diversions reduced, allowing the lake to recover partly. The story is a landmark of environmental activism, and a visitor centre in the town tells it well.

The Tioga Road climbs from here to Tioga Pass, at about ninety-nine hundred feet the highest highway pass in California, with a steep climb up Lee Vining Canyon in a series of bends and switchbacks, then enters Yosemite National Park, the way to meadows, lakes and granite domes. The road is usually closed by snow from November to late May, and the opening date varies. There is fuel in Lee Vining, and it is sensible to fill up here, as there are very few services on the high road. Mammoth Lakes, about thirty-seven kilometres south, is the larger town. Dress warmly, and watch for thunderstorms in summer.
t.death valley junction@36.3,-116.4:
Death Valley Junction is barely a place at all: a crossroads in the Amargosa Desert where California 127 meets the road that leads west into the national park, and a cluster of old Spanish-revival buildings left over from the borax days. The Pacific Coast Borax company built the town in the 1920s as a railway hub on the Tonopah and Tidewater line, and when the trains stopped, the place slid toward ghost status. What saved it is one of the odder stories in the desert. In 1967 a New York dancer named Marta Becket had a flat tyre here, peeked into the shabby community hall, and decided to stay. She restored the building as the Amargosa Opera House and performed there for decades, painting the walls with an audience of imaginary spectators. The hotel next door is still open, and the whole thing has a haunted-theatre charm that makes the desert feel stranger than usual.

For a rider, this is the doorstep rather than the destination. The terrain around here is open basin and range country: pale flats, dark ridges, a sky that fills most of the view, and the Funeral Mountains on the horizon to the west. Wind can be fierce, with gusts across the flats that shove a bike sideways, and summer heat is serious. Between June and September, temperatures can pass forty degrees Celsius in the early afternoon, so start at dawn, carry plenty of water, and treat the stretch to the park as a place where breakdowns have consequences. Winter nights can drop below freezing, and spring brings wildflowers in good years.

Services are almost nonexistent, which is the practical point. The nearest proper town is Pahrump, about forty kilometres away on the Nevada side, and that is where you should buy fuel and food. Inside the park, you will find fuel at Furnace Creek and Stovepipe Wells, but expect desert prices. Cell coverage is patchy, so tell someone your plan.

From here, the road drops through a gap in the Funeral Mountains toward Furnace Creek, passing viewpoints like Zabriskie Point, where golden badlands erode into folds, and the turn for Dante's View, which looks down on the salt flats from a mile up. The land below you is the lowest in North America. A short detour to Badwater, more than eighty metres below sea level, is easy to make and always a little surreal.

Take the opera house photo, check your tyre pressure, and go.
t.dantes view@36.2,-116.7:
Dante's View is the place to stand when you want to understand Death Valley in one glance. From a cliff on the crest of the Black Mountains, at about five thousand five hundred feet, you look straight down on the salt flats of Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America at 282 feet below sea level. Across the valley rise the Panamint Mountains, with the snow-capped summit of Telescope Peak, over eleven thousand feet, facing you. The difference in height between the two is almost two miles, and the view is a kind of geology lesson in a single frame.

The road up is a spur of about thirteen miles from the main highway near Furnace Creek, climbing steadily and then more steeply through the rugged Black Mountains. It is paved and well-maintained, with a few tight bends near the top, and the views grow with every turn. Large trailers and long vehicles are restricted near the top, but a motorcycle copes easily. The air at the lookout is noticeably cooler than on the valley floor, which can be a relief in summer, and the wind can be strong, so a windproof layer is wise.

The valley itself is a place of extremes. The hottest air temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth, about 134 degrees Fahrenheit, was measured at Furnace Creek in 1913. It is also very dry, with only a couple of inches of rain a year, though when storms do come they produce spectacular flash floods. Despite appearances, the park supports a surprising amount of life, from desert bighorn sheep on the slopes to the tiny pupfish that survive in isolated pools.

Furnace Creek, Stovepipe Wells, and Panamint Springs have pumps, and the sensible rule is to fill whenever you pass one. Carry plenty of water, wear sunscreen, and plan to ride in the cooler hours. Winter and early spring are by far the best seasons. Sunrise and sunset are the best times at Dante's View, when the light turns the salt flats pale gold and the mountains purple, and the silence is almost physical.
t.badwater basin@36.2,-116.8:
Badwater is not a place you stay long, but it is one you remember. A boardwalk leads out from a small parking area to a shallow pond, and beyond it stretch the salt flats, a white and crusted plain that reaches miles toward the opposite mountains. The sign on the cliff above marks sea level, a long way overhead. You are standing at 282 feet below it, the lowest point in North America, and the sun reflects off the salt with a brightness that makes sunglasses essential.

The name comes from a surveyor's story, in which a mule would not drink from the pool because the water was salty and bitter. The water is in fact full of dissolved minerals, washed down from the surrounding hills and concentrated by evaporation, and the salt crust forms intricate polygon patterns where the surface dries. Tiny snails and a few unusual insects live in the pools, which makes this an odd and delicate ecosystem. Walk on the boardwalk and a short way beyond, and avoid damaging the crust.

The ride to Badwater runs along the valley floor on Badwater Road, a well-surfaced highway that gets almost no shade. The riding is easy, with long straight stretches and gentle curves, and the scenery dominates: the Black Mountains on one side, the salt flats and Panamints on the other. Heat is the issue. In summer, temperatures can exceed forty-five degrees Celsius, and the pavement itself is scorching, so ride in the early morning or late afternoon and carry far more water than seems necessary. Never ignore heat exhaustion; it creeps up on riders more quickly than they expect.

Furnace Creek, about seventeen miles north, is the nearest place with pumps, a store, and a restaurant, and it is wise to fill up there and check your reserves. The best time to visit is in winter or early spring, when the days are warm rather than hot, and the dawn light across the flats is exceptional. Wildflowers sometimes bloom in a wet year, and the sight of the salt flat under a rare pool of water, reflecting the mountains, is hard to forget.
t.artists palette@36.3,-116.8:
The hills along Artist's Drive look as though someone has spilled a paint box over them. Pink, green, mauve, copper, and yellow streak the slopes in bands, and the colours shift with the light: dull at midday, glowing at dusk. At the high point of the drive, a viewpoint named Artists Palette gathers the best of it, with the multi-coloured hillside facing the road and the valley floor stretching away below.

The colours are chemistry. The hills are made of volcanic ash and sediment, and various metals have oxidised in them over time. Iron compounds give the reds, pinks, and yellows, mica produces a pale green, and manganese gives purple and lavender. Together they make a natural pigment chart, and the effect is greatest in the late afternoon, when the low sun intensifies each tone. Photographers come for this reason, and it is the one place in the park where a polarising filter does something miraculous.

Artists Drive is a nine-mile one-way loop, paved, narrow, and winding, leaving Badwater Road at the south end and rejoining it a little farther north. It is a short, lively ride, with dips, bends, and steep little rises, and the corners are tighter than anywhere else on the valley floor. Long vehicles are not allowed, but a bike has no problem. Watch for sand and gravel washed onto the road after storms, and for the occasional tourist stopping suddenly. Ride it slowly, because the point is the colour, not the speed.

Bring water, and carry more than you think necessary. In summer the heat is dangerous, and even in winter the sun can be strong. The best season is from November to March, and the best time of day is late afternoon, when the colours deepen and the temperature falls. If there has been rain, the hills can have a fresh brightness, and a rare wildflower bloom can add yet another colour to the palette.
t.zabriskie point@36.4,-116.8:
Zabriskie Point is the place that photographers drive to before dawn, and that most people see in the afternoon, and both are right. A short, steep path leads from the car park to a rocky platform that looks out over a landscape of eroded golden mudstone, ridged and folded like some enormous crumpled blanket. Beyond it the Panamint Range rises, and in the early light the whole badland glows in shades of honey and cream.

The badlands are the remains of an ancient lake bed. Millions of years ago, the region held a lake, and sediment from the surrounding mountains settled in layers on its floor. Later, the land was uplifted and torn apart, and rain carved the soft layers into the folds and gullies you see now. Borax, the mineral that made Death Valley economically important, was mined from similar deposits nearby, and the famous twenty-mule teams hauled it out across the desert in the 1880s. The point itself is named for Christian Brevoort Zabriskie, an executive of the company that ran the mines.

The road to the point is a spur off Highway 190, east of Furnace Creek, and it is short and easy. The main highway heading east climbs out of the valley with long, open bends, and the contrast between the stark badlands and the vast sky is very strong. It is a straightforward ride, with good surface and clear sightlines, though sand can drift across the pavement and the heat in summer is punishing. Italian director Michelangelo Antonioni gave the point a second life in a 1970 film of the same name, though the story has little to do with the place.

Furnace Creek, only a few miles away, has fuel, a store, and food, so it is the sensible base. Expect crowds at sunrise and sunset, and arrive early to get a good place on the platform. The light changes quickly, so be patient: the best colours often arrive a few minutes after you think you have seen them all. Wind and cold can catch riders out in winter mornings, so bring an extra layer. In summer, ride in the first hours of the day and rest in the shade when the heat arrives.
t.stovepipe wells@36.6,-117.1:
Stovepipe Wells takes its name from a scrap of iron and a bit of desperation. The story is that early prospectors, crossing the sand dunes here, found it hard to locate the one reliable well in all the shifting hummocks, so they stuck a length of stovepipe in the ground to mark the spot. It is a good detail, and the place has leaned into it ever since. Today, Stovepipe Wells is a small village with a motel, a general store, a restaurant, a ranger station, and a pump, set on the northwest edge of the great salt basin of Death Valley, with the Cottonwood Mountains behind and the pale Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes a few kilometres to the northeast.

Those dunes are the real attraction, and worth a walk at sunrise or sunset when the light rakes across the ripples and the heat is bearable. They are not huge by world standards, but they are photogenic, with mesquite bushes stubbornly holding on at the edges, and they show tracks of beetles, lizards and kit foxes in the morning. A little farther west, Mosaic Canyon cuts into polished marble and breccia, a short rough road away.

The road through here is California 190, and it is the best stretch of the Death Valley crossing for a rider. To the east, the road drops over a long, smooth ramp toward Furnace Creek, past the lowest places in the country. To the west, it climbs through Towne Pass at about fifteen hundred metres, with a series of broad, fast curves and views back over the salt flats, then drops again into the Panamint Valley. The surface is generally good, the traffic is light outside the winter holidays, and the wind can be heavy. Summer is brutal, with temperatures that regularly exceed forty-five degrees. The hottest air temperature ever recorded on earth, nearly fifty-seven degrees Celsius, was measured at Furnace Creek in July 1913. In winter, it is cool and clear, and the best season by far is from October to April.

Fuel is available here, but it is pricey, as you would expect when the nearest large town is a long way off. If you have a choice, fill up before you arrive, and always carry water. The store has cold drinks, ice and a few supplies, and the village is a decent place to eat and rest in the shade.

Sit on the porch and watch the heat shimmer over the flats. It is a reminder that this place does not forgive carelessness.
t.valmayor v@40.8,0.2:
The Matarraña, in the far east of Teruel province, is often called the Tuscany of Aragon, and for once the comparison holds. Stone villages crown hilltops above olive groves and vineyards, rivers run clear through limestone gorges, and the light in the evening is honey-coloured. Valmayor is a ravine in the hills here, between Valderrobres, Fuentespalda and the Catalan border, and its shelters hold prehistoric paintings, part of the UNESCO-listed Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin. As elsewhere, they are protected, and visits are best arranged through local tourist offices.

Valderrobres, a dozen kilometres away, is the obvious base, a village of two thousand people with a medieval bridge over the Matarraña river, a Gothic castle and church crowning the hill above, and narrow lanes winding between them. It is one of the most photographed villages in Aragon, and rightly so. The area is popular with walkers, cyclists and climbers, who come for the gorges and the Els Ports massif to the south, where Iberian ibex graze on ledges above the river at Beceite.

The riding is superb. Narrow roads twist through the hills between villages like Beceite, Cretas, Calaceite and Fuentespalda, with constantly changing views, very little traffic outside holidays, and surfaces that are mostly good. Further south, the Els Ports massif offers more dramatic mountain roads, and east, across the border into Catalonia, the Terra Alta wine region and the Ebro valley around Tortosa open up.

Services are limited in the smaller villages, so plan fuel carefully; Valderrobres has a station, and Alcañiz and Tortosa are the nearest larger towns. The local food is hearty and full of flavour: Teruel ham, olive oil from the Matarraña's own designation, lamb, and the local almonds. Peaches from Calanda, just to the west, are bagged on the tree to protect them and sold in September with their own designation of origin. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the weather is mild, the light clear and the hills fragrant with rosemary.
t.val del charco del agua amarga@41.1,0.0:
Around ten kilometres from Alcañiz, in a dry ravine among olive groves and limestone ledges, a rock shelter holds one of the most celebrated scenes of Levantine rock art in Spain. The paintings at Val del Charco del Agua Amarga show archers in motion, hunting and perhaps fighting, their thin bodies drawn with a few confident strokes in red. Many experts consider it one of the finest examples in the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art, and seeing it, even protected behind a fence, gives a real jolt of connection to people who lived here several thousand years ago.

The shelter lies in the Bajo Aragón, a landscape of ochre hills, terraced olive groves and pine-dotted ridges, cut by the valleys of the Guadalope and Matarraña rivers. The olive oil from here carries its own designation of origin and is sweet and fruity. Calanda, a few kilometres away, is famous for its Easter drumming, when thousands beat drums through the night, and it was the birthplace of the filmmaker Luis Buñuel. Alcañiz itself is crowned by a castle of the Order of Calatrava, now a parador, with a Gothic town hall and a lively main square below.

For riders, the name Alcañiz means one thing: MotorLand Aragón, the international circuit just outside town that hosts MotoGP and track days. Even if you do not ride on it, the surrounding roads are a delight, with fast, open bends across the hills, and quieter routes south into the Maestrazgo and east towards the Matarraña that wind through gorges and old stone villages. Traffic is light. Summer heat can be fierce, the cierzo wind from the northwest can push you around on exposed ridges, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Alcañiz has over sixteen thousand people, plenty of fuel stations, restaurants and hotels. Visits to the rock shelter are typically arranged with local guides or the regional interpretation centres, so check before turning up. Afterwards, try a plate of local ham, olives and bread drizzled with Bajo Aragón oil, and the peaches of Calanda in late summer, each one famously grown inside its own paper bag on the tree.
t.mallata c@41.7,0.1:
Ontiñena is a small farming village on the Alcanadre river, at the edge of the Monegros, the dry, wind-scoured steppe of central Aragón. Out in the ravines around it, prehistoric people left painted figures in rock shelters, among them the site labelled Mallata C, one of the many small components of the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art. The paintings are small, simple and best seen with a local guide, and the walk there crosses a landscape that seems built for epic films: gypsum hills, eroded gullies and wide skies.

Despite the barren reputation, life clusters along the rivers. The Alcanadre and the nearby Cinca support irrigated orchards and fields, and the contrast with the dry hills above is striking. A few kilometres away at Villanueva de Sigena stands the Royal Monastery of Santa María de Sijena, founded in the twelfth century by the Aragonese royal family for noblewomen of the Order of St John. Its story is turbulent, including a fire during the Civil War and a long legal battle over its art. The theologian Miguel Servet, burned in Geneva for heresy in 1553, was born in Villanueva de Sigena, and there is a small museum in his family home.

The riding is about space rather than curves. Long straight roads cross gentle hills, with few villages and very little traffic, and the light at dawn and sunset turns the earth into shades of gold and pink. Wind can be strong, especially the cierzo, which blows hard from the northwest across these plains, and summer heat is intense, regularly topping forty degrees. In winter, morning fog can settle along the river valleys.

Ontiñena and the nearby villages have bars but limited services; for reliable fuel, head to larger towns such as Fraga or Binéfar. Carry water at all times. Local cooking leans on lamb, the Ternasco de Aragón, roasted with potatoes, and the irrigated land around Fraga is famous for its figs. Bring sun protection, as shade is in short supply away from the riverbanks.
t.royal capetian fortresses of languedoc@4:
The Corbières are a rugged knot of hills between Carcassonne and the Pyrenees, covered in garrigue, vineyards and dark oak woods, and dotted with castles that seem to grow out of the rock. After the crusade against the Cathars in the thirteenth century, the French crown took over the region and rebuilt a string of fortresses to guard the border with Aragon: Peyrepertuse, Quéribus, Puilaurens, Termes, Aguilar and the walled city of Carcassonne itself, often called the five sons of Carcassonne. These coordinates sit in the upper Aude, between Couiza and the Corbières heights, in the heart of this castle country.

Peyrepertuse, stretched along a knife-edge ridge, and Quéribus, perched on a pinnacle with views to the Mediterranean, are the most dramatic, and visiting them involves steep climbs on rocky paths, rewarded by extraordinary views. The landscape is rich in legend: the Pech de Bugarach, the highest summit of the Corbières, attracts mystics, and the village of Rennes-le-Château has a long-running treasure story centred on its nineteenth-century priest. The air smells of thyme and wild lavender, and eagles and vultures circle overhead.

This is wonderful riding country. Roads wind through gorges and over passes, with tight bends, narrow sections and very little traffic. The Gorges de Galamus, where the road is carved into the cliff high above the river, is spectacular but narrow, with limited passing places, so take it slowly and be ready to stop.
