Other routes cross the Corbières between vineyards and villages, climb to the castles and drop into the Aude valley towards Quillan and Limoux. Summer is hot and dry, with occasional violent storms, while the tramontane wind can blow hard and cold.

Fuel is available in Couiza, Espéraza, Quillan and Limoux, but villages in the Corbières are small and pumps scarce, so plan ahead. Limoux is famous for its sparkling wine, the Blanquette, which locals claim predates champagne, and for its long carnival. Try cassoulet, the rich bean and meat stew of the region, and a glass of Corbières red, ideally at the end of the day's riding.
t.els figuerals@40.8,0.1:
The Matarraña, or Matarranya in Catalan, is the corner of Teruel that tourism brochures like to call Spain's Tuscany, and for once the comparison is not silly. Olive groves and almond orchards climb rolling hills topped by stone villages with church towers, while to the south the limestone wall of the Ports de Beseit rises abruptly, cut by gorges and clear rivers. Near the village of Fuentespalda, a painted shelter called Els Figuerals adds this valley to the long UNESCO roll of Iberian rock art.

Valderrobres, the main town of the area, is one of the most beautiful villages in Aragón, with a medieval bridge over the Matarraña river leading through a gateway into the old town, and a castle and Gothic church crowning the hill. Beceite, further south, is the gateway to the Parrizal, a narrow gorge with a wooden walkway above the river, and to rock pools where locals swim in summer. The area is bilingual, with Catalan spoken alongside Spanish, and has a long tradition of olive oil and cured ham.

The roads around here are a delight, with smooth tarmac, little traffic and constant curves through hills and valleys. Short loops link Valderrobres, Fuentespalda, Monroyo, Peñarroya de Tastavins and Beceite, with views of the Ports mountains and stone villages, and the route towards Morella in the Maestrazgo of Castellón is one of the great motorcycle roads of eastern Spain. Watch out for gravel on bends, especially after rain, and for wild boar at dusk. Summer days are hot, but evenings are cool, and spring and autumn are perfect.

Fuentespalda is a small village, so for fuel head to Valderrobres or one of the larger towns. Many villages have a bar or a small dining room offering rabbit with snails and garlic mayonnaise, and pastries made with almonds and honey. The local olive oil, from the Empeltre variety, is soft and fruity, perfect on toasted bread with tomato. Bring water and sturdy shoes for the walk to the rock shelters, which often involves steep paths, and check whether a guide is needed.
t.roca dels moros@41.0,0.2:
In 1903, a young man from Calaceite named Juan Cabré, who would go on to become one of Spain's pioneering archaeologists, found painted figures of deer and other animals in a rock shelter in the Calapatá ravine, between Calaceite and Cretas. The Roca dels Moros became one of the first sites of Levantine rock art identified in Spain, and it helped open up a whole new field of study. Today it is part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, and a visit here is a small pilgrimage to the beginnings of that story.

Calaceite itself is a handsome village of honey-coloured stone, with a large baroque church, an arcaded town hall and narrow streets lined with mansions, many restored by artists and writers who have settled here. On a hill outside the village lie the ruins of San Antonio, an Iberian settlement from the centuries before the Romans, with walls and house foundations visible on the summit. The surrounding Matarraña countryside is a patchwork of olive and almond groves, vineyards and pine woods, cut by ravines and dotted with farmhouses, the masías.

The riding here is relaxing and scenic. Roads are generally in good condition, with little traffic and a mix of gentle curves and sharper bends through the hills. The N-420 passes nearby, linking Alcañiz with Gandesa and the Terra Alta wine region in Catalonia, a fine road in its own right, and smaller routes lead through Cretas, Valderrobres and the villages towards the Ports de Beseit. The Ebro valley to the east, with its Civil War battlefields around Gandesa, adds a layer of more recent history.

Calaceite has a few bars and restaurants, and fuel is available in larger nearby towns such as Valderrobres or Alcañiz, though it is wise to check opening hours. The region produces excellent olive oil, and Terra Alta wines are well worth trying. Look for local dishes such as roast kid, potatoes with garlic and olive oil, and almond biscuits. Walking to the shelter involves a short hike, so bring water and sun protection, especially in summer.
t.mas de torres@41.4,0.0:
The Monegros in high summer is the closest thing Europe has to a desert, a wide, dry plateau of gypsum hills, wheat stubble and steppe scrub under a hard, white sky. Near the village of Candasnos, close to the main road between Zaragoza and Lleida, the shelter labelled Mas de Torres is one of the rock art sites of the Mediterranean Basin listed by UNESCO, a reminder that people lived and hunted here long before the land dried out to its present state.

The steppe is far from lifeless. It is home to rare birds such as the Dupont's lark, the little bustard and the sandgrouse, and in spring the plains are carpeted with wildflowers. Near Bujaraloz lie the saladas, shallow salt lagoons that fill after rain and dry to white crusts in summer, a strange and beautiful sight. To the south, the Ebro has been dammed into a huge reservoir at Mequinenza, known as the Sea of Aragón, where anglers come for giant catfish, and the town of Caspe is remembered for the Compromise of Caspe of 1412, when representatives chose a new king for the Crown of Aragón.

For riders, the Monegros means long straight roads, wide horizons and very little traffic, with occasional gentle curves and climbs onto the plateau edges. The A-2 motorway and the old N-II cross the region, with large truck stops and service areas at Candasnos and Bujaraloz, while side roads lead to quiet villages and the Ebro valley. Heat in summer is intense, often well above forty degrees, and the cierzo wind can blow hard across the plains, pushing bikes around on exposed stretches. Winter brings cold, fog and occasional frost.

Fuel is available at the service areas along the main road, and Caspe, Fraga and other towns are within reach. The truck stops serve hearty meals at reasonable prices, and village bars offer coffee and sandwiches. Local cuisine features lamb, the famous Ternasco de Aragón, as well as migas and roasted vegetables. Carry water and sun protection, and if you visit the shelters, check access arrangements in advance.
t.cueva pena miel i@42.3,0.1:
The Sierra de Guara, in the province of Huesca, is a limestone range riddled with canyons, and the river Vero cuts one of the most beautiful of them, a deep, narrow gorge of grey and ochre cliffs where vultures nest and the water runs clear over pale stones. Along its walls, prehistoric people left paintings in dozens of rock shelters, and the Cueva Peña Miel I is one of them, part of the UNESCO listing of rock art of the Mediterranean Basin. The Río Vero Cultural Park protects the area, with an interpretation centre in Colungo and guided visits to some of the shelters.

Alquézar, perched on a crag above the Vero canyon, is one of the most striking villages in Spain, with a collegiate church and castle at the top, built on the site of a Moorish fortress, and steep streets winding down to the river. A walkway along the cliffs below the village offers spectacular views of the gorge. The Sierra de Guara is one of Europe's best-known canyoning destinations, and in summer groups in wetsuits can be seen jumping into pools and abseiling down waterfalls. Around it, the Somontano wine region produces fine reds and whites, with modern wineries among the vineyards near Barbastro.

The riding in this area is superb. Roads climb from the Somontano plains into the sierra, with tight bends, narrow sections and wonderful views of the canyons and the Pyrenees beyond. Routes towards Aínsa and the high Pyrenees pass through gorges and over passes, while others link small villages of stone houses, many partly abandoned. Expect gravel on some corners, livestock, and in summer, more traffic around Alquézar. Winters can bring snow on the higher roads.

Fuel is available in Barbastro and in Aínsa, while small villages may have limited or no services. Alquézar has bars and restaurants, and Barbastro has plenty of choice. Local cuisine includes ternasco, roast lamb, and dishes with mushrooms and game. Try a glass of Somontano wine, ideally at the end of the day. Bring sturdy shoes and water for walks to the rock shelters, which often involve steep paths.
t.poblet monastery@41.4,1.1:
Few places in Catalonia carry as much weight as Poblet. The Cistercian monastery was founded in the middle of the twelfth century on land granted by Count Ramon Berenguer IV, and over the following generations it became the royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon, the place where kings chose to be buried under carved alabaster. It is still a working community of monks, which gives the vast walled complex a quietness that the coach parties never quite manage to break. UNESCO listed it in 1991, and walking through the outer gates, past the first enclosure and into the cloister, you feel the scale of medieval monastic power in a way that a textbook never conveys.

It sits at the foot of the Prades mountains, between the villages of Vimbodí and L'Espluga de Francolí, in the wine country of the Conca de Barberà. The landscape is a broad, bowl-shaped plain of vineyards and almond trees rimmed by wooded ridges, and that rim is where the riding gets interesting. The roads that climb into the Prades massif towards Prades village and Siurana are narrow, twisting and often deserted, with red sandstone cliffs and long views back over the plain. Down on the valley floor things are faster and more open, with a fair amount of agricultural traffic at harvest time in September.

Poblet is also one of three great Cistercian houses within an easy ride of each other. Santes Creus lies to the east and the nuns' monastery of Vallbona de les Monges to the north, and the loop linking them is signposted as the Ruta del Cister. It makes an excellent half day on a bike, all minor roads and small villages, with a cooperative winery somewhere along most stretches.

For practical matters, head for Montblanc, about seven kilometres away. It is a walled medieval town in remarkably good condition, and local tradition places the legend of Saint George and the dragon right outside its gates. You will find fuel there and in L'Espluga, plus plenty of places for lunch, and the local cava and trepat reds are worth a bottle in the panniers for later. Summers are hot on the plain, so plan the monastery visit for the morning and save the mountain roads for the softer evening light.
t.cova dels vilasos o dels vilars@41.9,0.7:
Os de Balaguer is a small village on the edge of the pre-Pyrenean hills in the Noguera district of Lleida, and the Cova dels Vilasos, also known as the Cova dels Vilars, lies just outside it. The site is one of the painted rock shelters of Catalonia counted within the Mediterranean rock art group protected by UNESCO, and its figures are small and reddish, drawn by people who lived from hunting and gathering in what was then a far wilder landscape. Like its neighbours it is protected and rarely dramatic at first sight; give your eyes a moment in the shade and the shapes begin to come out of the stone.

The ride in tells you a lot about this part of Catalonia. To the south lies the flat, irrigated plain of the Segre, a patchwork of fruit orchards, maize and canals, and then the ground starts to rise into a series of low sierras that build up towards the Montsec further north. The roads around Os de Balaguer, Algerri and Alfarràs are quiet country lanes, fairly narrow, with some broken edges and gravel thrown up by farm vehicles. They are not demanding, but they are pleasant, with a rhythm of gentle bends and short climbs that suits an easy pace.

Just north of the village is the monastery of Santa Maria de Bellpuig de les Avellanes, founded by the Premonstratensian order in the twelfth century and long connected with the Counts of Urgell, whose tombs were once housed there. Several of those tombs were later sold abroad and now sit in a museum in New York, a sore point locally. The monastery itself is worth the short detour for its setting alone, backed by wooded hills and looking out over the plain.

Balaguer, thirteen kilometres away, is the town to aim for. It sits on the river Segre beneath the remains of the Castell Formós, the stronghold of those same counts of Urgell, and its arcaded main square is a good place for lunch. You will find fuel and all the usual services there. In summer the plain can be stiflingly hot, and in winter dense fog sometimes settles over the Lleida lowlands for days, so check conditions if you are riding early in the morning.
t.l enceinte@42.6,2.4:
Villefranche-de-Conflent is a whole town inside a wall. Squeezed into the narrow valley of the Têt where it meets a side stream, it was founded in the eleventh century as a stronghold of the Counts of Cerdanya, and after the Treaty of the Pyrenees turned this area French in 1659 it was refortified by Vauban to hold the valley against Spain. The ramparts that give the place its label, l'enceinte, are part of the UNESCO listing of Vauban's fortifications, and you can walk along the covered galleries inside the walls. High above the town on the mountainside sits Fort Liberia, linked to the village by a long underground stairway.

The main road up the Têt valley runs right past the walls, and it is the route from Perpignan towards the high Cerdanya plateau and Andorra. It is a busy road by local standards, carrying trucks and holiday traffic, but once you leave it the riding changes completely. The lanes climbing towards Vernet-les-Bains and beyond into the foothills of the Canigou, the sacred mountain of the Catalans, are narrow and twisting, with steep gradients and views opening up towards the summit. Off to the side, the road to the abbey of Saint-Martin-du-Canigou ends at a car park, with the monastery perched high above on its rock.

Villefranche is also the starting point of the Train Jaune, the little yellow electric train that climbs through tunnels and over viaducts up to the Cerdanya. Watching it leave the station is a small pleasure in itself. Near the town are the Grottes des Canalettes and the Grandes Canalettes, show caves with impressive formations that stay cool in summer.

The village itself is very much geared to visitors, with crafts shops, cafes and creperies along the two main streets, and parking can be tricky in high season. For fuel and a wider choice of shops, go to Prades, a town of almost seven thousand people a few kilometres down the valley, which is also known for the music festival founded there by the cellist Pablo Casals after he settled in the town in exile. The climate is a pleasant mix of Mediterranean warmth and mountain air, though the tramontana can blow hard down the valley.
t.l enceinte et la citadelle de mont louis:
At around sixteen hundred metres, Mont-Louis is often described as the highest fortified town in France, and it feels like a frontier outpost even today. Vauban designed it in 1679 to guard the newly drawn border after the Treaty of the Pyrenees, placing it on a strategic shelf at the meeting of three valleys: the Têt dropping towards Perpignan, the Aude running north, and the wide basin of the Cerdanya opening to the west. The citadel is still used by the French army, home to a commando training centre, so parts of it are closed to visitors, but the walls and the small grid of streets inside them are free to wander.

The town's oddest treasure is its solar furnace, built in 1949, the first of its kind in the world. A field of mirrors concentrates sunlight onto a target, producing extreme temperatures, and it is possible to visit. The much larger furnace at Odeillo, near Font-Romeu, followed later and is visible from the road, its huge curved mirror reflecting the mountains.

The riding around Mont-Louis is some of the most varied in the eastern Pyrenees. Climbing up from Villefranche, the road twists through the Têt gorges in a series of hairpins and long, swooping bends, with the yellow train often keeping you company on its narrow tracks. Just above town, the Col de la Perche at 1,581 metres leads gently into the sunny Cerdanya plateau, with long open roads and views towards the peaks on the Spanish side. North, the road towards the Capcir plateau and the Aude gorges is quieter and slightly wilder, crossing pine forests and high meadows.

It can get surprisingly cold here, even in summer, and snow can arrive early in autumn and linger late into spring, so check the forecast and pack layers. Fuel and supplies are available in Font-Romeu and the surrounding villages, while Puigcerdà, just over the Spanish border eighteen kilometres away, is the largest town in the area and a lively place to stop for lunch. It is also worth knowing that the Cerdanya is one of the sunniest corners of France, which is why the solar scientists came here in the first place.
t.cova del tabac@41.9,0.9:
Above the village of Camarasa, where the Segre comes out of the pre-Pyrenean hills onto the plain of Lleida, a cave in the limestone holds some of the most interesting rock paintings in Catalonia. The Cova del Tabac, the tobacco cave, is a wide shelter with schematic paintings, simplified human figures, animals and symbols in red, and it is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of Mediterranean rock art on the Iberian Peninsula. A short walk leads up from the road to the shelter, which also offers a fine view over the valley, and on a clear day the Pyrenees rise white on the northern horizon.

Camarasa sits at an important crossroads. Just upstream, the Noguera Pallaresa, coming down from the high Pyrenees, joins the Segre, and the two rivers have been dammed to create reservoirs that provide water for irrigation and power for the region. The Camarasa dam, built in the 1920s, was one of the great engineering works of its time, and the reservoir behind it fills a deep, winding gorge. The village itself has a ruined castle on a hill above the houses, a reminder of its role in the medieval wars between the Counts of Urgell and their enemies.

For riders, this is the gateway to some of the best roads in Catalonia. Heading north, the road follows the Noguera Pallaresa through the Congost de Terradets, a dramatic gorge where the road is squeezed between sheer limestone cliffs and the river, with tunnels and galleries cut into the rock. Beyond it lies the Pallars valley and the high Pyrenees. To the west, the Montsec range, a long limestone ridge, offers twisting roads, viewpoints and an astronomical observatory, and its skies are among the darkest in Catalonia. The roads are generally good, but rockfall and gravel are common in the gorges.

Camarasa is a small village with limited services, so fill up in Balaguer, about fourteen kilometres away, a town of nearly seventeen thousand people on the Segre, with a lively Saturday market and an arcaded main square. The local food includes coca de recapte, a flatbread topped with roasted vegetables and anchovies or sausage, and the olive oil of the Garrigues to the south is excellent. Summers are hot on the plain, and winters can bring thick fog that lingers for days.
t.chateau de termes@43.0,2.6:
In the summer of 1210, Simon de Montfort, leader of the crusade against the Cathars, brought his army to the remote castle of Termes, in the heart of the Corbières, and laid siege to it. The castle's lord, Raymond de Termes, held out for four months, and the defenders only surrendered when their water supply was contaminated and disease broke out, or so the story goes. The castle became a royal fortress, guarding the border with Aragon, and was eventually dismantled in the seventeenth century. Today, its ruins sprawl over a rocky spur above the village, with remains of walls, towers and a chapel, and the views over the wild hills of the Corbières are tremendous.

Termes is one of the so-called Cathar castles, a group of fortresses in the Aude and the eastern Pyrenees, many of which were rebuilt by the French kings after the crusade and form part of the history of the region's conquest. Others include Peyrepertuse, Quéribus, Puilaurens and Aguilar, all perched on high rocks with dramatic views. The village of Termes itself is tiny, with a handful of stone houses, a small museum and a cafe, and the Gorges du Terminet, a narrow gorge cut by a stream just below the village, makes a fine short walk or ride.

The riding in the Corbières is some of the best in southern France. The hills are wild and rugged, covered in garrigue scrub, vineyards and patches of forest, and the roads wind endlessly through them, with tight bends, steep climbs and descents, and very little traffic. The surfaces are generally good, but narrow, and there are often no barriers on the edges. The wine of the Corbières is excellent, and there are many small producers along the way. The tramontane, a strong, dry wind from the north west, can blow hard here, especially in winter and spring, making riding challenging.

Services in the Corbières are limited. Lagrasse, with its great abbey and medieval bridge, is a lovely village to the north, and Carcassonne, with its famous walled city, is a short ride away. Summers are hot and dry, so carry plenty of water.
t.historic centre of avignon papal palace@:
For most of the fourteenth century, the popes lived in Avignon rather than Rome. In 1309, Pope Clement V, a Frenchman, settled here to escape the turmoil of Italian politics, and his successors built a vast palace, the Palais des Papes, the largest Gothic palace in Europe, with massive walls, towers and halls, more fortress than residence. Seven popes reigned here until 1377, when the papacy returned to Rome, and then rival popes continued to rule from Avignon during the Great Schism. The palace, the cathedral, the ramparts and the famous bridge, the Pont Saint-Bénézet, were listed by UNESCO in 1995.

The bridge is famous from the song, Sur le pont d'Avignon, though it was probably danced under rather than on. It once had twenty two arches, spanning the Rhône, but floods repeatedly damaged it, and only four arches remain today, ending abruptly in the middle of the river. The old town, enclosed by a ring of medieval walls, is lively, with squares, cafes, theatres and markets. In July, the Festival d'Avignon, one of the most important theatre festivals in the world, fills the city with performances, and the streets with actors, musicians and crowds.

The riding around Avignon is excellent. To the east, Mont Ventoux, the giant of Provence, rises to 1,909 metres, and the roads to its bald, windswept summit, from Bédoin, Malaucène or Sault, are legendary among cyclists and riders, with steep gradients, tight bends and views over half of southern France. To the south, the Alpilles, a small limestone range, offers twisting roads, olive groves and the villages of Les Baux and Saint-Rémy. To the west, across the Rhône, the Gard has the Pont du Gard, the great Roman aqueduct, and Nîmes, with its Roman amphitheatre and the Maison Carrée.

Avignon, a city of about ninety thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Traffic can be heavy, and parking difficult, especially during the festival. The mistral, a cold, strong wind from the north, can blow for days, making riding challenging, especially on exposed roads. The local wines, from Châteauneuf-du-Pape, just to the north, and the Côtes du Rhône, are excellent. Summers are hot and dry, and spring and autumn are the best times to ride.
t.coveta de montegordo@40.4,0.0:
Up in the dry limestone uplands of inland Castellón, the Valltorta and Gasulla ravines hold one of the densest concentrations of Levantine rock art in Spain, and the Coveta de Montegordo is one of its many small shelters. Painted under rock overhangs some seven or eight thousand years ago, perhaps more, the figures here are tiny, often no taller than a finger, yet astonishingly alive: archers running with bows drawn, goats and deer leaping, hunters following wounded animals. The whole region is part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listing inscribed by UNESCO in 1998, and the famous Cova dels Cavalls in the Valltorta shows a deer hunt with a line of archers waiting in ambush.

This is the Maestrat, or Maestrazgo, a harsh and beautiful land of high plateaus, stone terraces, drystone huts and fortified villages that once belonged to the military orders of knights. Albocàsser and Catí are the closest villages, small and stony, with arcaded squares and Gothic churches, and the Valltorta museum at Tírig explains the paintings and offers guided visits to the shelters. Almond and olive trees cling to the terraces, and in winter the high villages can be bitterly cold, with a wind that cuts through any jacket.

For riders, the Maestrat is one of Spain's great unsung regions. The roads twist across plateaus and down into ravines, with long views over endless ridges and very little traffic. The CV-15 and the smaller roads towards Morella, the walled hilltop town that crowns the region, are a joy, with fast sweepers on the plateaus and tight hairpins on the descents. Surfaces are mostly good, though gravel and rockfall can appear, and wildlife, including wild boar and the occasional ibex, can cross without warning.

There is little fuel in the high villages, so fill up in Alcalà de Xivert or other coastal towns before heading inland, or in Vilafranca or Morella. Albocàsser has a few bars, and the Maestrat cooking is mountain food: lamb, cured ham, truffles in winter, and hearty soups. Carry water in summer, when the plateau bakes under a fierce sun.
t.valcomuna@41.1,0.0:
Lower Aragon is a country of dry hills, olive groves and red earth, and in its ravines people painted on the rock thousands of years ago. Valcomuna is one of those rock art sites, between Alcañiz and Caspe near the village of Maella, part of the great family of painted shelters running down Spain's Mediterranean side that UNESCO listed as the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula. The figures in this tradition are small and lively, archers, deer, goats and people in motion, painted in red and black under overhangs where the weather could not wash them away.

Most of these shelters are protected by fences and grilles, and visits are often guided or need arranging through the local tourist office or the rock art centres in the area, so look into that before you set off. Even from outside the fence, the setting is worth the ride: a quiet barranco of pale limestone, holm oak and rosemary, with the smell of thyme when the sun warms the slopes.

For riders, Alcañiz has a special pull. Just outside town is MotorLand Aragón, the circuit that hosts international motorcycle racing, and on a race weekend the whole district fills with bikes. The town itself is crowned by a castle of the Order of Calatrava, now a parador, and has a fine arcaded main square. Caspe, to the northeast, sits above the vast reservoir of the Ebro known locally as the Mar de Aragón, and gave its name to the Compromise of Caspe of 1412, when delegates chose a new king for the Crown of Aragon.

The roads between Alcañiz, Maella and Caspe are a pleasure: mostly quiet, well surfaced, with long fast bends over the hills and tighter sections where they drop into river valleys. Summer heat is intense, often well above thirty five degrees by midday, so ride early and late and carry water. Wind from the northwest, the cierzo, can be strong and gusty on exposed ridges. Spring, when the almond and olive country is green, is the best time.

Fuel is easy in Alcañiz and Caspe, both towns of eight to sixteen thousand people with plenty of bars and restaurants; Maella, smaller, has the basics. Try the Bajo Aragón olive oil, which has its own protected designation, and the local peaches if you come in late summer. A plate of migas with grapes is a classic in these parts.
The Añisclo canyon is one of the deepest and narrowest in the Spanish Pyrenees, a cleft in the limestone of the Ordesa and Monte Perdido National Park, and the road that runs through its lower section is one of the most remarkable in Aragon. At its southern end, beside an old stone bridge over the Bellós river, stands the hermitage of San Úrbez, built half into the cliff, with a cave behind it where tradition says the saint lived as a hermit. Close by, rock shelters hold traces of prehistoric painting.

The road through the canyon is narrow, carved into the rock, with overhangs, tunnels and sheer drops, and part of it has long been one way, heading south. Traffic restrictions and closures happen in high summer and after rockfall, so check before you go. Ride slowly: the views up to the canyon walls and down to the turquoise water are reason enough, and there are cyclists, walkers and cars coming round blind corners. Rockfall after rain is real.

The whole area is part of the Pyrenees–Mont Perdu World Heritage Site, shared with France. Monte Perdido, at about 3,350 metres, is the highest limestone massif in Western Europe, and its glaciers and canyons drain south into Spain. Bearded vultures, griffons and chamois are commonly seen, and the beech and pine forests are cool even on hot days.

Around the canyon, the riding is magnificent. The road from Aínsa up the Cinca valley to Bielsa and the tunnel to France, the climb to Fanlo, and the road from Broto into the Ordesa valley are all twisting mountain roads with stunning scenery. The Broto valley is the main gateway to Ordesa, where private vehicles are restricted in summer and shuttle buses take over.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Boltaña and Aínsa, south on the Cinca, have filling stations, as does Broto, and Bielsa toward the French border. Sabiñánigo, thirty five kilometres away, is the nearest town of ten thousand. Aínsa's medieval walled hilltop town, with its arcaded plaza, is one of the loveliest places to eat and sleep in the Pyrenees. Bring water and snacks into the canyon, as there is nothing there.
t.paleochristian cemetery@41.1,1.2:
When the Roman city of Tarraco converted to Christianity, its people began burying their dead beside the Francolí river, west of the town, and the necropolis that grew up there over the fourth and fifth centuries is now one of the most important early Christian burial sites in the western Mediterranean. Hundreds of tombs were found, from simple graves to carved marble sarcophagi, along with remains of a basilica. Tradition links the site with Saint Fructuosus, the bishop of Tarraco burned in the amphitheatre in the year 259 along with two deacons.

The site was found in the 1920s during construction of the tobacco factory next door, and it has its own museum, part of the National Archaeological Museum of Tarragona; check whether it is open, as access has varied over the years with restoration work. The whole ensemble of Roman Tarraco is a World Heritage Site, and Tarragona makes it easy to walk from monument to monument.

Riding into Tarragona is coastal city riding, with traffic, roundabouts and port traffic near the Francolí, but parking a bike is easier than parking a car. Once you have seen the amphitheatre by the sea, the circus vaults, the walls and the old town around the cathedral, head out to the Pont del Diable, the Roman aqueduct a few kilometres north, which you can walk across. Inland, the roads climb into the Priorat and the Montsant, with tight, scenic bends through terraced vineyards.

Tarragona has a fishermen's quarter, El Serrallo, where restaurants serve the day's catch and the local sauce, romesco, made with dried peppers, almonds and garlic. In late winter and spring, calçots, grilled spring onions dipped in a romesco-style sauce, are the regional obsession around Valls, just inland. Human towers, castells, are another Catalan tradition with deep roots here, and the city hosts major competitions.

Fuel and services are plentiful throughout the city and in Constantí and La Canonja nearby, though La Canonja borders the petrochemical complex, which is not much to look at. Summer is hot and humid on the coast, and spring and autumn are ideal. Watch for the many speed cameras on the main roads around the city.
t.abric de la vall d ingla@42.3,1.8:
The Cerdanya is a high, wide, sunny valley in the eastern Pyrenees, shared between Catalonia and France, and its southern wall is the long limestone barrier of the Serra del Cadí. The Vall d'Ingla cuts into that wall just above Bellver de Cerdanya and the neighbouring village of Éller, and the rock shelter there is one of the archaeological traces of people who used these valleys long before towns and borders. You are inside the Cadí-Moixeró Natural Park, a protected area of pine forest, cliffs and high pasture.

Bellver de Cerdanya, a village of under two thousand people, sits on a hill above the Segre river, with a fortified old core and a small square. Puigcerdà, the capital of the Cerdanya, is sixteen kilometres east, and next to it lies Llívia, a little Spanish enclave entirely surrounded by France, left over from the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659, which handed villages to France but not towns. Llívia counted as a town, and so it stayed Spanish.

The riding here is some of the best in Catalonia. The N-260 runs along the valley floor with fast, open curves and snow peaks on both sides. Climbing south, the road over the Collada de Toses toward Ribes de Freser is a classic of hairpins and long views, and the Cadí tunnel takes the C-16 under the range toward Berga, with a toll. Further west, the road to La Seu d'Urgell follows the Segre and leads to Andorra.

The Cerdanya is known for its sunshine, and the valley floor is broad and flat, which makes it feel almost like a plateau. Mornings can be cold even in summer. Cows graze in the meadows, trout fishermen work the rivers, and in autumn the larches turn gold on the slopes. Snow closes higher passes in winter, though main roads are kept open.

Bellver has a filling station and places to eat, and Puigcerdà has everything, including good restaurants serving trinxat, a dish of cabbage and potato with bacon that is the Cerdanya's signature. The roads up into the Vall d'Ingla are narrow and in places unpaved, so check the surface before taking a road bike up.
t.mas de patriciel i@41.3,0.2:
Where the Ebro and the Segre meet near Mequinenza, the rivers have been dammed into two long reservoirs, and the result is a strange, beautiful landscape of blue water filling deep valleys among dry, terraced hills. The rock shelters of Mas de Patriciel lie in the hills between Mequinenza, Nonaspe and Fayón, part of the network of painted sites that UNESCO listed as the Mediterranean rock art of Iberia.

The dams changed everything here. Old Mequinenza, a town of coal miners and river boatmen, was flooded in the 1970s and rebuilt higher up; its museums in the old town site tell the story of the lost town and its lignite mines. At Fayón, the bell tower of the old church still stands out of the water of the Riba-roja reservoir, a ghost of the village that was drowned, and it is one of the most photographed sights on the lower Ebro. The reservoirs are now famous among anglers for wels catfish, huge fish introduced decades ago that can grow to over two metres long, and you will see fishing camps and boats along the shores.

The riding here is pleasant and quiet, with the reservoirs providing constant scenery. The roads follow the water and climb into the hills with good curves and wide views, and traffic outside the towns is light. Surfaces are mostly good, and the area is easy to combine with the Matarraña country to the south, with its stone villages and gorges. Wind can be strong, and summer heat makes midday riding unpleasant.

Mequinenza, with about two and a half thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Caspe, twenty two kilometres away, has more. Nonaspe and Fayón are small villages with limited services. In the restaurants, look for fish from the river, local olive oil and peaches in season, and the hearty cuisine of Lower Aragon, with lamb and game dishes.
t.cova dels cavalls@40.4,0.1:
A line of archers closing in on a herd of deer, one animal already wounded and fleeing: the hunting scene in the Cova dels Cavalls is one of the most reproduced images of Spanish prehistoric art, and it sits in the Barranc de la Valltorta, a dry limestone gorge in the Castellón hinterland between Albocàsser and Tírig. The Valltorta shelters, together with nearby Gasulla, form one of the key groups of Levantine rock art, and the Museu de la Valltorta near Tírig runs guided visits to the main shelter and explains the paintings with replicas and finds. Check visiting times at the museum before you set off, because the shelter is only seen with a guide.

The Maestrat, as this upland country is called, is a land of dry stone walls, almond and olive terraces, holm oaks and isolated stone farmhouses, the masos, many of them abandoned. Villages like Catí, with its Gothic stone houses, and Albocàsser, with its arcaded square, grew rich on wool in the Middle Ages, when flocks moved along drove roads between the coast and the Aragonese mountains. Ares del Maestrat, a little further inland, perches on a cliff with a ruined castle and huge views.

On two wheels, the Maestrat is a treat. The roads climb from the coastal plain into the hills in long series of bends, wind between villages on high plateaus and drop into gorges, with good surfaces, light traffic and very few towns. The CV-15 is the main artery, fast and flowing; the smaller roads off it are narrower and more fun. In winter it can be cold and foggy up here, and in summer the midday sun is relentless, so plan for early starts.

Services are thin. Albocàsser and Coves de Vinromà are villages of under two thousand people with a bar or two; for reliable fuel, head to Alcalà de Xivert on the coast, eighteen kilometres away, or to Vilafranca or Morella further inland. Local food is hearty: lamb, cured sausages, truffles from the Maestrat in winter, and the cheese of Catí.
t.abric d esquarterades i@40.6,0.5:
In the dry hills behind Ulldecona, near the southern tip of Catalonia, small figures painted in red ochre run, hunt and gather across the walls of shallow rock shelters. These are the paintings of Levantine rock art, made by prehistoric people some seven to eight thousand years ago, and the shelters of the Serra de Godall, including the Abric d'Esquarterades, are among the best examples. They are part of the World Heritage site that covers rock art in the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula.

The figures are small, often just a few centimetres high, but full of life. Archers draw their bows, deer and goats leap, and people move in groups. The style is dynamic, almost narrative, and it tells us a lot about the lives of the hunter-gatherers and early farmers who lived here. The paintings are fragile, and access is usually by guided tour, often starting from the interpretation centre at the Ermita de la Pietat, a hermitage just outside Ulldecona.

The landscape is dry and Mediterranean, with olive groves, almond trees, carob and scrub covering the low hills. To the east, the Ebro Delta stretches out into the sea, a flat world of rice fields, lagoons and beaches, rich in birdlife, including flamingos. To the north, the Montsià mountains rise sharply above the coast, and inland, the Ports de Beseit offer rugged limestone peaks and gorges.

The riding is varied and fun. The roads around Ulldecona are quiet and winding, with good surfaces and views over the olive groves. The road over the Montsià to the coast, and the routes into the Ports, are particularly good, with tight bends, steep gradients and spectacular scenery. The flat roads of the Ebro Delta are a different experience, through rice fields and along lagoons, with the sea always close. Wind can be strong here, especially the mestral blowing down the Ebro valley.

Ulldecona, about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Amposta and Sant Carles de la Ràpita are larger towns nearby. The area is famous for its olive oil and its rice, and you can eat excellent paella and arròs negre, rice cooked with squid ink, in the delta restaurants. The oysters and mussels farmed in the bays of the delta are also worth seeking out.
t.roques guardies ii@41.5,0.8:
Les Garrigues is the dry, stony corner of western Catalonia, south-east of Lleida, a land of low hills, terraced olive groves, almond trees and stone huts, where the light is hard and the summers are hot. Roques Guàrdies II is a rock shelter in these hills near Juneda and Arbeca, with traces of prehistoric paintings in the Levantine style, part of the World Heritage site of rock art in the Mediterranean Basin of the Iberian Peninsula.

The most famous rock art site in the area is the Roca dels Moros at El Cogul, a short ride south-west, where figures of women dancing around a man, as well as animals and hunters, were painted on the walls of a shelter thousands of years ago. It was one of the first Levantine sites to be studied, in the early twentieth century, and it has an interpretation centre. Roques Guàrdies is more modest, but it shares the same landscape and the same sense of the deep past.

Arbeca is the home of the Arbequina olive, a small, fruity variety now grown worldwide, and the olive groves around the town produce some of the best oil in Catalonia, sold under the Les Garrigues designation of origin. The village has a ruined castle and a pleasant old centre. Juneda and the other villages in the area are small and quiet, with churches, squares and cafés.

The riding here is pleasant and relaxed. The roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, with good surfaces and little traffic, winding through olive groves and almond orchards. To the south, the hills become steeper as you approach the Serra de la Llena and the Priorat, with its famous wine villages and twisting mountain roads. Summer is very hot, so ride early or late, and carry plenty of water. Spring, when the almond trees blossom, is especially beautiful.

Juneda, about six kilometres away, has fuel and basic services. Mollerussa and Les Borges Blanques are larger towns nearby, and Lleida, the provincial capital, is about twenty minutes away. The Garrigues is also known for its snails, cooked a la llauna, grilled on a metal tray, and for calçots, sweet green onions grilled over a fire and dipped in romesco sauce, eaten in late winter and spring.
t.cova alta del llidoner@40.1,0.1:
Most people come to this stretch of the Castellón coast for the beaches at Benicàssim and Oropesa, and they never look up at the dry, scrubby hills a few kilometres inland. Up there, among the pines, rosemary and limestone ledges near Cabanes, the Cova alta del Llidoner is one of the rock shelters with prehistoric paintings that belong to the World Heritage site of Levantine rock art. It is a quiet, unshowy place, more about the feel of the land than about anything you can photograph.

The landscape changes abruptly as you climb away from the sea. Behind Benicàssim rises the Desert de les Palmes, a natural park of rugged hills named after the dwarf palms that grow there and the Carmelite monastery, the desert in the sense of a place of retreat. Further north, the plain around Cabanes is dotted with olive and almond trees, and in Cabanes itself a single Roman arch stands alone in the fields beside the old Via Augusta, the road that ran along the Mediterranean coast from the Pyrenees to Cádiz.

The riding is surprisingly good. The coastal strip is busy and built up, but the roads that climb into the Desert de les Palmes are steep, winding and full of views over the sea. Inland, the roads towards Vilafamés, a hilltop village with a castle and a contemporary art museum, and onward into the mountains of the Maestrat, are quiet and twisting, with good surfaces. Summer heat and coastal traffic are the main drawbacks, so spring and autumn are ideal.

The coast here has its own natural treasure: the Prat de Cabanes-Torreblanca, a wetland between the sea and the hills, home to many birds and a rare species of fish. The hills are covered with Mediterranean scrub, smelling of thyme and rosemary in the heat, and in spring they are full of wildflowers.

Oropesa del Mar, about four kilometres away, has fuel, restaurants and shops. Benicàssim and Castellón de la Plana are larger towns nearby with all services. The coast is famous for its rice dishes, and a good arroz a banda, rice cooked in fish stock, served with alioli, is the perfect end to a day in the saddle. The local oranges, sold at roadside stalls in winter, are superb.
t.chateaux de lastours@43.3,2.4:
Four castles perch on a narrow rock ridge above the village of Lastours, in the Montagne Noire north of Carcassonne, and they look so improbable from the viewpoint across the valley that most people stop talking when they see them. The two streams, the Orbiel and the Grésilhou, wrap around the ridge, and the castles, Cabaret, Tour Régine, Surdespine and Quertinheux, stand along its length like beads on a string.

These are Cathar-country fortresses, and their story is hard and human. In the early thirteenth century the Albigensian Crusade was launched against the heretics of Languedoc, and the lords of Cabaret sheltered them. Simon de Montfort's army besieged the castles in 1209 and again in 1210 and 1211, and eventually the defenders gave way. Later the castles were rebuilt as royal fortresses of the French crown, which is why they sit within the group recognised by UNESCO as the Royal Capetian fortresses of Languedoc. The ruins you climb through today are the later, harder stonework.

You park in the village and walk up. The path is steep and stony, takes under an hour for a slow circuit, and there is a belvedere on the opposite hillside with a cheap telescope that gives the postcard view. Good boots beat motorcycle boots here, so a light pair of trainers in the pannier helps.

The approach is the better part for a rider. From Carcassonne the D118 heads north to Conques-sur-Orbiel and then the smaller D101 climbs along the Orbiel gorge to Lastours, a series of easy bends with a lovely view over vines and scrub oak. Further up, the road to Mas-Cabardès and the Pic de Nore mountain wanders through chestnut woods and offers some of the quietest riding in the Aude. Wind is common, the Cers coming from the north-west, and summer afternoons can be hot, so go early. Cabardès wines are made nearby, a blend of Mediterranean and Atlantic grapes, and most villages have a cellar door.

Carcassonne, fourteen kilometres away, is the place for fuel, and Conques-sur-Orbiel, with a couple of thousand people, may have services too, though check before you rely on it. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; July and August are busy and baking.
t.mas d en llort@41.4,1.1:
Montblanc is one of those small Catalan towns that still has its medieval walls, and the Mas d'en Llort label lies a few kilometres from it in the Conca de Barberà, a basin of vineyards and wheat fields ringed by low, scrubby mountains. A mas is a farmhouse, so the spot is probably a rural building or a field track rather than anything with a name on the map, and what you are really riding into is the countryside around it.

The district has a deep history. Shallow rock shelters in the surrounding hills were painted by prehistoric people, and Catalonia's share of that Levantine rock art is protected as part of a UNESCO group of sites. Many of the paintings are small, red, and hard to find without a guide, and the shelters are fragile, so look for local information in Montblanc before you go wandering. Montblanc itself carries the legend of Saint George and the dragon, which the town claims for its own, and each April the old streets fill up with stalls and costumes around Sant Jordi's day. Ten kilometres south, the Cistercian monastery of Poblet, begun in the twelfth century and a royal burial place, is one of the finest medieval monasteries in Spain.

The roads here are easy and rural. The C-14 and the smaller roads towards Vimbodí and Prades twist up through oak and pine, with views over terraced hillsides and lots of slow, satisfying bends. Prades, in the mountains to the south, is a stone village with a big arcaded square and cool air in summer. Traffic is light outside the weekend, though tractors move slowly at harvest, and in October the vineyards turn red and gold.

Montblanc has just over six thousand people and is the place for fuel, a coffee, and a meal. Wine from the Conca de Barberà is the local pride, and the area makes much of the base wine for cava, so cellars and cooperatives are easy to find if you want to taste. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights, and August can be fiercely hot in the afternoons, so ride in the morning if you come then. Carry some water if you plan to walk anywhere.
t.chateau et remparts de carcassonne@43.2,:
Carcassonne has two faces. Down by the river Aude sits the ordinary lower town, a grid of streets laid out in the thirteenth century around a market square, and on the hill above rises the Cité, a double ring of walls and fifty-odd towers that looks like the illustration to a children's book about knights. The Cité was inscribed by UNESCO in 1997, and it is one of the most visited monuments in France, with the nearest sizeable roads and everything a rider needs just a kilometre away in the modern town.

The hill had a fortified settlement since Roman times, and the inner wall still has Roman and Visigothic stonework at its base. In the Middle Ages the viscounts of Trencavel held it, and in August 1209 the army of the Albigensian Crusade besieged it, cut off the water supply in a hot summer, and took the town. The young viscount, Raymond-Roger, died in his own dungeon a few months later. Later the French crown strengthened the walls into a frontier fortress facing Aragon, and when that border moved south the whole place decayed. In the 1850s the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc was sent to rescue it. He added steep slate roofs to the towers, which historians have argued about ever since, since local building traditions call for tile, but without him the Cité might well have been quarried away.

There is a story of Dame Carcas, a lady who held the town against Charlemagne and, when food ran low, threw the last pig over the walls, so that the besiegers gave up and a trumpeter cried that Carcas was calling them. It is not history, and every guide tells it anyway. Eat the real thing at lunch: cassoulet, a slow-cooked casserole of white beans, sausage and duck confit, which the whole district argues over.

For a rider, Carcassonne is a gate to the south. The old Midi canal, dug by Pierre-Paul Riquet in the seventeenth century, runs through the lower town. The Corbières hills begin a short way to the south and offer twisting roads towards Cathar castles such as Peyrepertuse and Quéribus, and the Pyrenees are a couple of hours away. Walk the Cité on foot, since vehicles are restricted, and park outside the gates. July, with its great fireworks on the fourteenth, is crowded and hot, and spring and autumn are far more pleasant. The Cers wind can be fierce.
t.abric mas de la roca@40.5,0.1:
Northern Castellón is a hard, empty, beautiful part of Valencian Spain, a country of limestone ridges and terraced slopes some thirty kilometres back from the Mediterranean, and the Abric Mas de la Roca belongs to it, about six kilometres from the village of Xert, whose name is spelled Chert in Catalan and Valencian. Xert has fewer than a thousand people, Canet lo Roig and Catí are similar, and everything here is small and old.

An abric is a rock shelter, a shallow overhang in the cliff, and the shelters of this district were painted by prehistoric hunters. The images, known as Levantine rock art, show tiny red archers, deer and wild goats in motion, and they are protected by UNESCO as a group together with other sites across the Spanish Mediterranean. I cannot tell you exactly what stands at the point on your map, but sites like this are usually fragile and sometimes closed, so ask at a local museum or tourist office before heading into the scrub.

Behind the village the land climbs westward, and farther on the high point of the region, Penyagolosa, a bald, pointed mountain of nearly eighteen hundred metres, dominates the horizon. A hermitage stands below it, and on certain days pilgrims walk through the forest from the surrounding villages in a long procession. Towards the coast, the old town of Sant Mateu, once the capital of the Maestrat under the military order of Montesa, still has handsome Gothic houses and a fortified church, and Peñíscola, on the coast, has the castle that sheltered the schismatic pope Benedict XIII, known as Papa Luna.

The riding is open, rural and light on traffic. The small roads that connect Xert, Catí and Canet climb over low passes between almond groves and stone walls, and the surface is usually fair, though in places you will find patches and loose gravel from the fields. The wind is strong in the afternoons, spring brings blossom, and summer is intensely hot and bright. Winter nights fall below freezing.

Fuel is thin on the ground. The villages are tiny, so plan to fill up on the coast, at Vinaròs or at Alcalà de Xivert, twenty-two kilometres away, which has nearly seven thousand people and several stations. Local food is simple and strong: olive oil, cured sausages, lamb, honey and a very good local cheese.
t.mas d en ramon d en besso@41.4,1.1:
Behind the Conca de Barberà, where the Catalan plain begins to lift towards the Serra de Prades, a small valley holds the monastery of Poblet, one of the largest and best-preserved Cistercian abbeys in Europe. The Mas d'en Ramon d'en Besso is a farmhouse a few kilometres from Montblanc and from the village of Vimbodí, in wooded country of holm oak, pine and dry-stone terraces with the red cliffs of the Roques Guàrdies nearby.

Poblet was founded in 1151, after Ramon Berenguer IV conquered these lands from the Moors, and settled by monks from the abbey of Fontfroide in southern France. Over the following centuries it grew rich and powerful, a burial place for the kings of Aragon and a centre of learning, with a great fortified wall, a cloister, a library and a dormitory on a huge scale. In 1835, during the anticlerical upheavals of the Spanish state, the monks were thrown out, the buildings were looted and burned, and it lay in ruins for a century before a patient restoration began. Monks came back in 1940 and still live there. The abbey belongs to the Cistercian route that links it with the monasteries of Santes Creus and Vallbona de les Monges, and was inscribed by UNESCO in 1991.

The prehistoric side of the district is less obvious. Rock shelters in the cliffs near Montblanc and Prades contain painted figures in the Levantine style, protected as part of a wider UNESCO group. Many are hard to reach, small and fragile, and I cannot say what you will see at this point, so check locally.

The riding is on rural roads that climb out of the Conca de Barberà into the hills of Prades, with a mix of tight corners and smooth stretches under pine and oak. The road to the village of Prades, built of red stone around a big arcaded square, is enjoyable and ends in cool, fresh air at nearly a thousand metres. Weekends bring cyclists and walkers, and tractors appear at harvest. Autumn colour in the oak woods is a delight, while August afternoons are scorching and thunder can come quickly.

Montblanc, five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Vimbodí has a couple of bars and a bakery. The monks of Poblet sell their own products, and the local wines of the Conca de Barberà are worth tasting. Calçots, grilled spring onions dipped in romesco sauce, are a Catalan tradition in winter and early spring.
t.abric de la mostela@40.4,0.1:
The hill country around Albocàsser and Catí, in the north of Castellón province, is a landscape of terraced slopes, almond trees and limestone ravines that few visitors cross on their way from the coast to Morella. The Abric de la Mostela is a rock shelter here, about ten kilometres from Catí, and the coordinates take you into the heart of the Maestrat, among small farms and old stone walls.

The ravines were home to some of the earliest known art of the Mediterranean coast. The nearby Valltorta gorge, a short way south, is a famous concentration of Levantine paintings, small and lively red figures of archers, hunters and animals, and there is a museum at Tírig that explains them. Together they are part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin protected by UNESCO. The shelters themselves are often closed and fenced, and the paintings are fading, so see them with a guide or a local office rather than by climbing about on your own.

Catí is known for its cheese, a soft, tangy goat's cheese that is the pride of the district, and the village has a fine old centre with Gothic houses and a fair in its honour. Albocàsser has a church, a few bars and views over the surrounding ridges. Chert, or Xert, farther north, is a gorgeous small place with steep streets. The area has always been poor, and it shows in the stone shepherds' huts and the dry-stone walls that cover the hills in lines.

The riding is a pure delight for those who like empty roads. The CV roads between Catí, Albocàsser and Tírig rise and fall over small passes with lots of bends and no traffic, the surface is decent most of the way, and in spring the fields are green and the almond and cherry blossom lights up the valleys. The wind picks up in the afternoons, and winter nights are cold, with the odd frost on the shaded bends. In midsummer the heat is intense and the best time is early morning.

For fuel, the towns are small, so fill up before you leave the coast road. Alcalà de Xivert, sixteen kilometres away, has nearly seven thousand people and several stations, and Catí and Albocàsser have bars where you can get a coffee and a plate of local sausage or lamb. Plan your timing, because many places close from three to six in the afternoon.
t.abric del barranc d en cabrera@40.4,0.1:
The Maestrat is a quiet corner of Castellón, a country of dry-stone walls, almond groves and villages built on knolls, and the ravines that cut through it hide shelters painted with scenes from the Mesolithic and Neolithic. The Abric del Barranc d'en Cabrera belongs to the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean Basin, a tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 1998, and it lies in the hills above Albocàsser, near the little towns of Catí and Les Coves de Vinromà. The best-known cluster, the Valltorta gorge, lies not far away, with a museum at Tírig that explains the art and gives access to some sites.

Walking to a shelter here is part of the point. Paths drop into ravines scented with thyme and rosemary, crossing terraces held up by dry-stone walls that took generations to build, and lizards flash across the rocks. The paintings themselves are small, red and easily missed, so go with the right expectations and look at them quietly. They are fragile, and many are fenced, so follow the rules and do not touch.

Albocàsser is a village of about fourteen hundred people, and Catí, a bit larger, is known for its goat's cheese, which has protected status, and for a handsome old centre with Gothic houses. Fuel is limited in these hills, and the nearest sizeable town on the list, Alcalà de Xivert, is some distance away on the coast, so top up before you climb. Local food leans on lamb, wild boar and stews, with honey and olive oil as the staples.

The riding is peaceful and varied. The roads climb out of the coastal plain through olive terraces, then roll across a high plateau, with views toward the sea on clear days and long, empty stretches where you may see no other vehicle for half an hour. Surfaces are mostly decent, but patchy in places. Spring is the finest time, with wildflowers and green slopes, while summer is hot and dry, and winter nights bring frost to the heights.
t.balma del panta@41.9,0.9:
Camarasa is a small town beneath a big wall of water. The dam across the Noguera Pallaresa, built in the early twentieth century, holds back a long reservoir, the Pantà de Camarasa, in a dry, rocky corner of Lleida where the pre-Pyrenees fall toward the Ebro plain. The cliffs rise steep and ochre above the water, and in the folds of that rock, shelters hold painted scenes from long before there was a dam or even a town. The Balma del Pantà is one of the sites of the Levantine rock art of the Iberian Mediterranean, a tradition listed by UNESCO in 1998.

The place is dry and sunlit, and the scent is hot stone, rosemary and almond. Hawks and vultures circle on the thermals above the gorge, and kingfishers flick over the water. Balaguer, fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with about seventeen thousand people, a good market and an old centre on the Segre river, and it is the place to buy fuel and a proper meal. Camarasa itself is small, with only a few hundred people.

Other sites in the area, such as Monderes and the Cova del Cogulló, belong to the same family. The cave at El Cogul, a short way south, is celebrated for its scene of women dancing around a male figure, one of the best-known compositions in the art, and it has a visitor centre. Check opening times and book ahead if you plan to go, as sites are small and numbers are controlled.

For riders, this is a lovely region of gorges and reservoirs. The C-13 along the Noguera Pallaresa follows the river through narrow limestone cuts, with tunnels and cliffs towering overhead, and farther north the gorge of Mont-rebei, on the Aragonese border, is spectacular. Traffic is light, except on summer weekends. Spring and autumn are best, and winter mornings can be icy in the shadow of the cliffs.
t.aqueduct@41.1,1.2:
The Pont del Diable, the Devil's Bridge, is not a bridge for people. It is a Roman aqueduct, a tall, two-tiered stone arcade that carried water to Tarraco, modern Tarragona, from the Francolí river, about fifteen kilometres away. It spans a small valley near the road to Constantí, two hundred metres long and about twenty-seven metres high at its tallest point, built of big dressed stones without mortar, and it has stood for roughly two thousand years. UNESCO included it in the Archaeological Ensemble of Tarraco in 2000.

The legend is charming. A woman was tired of carrying water to her village, so the story goes, and offered her soul to the Devil if he built a bridge in a single night. He nearly finished it, but a clever woman, or a cock crowing too early, depending on the version, cut the deal short, and the last stone was left missing. Hence the name. You can walk along a path beside the arches and, in certain places, along the top, with a good view over pine woods and orchards.

Tarragona is only a few kilometres away, a city of 140,000 with a magnificent amphitheatre above the sea, a Roman circus, the forum and a cathedral on the hilltop of the old town. Fuel and food are abundant, and the Mediterranean seafood is superb, particularly in the fishermen's quarter, the Serrallo. Constantí and Els Pallaresos are smaller towns nearby.

For riding, you are in a busy corridor. The AP-7 toll motorway and the N-240 roar close by, so this is not a quiet spot, but just inland the Priorat wine country and the Prades mountains offer rewarding roads with tight bends and fine views. Hot summers make early starts wise, and winter is mild. Spring brings wildflowers and soft light on the stone, while autumn is cooler and the harvest is under way in the vineyards.
t.la saltadora abric i@40.4,0.1:
Albocàsser sits on a limestone shelf in the northern Maestrat, a farming village of about fourteen hundred people with a stone church, a market-day bustle and almond trees all around. A few kilometres from it, the Gasulla ravine and its neighbours hold Levantine rock paintings, and La Saltadora, the Jumper, is one of the shelters, named perhaps for a leaping figure or a nimble ledge. The Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula was added to the UNESCO list in 1998, and Abric I is a small but significant piece of that story.

The country around it is quietly beautiful. Olive terraces climb the slopes, shepherds' huts of dry stone, the barraques, dot the fields, and the smell of wild rosemary is constant. In spring the hills are green and spangled with wildflowers; in late summer they are tawny and loud with cicadas. Birds of prey ride the thermals above the ridges, and wild boar leave their tracks on every path.

The ride out is simple. Albocàsser is on a fine network of country roads that connect the villages of the Maestrat, and the surfaces are generally good, with gentle gradients and curves that fit a relaxed pace. Fuel and shops are limited, though the village has basic services, and the larger coast town of Alcalà de Xivert is the better bet for filling up before climbing into the hills. Nights can be cold even in spring, with a sharp drop after sunset.

For lunch, look for a village restaurant serving rabbit with snails, lamb with garlic, or a thick vegetable stew, with a glass of the local red. Tourism here is calm and respectful, and the rock shelters deserve the same attitude: look, photograph without flash, and leave everything as you found it. If you plan to see the paintings, find out first which sites are open and when, since access is controlled and some require a guide. Early morning is the best time to enjoy the silence of the ravines.
t.abric d esquarterades ii@40.6,0.5:
Ulldecona stands where the foothills of the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit slope toward the plain of the Ebro, in the south of Catalonia, and it is a town of about six thousand people with olive groves in every direction. The Serra de Godall rises behind, and under its cliffs, the shelters known as the Abrics de l'Ermita, near the hermitage of La Pietat, hold prehistoric paintings, with a small visitor centre that makes it one of the easier places to see this art. Esquarterades is another shelter in the same tradition, part of the Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Ulldecona has a long history, and its castle was held by the Order of the Hospital in the Middle Ages, a reminder that this was frontier country between Christian Catalonia and the Muslim south. The old streets, the church and the nearby hermitage are worth a stroll. The local olive oil is excellent, and the town celebrates it with festivals and tastings. In the surrounding hills, you will find dry-stone huts, ancient terraces and tracks used by shepherds for centuries.

Fuel, supermarkets and restaurants are all available in town, and the coast at Sant Carles de la Ràpita, with its seafood and its access to the Ebro Delta, is about half an hour away. The delta is a flat world of rice fields, lagoons and flamingos, and it makes a good contrast to the dry hills. Try the local arròs negre, rice with squid ink, or the grilled calçots in season.

The riding is varied. Roads wind through olive terraces and low hills, with views of the mountains of the Ports to the west, and the surfaces are generally good. Heat can be intense in July and August, and the wind, the mestral, blows hard from the northwest at times. March to June and September to November are best. Respect the shelter sites, which are fragile, and follow the guidance at the visitor centre.
t.cingle dels tolls del puntal@40.4,0.1:
Cingle means a cliff in Valencian, and the Cingle dels Tolls del Puntal is one of the rocky bands that cut across the hills of northern Castellón, in the Maestrat region. The shelters in these cliffs hold paintings of the Levantine rock art tradition, red figures of archers, goats and deer, protected by UNESCO as part of the Mediterranean Basin group. The Valltorta gorge nearby is one of the richest concentrations of this art, and there is a museum in the village of Tírig that explains the painted shelters. The shelters themselves are fragile and often restricted.

Albocàsser, the nearest village, lies in a farming basin of almond, olive and carob trees, with stone farmhouses scattered across it and a ring of sharp, grey-white hills. Cuevas de Vinromà and Catí are small, old and quiet, and Catí is known for its goat's cheese, which is soft, tangy and a good reason to stop at a local shop. The country smells of pine resin and wild herbs after rain, and in spring the hillsides are bright with yellow broom.

For a rider the Maestrat is a find. Narrow roads wind among terraces and rocky outcrops, with a pleasing mix of fast curves and tight corners, steep gradients and sudden views to the Mediterranean on a clear day. The traffic is light, and the villages rarely seem to have more than a few people in the street. Surfaces vary, with patches of rough tarmac and the occasional stray goat or sheep, and in summer the heat on the plateau is fierce. Early morning is the best time, with cool air and long shadows.

Fuel is available in larger towns, and the small villages here do not all have petrol stations, so it is wise to fill up in a bigger town before heading into the hills. Albocàsser has several bars for coffee and the local almond cakes, and Catí has a few restaurants serving lamb and local cheese. The best times of year are spring, when the wildflowers are out, and autumn, when the heat has eased. In winter the hills can be misty and cold, with an occasional dusting of snow.
t.abric d ermites vi@40.6,0.5:
Ulldecona sits at the foot of the Serra de Godall, in the southern tip of Catalonia, close to the border with Valencia and a short distance from the Ebro delta. The town is an old one, set among olive groves that produce a good oil, and above it stands the hermitage of La Pietat, with long views to the sea. The Abric d'Ermites VI is one of the rock shelters of the Ermites group, painted in the Levantine style with small red figures of hunters, and part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art inscribed by UNESCO in 1998. The shelters lie in the cliffs of the Godall range, and access is by foot with regulations to protect the paintings.

The country is dry and fragrant, with grey limestone ridges, scrubby pines, rosemary, and olive terraces climbing the slopes. The Serra de Godall is a modest range, but its cliffs hold griffon vultures, and in spring the ground is covered with flowers. The air is warm, and the smell of herbs is strong after rain. On a clear day you can see the sea, with the delta and its rice fields a flat green and gold plain beyond the hills.

For a motorcyclist, the road network of the Montsià and the Ports de Beseit is a fine area. Roads climb through olive groves with a series of long, easy bends, then wind into the hills with tighter corners and good views. Traffic is thin, and the surface is usually fair. In summer, the heat on the coast is intense, and the mountain roads are a relief. Winter is mild, though high roads can be misty.

Ulldecona is a town of over six thousand people with fuel, supermarkets and bars, and Santa Bàrbara and Masdenverge are smaller villages nearby. The local food is simple and good: olive oil, grilled vegetables, rice, and fish from the coast. Visit in spring, when the hills are green, or in autumn, when the heat has eased and the olive harvest begins.
t.hospital de sant pau@41.4,2.2:
There is a hill in Barcelona that most visitors reach by accident, on the walk from the Sagrada Família down a long avenue named after Gaudí. At the end of it stands the Hospital de Sant Pau, one of the greatest works of Catalan Modernisme, designed by Lluís Domènech i Montaner and built between 1902 and 1930 with money left by a banker called Pau Gil. The architect rejected the idea of a single block. Instead he built a garden city of pavilions, joined by underground tunnels, each with brick walls, tiled roofs and mosaics, so that patients could look out on trees and sky. It worked as a hospital until 2009, and has since been restored as a museum and cultural centre. UNESCO listed it in 1997 together with the Palau de la Música Catalana, also by Domènech.

Inside, the colours are the surprise. Sunlight comes through stained glass, domes glitter with tile and the sculpture is full of flowers and birds. The administration building has a grand staircase, and the pavilions are decorated with the names and arms of donors. The idea behind it was that beauty heals, which is as good a theory as any, and the place feels like a palace for the sick.

Riding in Barcelona is a matter of patience. The city is dense and busy, with a grid of one-way streets, tram lines, and fast-moving scooters, and parking for motorbikes is common on pavements marked for it, though rules vary and fines are real. Low emission zone rules apply to older vehicles, so check before entering. The surface is decent, but manhole covers and painted lines are slippery in the wet. On a weekday morning the traffic is heavy, and Sunday morning is calmer.

Fuel is available at stations around the edge of the central area, and the neighbourhoods around Sant Pau, Guinardó and Clot, have cafés and bakeries in every street. A coffee and a pastry in a local bar is the best way to recover. The hospital is open to visitors daily with some exceptions, and queues build in the middle of the day, so plan for the morning. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild temperatures and clear light on the tiles.
t.bco de la plana ii@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza is a town that was moved. In the 1960s the Ebro was dammed below the confluence with the Segre and the Cinca, and the new reservoir, known as the Mar de Aragón, drowned the old river valley. The old town was largely abandoned and its people rehoused up the slope, which is why the place feels more planned than ancient. What remained was the castle on its rock, a coal-mining history that fed the power stations of the lower Ebro, and a landscape of limestone ridges, pine and rock rose dropping to a long, green-blue lake. The Barranco de la Plana is one of the dry ravines running down to it, and the shelter that gives this stop its name sits among the rock art of the Mediterranean Basin that UNESCO listed in 1998.

The shelters in this part of the Ebro country are small and easily missed, with red figures painted in the Levantine style that suggest hunters, animals and groups of people. Finding them takes a guide or a good map, and the paintings are fragile, so regulations apply. The surroundings are better known to anglers, since the reservoir is famous across Europe for its huge catfish, introduced decades ago and now enormous. The local restaurants will happily serve river fish and rice, and the town has a small museum devoted to the mining past.

For a motorcyclist, Mequinenza sits where Aragon, Catalonia and the dry flat plains of the Ebro basin meet. Roads along the lake run through low hills with an easy rhythm of curves, and the views of the water against pale ground are surprisingly handsome. Traffic is light, the surface generally reasonable, and the scrub smells of thyme in the evening. In summer the heat is severe and the best riding is before ten in the morning and again after sunset. A cold wind called the cierzo comes down the valley in winter and can blow a bike sideways.

The town itself, under a kilometre away, has fuel, a supermarket and a handful of bars, and Fayón, across the water, is much smaller. Seròs, a little further along the Segre, has a few shops as well. Carry water on the walk to the shelter, wear solid shoes on the loose stone, and keep a close eye on your phone battery, because signals fade in the ravines.
t.cova de l escoda@41.0,0.8:
The Mediterranean Basin rock art does not end at the Valencian border, and the Cova de l'Escoda is a reminder that the painted shelters stretch up into Catalonia. This one lies in the hills inland from the Costa Daurada, in the dry, rugged country of the Baix Camp and the Ribera d'Ebre, with the Serra de Llaberia to the north and the Ebro valley to the south-west. The shelter belongs to the group listed by UNESCO in 1998, and its paintings are in the Levantine style. The nearest places on the map are El Perelló and Ginestar, though the largest town in the area is Mont-roig del Camp, some sixteen kilometres away.

Mont-roig has a particular claim to fame. It was the family farm of Joan Miró, who spent childhood summers there and returned throughout his life to paint, and the farmhouse, Mas Miró, appears in one of his best-known early works. The artist said the landscape of this part of Catalonia, with its red earth, carob trees and bright sea, shaped everything he later did. It is not hard to see why when you look at the colours here in the late afternoon.

The country is hard and fragrant, a mix of scrub, pine woods and terraced fields of almonds, olives and hazelnuts. The Ebro is not far, and the delta, with its rice fields and its birds, is a short ride south. The smell, on a warm day, is of thyme and resin and the faint salt of the sea. Wild boar are common and the cliffs hold eagles.

Riding here is easy and rewarding. The roads climb from the coast in a series of gentle bends, cross low passes with views of hills and sea, and wind through villages with narrow streets. Traffic is heavy near the coast in summer, because of the resorts, but the inland roads are quiet. The surface is generally good. Fuel is plentiful at the larger towns, including Mont-roig del Camp and El Perelló, and bars serve local food including calçots, the grilled spring onions of Catalonia, in season. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.eglesia de santa eulalia@42.5,0.8:
The little Romanesque church of Santa Eulàlia stands at Erill la Vall, one of the villages of the Vall de Boí in the Catalan Pyrenees, and its tall, slim bell tower is a landmark from the road. Together with ten other churches and hermitages in the valley, it was listed by UNESCO in 2000, and the whole group is a small marvel. They were built in the early twelfth century, in a style borrowed from Lombardy, with stout stone walls, round arches and bell towers decorated with blind arcades. Inside, the frescoes that once covered the walls were taken down in the early twentieth century and are now in the museum in Barcelona, while replicas have been placed on site.

The valley is a rider's treat. The road climbs from the Noguera Ribagorçana in a ribbon of tight bends and gentle straights, with the peaks of the Aigüestortes National Park rising ahead and the slopes covered in meadows, beech and fir. Traffic is light for most of the year, though the roads to the ski resort at Boí-Taüll fill in winter, and snow can close higher roads from November to April. Summer mornings are crisp, with mist in the hollows, while autumn colours are spectacular, with larches turning gold.
