Vielha, in the Val d'Aran, is about nineteen kilometres away by the crow, but the road distance is longer, and it has about five thousand people and reliable fuel. Closer by, small shops in the valley villages sell cheese, sausage and honey, and the local food is warming mountain cooking, with stews, grilled lamb and a hearty soup called olla. For a larger town on the southern side, El Pont de Suert is the usual stop.

Take your time at the church. The cool, dim interior and the thick stone walls are a pleasure in hot weather, and the view from the churchyard across the roofs of the village toward the mountains is lovely. Visits to some churches are by guided tour, so check the times, and keep your voice low, because this is still a place of worship.
t.cova del ramat@41.0,0.7:
The Ebro makes a great loop through southern Catalonia, and the Cova del Ramat lies in the dry hills just west of it, above the villages of Ginestar and Rasquera. The river here is broad and slow, lined with orchards and reed beds, and in 1938 it became the site of the Battle of the Ebro, the longest and bloodiest battle of the Spanish Civil War, which raged for nearly four months in the summer and autumn and left the hills riddled with trenches. Their traces survive in the landscape, and several memorial sites and museums, notably around Gandesa, tell the story.

The riding is rewarding and varied. Roads leave the river valley into the Serra de Cardó and neighbouring ranges, a land of scrub, pine and rocky ridges, with long views across the Ebro and the lowlands toward the Mediterranean. The bends are open and the tarmac holds up well, with little traffic outside the summer weekends. To the north lie the vineyards of the Priorat and Montsant, where slate soils produce some of Spain's most admired wines, and the roads there are twisting and scenic. Spring is the best season, with wildflowers and soft air, followed by autumn when the vineyards turn red and gold. Summer afternoons can be punishing, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees.

Fuel is a question of planning. Ginestar and Rasquera have a few hundred to a thousand inhabitants each, so look for stations in the bigger towns strung along the Ebro, such as Móra d'Ebre, or head toward the coast. Mont-roig del Camp, on the other side, is bigger, and the painter Joan Miró had a family farm there, which he loved and painted often. The local food is Mediterranean, with olive oil, almonds and good bread.

Cova del Ramat is one of several rock shelters here, and the paintings are of a style found all along the Spanish Levant. Visit with care, keep to the paths and take nothing but photographs. In the evening the hills fall quiet, and the smell of thyme and warm stone rises from the slopes.
t.punta del alcanizano@41.0,0.1:
Bajo Aragón has the look of a country that works for a living. Olive trees climb the terraces in tidy grey-green rows, almond orchards fill the gaps, and every village seems to own a mill or a cooperative that presses oil under a protected regional name. The Punta del Alcañizano sits in the rolling hills of the Matarraña district, near Valdeltormo and Mazaleón, two villages of a few hundred people each, on the southern edge of Aragón where the land begins to tilt toward Catalonia and the Ebro. The name, the Alcañiz point, suggests a landmark on the old boundary of the town's territory, though I cannot say what the marker is.

For a rider, this is easy-going country. The roads between villages are smooth, lightly trafficked and full of long, open curves, with fields of olive and vine on both sides and stone farmhouses scattered through them. Heat is the main issue in July and August, with afternoon temperatures that can be fierce, so go early. Spring, when the almond blossom fades and the poppies come out, is lovely, and so is October, when the light turns soft and the olive harvest begins. If you head south and west toward the Matarraña river, the scenery grows more dramatic, with limestone gorges and the medieval bridge and castle of Valderrobres.

Alcañiz, twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with about sixteen thousand people, so fill up there. It has a castle that is now a parador, a handsome arcaded main square and, for motorcyclists, a special draw: the Motorland circuit just outside town, where world championship races are held, and where track days are sometimes open to ordinary riders. Even if you are not racing, the sound of engines carries on a quiet afternoon.

Eat the local oil on bread, with tomato and a thin slice of cured ham, and you will understand why people here are proud of it. In spring the whole district smells of thyme and warm earth, and the stone walls keep the heat well after the sun has gone.
t.abric d ermites i@40.6,0.5:
Where Catalonia runs out, the Serra de Godall stands guard over Ulldecona, and in the rock faces under its ridge the oldest residents of the district left their paintings. Ulldecona is the southernmost town in the Tarragona province, a few kilometres from the Valencian border, and the shelters known collectively as Abrics de l'Ermita lie on the hill above the old hermitage. The Levantine paintings here, small and red, are part of the group UNESCO listed in 1998, and they are among the best preserved in Catalonia.

What makes the Ermites shelters special is the quality of the figures. Archers with long legs and tiny waists, animals that look about to bolt, and the sense of a scene being caught rather than composed. Some paintings here are protected by grilles, others by distance, and it is wise to look at the information on site rather than wander off unprepared. Whatever you find, treat the rock as you would a painted ceiling in a museum.

Ulldecona itself is a pleasant working town of about six thousand people, with a castle remnant and a long tradition of olive growing. The oil from this corner of the Montsià is a regional point of pride, and so are the carob trees and almonds that crowd the dry fields. A reservoir lies to the west, and beyond rises the great limestone wall of the Ports de Tortosa-Beseit, a natural park of ridges and goat tracks where you can see Spanish ibex if you are lucky.

For riders the surroundings are a treat. Leave the coast and its motorway behind, and you quickly reach roads that thread between olive terraces and rise toward the Ports with long, readable corners, decent tarmac and almost nobody on them outside weekends. Spring brings wildflowers, autumn smells of crushed grapes and woodsmoke, and summer is best saved for early mornings. The wind can be sharp when the mestral blows down from the north-west.

Ulldecona has several pumps and a good choice of bars and restaurants; this is the place to fill up before heading into the mountains, where villages are small and far apart. Take water and a hat if you walk to the shelters, because shade is scarce.
t.mas d en salvador abric i@40.4,0.0:
The Valltorta is the name that matters in this corner of Castellón, and everything about this shelter makes more sense once you know why. The Barranc de la Valltorta, a deep, narrow gorge cut through the limestone of the Alt Maestrat, holds one of the great concentrations of Levantine rock art, including scenes of hunting and fighting that were among the first to make archaeologists understand that these paintings tell stories. A small museum in nearby Tírig explains the gorge and its art, and it is a sensible starting point before you set out.

Mas d'en Salvador lies a few kilometres from Albocàsser, a village of fewer than fifteen hundred people on a plateau of olive and almond fields. The name Cova de Gargán sits on the region label here, and it tells you how many shelters crowd this landscape. The painted figures are tiny, red and sometimes so faded that you need a guide or a good photograph to make them out. What they show is people hunting deer and wild goats with bows, a world of movement drawn by someone who loved to watch it.

The Alt Maestrat is a landscape of stone: dry-stone walls, stone farmhouses, and peaks that rise toward Penyagolosa further inland. The people here live by olive oil, almonds and sheep, and the best thing to eat in the local bars is something simple like grilled lamb, cured sausage or a plate of local cheese with bread.

The riding is wonderful if you like quiet. Roads leave the coastal plain at Alcalà de Xivert and climb into the Maestrat with long, sinuous stretches over open country, little traffic, and views to the Mediterranean on a clear day. Corners are medium in speed, the road surface is generally good, and there are many places to pull over. The best light comes in the morning, when the hills turn gold and the air is cool.

For fuel, the nearest larger town is Alcalà de Xivert, a long way off, so fill up on the coast before climbing. Albocàsser has a bar or two for a coffee and a bocadillo, and that is about it. Carry water.
t.cingle de l ermita abric v@40.4,0.1:
Ermità means hermit, and a cingle is a cliff band, so the name tells you what you are looking for: a ledge of rock above a hermitage. The fifth shelter in this group lies beyond Albocàsser, in the Alt Maestrat of northern Castellón, where the limestone has been split into gorges and overhangs. The paintings here belong to the Levantine tradition that UNESCO listed in 1998, red figures drawn thousands of years ago by people who hunted and gathered in these hills before farming arrived.

It helps to understand the geography. This part of the Maestrat is a high, dry plateau of olives, almonds and cereal fields, divided by narrow barrancs and punctuated by small stone villages. The coast is barely thirty kilometres away, but the land feels remote, and the sea breeze brings nothing but a faint salt tang. Albocàsser itself is a quiet village of around a thousand and a half residents, and a visit gives you a sense of how life goes on in rural Valencian Spain, with a bar full of old men, a church on the hill and a bakery that sells out by eleven.

The riding here is a pure pleasure for anyone who prefers quiet. The roads are narrow, well-surfaced and mostly empty, running between dry-stone walls and over small rises that give a view down toward the plain. The bends are friendly rather than dramatic, which suits the landscape, and in spring the roadside is bright with poppies and broom. In summer, start early. By noon the heat in these valleys is serious.

Nobody makes a fuss of the shelters, and that is one of the pleasures. Information boards exist in some places, but many of the paintings are known mainly to local guides and to the people who have walked these paths for years. Respect the rock and keep your hands off it.

Fuel is a problem to solve before you arrive. Alcalà de Xivert is the nearest sizeable town, and it is nearly twenty kilometres away, so fill up there or on the coast. Albocàsser has a bar for coffee and a simple meal.
t.cueva pena miel ii@42.3,0.1:
The Sierra de Guara is cut by gorges so deep that sunlight reaches the bottom only at midday, and the Cueva Peña Miel lies on the edge of that wild country, in the foothills of the Pyrenees in Huesca. It is part of the Río Vero Cultural Park, an area where painted shelters, some in the Levantine tradition and others in a later, more abstract schematic style, are scattered through the canyons and cliffs. The park is a UNESCO site, and Peña Miel, which translates as Honey Rock, is one of the smaller ones, a fact that keeps it quiet.

The nearest village is Alquézar, which should be on every rider's list. It stands on a rocky hill above the Vero gorge, with a Moorish castle that became a collegiate church and a village of narrow stone streets descending the slope. Walkways bolted to the cliff, called the passerelles, take walkers above the river, and the canyon below is a draw for canyoneers from across Europe. Vultures wheel overhead, including the rare bearded vulture that has been reintroduced to the Pyrenees.

The ride here is wonderful. From Barbastro the road winds up through the vineyards of the Somontano, whose wines are among the best in Aragon, and then into a dry, rocky landscape of oak and boxwood. Corners are medium to tight, sometimes with gravel at the edge, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. Spring and autumn are ideal, with soft light on the cliffs and cool temperatures, while mid-summer afternoons are hot and the canyons draw crowds.

Think ahead about fuel. Alquézar is a village of a few hundred and not a place to rely on for petrol, and the nearest large town is Barbastro, nearly thirty kilometres away. Fill up there. Bring water, because the paths to any shelter are dry, and watch the weather, since flash floods in the gorges are real and can come with little warning.

The cave is delicate and best seen only with permission or a guide.
t.massane@42.5,3.0:
Argelès-sur-Mer is known for its long beach, but the fun is in the hills behind it. The Albères are the eastern end of the Pyrenees, a low, forested range that drops straight into the Mediterranean, and the Massane is its secret. The Forêt de la Massane is a nature reserve of beech trees, some of them centuries old, growing on the cool northern slopes at a height where one would not expect them near the sea. In 2007 it was inscribed by UNESCO as part of the primeval beech forests of Europe, and scientists have studied its dead wood and insects for decades.

A rider cannot enter the beech forest, which is a walking reserve, but the approach is half the pleasure. From Collioure, the little fishing town with its blue-domed bell tower and its anchovies, roads climb into the hills through terraced vineyards that produce Banyuls and Collioure wines. In 1905 the painters Matisse and Derain worked in Collioure and gave birth to Fauvism with the explosive colours of the bay. The Tour de la Massane stands above the forest, one of a string of medieval watch towers that guarded the border.

The riding here is a mixture of coastal views and mountain roads. Narrow lanes climb steeply through vines and cork oak, there are lots of hairpins, and the surface is mixed, with some rough patches. The Tramontane, the dry north wind, can blow hard, especially in winter and spring, so be ready for gusts on exposed bends. Come on a clear day for views along the coast to Spain, and in autumn when the vineyards turn red and gold.

The border is only a few kilometres south, and the Col de Banyuls takes you over into Catalonia on a modest, pleasant road. Cross it for lunch if you like, but remember that rules and fuel prices differ.

Collioure has bars and restaurants, though little parking in summer, and Argelès, with ten thousand people, is the nearest place to fill up.
t.cova de les creus@41.3,1.1:
Montblanc is a walled town that looks almost too perfect, and then you realise it has been looking like this since the fourteenth century. The Conca de Barberà is a basin of vineyards and cereal fields ringed by low mountains, and Montblanc sits at its heart with over a kilometre of medieval walls, towers and gates still standing. The town claims to be the setting for the legend of St George and the dragon, and each April it celebrates the festival of Sant Jordi, with a medieval week of costumes and markets.

The shelter marked here lies a few kilometres out of town, among scrubby hills and dry valleys, in the Abric de Gallicant area. Rock art in Catalonia is less famous than that of Valencia or Aragon, but there are important painted places across the region, and some belong to the same Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO in 1998. The Cova de les Creus, Cave of the Crosses, tells you something about how later people have used these places, and at many shelters you may see more recent marks beside the prehistoric ones.

The surrounding area is full of history. Two great Cistercian monasteries, Poblet and Santes Creus, lie within easy reach, and together with a third at Vallbona they form the Cistercian Route. Poblet in particular is a large, serene complex of cloisters and royal tombs, and it was declared a World Heritage site in 1991. A visit is an easy addition to a day in the countryside.

The roads here are among the nicest in Catalonia for relaxed riding. They wander between vineyards, almond orchards and small villages, with gentle gradients, good surfaces and little traffic. The Prades mountains rise to the south, and the road toward them gets steeper and twistier. Spring brings flowers and autumn the grape harvest, and both are good seasons.

Montblanc has six and a half thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and shops. Try the calçots, grilled spring onions, in season, or a plate of local sausage and bread.
t.abric de la bonansa@40.5,0.1:
Bonansa means fair weather, a calm sea or that lull after a storm, and it is a rather hopeful name to give a shelter in a land of wind and drought. The place lies on the high ground of the Baix Maestrat, a few kilometres from the village of Xert, known in Spanish as Chert, where the olive terraces start to climb toward the dry mountains of the interior. The shelter is one of the painted places of the Levantine rock art tradition, red figures on limestone that the UNESCO list of 1998 brought to wider notice.

Xert is a village of fewer than a thousand people, and its charm is that nothing much has been done to it. Stone houses cluster around the church, the bars open early and close late, and most of the talk is about the olive harvest. Nearby, Sant Mateu was the medieval capital of the Maestrat, the district named for the military order of Montesa that ruled these lands, and its old streets and Gothic church give a sense of how important this quiet region once was. If you only have time for one extra stop, make it there.

The roads here are among the best-kept secrets of the Valencian side. They leave the coastal plain near Alcalà de Xivert and climb onto a plateau of rolling hills, dry-stone walls and scattered farmhouses. The corners are gentle, the views long, and traffic nearly nonexistent. There is wind on the open stretches, sometimes enough to lean on, and in summer the sun is relentless, so go early or late. April, May and October are the best months.

Wildlife is part of the scene. Red-legged partridges burst out of the verges, kestrels hover over the fields, and in the evening wild boar come to the edges of the olive groves. The scrub is full of rosemary, thyme and gorse, and the smell on a warm afternoon is something you carry home.

Practical matters need forethought. The nearest larger town is Alcalà de Xivert, over twenty kilometres away, so top up on the coast before you climb. Xert has a bar for coffee and a plate of something hot, and little more. Carry water for the walk.
t.medol quary@41.1,1.3:
Some quarries are ugly scars, and this one is a lesson in what the Romans meant by planning. The Médol quarry, a few kilometres east of Tarragona near Altafulla and Torredembarra, supplied the golden sandstone that built much of Roman Tarraco, the capital of a huge province. Blocks were cut here, hauled to the coast and shipped or carted along the Via Augusta to build temples, walls and the amphitheatre. The quarry is part of the archaeological ensemble of Tarraco inscribed by UNESCO in 2000.

What you see today is a series of deep, square-cut chambers in the rock, now partly overgrown with pine and rosemary. Standing in the middle is a tall pillar of stone left behind, known as the Agulla del Médol, the Needle, which may have been left as a marker of the original ground level or simply because it was not worth cutting. The cut faces still carry the marks of the tools, and in places you can see where blocks were half-detached and abandoned. It is a quiet, slightly eerie place on a still afternoon.

Altafulla, two and a half kilometres away, is a pleasure of its own. Its walled medieval core, the Vila Closa, is crowned by a castle and filled with narrow lanes, and just beyond lies a long, gentle beach. Torredembarra, a larger town, has a harbour and a seaside promenade, and Tarragona itself is a short ride away with its amphitheatre above the sea.

This stretch of the Costa Daurada is not a great riding area in the mountain sense. Roads run along the coast and through low hills of vines and pines, mostly busy and straight. The pleasure is the history and the sea air. Early morning or late afternoon in spring and autumn are the best times, when the traffic thins and the light turns golden, much like the stone.

Fuel and food are no problem. Torredembarra has pumps, supermarkets and many restaurants, and a plate of grilled seafood or an arròs is easy to find. Bring a hat in summer, because the quarry floor traps heat.
t.tower of the scipios@41.1,1.3:
Rome built a road through Spain, and this tower stands beside what was left of it. The Torre dels Escipions, the Tower of the Scipios, is a tall, square funerary monument, about nine metres high in its present state, on the old line of the Via Augusta a few kilometres from Tarragona. It was built in the first century AD, and for a long time people thought it was the tomb of the Scipio brothers, the Roman generals who died fighting the Carthaginians in Spain around 211 BC. That story is almost certainly false, but the name stuck.

On its faces you can still make out three carved figures, which most scholars read as the god Attis, a young man in Eastern dress associated with death and rebirth. They are worn and weathered, and a pair of inscriptions has long since vanished. The tower stands alone in a field beside a quiet road, which gives it an odd dignity, and it is part of the archaeological ensemble of Tarraco that UNESCO listed in 2000.

The region label mentions the Cova del Taller, a nearby cave, and the area is rich in ancient remains. Tarraco was the capital of Roman Hispania Citerior, and the city's amphitheatre, circus and walls are among the best in Spain. A short ride south you reach Altafulla and its medieval centre, and a few kilometres on the Arc de Berà, a Roman triumphal arch that still straddles the old road.

The ride is easy and pleasant rather than thrilling. Minor roads run between vineyards and pines, with some gentle curves, and the old N-340 follows the Via Augusta along the coast. Traffic can be heavy, particularly in summer, so choose early morning or late afternoon. Spring and autumn offer the softest light.

Tarragona is the place for fuel and food, a city of 140,000 people only six kilometres away, with a big port and a good seafood tradition. Altafulla also has pumps and restaurants. Bring a camera, and a hat for summer, since there is little shade at the tower.
t.eglesia de santa maria@42.5,0.8:
Nine Romanesque churches stand in the Vall de Boí, high in the Catalan Pyrenees, and together they make one of the most coherent medieval landscapes in Europe. They were built in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, in a style that came from Lombardy with masons who knew how to raise stone towers without much money. UNESCO inscribed the group in 2000, calling them outstanding examples of a distinctive Lombard-Catalan style in a remote mountain setting.

The Santa Maria churches of the valley belong to that group, with their tall, slender bell towers rising in several storeys of small arched windows. Their interiors once held frescoes of astonishing quality, painted in strong reds, blues and ochres, and the best of them were removed in the early twentieth century to the National Art Museum of Catalonia in Barcelona for safe keeping, with copies and projections now in place in the churches themselves. It is an odd experience to stand in a small stone church and see a ghost image of a giant Christ looking down.

The valley road runs up from El Pont de Suert through villages whose stone houses and slate roofs seem to grow out of the mountain. It is a good road, with tight bends, short climbs and spectacular views toward the peaks of the Aigüestortes National Park, which is a few kilometres away and has mountain lakes and granite crests. Traffic is light except in summer and at weekends, and the weather changes fast. Snow can close the roads in winter, and fog and thunderstorms are common in summer afternoons.

Practicalities need care. Castejón de Sos and Vielha are each over twenty kilometres away, and the valley villages are small, so do not assume fuel is available. Fill up in a larger town before you climb. Churches may be open only at set times, with guided tours or tickets from a central office in the valley, so check the schedule before arriving.

A bowl of hot soup or a plate of local sausage in a mountain bar is a pleasure after a cool morning.
t.centelles abric v@40.4,0.0:
Up on the Maestrat plateau in Castellón the country changes its mind about what it is. Below you the Mediterranean orchards give way to bare limestone, juniper, kermes oak and the stone-walled fields of a place that was once rich in sheep and wool. Centelles lies in that landscape between Catí and Albocàsser, and the shelter here is one of a scatter of rock paintings that make the Valencian hills one of Europe's richest outdoor galleries of prehistoric art.

I would not describe the ride in as thrilling, because the pleasure is subtler. The roads from Catí and Albocàsser wind across open upland between fields and old farmhouses, the surfaces are typically fair, the traffic is close to nothing, and corners come in easy sets that leave plenty of time to look at the Penyagolosa massif standing on the horizon to the west. The hills are cold in winter and sometimes snowy, and the wind can pick up hard across the open ground, so check the forecast. Late spring, when the broom is yellow and the barley is green, is the best moment.

Catí is worth knowing for its goat cheese, an old local speciality that you can buy in the village and eat on a bench with bread, and for the Gothic town hall that speaks of its medieval wealth. Albocàsser lies a few kilometres to the south and is another quiet farm town with a good square. Both are small enough that fuel is not guaranteed, so plan to fill in Alcalà de Xivert, the nearest town of any size, which is twenty-three kilometres away towards the coast, before turning inland.

As for the paintings, the typical pattern in this district is a low shelter along a barranc wall with a few faded red figures, often fenced to protect them. The nearby Valltorta museum at Tírig is the place to understand what you are looking at, and it is better to go there first than to arrive cold at a shelter and be disappointed that the images are smaller than the story.
t.mas d en carles@41.3,1.1:
Montblanc is a walled town with a dragon, and that alone makes it worth the detour. The thirteenth-century and fourteenth-century ramparts still circle the old centre almost intact, towers and gates and all, and the town has long claimed the legend of Saint George and the dragon as its own, which is why Catalans exchange roses and books on Sant Jordi in April. It sits in the Conca de Barberà, a basin of vineyards and fields surrounded by wooded ranges, and Mas d'En Carles lies in the hills to the south-east, on the edge of the Prades mountains.

The riding around here is quiet, easy and often lovely. Roads climb gently from Montblanc into oak and pine woods, curve through small farm country, and cross the hills at relaxed gradients with a mix of bends that favours a gentle tour rather than a hard ride. The traffic thins as soon as you leave the main roads. Spring brings fresh green and wildflowers, autumn gives colour and clear air, and winter can be cold enough in the higher parts that you should check for ice early in the morning.

This is also a region of Cistercian history. The monastery of Poblet, a few kilometres beyond Vimbodí, is one of the largest surviving Cistercian complexes in Europe, a royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon behind massive walls, and it is a World Heritage Site. If you only stop for one thing in this corner of Catalonia, stop there, and bear in mind that the monastery has strict visiting hours and that the car park is no place to leave expensive luggage on a bike.

Fuel is easy at Montblanc, only seven kilometres away, with Alcover as a second option, so there is no need to worry about range. Vimbodí is smaller but has bars and a bakery. The rock shelter here is part of the same Levantine and schematic art family that spreads from Catalonia down through Valencia and Andalusia, and in this area the paintings tend to be modest in size, so look for the informative panels rather than expecting a grand gallery.
t.centelles abric iii@40.4,0.0:
Some places on a map look like they were made for motorcycles, and the Maestrat is one of them, with its folded limestone and its small roads that rarely carry anything heavier than a delivery van. Centelles, between Catí and Albocàsser, is a quiet corner of that plateau, and it is where you leave the modern world for an hour and walk to a rock shelter that holds paintings from before farming took hold of the valleys.

The approach takes you across upland country that feels more Aragonese than Valencian, with long skylines of pale rock, oaks and juniper, and in the distance the pyramid of Penyagolosa, which at 1,813 metres is the highest point of Castellón. The roads here are narrow but clear, with bends that are easy to read, good for cruising rather than racing. Cold air lingers in the hollows in winter, so on frosty mornings ride with care, while in July the shade is a rare luxury.

The old economy of this part of the world was wool and cheese, and you can still see it in the sheepfolds and the stone barns that dot the landscape. In Catí the town hall and the old merchant houses reflect that wealth, and the goat cheese made around here is a good reason to carry a small cool bag. Albocàsser, on the other side, has a pleasant square and a few modest places to eat, and the whole Maestrat was a stronghold of the Carlist armies in the nineteenth century.

Towns here are small, so fuel is something to plan rather than assume. Alcalà de Xivert, twenty-three kilometres away on the road to the coast, is the nearest real town, and it is wise to arrive with a decent tank. The paintings, when you reach them, are modest, as is typical in the region: a few faded figures in red under a ledge of rock. They reward patience and a slow look more than a quick stop, and they stay far better when visited quietly and with respect.
t.cueva de la font de la bernarda@41.0,0.2:
Ask a rider where the best quiet roads in Aragon are and, sooner or later, someone says Matarraña. It is the river and the district at the southern end of Teruel province, a land of olive terraces, almond orchards, honey-coloured villages and low limestone ridges, and people in Zaragoza call it the Tuscany of Aragon without any irony. The Cueva de la Font de la Bernarda sits in the hills a few kilometres from Calaceite, with Valderrobres just over the hill and the Catalan border not far beyond.

Calaceite itself is a handsome little town of arcaded squares and Renaissance and Baroque houses, and it has fuel, bakeries and several places for a long lunch. Valderrobres, ten kilometres away, is the showpiece: a medieval fortified bridge over the Matarraña, a castle-palace of the archbishops of Zaragoza above it, and a Gothic church with a tall bell tower. If the light is right the reflection of the whole composition in the river is one of the best sights in the region. The local olive oil, protected under the Bajo Aragón designation, is worth putting in your panniers.

The roads between these villages are what riders come for. Smooth surface, light traffic, sequences of medium-radius bends over low passes, and in spring a green and gold landscape that makes you slow down, though summer heat can be fierce and the wind, the cierzo, can blow hard from the north-west. Out towards Alcañiz, twenty-eight kilometres away, you will find MotorLand, the circuit that hosts the Aragon MotoGP round, and the town itself has the larger shops and workshops you might need.

As for the cave, the area has a series of small rock shelters with paintings in the Levantine tradition, made by hunters and gatherers long before the Iberians built their hilltop villages here. Many are hard to find without a guide or local signs, and the terrain around them is rough scrub and rock, so wear boots and look closely. Valcomuna and the Ermites shelters share the same landscape, so you can spend a long, slow day in a district where history is layered up like pastry.
t.eglesia de la nativitat@42.5,0.8:
The Vall de Boí is a cul-de-sac with a gift in it. It lies at the head of the Noguera de Tor, tucked below the high granite of the Aigüestortes national park, and in the Middle Ages local people built a string of small stone churches along it, each with a tall Lombard bell tower, so that the valley's skyline reads like a row of exclamation marks. In 2000 UNESCO named them together as the Catalan Romanesque Churches of the Vall de Boí. The Església de la Nativitat in Durro is one of them, and its slim tower seems to catch the light better than almost any other.

The way in is part of the pleasure. From El Pont de Suert you follow the valley road up through Barruera, with the river below and the mountains ahead, and the bends grow tighter and the air cooler as you climb. The surface is good, the traffic modest apart from weekends in winter when skiers head for Boí-Taüll, and in high summer you will share the road with hikers and walkers heading for the park. Snow can close the upper part of the valley in winter, and early mornings in spring can be icy in the shaded bends.

The art that made the valley famous is mostly not here any more, though. The twelfth-century wall paintings of Taüll, including the great Christ in Majesty of Sant Climent, were removed in the 1920s to protect them, and now hang in the museum in Barcelona, with replicas in place in the churches. It is an honest compromise, and the replicas are well done, but it is worth knowing before you ride up expecting to see the originals in situ.

Vielha is the nearest town of any size, twenty-two kilometres away on the other side of the mountain, and the sensible fuel stop is at El Pont de Suert on the way in. Villages in the valley are small, with places to eat that serve mountain food such as stews, cured meats and local cheese. Parking a motorcycle by a Romanesque church wall is no problem, and a short walk through Durro's stone lanes, with their slate roofs and heavy doors, is a pleasant way to rest.
t.cueva de malifeto@42.3,0.0:
The Sierra de Guara is limestone country, and it behaves like it: the rivers have sliced through the rock in deep canyons, the villages sit on crags, and the sky is full of vultures. Cueva de Malifeto is in the foothills of the range, eleven kilometres from Alquézar, a village that grew up around a hilltop collegiate church above the gorge of the Río Vero. The name has a slightly sinister ring in Spanish, and shepherds in these hills have always had stories about odd and shadowy places.

The riding is memorable. The roads in this part of Huesca wind between stony ridges, drop into river valleys, climb again and run along ledges with views across the plains towards the Ebro, and each season gives them a different character. Spring brings flowers and swollen streams, autumn gives crystal air, summer is hot and lively with canyoners and climbers, and winter is quiet. Gravel is common near the canyon heads, so ride with a bit of caution. The road to Aínsa, nineteen kilometres away, is a classic: Aínsa's arcaded plaza and walled old town are one of the most beautiful in Aragon.

Alquézar deserves a stop. The Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor, begun in the eleventh century on the site of a Muslim fortress, looks down on the river from a rocky spur, and below it the Vero is crossed by a footpath of wooden walkways bolted to the canyon wall. The village is a good place for coffee, with narrow streets of stone houses and several terraces. The Vero canyon also holds painted rock shelters that belong to the same UNESCO listing as the Valencian ones.

Fuel is important here. Alquézar and the other small villages have no reliable pumps, so fill in Barbastro, twenty-eight kilometres away, a lively town and the capital of the Somontano wine district, where you can also buy supplies and see the cathedral. Griffon vultures are almost always overhead, and with luck you may spot the larger bearded vulture, once nearly extinct in Spain.
t.bco de campells ii@41.4,0.3:
Mequinenza has a double life. There is the town you can ride into today, a quiet place on a hillside above a vast stretch of water, and there is the town that lies underneath that water, the old Mequinenza, which was flooded when the reservoir was filled in the 1960s and whose people were moved up the hill. The writer Jesús Moncada grew up in the old town and made it the subject of his novels in Catalan, so if you want one book to read before coming here, that is the one to look for. The Bco. de Campells is a dry ravine two and a half kilometres out, with a small rock shelter holding prehistoric paintings.

The setting is the meeting of two big rivers. The Segre flows into the Ebro here, and the dams downstream turned the whole confluence into a long green lake that Aragonese people sometimes call their inland sea. Anglers come from all over Europe for the giant catfish that thrive in it. The landscape is dry and stony, with pale hills, pines, thyme and rosemary, and the surrounding terrain is often glaring in summer and surprisingly cold in January, when the cierzo wind can cut across the water.

For riders the roads are open and fast. They run along the lake, drop to the water, climb to a plateau, and cross it in long, easy bends, with plenty of room to see what is coming and not much traffic. Take care in the gravelly corners where tracks join the road, and remember that there can be strong crosswinds on the bridges and dams. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the light is clear and the temperatures kind.

Fuel can be found in Mequinenza itself, but Fraga, sixteen kilometres away on the road towards Lleida, has more choice and larger shops. Seròs lies across the river on the Catalan side with a lock and a modest riverside promenade. If you are hungry, local restaurants specialise in freshwater fish and in Aragonese lamb, and the castle hill above the town gives a good outlook over the reservoir. Take water for the walk to the shelter, and do not climb on the rock.
t.ermitage de sant quirc@42.5,0.8:
Durro is a village of about a hundred people and a church tower too tall for its size, which is typical of the Vall de Boí. The hermitage of Sant Quirc stands on a rise just outside the village, a plain Romanesque building from the same period as the great churches of the valley, and it looks out over the Noguera de Tor and its steep, fir-covered sides. The Nativity church in the village below shares a map with it, so the two work well together as a short walk.

The way up is one of the best rides in the Catalan Pyrenees, and the high passes towards the Val d'Aran lie not far to the north. From El Pont de Suert the valley road starts gently and then narrows between slopes of beech and pine, and as you gain height you cross small bridges over side streams. The bends are smooth and well banked, the surface good, and the traffic light apart from winter weekends. In spring the meadows are full of flowers and in autumn the beeches go copper.

What strikes you here, apart from the scenery, is the Lombard style of the churches. Masons from northern Italy, trained in the early Romanesque, came to the Pyrenees in the eleventh and twelfth centuries and left their bell towers with rows of small blind arches and shallow pilasters, which you can read at a glance as a signature. Together the churches are listed by UNESCO, and visiting them one after another is a lesson in how a small, remote valley can be rich in art.

Be prepared for the practicalities. There are no large towns, and Vielha, twenty-two kilometres away over the pass, is the nearest, so plan your fuel in El Pont de Suert or in Vielha. The upper valley is subject to snow in winter. Small restaurants in the villages serve mountain food, including stews and grilled meat, and the water from fountains is generally cold and good. Respect the hours of the churches, which are often open only at certain times.
t.eglesia de sant feliu@42.5,0.8:
Barruera is the main village of the Vall de Boí, and its church of Sant Feliu stands over the houses with a stout tower and a roofline that has been altered through the centuries. Here, more than in the smaller villages higher up, you get a sense of the valley as a living place, with a main street, a few shops, a café, and children heading to school. The valley is just over twenty kilometres from Vielha as the crow flies, but the mountains between make it a very different world.

The road in from the south is part of the experience. The L-500 and the roads that continue to Boí follow the Noguera de Tor upstream with the peaks of the Aigüestortes park rising ahead, and the surface is generally good with moderate gradients and smooth bends. In winter the valley can be icy and snowbound at the top end, but from May to October it is open and green. Early morning is the quietest time, and the light on the stone is lovely.

History here is dense. The valley was fought over in the early Middle Ages as Christian counts pushed back the Muslim frontier, and the villages built defensive towers that later became bell towers, which is one reason why they are so tall. In the twelfth century the region saw an extraordinary flowering of art, with wall paintings that are now considered masterpieces of European Romanesque. The best of them were taken to Barcelona in the 1920s, but copies in the churches give a feel for the original colours.

For fuel, the nearest sure place is El Pont de Suert, back down the valley, as the villages here are small. Vielha is about twenty-two kilometres away, over the mountains, and has everything. A walk around Barruera's lanes takes only a few minutes, and the village has a good place for a coffee and a slice of local cheese. The mountains around hold chamois and marmots, and golden eagles hunt along the ridges.
t.nativity facade and crypt of the basilic:
Gaudí took forty-three years of his life on the Sagrada Família and still did not see it finished. He began work in 1883, soon after taking over from another architect, and from the 1890s onward he devoted himself to it almost completely, living in a workshop on site in his last years. The Nativity Façade, on the east side, is the part that he built the most of, and it was the only one to be substantially completed in his lifetime. Its carved portals teem with plants, animals and figures, tortoises at the foot of its columns included, and the effect is like a cliff of stone coral.

Underneath is the crypt where Gaudí himself is buried, after being hit by a tram in 1926 and, at first, not being recognised because he was so shabbily dressed. The crypt was the first part of the church to be built and is much quieter than the nave above, a plain Neo-Gothic space with the architect's tomb in a side chapel. UNESCO has listed the façade and crypt with other works by Gaudí in Barcelona, and it is worth seeing them in daylight.

As for the riding, this is not a place to cruise. You are in the middle of Barcelona's grid, and the best approach is to arrive early, park the bike in one of the designated motorcycle bays on a nearby street, and walk. Traffic is dense and the cobbles are slick when wet, and tourists step off kerbs without looking. Check the rules for the city's low-emission zone before you go, as older bikes may be restricted, and keep your belongings with you, because Barcelona has a well-earned reputation for bag theft.

There is a good reason to come, though. A rider who has spent days in the empty hills of Valencia and Aragon will find that the contrast gives the city extra force. Pause on the pavement outside, look up at the towers and take in the shock of its detail. Fuel is available at several stations around the city, and the cafés nearby serve everything from strong coffee to a plate of tapas. Weekday mornings are the quietest time to visit.
t.catalan romanesque churches of the vall:
There are nine churches in the Vall de Boí listed by UNESCO, and the surprise is that they are not museum pieces. They stand in working villages, with cows in the lanes, firewood stacked against the walls and the bells still ringing, and together they make one of the best-preserved groups of Romanesque churches in Europe. Sant Climent and Santa Maria de Taüll, the pair that everyone comes for, stand a few hundred metres apart on the hillside above the Noguera de Tor, and they were consecrated within a day of each other in December 1123. The others, in Boí, Erill la Vall, Cardet, Durro, Barruera and Coll, are quieter but each has a character of its own.

Look first at the towers. They are slim, tall and decorated with rows of small blind arches, the Lombard fashion brought up from northern Italy, and they can be seen from across the valley, so that the road up feels like a count-off of villages by steeple. At Boí, the church of Sant Joan keeps a painted scene of the stoning of Saint Stephen. The great paintings from Taüll, including the Christ in Majesty of Sant Climent, were taken off the walls in the early twentieth century and are now in the museum in Barcelona, with replicas in the churches, but the buildings reward a visit on their own.

The riding up the valley is a joy. The road from El Pont de Suert runs for about thirty kilometres in a gentle climb, with views of the high peaks ahead, and the bends are open and well banked. The surface is generally excellent, but the valley is often shaded, so ice can linger in winter and spring. Weekends in July and August bring traffic, and in winter skiers heading for Boí-Taüll fill the road, so a weekday morning in May or October is the best time.

Fuel is at El Pont de Suert, not in the valley itself, and Vielha, twenty-two kilometres away over the range, is the nearest town of any size. Restaurants in Boí and Taüll serve the mountain food of this part of the Pyrenees, with stews, cured sausages and local cheeses, and half an hour in a cool church followed by a coffee is a fine way to close a day. Churches are not always open, so ask in the tourist office before you go.
t.covacho de labarta@42.2,0.0:
Somontano means under the mountain, and that is just what this district is: the rolling foothills of the Pyrenees below the Sierra de Guara, where the land opens from the stony gorges into a country of vineyards, almond groves and golden fields. The wine region of that name, around Barbastro, is one of the quiet success stories of Spanish viticulture, and its reds, whites and rosés are well worth carrying home. The Covacho de Labarta is six kilometres from Alquézar, in the hills that look down on the gorge of the Río Vero.

Riding here has an easy rhythm. The roads wind through vineyards and low hills, with views of the Pyrenees on clear days, and the bends are smooth and open. Surfaces are mostly excellent, and the traffic is light except on weekends in summer when canyoners and climbers come to the Guara. Early autumn, when the grapes are being picked and the light is golden, is the best time.

Barbastro, twenty-three kilometres away, is the sensible stop for fuel. It has a cathedral in late Gothic style, a long history, and a wide choice of restaurants. Torreciudad, a large hilltop shrine above a reservoir with a long view of the Pyrenees, lies well to the north and could be added for a longer day. Alquézar is a pleasure to wander through, with a collegiate church on a rock above the river, but it is a small village and you should not rely on pumps. Salas Altas and Angüés are smaller still.

The shelter is a small one, a covacho being a modest hollow, and its paintings belong to the tradition that spread across the Spanish Levant. Visitors should check locally before trying to reach it, and the information points in Alquézar are a good place to start. Take water for the walk, be mindful of the heat, and watch for griffon vultures, which nest on the cliffs above the Vero and are nearly always in the sky.
Menorca is the quieter of the Balearic islands, and its prehistoric heritage is the reason it appears on the UNESCO list as Talayotic Menorca, inscribed in 2023. From around the second millennium BC until the Roman conquest, the island's people built massive stone towers called talayots, T-shaped stone altars known as taulas, and burial monuments shaped like upturned boats, the navetas. They did it on an astonishing scale for an island of this size, and the stone ruins lie everywhere, in fields and pine woods.

The island's roads are a pleasure to ride. The main road crosses from Maó to Ciutadella along the spine of the island, and the minor roads run out to the coast between dry-stone walls, called parets seques, that divide every field. Corners are gentle, the surface is usually good, and speeds are low, so this is a place for a slow ride. The north wind, the tramuntana, can be strong in winter and spring, and the summer months fill the roads with rental cars, so spring and autumn are the best times.

Maó, seven kilometres away, is the capital and a handsome port on one of the largest natural harbours in the world. It is the home of Mahón cheese, of a gin distilled to a recipe left by the British, who held the island for much of the eighteenth century, and, according to a legend that the French dispute, of mayonnaise. The town has plenty of fuel and good restaurants, and the waterfront is excellent for a long lunch. Es Castell and Alaior are close alternatives with their own character.

The northern side of the island is wilder, with low cliffs, scrub and small coves. The Camí de Cavalls, an old bridleway, circles the whole island, and you can walk sections of it from many points. The ferry from Barcelona or Valencia is the usual way to bring a bike. Take water and sun protection if you plan to walk to a monument, because shade is rare, and do not climb on the stones, which have stood for three thousand years and do not need your help.
t.centelles abric ii@40.4,0.0:
Three or four shelters bear the name Centelles, and on a map they all collapse into one dot, which says something about how these places are catalogued: by the ravine, the farm and the order in which a surveyor stumbled across them. The Centelles of this ride lies in the upland country between Catí and Albocàsser, where the Maestrat plateau is broad, quiet and dry, and where the main event of the day is the sheep crossing the road.

There is almost nothing to ride against. The roads are smooth, the traffic almost nonexistent, and the corners come in steady, easy sets as the tarmac follows the contours. In clear weather you can see the Penyagolosa massif on the horizon, and on the plateau itself you might see a hare, a pair of red-legged partridges or a harrier over the barley. Winters are cold and wet, summers are hot and dry, and spring and autumn are the seasons to choose.

Catí, six kilometres away, is the place for goat cheese and for a beer in the square, and Albocàsser, eight kilometres away, has a quiet, handsome main street. Fuel is a different matter, since neither village can be relied upon, and Alcalà de Xivert, twenty-three kilometres off, is the sure bet. Benassal, thirteen kilometres, is an alternative for lunch, and its cool springs are a welcome sight on a hot day.

The shelter's paintings are of the Levantine type, red figures under a natural overhang, and they are often small and faded. The best way to understand what you are looking at is to visit the museum in Tírig, which is dedicated to the art of the Valltorta and Gasulla ravines, and which makes sense of the whole tradition in an hour. Go in with realistic expectations, and the faint marks become more interesting, not less.
t.roman walls@41.1,1.3:
The Romans did not take long to decide that Tarragona was worth fortifying. Scipio's army landed here in 218 BC during the war against Carthage, and in time the settlement of Tarraco became the capital of the Roman province of Hispania Citerior and later of Tarraconensis, and one of the largest cities in Roman Spain. Its walls started as a Republican fortification, with huge irregular blocks at the base, the so-called cyclopean masonry, which were later heightened and rebuilt in Roman and later periods. A good stretch survives in the Passeig Arqueològic, where you can walk along the top.

The city has a great deal more besides. The amphitheatre sits on a bluff above the sea, where, according to tradition, Christian bishop Fructuosus was burned in the third century. The Roman circus runs under the modern streets, and a ruined forum, a necropolis and an aqueduct, known as the Pont del Diable, lie around the outskirts. UNESCO listed the archaeological ensemble of Tarraco in 2000, and the city's human towers, the castells, are listed too, though you will see those only on festival days.

Riding in is easy but needs a little thought. From the coast road or the motorway you reach the upper town, with its cathedral and narrow lanes, and the old town is hilly and often closed to cars. Park in a designated motorcycle space near the walls and walk, and do not leave anything on the bike. Tarragona has plenty of fuel, from stations on the ring roads to the ones near the port, and the city is the obvious place to stock up.

The sea adds to the charm. From the Balcó del Mediterrani at the end of the Rambla Nova you can look out over the amphitheatre and the beach, and there are good seafood restaurants in the old fishermen's quarter at the harbour. Weekdays outside the high season are the quietest time. Constantí and Els Pallaresos, a few kilometres inland, are quiet small towns, handy for a break from the traffic.
t.arpan e 2@42.2,0.0:
The Río Vero is not a big river, but it has spent a very long time doing something clever with the limestone of the Sierra de Guara. Above Alquézar it has cut a gorge that narrows to a few metres in places and widens again into pools the colour of bottle glass, and the plateau on both sides is a dry country of box, holm oak and aromatic scrub that bears almost no relation to the water below. Arpán is a small side-valley three kilometres from the village, a short walk off the road, and its shelter is one of several in the Vero canyon system that carry painted figures from the ancient hunters of the Levantine tradition.

Riding out to it is a lesson in how quickly the Pyrenean foothills change character. Leave Barbastro among vineyards and peach orchards, and within half an hour the road is climbing through a rocky landscape with the first sharp ridges of the Guara rising ahead. The bends tighten, the surface is generally good, and the traffic consists mostly of vans carrying canyoning gear. Late spring and early autumn are kindest. In August the plateau bakes and the gorge floor is full of people; in January the shady curves keep frost until noon.

Alquézar itself deserves a longer look than the average rider gives it. The village hangs on a rocky spur above the river, topped by a collegiate church that began life as a Muslim fortress and was converted into a Christian stronghold in the eleventh century, and the lanes between the stone houses are steep and narrow enough that you leave the bike at the entrance. There are terraces for coffee and a few places that serve local lamb, and the walkways bolted to the canyon wall are well worth an hour.

Fuel is the weak point. Salas Altas and Angüés are small villages with bars. Treat the shelter with the care it needs; the Aragonese government protects the rock art of the Vero as a cultural park, and some sites are open only with a guide.
t.mallata b 1@42.2,0.0:
There is a shelter near Alquézar that people call Mallata, and a ravine of the same name, and on a summer weekend you could miss both while looking for a parking space. The Barranco de la Mallata is a narrow side-canyon of the Vero, a few kilometres from Alquézar, and it holds shelters that have become famous among specialists for their Levantine paintings. Mallata B1 is one of them, a small, shaded hollow where the paint has survived better than you might expect.

From Alquézar the road runs up the Vero valley to Colungo, a small village that has an interpretive centre for the rock art of the canyon, and this is the best place to start, because it explains the sites you cannot visit and tells you which are open. The road is narrow, winding and well surfaced, with bends that hug the hillside and views over the river, and it is lightly trafficked outside the school holidays. On a clear spring morning it is one of the best short rides in Aragon.

Alquézar's Collegiate Church overlooks the gorge, and below it the footpaths along the river are a pleasure for a stroll. The village has plenty of terraces, and local products include olive oil, honey and the wines of the Somontano. Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres away, has the fuel, as do larger villages on the plain. Salas Altas and Angüés have bars, but little else.

Treat the paintings with care. Do not wet them or touch them, and follow the instructions of the park staff. A little water makes the pigment glow for a moment and does lasting harm, and people have done it in good faith for generations, which is part of why so many panels are now behind grilles.

The light matters more than anything else you can control. The ravine runs between tall walls, so a shelter that is bright at ten can be in shade by two, and a photograph taken in flat midday glare shows almost nothing. Take your time, let your eyes adjust, and look for the faint orange line before you look for the figure. Dress for a walk, not a ride, because the paths from the road are rough, and keep an eye on the weather in the Guara, where storms build quickly over the ridges in late summer.
t.val de mamet ii@41.3,0.1:
In 1412 nine delegates met in the little Aragonese town of Caspe to decide who should be king of Aragon after the death of Martin the Humane without an heir, and the choice they made, Ferdinand of Antequera of the Castilian royal house, changed the course of Spanish history. The Compromise of Caspe is the thing most people know about the town, which sits on the Ebro seventeen kilometres from here, and it gives this dry, wide, thinly peopled corner of Aragon an unexpected sense of having once been at the centre of things. Val de Mamet is a quiet barranco in the hills to the east, on the border country between Aragon and Catalonia.

The land is steppe-like. Pale hills carry thyme, rosemary and Aleppo pine, and the fields in between grow cereals, almonds and olives. Villages are small and far apart: Fabara, Nonaspe and Mequinenza each count a few thousand people at most, and Mequinenza has the old town now lying under the reservoir of the Ebro. Fabara has a surprise, a Roman mausoleum of the second century standing in a field just outside the village, a tall, tower-like tomb with columns, one of the best preserved in the region.

The roads are uncrowded and fast. They run in long, open stretches across the plateau and then dip into river valleys where bends tighten and the surface is somewhat patchy. Wind is a constant companion, especially the cierzo from the north-west, which can be strong enough to push a bike across the lane, so hold the bars firmly on exposed stretches. Summers are hot and winters cold and clear, and spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons.

The shelter itself is typical of the region: modest, protected, with a few painted figures of the Levantine tradition. Caspe, with about eight thousand people, is the sensible choice for fuel, supplies and a meal, and its fortified church and old centre are worth a short stop. Take water, wear walking shoes, and remember that these shelters survive only because visitors treat them gently.
t.abric del barranc de cana o de la mina f:
Before the reservoir and the anglers' boats, Mequinenza was a coal town. The seams of lignite that run under the hills around the confluence of the Segre and the Ebro were dug for generations, and the coal was shipped down the river to feed the furnaces and power stations of a growing Spain. When the mines faded and the old town was submerged, a good part of the population left, and the people who remained are proud of a heritage that is half underground and half underwater. The Barranc de Canà shelter lies five kilometres out, in dry hills between the town and the road to Fraga.

The surrounding landscape is pale and austere. Low, eroded hills carry rosemary and pine, the fields are small and terraced, and the sky seems very large. The roads are open, quiet and fast, with wide views across the water, and corners come at long intervals. Autumn and spring are the sensible seasons. In summer the heat in this trough of the Ebro is formidable, and winter brings the cierzo, a cold wind that has been known to bring cyclists to a standstill.

Mequinenza has the fuel and a few places to eat, and in the old centre you can find the local specialities of freshwater fish. Seròs, nine kilometres away, is smaller and pleasantly sleepy. Fraga, thirteen kilometres off, is the real town of the district, with nearly fourteen thousand people and a history that includes the battle of 1134, in which Alfonso the Battler of Aragon met a defeat that proved fatal. It is also a centre for fruit, particularly peaches, grown in the irrigated plain of the Cinca.

Reaching the shelter takes a little local knowledge, and the paintings, like others in the region, are small and weathered. Ask at the tourist office in Mequinenza for the latest advice, bring plenty of water, and wear shoes with a grip.
t.el portell de les lletres@41.4,1.1:
Montblanc has been a town of walls since the Middle Ages, and the walls are still most of what you see: a circuit of about a kilometre and a half of ramparts, with thirty-odd towers and gates that make it one of the best-preserved medieval enclosures in Catalonia. El Portell de les Lletres lies a short way beyond them, in the folds of the hills south-east of the town, and its name, which suggests a little gap or notch, fits the way a path slips between two rock faces. A rider can combine the shelter with a day of monastic and medieval sightseeing.

The monasteries are the main draw. The Cistercian Route links the great houses of Poblet, Santes Creus and Vallbona de les Monges, and Poblet, on the edge of Vimbodí a few kilometres from here, is the finest, a vast walled complex that served as a royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon and is on the UNESCO list. The cloister and the fortified gates are worth a slow hour. Santes Creus is a little further, and Vallbona, a convent of nuns, is a quiet visit in the countryside.

Roads in the Conca de Barberà are among the most pleasant in Catalonia for easy riding. They run over rolling country of vineyards and wheat, climb into the wooded Serra de Prades, with its red sandstone and the village of Prades, and wind through the oaks and pines. The bends are easy and the surface good, and with fuel at Montblanc, five kilometres from the shelter, you are never far from supplies. Alcover, eleven kilometres away, is another option.

The wine of the Conca de Barberà is white or red, light and fruity, and most local restaurants serve it with grilled meat and calçots, the long spring onions that Catalans eat in winter and early spring with romesco sauce. Autumn, with the colour in the vines, is a beautiful time. As for the shelter, treat it gently and ask locally about access.
t.cova del raco d en perdigo@41.0,0.8:
Joan Miró painted his farm. The great Catalan artist's family owned a farmhouse at Mont-roig del Camp, a few kilometres from the coast of Tarragona, and he came here every year from his youth, and in 1921 and 1922 produced there the large painting called The Farm, which captured the landscape of rocks, carob trees, chickens and tools with an obsessive tenderness. The village, sixteen kilometres from the Cova del Racó d'en Perdigó, is a reminder that this corner of Catalonia has been seen by artists as well as by hunters.

The hills inland from Mont-roig are rugged and dry, with scrub, rock and terraces of almond and hazel. The Serra de Llaberia, a range of low, craggy mountains, rises behind, and the land to the north and west is the Priorat, home of some of the most celebrated wines in Spain, grown on steep slopes of dark slate. The village of Siurana, perched on a cliff above a reservoir, was the last Muslim stronghold in Catalonia, and the legend says that the last queen leapt from the cliff on her horse rather than surrender, leaving a hoofprint in the rock.

For a motorcyclist this is excellent country. The roads over the Serra de Prades and the Priorat are twisting and well maintained, with views over terraced vineyards, and they are popular with cyclists and riders, so expect company on a spring weekend. Take care on the bends, where gravel and the odd wild boar can appear, and avoid the midday heat in summer. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Mont-roig del Camp, with nearly thirteen thousand people, is the town for fuel and supplies, and it has beaches nearby if you want to end the day in the sea. Ginestar and El Perelló are smaller. The cave is a small shelter with painted figures, and access may be limited, so ask locally before you set off. Bring water, and take care with the rock.
t.palau de la musica catalana and hospital:
Lluís Domènech i Montaner built hospitals the way other people build palaces. The Hospital de Sant Pau, which stands about a kilometre from the Sagrada Família along the broad Avinguda de Gaudí, is a campus of brick pavilions covered in coloured tiles, domes and mosaics, set in gardens, and linked by underground tunnels so that patients could be moved without going out into the weather. It was paid for by a banker's bequest, begun in 1902 and finished, with his son Pere taking over, in 1930, and it continued as a working hospital for decades before the patients moved to a new building and the old one became a museum and cultural centre. Together with the Palau de la Música Catalana, it was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1997.

The idea behind the design was that beauty heals, or at least helps, and so the wards are lined with tile, and the pavilions face the sun and the sea breezes. You can walk around the grounds, go into the Administration building with its stained glass and mosaic ceilings, and descend into the tunnels. It is one of the best things to see in Barcelona, and generally less crowded than the Sagrada Família.

Barcelona is a city of motorcycles, and a rider will fit in easily, with designated motorbike parking along many streets. Traffic is dense, though, and you should plan to arrive outside rush hour. The city has a low-emission zone, so check its rules for your bike before you go, and do not leave luggage on the machine, because bag theft is a real problem. Fuel is available at stations around the ring roads.

After a visit, the café terraces on the Avinguda de Gaudí are a pleasant place to sit, and the walk to the Sagrada Família takes a quarter of an hour. The Palau de la Música Catalana, where this stop is marked, lies in the old quarter near the Via Laietana, a short Metro ride or a pleasant walk away, and Domènech i Montaner's concert hall, with its inverted skylight of stained glass and its ceramic flowers, is a fitting partner to the hospital. Together they make a good day, and the UNESCO listing treats them as a pair.
t.cenrelles abric iv@40.4,0.0:
From the sea to the plateau is a climb of several hundred metres in less than fifty kilometres, and a rider who starts at Alcalà de Xivert, on the Castellón coast, can feel the world change on the way. Alcalà itself is a market town with a ruined Templar castle nearby at Xivert, orange groves and a long beach down the road at Alcossebre, and behind it the wild Serra d'Irta, a natural park of unspoilt cliffs and scrub. Inland, the land rises through olive and almond terraces to the Maestrat plateau, and by the time you reach Catí and Albocàsser, twenty-three kilometres from the coast as the crow flies, the air has changed.

The roads that make the climb are some of the finest in the province. They wind up through the foothills, cross the ridges and join the quiet roads of the plateau, and the bends tighten and relax as the terrain demands. The surface is mostly good, traffic is light, and the views behind you get larger with every bend. Looking back on a clear morning you can follow the line of the coast for miles, though in summer there is often a haze.

Centelles, in the district between Catí and Albocàsser, is the end of the climb, and the shelter is a modest place, one of several that bear the name. It holds a few red figures of the Levantine tradition, and it makes a good excuse for a walk. The village of Catí is known for its goat cheese, and Albocàsser, with its square, is a pleasant stop.

Fuel is at Alcalà de Xivert, so fill the tank before you leave the coast. Take water, wear good shoes, and treat the paintings with care. In winter, check the forecast, since snow and ice can appear on the plateau when the coast is mild.
t.palau de la musica catalana@41.4,2.2:
The Palau de la Música Catalana is hidden. It stands on a narrow street in the old quarter of Barcelona, so close to the buildings opposite that you cannot step back far enough to take it in, and it was built between 1905 and 1908 for the Orfeó Català, a choral society that was the pride of Catalan cultural life at a time when Catalonia was finding its voice again. Lluís Domènech i Montaner designed it, and he threw everything at it: brick, mosaic, ceramics, sculpted flowers, stained glass, an iron frame so open that the walls are almost glass.

Inside, the concert hall is a revelation. Its ceiling is a great inverted dome of stained glass in gold and blue, with a sun at the centre, and around it the walls are covered with colour. Above the stage a ring of sculpted Muses seems to step out of the wall, and the sound, in a hall designed for choirs, is warm and clear. If you can, go to a concert; a guided tour is the next best thing. UNESCO listed it in 1997 with the Hospital de Sant Pau.

The district around it, the Born and Sant Pere, is a good place to walk. Narrow medieval streets, the market of Santa Caterina with its roof of coloured tiles, small bars and the basilica of Santa Maria del Mar lie within a few minutes. Barcelona is a city for walking, and a rider should leave the bike in a designated parking space and go on foot. Traffic and the one-way system in the old quarter are confusing, and thieves are active, so never leave bags on the bike.

Fuel is at stations on the ring roads and in the outer districts. In the evening, the Palau's lit windows are a fine sight from the street. A short ride beyond the city takes you to the hills of Collserola, where roads wind up through the forest to a ridge with views over the whole city and out to the sea.
t.fajana de casabon@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar sits on a rock above the Vero river like a village in a children's book, with a golden collegiate church crowning the hill and houses stacked beneath it. About five kilometres from here, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, the sandstone and limestone cliffs hold small shelters with prehistoric paintings, and Fajana de Casabón is one of them. The painted shelters of the Vero valley are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot describe what is painted in this particular shelter, and visits to many of them are controlled, so it is worth asking locally before you set out.

What you can enjoy freely is the village. Alquézar has about three hundred permanent residents, but in summer it fills with visitors, so the streets, with their arcaded square and old stone houses, can be crowded. The collegiate church of Santa María la Mayor stands on the site of a Muslim fortress, the name Alquézar coming from the Arabic for castle, and it was a stronghold of the frontier until the Christian king Sancho Ramírez took it in the late eleventh century. The church's Romanesque cloister has carved capitals that repay a slow look, and the view from its terrace over the river gorge is excellent.

The roads here are best taken slowly. From Barbastro the road to Alquézar follows the Vero upstream, then climbs through almond and olive terraces in a series of easy bends. Beyond the village the lanes narrow, the surface grows rougher, and the corners are sharper, so it is a ride for a light bike and a patient mind. Weekends can be busy with walkers, cyclists and canyoning vans, so early starts are wise.

Alquézar is too small to count on for fuel, so fill the tank at Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, where you will find larger shops and many places to eat. The local specialities are lamb from Aragon, game, mountain vegetables and the red wines of the Somontano. A glass of wine and a plate of ham on the village terrace is a very fine way to end a morning.

Come in spring, when the terraces are green, or in October, when the light is softer and the crowds have gone.
t.casa batllo@41.4,2.2:
Passeig de Gràcia is the grand avenue of Barcelona, and on its sunny side stands a building that looks like it was made out of something living. Casa Batlló, remodelled by Antoni Gaudí between 1904 and 1906 for the textile industrialist Josep Batlló, is a facade of mottled glass and ceramic, with balconies shaped like masks or skulls and bone-like columns, and a roof ridge that arches like the back of a dragon, with a tower topped by a cross. Locals call it the House of Bones, and the roof is said to represent the dragon slain by Saint George, patron saint of Catalonia.

The house stands on the Block of Discord, a stretch of the avenue where several of the leading Modernista architects built neighbouring houses in competing styles, and a few steps away are works by Domènech i Montaner and Puig i Cadafalch. Gaudí did not build from scratch, but rebuilt an older house, and he turned the interior into a flowing series of curved walls, wooden doors and a central light well tiled in shades of blue, graded so that the light seems even at every level. The building is part of the group of Gaudí works listed by UNESCO.

Barcelona is a city for motorbikes, with more of them per head than almost anywhere in Europe, and riding here is easy once you learn the rhythm. Scooters and motorcycles share the lanes and park in marked bays on the pavements, and the grid of the Eixample makes navigation simple. The traffic is fast and close, so keep your wits about you, and note that a low-emission zone restricts older vehicles, so check the rules before you arrive. Cobbles, tram tracks and painted lines can be slippery when wet.

Fuel is easy to find on the edges of the city but sparser in the middle, so fill the tank when you can. The Eixample has endless cafés, bars and restaurants, and a plate of tapas or a bowl of fideuà at a local place is a pleasant lunch.

The ride combines Casa Batlló with the Cova de Vallmajor, an excursion into a very different, older Catalonia. Entrance to the house is by timed ticket, and queues form in high season, so book ahead.
t.mallata ii@42.2,0.0:
The Sierra de Guara is the canyoning capital of Europe, or near enough, and Mallata II sits in country that owes its character to the water that carved it. The limestone and conglomerate of the range has been cut by streams into narrow gorges, with pools, waterfalls and polished rock, and each summer the roads of Alquézar and Rodellar fill with vans carrying wetsuits and ropes. Mallata II lies about four and a half kilometres from Alquézar, in the same landscape of cliffs and overhangs.

Overhangs are the key to the story. Out of the rain, with a ledge to sit on and a view over the valley, they were the obvious shelters for people who lived on the move thousands of years ago, and a number of them were painted. The shelters of the Vero valley, which UNESCO included in its Mediterranean Basin rock art listing in 1998, are small and delicate. I cannot say what Mallata II contains, and I would suggest asking in Alquézar about guided access, since many shelters are protected and not open without permission.

Riding in the area is a pleasure, especially if you like roads that go somewhere slowly. The lanes around Alquézar climb and fall between stone walls, almond groves and oak scrub, with bends that tighten in the gorges and views of the pale cliffs. The surface is generally fair, with some rough patches and gravel on the verges, and a sudden stream crossing is possible after storms. Traffic is light on weekdays, but on summer weekends canyoning minibuses and cyclists make it busier.

Alquézar has a few hundred inhabitants and is too small for reliable fuel, so use Barbastro, a town of seventeen thousand about twenty kilometres away, with supermarkets, restaurants and the cathedral. A good local lunch is the lamb of Aragon, which has its own protected status, with roast potatoes and a glass of Somontano red. The village itself has cafés on the arcaded square.

Summer is hot and best avoided in the afternoon. Spring and early autumn, when the water is cool and the cliffs are warm in the sun, are the best seasons. Take care on gravel and do not leave the track, as the vegetation is thin and fragile.
t.mallata i@42.2,0.0:
Mallata I lies four and a half kilometres from Alquézar in the heart of the Vero valley, and to understand it you have to follow the river. The Vero rises in the Sierra de Guara and flows south-east through a deep, winding gorge, past Alquézar and Barbastro, before joining the Cinca. The gorge is lined with cliffs of sandstone and limestone, stained in orange and grey, and in places it narrows so that a footpath has been bolted to the rock face above the water. It is a hawk's-eye view of a river carving a valley.

The Sierra de Guara is also one of the places where the bearded vulture, the lammergeier, still breeds, and it is not unusual to see griffon vultures wheeling over the cliffs. The birds follow the thermals along the gorge in the afternoon, and on a still day you hear the wingbeats. Eagles and choughs are also common, so keep an eye on the sky.

Mallata I is one of the rock shelters of the valley that contain prehistoric paintings. The Vero area has one of the densest groups in Aragon, with several dozen shelters, and they are part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what is painted in this particular one. The best way to see the art is with someone who knows the valley, as the sites are fragile, some are closed to the public and the paths can be steep and slippery.

The riding around Alquézar is enjoyable but not fast. The road from Barbastro follows the river upstream, with views of the pale cliffs, and beyond the village the lanes climb through oak scrub and farmland, narrow and winding, with the odd gravel patch. Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, is the place for fuel and supplies, a lively town of some seventeen thousand people with a fine Gothic cathedral and a good range of restaurants. Somontano is also a wine region, and you can visit some of the cellars.
