Spring is the best season, with the river full and the terraces green, followed by early autumn. Midsummer is hot and busy. Bring a hat and water if you plan to walk.
t.la cova dels tolls alts@40.4,0.1:
The high, folded country behind the Valencian coast, the Maestrat, has long been a land of isolated farms, stone walls and windy ridges, and it is one of the least known parts of eastern Spain. La Cova dels Tolls Alts lies five kilometres from Albocàsser, in limestone hills dotted with holm oak, pine and almond, where the ravines run down toward the lowlands and the sea. The name means cave of the high pools, a reminder that water, even in this dry region, is what makes a place habitable.

The area is rich in prehistoric rock art, belonging to the Mediterranean Basin tradition that UNESCO listed in 1998. The ravines of the Valltorta and the Gasulla, a short distance away, hold some of the best-known examples, and the museum at Tírig explains them well. I cannot tell you what the paintings at Tolls Alts show, and I would advise asking at the museum or in Albocàsser about guided access, since the sites are fragile and some are closed.

Albocàsser itself is a village of about fourteen hundred people with a long stone-built centre, and nearby Cuevas de Vinromà and Catí are similar in size. These are places where old men still sit in the shade and the pace of life is slow. Farming, olives, almonds and sheep have shaped the landscape, and the stone huts and drystone walls of the hills are part of the pattern, built over centuries by shepherds and farmers.

For riders the region offers quiet, flowing roads over low passes, through valleys of orchards and across open uplands, with enough bends to be interesting but no great drama. The surface is mostly good, and there is little traffic once you leave the main routes. Wind can sweep across the plateaus, and in winter the nights are cold and frosty, though snow is rare at this altitude. Villages are small, so keep the tank full, and know that Cuevas de Vinromà or Albocàsser are the likely places for fuel.

Local cooking includes lamb, rabbit with snails, rice cooked in a pan, and cured meats, with good olive oil and local honey. The ride joins this cave with the Abric de la Tenalla and the Mas d'en Badenes, a pleasant circuit of small roads. Spring is green and cool, and autumn brings softer light.
t.barfaluy ii@42.2,0.0:
The Barranco de Barfaluy is a gorge that looks as though someone had cut it with a ruler. Its walls rise sheer on either side, in places only a few metres apart, and the stream at the bottom winds between rocks and pools. The path through is short but memorable, and the narrowness gives the place a cathedral hush. Barfaluy II, five kilometres from Alquézar, is one of the shelters in the gorge that carry prehistoric paintings, a part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998.

I cannot describe the figures in this particular shelter, but the Barfaluy gorge is well known among people who study the Vero valley's art, and it is one of the sites where visits have been organised with a guide, so it is worth asking about. The gorge is small and fragile, and the paintings are close to the walkways, which is why access is regulated. The sense of walking into a narrow place where people came thousands of years ago to leave a mark is very strong.

The gorge lies on the edge of the Sierra de Guara natural park, a country of limestone cliffs, holm oaks and scrubby slopes, with villages that seem to cling to the rock. The roads that reach it are quiet and narrow, climbing out of the Vero valley through terraces of almond and olive, with plenty of bends and some rough surface. A light bike and a relaxed pace suit them. After heavy rain, gravel washes onto the tarmac, and the gorge itself can flood, so check the weather.

Alquézar has only a few hundred inhabitants and a handful of cafés, so plan to fill the tank at Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, a lively town of around seventeen thousand with a Gothic cathedral and plenty of restaurants. The surrounding Somontano region produces good red and white wines, and the local lamb, roasted with potatoes, is a classic. In the village, the terrace of a bar over the gorge is a fine place for a coffee.

Spring and early autumn are the best seasons. In midsummer the heat in the gorge is trapped by the rock and the afternoon can be oppressive, so start early.
t.chimiachas l@42.2,0.0:
Almond blossom comes early to the Somontano, and in February the terraces around Alquézar turn pink and white before anything else has woken up. The word means under the mountain, and it describes the strip of land between the high Pyrenees to the north and the dry plains of the Ebro to the south. Chimiachas L lies about four kilometres from Alquézar, in the foothill country where the limestone ridges run in long parallel waves, with farmland in the hollows.

The shelters of the Vero valley, scattered through the cliffs, include several with prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. Chimiachas is among the names known to specialists, though I cannot tell you what this particular shelter holds, and I would sooner say so than invent something. Many of the shelters are small, under shallow overhangs, and the paintings are faint, so the experience is as much about the walk and the place as about the image.

This is excellent country for unhurried riding. The back lanes link farms, stone barns and tiny hamlets, rolling over ridges and dipping into dry stream beds, and the corners are open, with views that run all the way to the high Pyrenees on a clear day. The surface can be rough, with patches of gravel, and farm tracks look tempting but turn muddy after rain. In summer the land is parched and golden, with the hum of cicadas, while spring and autumn bring greener hills and softer air.

The Somontano is also one of the quiet wine regions of Spain, with a good reputation for its reds and whites, produced around Barbastro, which is also the nearest town for fuel and supplies, about twenty kilometres from Alquézar. Barbastro's centre has a pleasant Gothic cathedral, arcaded streets and a lively food scene. Local specialities include borage, a vegetable found in this part of Aragon, cooked with potatoes, and the lamb known as ternasco.

If you can, plan the day so that you are walking in the cool of the morning and riding in the warmth, and keep a bottle of water handy, since shade is thin on these dry hillsides. The ride joins this shelter with the Cueva de los Moros.
t.casa vicens@41.4,2.2:
Casa Vicens is where Gaudí began, and you can see him working out his ideas. He was in his early thirties when he took on the commission, between 1883 and 1888, for Manuel Vicens i Montaner, a stockbroker and ceramics manufacturer who wanted a summer house in what was then the separate town of Gràcia. The result is a small, colourful building with a Moorish air, built of rough stone and brick, striped with glazed tiles in green and white, and covered in tiles painted with marigolds, a flower that grew on the site.

The tile work is the signature. The yellow marigolds repeat across the wall, set among geometric patterns, and the iron railings echo the shape of the palmetto leaf. Inside, the dining room and smoking room have ceilings of moulded papier-mâché and painted walls, where Gaudí's love of nature is already at work. The house was extended and altered over the years, and it was opened as a museum in 2017. It is part of the group of Gaudí works that UNESCO listed.

Gràcia has changed from a village to a lively neighbourhood. It was annexed by Barcelona in 1897, but it has kept its own character, with small squares, narrow lanes, independent shops and bars where locals gather in the evening. The festival of Gràcia in August fills the streets with elaborate decorations, and it is one of the best street parties in the city.

Riding in Barcelona is easy and fast, with motorbikes parked in marked bays on the pavements and a grid of avenues, but Gràcia's streets are narrow, steep and often one-way, so leave your bike at a car park on the edge and walk in. Watch tram lines, painted road markings and manhole covers in the wet, and check the rules for the low-emission zone before you arrive.

With some hundred and twenty thousand people in the district, you will find everything within a few streets. The tapas bars of Gràcia serve patatas bravas, croquettes and grilled vegetables, and a vermouth on a terrace before lunch is a very good habit.

The ride links the house with the Abric de Can Ximet, an excursion into the countryside beyond the city.
t.abric de la baridana i@41.3,1.1:
The Conca de Barberà is a basin of vineyards and wheat, ringed by the Prades mountains, and Montblanc is its capital. The town is still wrapped in medieval walls, with towers and gates that have survived mostly intact, and the narrow streets inside are lined with Gothic houses and a church with a notable altarpiece. Local legend places the story of Saint George and the dragon here, and at the festival of Saint George every year the town re-enacts it with great enthusiasm. The Abric de la Baridana I lies about seven and a half kilometres from the town, in the hills to the south-west.

It is one of the rock shelters of the region that carry prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. The shelters of the Prades hills are small and shallow, and the figures are few and faint. I cannot say what this one preserves, so ask locally for any signed access, as some are open and others are protected.

The Conca is also the heart of the Cistercian Route, which links the great monasteries of Poblet, Santes Creus and Vallbona de les Monges, three abbeys founded in the twelfth century as Catalonia expanded south. Poblet in particular, a few kilometres from Montblanc, is a vast fortified monastery that was a royal burial place, and it is one of the finest of its kind in Europe, listed by UNESCO in 1991. It is well worth combining with the shelter.

The riding here is relaxed and lovely. Roads wind between vineyards and almond groves, climb gently through pine woods, and descend into valleys, with moderate bends and good surface, and the traffic is light outside the weekends. The Prades hills have sharper roads for those who want more, though the climbs are not long. In summer the heat is fierce, and in winter the wind can be sharp.

Montblanc has some six and a half thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and several restaurants, and Vimbodí and Alcover are smaller neighbours. The local cooking features calçots, grilled spring onions dipped in romesco sauce, in the winter and early spring, and the wines of the Conca de Barberà are a pleasant surprise. Visit in spring or autumn for the best light.
t.quizans ii@42.2,0.0:
The Vero valley does not look like a place that hides a great deal. The river runs through low hills of oak and box, and the cliffs that line its banks are warm orange and pale grey, but the way the rock folds into small overhangs is what attracted the people who painted here thousands of years ago. Quizáns II, three kilometres from Alquézar, is one of those shelters, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998. I cannot say what this particular shelter contains, and I would encourage you to ask about guided visits rather than search the cliffs alone.

What gives the valley its feel is the combination of dry land and steady water. The Vero is not a large river, but it runs clear, with pools of green and blue, and in summer people swim in the places where the road runs beside it. Kingfishers, dippers and herons live along its banks, and the oak woods above are full of jays and woodpeckers. Wild boar are common, although rarely seen. The smell of box and thyme is strong after rain.

The roads in this part of Aragon are lovely for slow riding. The lane from Alquézar toward the shelters is narrow and winding, with tight bends, loose gravel and the odd stray sheep. The wider roads from Barbastro offer longer, easier curves, with good views of the foothills and the far white line of the Pyrenees. Midsummer afternoons are very hot, and autumn is mild, with golden light through the oaks. Winter can be cold, and ice forms in the shade of the gorge.

Alquézar's cafés and restaurants make a good base for a day, but fuel is a question for Barbastro, twenty kilometres away, which has everything a rider needs, including a cathedral and a lively old quarter. The ride also takes in the Church of Santa Maria de l'Assumpció, in a very different village, so there is variety in the day.

Try the local olive oil, which is peppery and green, drizzled on toasted bread with tomato, and a plate of cured ham. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for riding, walking and swimming.
t.fajana de pera i@42.2,0.0:
If you want to understand the cooking of Alto Aragón, begin with what grows on a dry, stony hillside: olives, almonds, borage, wild herbs, and what can be grazed there, lamb above all. Fajana de Pera I, a painted shelter some five kilometres from Alquézar, belongs to the same hill country, and the shelters of the Vero valley, which UNESCO included in the Mediterranean Basin rock art listing of 1998, are a reminder that people have been feeding themselves from this land for a very long time. I cannot say what is painted at this particular shelter, and guided visits are the safest way to see any of them.

Aragonese lamb is the pride of the table. The ternasco, a young lamb roasted in the oven with potatoes and a splash of white wine, has its own protected label and turns up in every village restaurant. Alongside it come migas, fried breadcrumbs with garlic and peppers, and borage stalks cooked with potato, a green vegetable that most visitors have never met. In late summer, local peaches and figs fill the markets, and in autumn the olive oil from the new harvest is cloudy, green and peppery enough to catch your throat.

Wine is the other pillar. The Somontano denomination, centred on Barbastro, has grown over the last decades into one of the better-regarded regions of northern Spain, with Cabernet and Tempranillo alongside the local Moristel and Parraleta grapes. Several cellars welcome visitors, and a tasting makes a civilised break from a day in the saddle, provided you leave the bike for a few hours.

As for the riding, the lanes between Alquézar and the shelters are narrow, with tight bends, gravel patches and sheep, and a calm pace is best. The main roads from Barbastro are smoother and faster, with long curves and good views. The village has too few people for dependable fuel, so use Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away, where supermarkets and restaurants abound.

Aim for lunch at a village place rather than a tourist spot. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for the whole day, from the walk to the table.
t.litonares l@42.2,0.0:
In the late eleventh century, Alquézar was a frontier fortress, and its walls were the front line of a long war. The Muslim rulers of the Ebro valley held the castle as part of a defensive chain against the Christian kingdom of Aragon, until King Sancho Ramírez captured it around 1067 and made it a base for the conquest of Barbastro and the plains beyond. The name itself comes from the Arabic for castle, and the church that was built on the rock, the Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor, took over the castle's commanding position.

Litonares L, three kilometres from the village, is one of the shelters in the valley that hold prehistoric paintings, far older than any of this. The Vero valley's art, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, is thousands of years old, and I cannot say what this shelter contains. The contrast between the medieval fortress and the prehistoric shelter is part of what makes the area interesting, since people have found this narrow canyon a good place to live, to hide and to worship for a very long time.

The collegiate church is the best place to start. Its Romanesque cloister has capitals carved with scenes and monsters, and the terrace below it looks out over the gorge and the river. The village streets, with their stone arches and old houses, wind up the hill in a pleasant tangle, and the arcaded main square is a good place for a drink.

The roads are narrow and winding. The approach from Barbastro follows the river and climbs in easy bends, and beyond the village the lanes are tighter, with rough patches and gravel. A small, light bike and a calm hand suit them. Traffic is light on weekdays, though summer weekends bring a stream of visitors, and the hairpins near the village are tight enough to demand a slow pace.

Alquézar has only a few hundred inhabitants, so fuel is a matter for Barbastro, about twenty kilometres away. The village has cafés and restaurants for lunch. Aim for the early morning, when the light is soft and the crowds have not arrived, and the old stones are warm.
t.gallinero ii@42.2,0.0:
Underneath the story of the paintings is a story of rock. The Sierra de Guara is made largely of limestone and sandstone laid down in warm seas tens of millions of years ago, then pushed up as the Pyrenees rose to the north, and then cut by rivers into the gorges you see today. The Vero has carved a deep canyon through the layers, and where softer bands of rock have weathered away, they have left overhangs, shallow caves and ledges that were perfect for shelter. Gallinero II, five kilometres from Alquézar, is one of those natural shelters, and it holds prehistoric paintings, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what this one shows.

Geology also explains the colours. The cliffs here are pale grey where the limestone is fresh and orange or ochre where iron has stained the surface, and in the right light the whole valley glows. The red tones used by the painters were probably made from iron-rich earth, which was ground and mixed with a binder, and which is part of the reason the paintings have lasted so long under their overhangs.

The Sierra de Guara is also fossil country, and in some places on the hillsides you can find the shells of marine creatures from the ancient sea. It is a quiet and bare country in places, with scrub oak, box and juniper, and in winter the grey rock and the dark green trees have a stern beauty. Spring brings wildflowers, orchids among them, and the first greens.

Riding here is enjoyable at a moderate pace. The roads follow the contours of the land, and bends are frequent and not always well signed, with gravel in the gutters and the odd rock on the road after storms. On the main road from Barbastro the surface is generally good. The nearest place for fuel and shops is Barbastro, about twenty kilometres from the village, a town of some seventeen thousand people with plenty of restaurants.

Bring water and sturdy footwear if you plan to walk, and follow local guidance on access, since the shelters are fragile and some are protected by law.
t.argantin ii@42.2,0.0:
Nobody saw the painters at work, so everything we say about the rock art of eastern Spain is inference, and the inferences have changed over the years. The shelters of the Vero valley hold two broad families of images, as elsewhere in the region: naturalistic figures of people and animals, often in red, called Levantine art, and later, simpler, more abstract signs known as schematic art. The first is usually attributed to hunter-gatherers and the second to farming communities, though the dating is still debated, and many specialists are cautious about exact numbers. Argantín II, five kilometres from Alquézar, is one of the shelters in this valley, listed with the others in the Mediterranean Basin rock art inscription of 1998, and I cannot say which kind of image it holds.

That caution is a good thing to carry with you into the landscape. The cliffs above the Vero are weathered, honey-coloured and pocked with overhangs, and standing under one, you can see how such a shelter would work: out of the rain, facing the light, with a view over the river. What people did there, and what the images meant to them, is a matter of theory, and local museums and guides are a better source than a roadside sign.

The valley is a very pleasant place to ride. The road from Barbastro rises gently along the river, with the cliffs closing in, and beyond Alquézar the lanes climb and twist through olive terraces and oak scrub. Bends are often tight, and gravel is common, so ride within your sight. The country is drier than it looks, and in midsummer the heat bounces off the rock, so keep to the cooler hours.

Barbastro, about twenty kilometres from Alquézar, is the nearest town with fuel and services, and Alquézar has cafés and a few bars for lunch. The local lamb, olive oil and Somontano wine are all worth trying. A short walk from the village leads to viewpoints over the gorge, and the walkways along the cliff are an easy way to see the river from above.

April and May, when the hills are green and the river runs fast, are the best months.
t.litonares e 3@42.2,0.0:
Every season has its own character in the Vero valley, and the riding is better in some than in others. In spring the almond blossom comes first, then the oak leaves open, and the hills turn the fresh green that makes the cliffs look more orange by contrast. The river is full from snowmelt in the Pyrenees, and the air smells of wet earth and rosemary. This is the best season, and Litonares E3, three kilometres from Alquézar, is a pleasant place to walk to in the morning light.

Summer is hot. By July the valley is dry and yellow, and temperatures regularly pass thirty-five degrees in the afternoon, which makes a motorbike jacket an effort. Cicadas whine in the pines, and the river drops to a trickle in places, though the pools remain cool enough for swimming. The shelters give some shade, which may be one reason people chose them, and you will understand it if you sit in one at midday. The painted shelter here is part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what this one shows, and you should ask about access.

Autumn, from late September to November, is mellow, with soft light, the smell of new olive oil and woodsmoke in the villages, and the colours of oak and wild cherry turning bronze. Mist lies in the valley in the early mornings. In winter, the nights are cold, and frost can lie in the gorge in the shade, so black ice is a real risk on north-facing bends, while on the sunny side the days can be bright and mild.

The roads are narrow and winding near the village, and wider and faster toward Barbastro, which is also the place for fuel, about twenty kilometres from Alquézar. In the village you will find coffee, tapas and simple meals, and the Somontano wines are a fair match for the lamb. Weekdays outside July and August are far quieter than weekends.

My advice is to come in the second half of April or in October, when the weather is kind and the valley is at its best.
t.las escaleretas@42.2,0.0:
Escaleretas means little stairs, and the name probably describes the way the rock rises in short, stepped ledges. It is a common kind of name in these hills, where the cliffs are terraced by the layers of sandstone and limestone, and a path may follow a natural staircase up to a shelter. Las Escaleretas lies about five kilometres from Alquézar, and I cannot tell you what is painted there, though it is one of the shelters of the Vero valley that belong to the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Getting to a shelter like this usually means a walk, and that is part of the point. The paths are narrow, sometimes steep and loose, and they cross open slopes with little shade, so wear proper shoes rather than riding boots if you can, and take water. After rain, the clay can be treacherous, and in storms the gullies fill fast. If you are not sure of the way, ask at a local information office or take a guide, because the shelters are not marked on most maps, in order to protect them.

Etiquette matters. The paintings are fragile, and they have survived for thousands of years because they are protected from weather and from people. Do not touch them, do not wet them to improve the colour, a bad habit of earlier generations, and keep to the paths. A good camera and a bit of patience will reward you more than a hand on the wall.

The ride to the starting point is a pleasure in itself. Narrow lanes link farms and stone barns, climbing over low ridges and dropping into stream beds, with views over the valley. The surface is mixed, with gravel and the occasional bump, and traffic is light. The village of Alquézar, with its collegiate church, is the natural base, though it is too small for reliable fuel, so rely on Barbastro, twenty kilometres away, where you will find a good range of shops and restaurants.

Plan to arrive early, walk in the cool of the morning and be back for a long lunch.
t.fajana de pera ii@42.2,0.0:
Barbastro is the gateway to this country, and most riders pass through it without a second look, which is a mistake. The town, with some seventeen thousand people, sits on the Vero where it leaves the hills, at the edge of the Somontano wine region, and it has a handsome old centre with arcaded streets, a Gothic cathedral begun in the sixteenth century and a long tradition of markets and trade. It is the practical centre of the district, with the fuel, supermarkets, banks and restaurants that the small villages of the valley lack.

Fajana de Pera II is a painted shelter about five kilometres from Alquézar, in the cliffs that line the upper Vero. The shelters of the valley belong to the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and I cannot say what is painted at this particular spot. If you want to see the art, the best plan is to ask in Barbastro or at the park's information points about guided visits, which can save you a lot of wandering.

From Barbastro the road to Alquézar follows the river up into the hills, a distance of some twenty kilometres. It starts as an easy road through farmland, with almond and olive terraces on either side, then closes in as the cliffs rise, with bends that tighten gradually. The surface is generally good, and the traffic is moderate, with a few tourist vehicles on summer weekends. Past the village the lanes narrow, with gravel and rough patches, so a light bike and a patient hand suit them.

Before you leave Barbastro, fill the tank, buy water and food, and consider visiting a winery. Several cellars around the town welcome visitors, and a tasting of Somontano red or the fresh whites is a good way to understand the region. The local specialities are lamb, borage, cured ham and the almond-based sweets of Aragon.

Spring and early autumn are the best seasons. The market days are lively, and the old centre is a pleasure for a stroll before the day's riding begins.
t.ereta de litonares@42.2,0.0:
On a clear day, from the high ground north of Alquézar, you can see the Pyrenees laid out like a wall, with snow on the crests until June and the long grey ridge of the Sierra de Guara in the foreground. Ereta de Litonares lies about three kilometres from the village, and the word ereta, a small threshing floor, hints at the open, level patches of rock and earth that farmers used to thresh grain in the wind. A threshing floor needs a breeze and a view, and so does anyone who wants to look at mountains.

The shelter at Ereta is one of the painted shelters of the Vero valley, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what it contains and I would sooner tell you so than guess. Most of the images of the region are small, in red and dark tones, and only visible when the light falls at the right angle, so a visit is as much about patience as about finding anything, and for that reason I would advise going with a guide.

Alquézar itself is the natural viewpoint. The collegiate church stands on the rock above the river, and from its terrace you look over the gorge and the terraced fields to the foothills beyond. The village has an old arcaded square, a few cafés and restaurants, and a quiet that returns in the evening when the day visitors have gone. The Church of Santa Maria de l'Assumpció, which shares the ride, is a village church elsewhere on the ride, in a different valley and a different mood.

The roads around are generally narrow and winding, climbing over small ridges between oak scrub and olive terraces. Surfaces vary, and gravel is common in the bends, so a relaxed pace is best. For fuel and shops you need to drop down to Barbastro, about twenty kilometres from Alquézar, where you will also find a good variety of restaurants and a cathedral. The best light for the view of the Pyrenees is early in the morning or in the hour before sunset.

Spring is excellent for snow-capped peaks, and autumn for the clarity of the air.
t.casa mila la pedrera@41.4,2.2:
La Pedrera, the stone quarry, is what Barcelonans call Casa Milà, and the nickname is fair. The building, designed by Gaudí for Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon and built between 1906 and 1912, has a facade of pale limestone that rolls along the corner of Passeig de Gràcia and Carrer de Provença like a frozen wave, with balconies of twisted wrought iron that look like seaweed. There are no straight lines on the facade, and no load-bearing walls inside, since the structure is carried by columns and the floors can be arranged freely.

The roof is the most surprising part. The chimneys, stairwell exits and ventilation towers are modelled as strange hooded figures, which people compare to knights or to the soldiers of a fantasy army, and the roof undulates between them in a series of low hills. It is one of the best places in Barcelona to look out over the city, with the towers of the Sagrada Família visible in one direction and the sea in the other. The building was controversial in its day, and the city council even fined the owners for exceeding the permitted height. It is now one of the group of Gaudí works that UNESCO listed.

For riders, the Eixample is the easy part of Barcelona. The grid of wide avenues with chamfered corners makes orientation simple, and motorcycles have designated bays along the pavements, so parking is better than in most cities. Traffic is dense and quick, with taxis, buses and scooters in a fluid mass, and the low-emission zone applies to older vehicles, so check the rules before you arrive. Paint, tram lines and manhole covers are slippery in the wet.

Fuel stations are fewer in the centre, so fill up on the outskirts. Around the building you will find cafés, bakeries and restaurants in plenty, and a slow lunch at one of the neighbourhood places in the side streets is a good deal better than the tourist menus on the main avenue.

Entry is by timed ticket, and the rooftop is open in the day and sometimes in the evening for events. Book ahead in summer. The ride pairs the house with the Cova de Vallmajor.
t.archaeological ensemble of tarraco@41.1,:
Tarraco was Rome's first permanent foothold in Spain. The Scipio brothers landed on this coast in 218 BC to cut Carthaginian supply lines and built a fortified base on the rock above the harbour, whose huge stone walls, in part from that early period, still stand along the edge of the upper town. Under Augustus the city became the capital of the largest Roman province in Spain, Hispania Tarraconensis, and the emperor himself lived here for a time in 26 and 25 BC, ruling the empire from a Spanish town while he recovered his health and led a campaign in the north.

The remains are spread through the modern city. The amphitheatre sits on a slope above the sea, with the waves beyond the arena, and was the scene of games and executions, among them, according to tradition, the burning of the bishop Fructuosus in the third century. The long hippodrome of the circus lies under the old town, with its vaults used as foundations for houses, while the forum and the provincial forum, the imperial cult area, occupy the heights. Just outside the city, an aqueduct, the Pont del Diable, strides across a valley on two tiers of arches. UNESCO listed the Archaeological Ensemble of Tarraco in 2000.

Tarragona today is a lively port city of some hundred and forty thousand people, with a beach, a cathedral, a pretty old quarter and a calm Mediterranean air. It is also the heart of the Catalan tradition of building human towers, the castells, which are performed on feast days in the squares and are well worth watching. Fuel, food and beds are easy to find, and in the seafood restaurants of the Serrallo fishing quarter you can eat the catch of the day with local wine from the Priorat and Penedès.

The coast road from Barcelona is fast and busy, but the inland roads through the vineyards and low hills, such as those toward the Prades mountains, are twistier and quieter. The old town is hilly and partly pedestrian, so leave the bike in a garage and walk. Summer is hot, humid and crowded, and the best months are April, May, October and early November.

The ride links the Roman city to Gaudí's crypt at the Colònia Güell, with a wide gap in time between them.
t.litonares e 1@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar has about three hundred inhabitants, and in many ways it is the best place to understand the valley, because it is a village where people still live, and not only a place to visit. In the morning, the baker's van comes through, old men sit on the benches of the square and the cats occupy the church steps. By midday the day visitors arrive, and by evening they have gone. Litonares E1, three kilometres from the village, is a painted shelter in the hills above it, part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and I cannot say what is painted there.

The village is stacked up a rock above the Vero, with its collegiate church at the top, in a tangle of stone houses, arches and stairways. The collegiate church holds a Romanesque cloister with carved capitals and a long terrace over the river. The best way to see it is to walk slowly, take a coffee in the arcaded square and then follow the walkways along the cliff above the gorge, which are well made and easy to follow.

Farming still shapes the surroundings. Almonds, olives and some vines grow on the terraces, and the old stone barns and drystone walls are part of a pattern that has hardly changed. In late winter the almond blossom turns the hills white, and in early summer the hay is cut and the fields smell sweet. Griffon vultures soar over the cliffs, and the evening light turns the walls of the gorge to copper.

Getting here by bike is a pleasure. The road from Barbastro, some twenty kilometres of gentle bends along the river, is a good introduction, and the lanes beyond are narrower and more demanding. The surface is mostly sound, with some gravel, and the traffic is modest except on summer weekends. Fuel is a matter for Barbastro, as the village has none that you can rely on, and groceries and a good lunch are also easier there.

Stay the night in the village if you can. The place changes completely after the day visitors leave, and the stars over the gorge are unforgettable.
t.the imperial cult enclosure@41.1,1.3:
When the Emperor Augustus died in AD 14, the people of Tarraco asked permission to build a temple to him, and Tiberius agreed. Tacitus records the request, and the rhetorician Quintilian preserves a joke from the emperor's lifetime: when the people of Tarraco reported that a palm tree had sprouted on his altar, Augustus replied that it showed how seldom they lit the fire on it. The imperial cult enclosure, the sacred precinct of the provincial capital, occupied the top of the hill, and what survives of it now lies under and beside the cathedral of Tarragona.

The idea was to bring the provinces together in worship of the emperor, which meant that every year delegates from across the province gathered here, to honour Rome and, not incidentally, to discuss local politics. A great terrace was built on the heights, with a temple and a surrounding portico, and the result was one of the most visible symbols of imperial power in the Spanish provinces. Fragments of the precinct wall can be seen in the cathedral cloister and in the old town, and the whole area belongs to the Roman Tarraco ensemble listed by UNESCO in 2000.

The cathedral itself is a fine Romanesque and Gothic building, begun in the twelfth century on the same hill, and its cloister has carved capitals worth a slow look. The street plan of the old town follows in part the lines of the Roman streets, and walking the lanes you will cross from one era to the next several times in a minute.

Tarragona is a city of about a hundred and forty thousand people, with fuel and every service, and the easiest approach is by the coast or by the motorway from Barcelona. Inland, the roads wind through vineyards and hills, and the Mas de Torres, which shares the ride, is a countryside stop. The old town is hilly and paved with stone, so park in a garage and walk.

Aim for the morning, when the stone is cool and the light is clean, and avoid the heat of August afternoons.
t.cova de l arc@40.4,0.1:
Albocàsser, Catí and Les Coves de Vinromà share a landscape of limestone ridges and wide, dry valleys, in the north of Castellón, where the first foothills of the Maestrat meet the plain. Cova de l'Arc, six kilometres from Albocàsser, is one of the shelters of this country, and its name, the cave of the arch, suggests the shape of the rock. The district is known to archaeologists for its painted shelters, which form part of the Mediterranean Basin rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998. I cannot say what is painted in this one, and I would advise a visit to the museum at Tírig, which explains the art of the nearby ravines and the best way to see them.

The people who painted here lived in a landscape quite like the present one, though more wooded, with deer, wild boar and wild goats on the slopes. Today the land is farmed with almonds, olives and some vines, and the stone farmhouses called masos, such as the Mas d'en Badenes that shares the ride, dot the hillsides. Drystone walls and small stone huts for shepherds and farmers are part of the pattern.

The riding is excellent for those who like open country. Roads link the villages over low passes, through avenues of almond trees that bloom in late winter and across plateaus where the wind blows steadily. The curves are easy and the surface is good on the main roads, though side lanes are narrower and rougher. Traffic is light, apart from tractors in the harvest season. In summer it is hot and dry, and in winter the nights can be frosty.

Albocàsser has about fourteen hundred people and the basics, with a few bars, a bakery and a shop. Cuevas de Vinromà, with nearly nineteen hundred, is nearby, and Catí, smaller, is famous for its cheese. For a bigger choice of fuel and food, you would head toward the coast or the main road. Local dishes include rice with rabbit, grilled lamb and the sweet pastries of the Maestrat.

Spring, with its green fields and blossom, and autumn, with a soft light, are the best times to visit.
t.arpan e 1@42.2,0.0:
Alquézar has about three hundred permanent residents, and the shelter named Arpán E 1 lies only three kilometres from it, up in the dry limestone country on the edge of the Sierra de Guara. The name Arpán belongs to a side ravine and a scatter of old fields rather than a village, and the pin marks one of the numerous painted rock shelters in the Vero valley. These belong to the Levantine art of eastern Spain, protected by UNESCO since 1998, which means small, mostly red figures of hunters and animals, made by people who lived here some six thousand years ago or more.

The valley itself is why you come. The Río Vero cuts a deep, twisting canyon through soft rock between Barbastro and the high Sierra, and the road along it, the A-1232 from Barbastro towards Alquézar and on to Colungo, is an honest motorcycle road: some tight bends, a couple of blind crests, a patchy surface in places, and between the bends views of cliffs, oak scrub and cypress-like junipers. Traffic is thin on weekdays, heavier at weekends when climbers and canyoners from all over Europe use the Sierra de Guara as a playground.

Alquézar is built on a rock above the river and is wrapped around its collegiate church, which began as a Moorish fortress and was taken by the Aragonese kings in the eleventh century. Wooden walkways in the gorge below let you stand over the water. Vultures circle over the cliffs most days, griffons for certain, and in the right light the stone turns from grey to honey colour at about six in the evening.

Practical matters: Alquézar has bars and a couple of restaurants but it is a village, so go to Barbastro, twenty kilometres away, for fuel. That town is also the capital of the Somontano wine district, where cool nights give crisp whites and a good local red, and its Gothic cathedral is worth a short look. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the heat is mild, the light is clear and the grapevines on the lower slopes are green or gold. The cierzo wind can howl down the valleys in winter, and you will feel it.
t.gallinero i@42.2,0.0:
Gallinero is a name that turns up among the scattered painted shelters of the Vero valley, and the pin lies five kilometres from Alquézar and about twenty-two from Barbastro. That puts it in the gap between the last decent town and the first real mountains, where fields of almond and olive trees give way to oak, box and rock. The shelters here belong to the Levantine tradition, small figures in red pigment made by hunter-gatherers and early farmers, and the whole group is listed by UNESCO as part of the Mediterranean rock art of the peninsula.

The honest truth is that most of these overhangs are not signposted for the casual passer-by, and they are not the kind of place you ride up to and photograph from the seat. The paintings are fragile, and some are on protected ground with limited access. What the ride gives you is the setting: the approach to the Sierra de Guara from the south, with the Pyrenees faintly visible to the north on a clear winter day and the plateau of the Somontano below.

From Barbastro the road narrows quickly after the last roundabout. You wind up through low hills, over short rises, past little farms with big stone barns, and then drop into the Vero canyon. The bends are medium in size, the surface is mostly good, and the places where it breaks up are usually the places where a stream crosses. There are few barriers, so keep your speed honest on blind left-handers. In summer you want to start early, because the rock radiates heat in the afternoon, while in March the almond blossom brings a pale pink flush to the lower terraces.

People have lived off this country for a very long time. Before the shepherds came, someone had cause to climb into these overhangs and paint on them, and thousands of years later the local people still talk about the Moors who were supposedly the painters, a folk tale that has produced a good many cave names. Fill the tank in Barbastro before you set off, since the villages along the valley are small and pumps are scarce, and carry a bottle of water if you plan to walk.
t.litonares e 2@42.2,0.0:
Litonares is another of the small ravines and field names that the archaeologists have used to catalogue painted shelters in the middle Vero, and its pin lies three kilometres from Alquézar. The code E 2 tells you it is part of a numbered series, which is how these shelters are known on paper. In the field it will be a low overhang in pale limestone, probably under a juniper or an oak, with a view over a dry gully. What was painted on the rock is a question for the specialists, who date the Levantine art of Aragon to the period between hunting and farming.

Think of this one as a pause in a bigger day. The ride from Barbastro follows the Vero upstream and the road gets better as it narrows, with a repeating pattern of short straights and tight bends where the valley wall pushes in. The A-1232 rises and falls along the side of the canyon, with a patchwork of grey cliffs and green hillsides, and the sun reaches the bottom of the gorge only late in the morning. After heavy rain a little mud washes across the road at the stream crossings, so look at the surface before you lean.

Alquézar, the nearest village, is worth the time you spend on it. Its streets are steep and cobbled, so park at the lower end and walk, and take the footpaths that run beside the river below the town. The collegiate church above it was once part of a Moorish stronghold, and the castle is more or less a watchtower with a view. Inside the village you will find a handful of small restaurants where lamb, local oil and the cheese of the high Pyrenees appear on the menu. I would choose the sunny terrace of a bar for a coffee and a slice of tortilla before you go any further.

Barbastro, the market town at the foot of the sierra, has several stations and is the place to top up before and after, as it lies twenty kilometres away along an easy road. Spring is lovely, summer is hot and busy with canyoning groups, and November often brings the clearest, calmest days.
t.cueva de la fuente de trucho@42.2,0.0:
The name suggests a spring and a trout, and you can hold on to the idea of water even if the shelter itself is dry. The Cueva de la Fuente de Trucho is one of the rock shelters that the archaeologists place in the Vero valley, two and a half kilometres from Alquézar, and it belongs with the painted overhangs of the Iberian Mediterranean arc that UNESCO recognised in 1998. Springs matter in this part of Aragon, which is dry for most of the year, and prehistoric people came to places like this for the same reason that modern walkers do: water, shade and a view.

The setting is the Sierra de Guara, the last big limestone upland before the Pyrenees proper. Riding in from the south you leave the wine and almond country of the Somontano and climb into scrub oak, box and pine. The Vero has carved a long canyon in soft rock, and the road beside it, a typical Aragonese secondary route, is narrow and winding but mostly good tarmac. Expect a little gravel at the edges, tractors in the harvest season and cyclists in the early morning. Take it slowly and the valley is a real pleasure; take it fast and you will meet a van on a blind bend.

Alquézar itself is the natural place to rest. It has a few bars, a couple of restaurants and a collegiate church standing on a rock that the Moors once fortified, and the late afternoon light on its walls is the best thing in the village. Footbridges and walkways take you above the river in the gorge. Eagles and vultures use the thermals along the cliffs, and in spring the air carries the smell of wild thyme and rosemary, both of which grow in thick tufts on the rocky ground.

Fuel is the thing to plan for. There is none in Alquézar, and the nearest sizeable town is Barbastro, nineteen kilometres away, where you will also find supermarkets and a good Gothic cathedral. The valley is busy with canyoners from Easter to October, so weekdays are calmer for riding. If you want a drink of local wine, the Somontano reds and rosés are easy to drink and kind on the wallet.
t.barfaluy iii@42.2,0.0:
Barfaluy is among the best-known names in the Vero valley, because the gorge that carries it is one of the classic short walks in the Sierra de Guara, a narrow slot of rock where the walls close in overhead. The pin, labelled Barfaluy III, is five kilometres from Alquézar and a little over twenty from Barbastro. The shelters of this area belong to the Levantine tradition of rock painting and are included in the UNESCO listing of 1998, and the third in the series sits in the broken limestone above the ravine.

Where Barfaluy is concerned, it helps to know what you are looking at on the way. The Vero canyon is cut into limestone laid down in a warm shallow sea tens of millions of years ago, then lifted as the Pyrenees rose and carved by water since. That is why the shelters exist at all: soft layers erode faster than hard ones and leave overhangs under the cap rock. The painters picked dry, shaded spots with a view, and the species they portrayed, deer, wild goats and bulls, still live in the neighbourhood, or at least their descendants do.

On two wheels the valley road is the draw. It is the A-1232 from Barbastro, winding through low hills, then following the river upstream beyond Alquézar. Bends are a mix of tight hairpins and quick left-rights, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is light outside of holiday weekends. Wind blows down from the north in winter, and in summer the temperature at midday can climb above thirty-five. Aim for the first hours of the day, or for an afternoon in October, when the oak leaves turn and the light is long.

That town sits at the junction of the mountains and the plain, with a good market and a collection of wine bars serving the Somontano reds and whites. Walking in the ravine proper is mostly a summer activity, and the water can run high after storms, so look at the sky before you go.
t.quizans i@42.2,0.0:
Where the Vero canyon opens out above Alquézar, the land is partitioned into dry terraces that once held wheat and olives, and one of those fields or slopes carried the name Quizáns. The shelter listed as Quizáns I is the first of its group, a little over three kilometres from the village and twenty from Barbastro. It belongs to the family of painted shelters of the Aragonese Pre-Pyrenees, which are part of the Levantine art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and in this area it often means lines of tiny archers and animals in a dull red pigment.

The view from this level, if you can find a clear patch of ground, is generous. Southward the Somontano rolls out in a patchwork of vineyards and almond trees, and on a crisp winter morning the Pyrenees show up in the north as a serrated white line. The name Somontano itself means at the foot of the mountain, which is exactly where you are. The wine trade here has grown since the late twentieth century, and Barbastro is full of tasting rooms and cooperatives where you can buy a bottle for the evening, if you have space in the panniers.

Roads in the district are the kind that tourists tend to underrate. They are narrower than the signs suggest, with edges that crumble where tractors have passed, and short, steep ramps that follow the hillside. Take it easy for the first ten kilometres and the surface will tell you what to expect. October is a particularly good month, because the grape harvest has just finished, the stubble is gold and the air is clear.

Barbastro has the nearest stations, and a good Saturday market. Its cathedral is a big late Gothic hall church with a fine altarpiece, and the old quarter is quietly handsome. There is a small supply of water at the village, and the rest of the route is dry, so bring plenty if you plan to walk to the shelter.
t.mallata iv@42.2,0.0:
Is it windy? In the Ebro basin it nearly always is, and the cierzo, the dry north-westerly that funnels down the valley from the Pyrenees to the Mediterranean, is part of the character of Aragon. It dries the soil, bends the almond trees into one shape, and can make a loaded motorbike on an exposed ridge lean at an unsettling angle. The pin at Mallata IV, four and a half kilometres from Alquézar, sits in the broken country on the edge of the Sierra de Guara, which is one of the places where you notice this most. Learn to read the trees and keep your elbows loose.

Mallata itself is a hamlet name, and the shelter is the fourth of its series in the catalogue of the Vero valley's painted rocks. They are part of the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula that UNESCO listed in 1998, small red figures and signs whose makers lived long before any local village was founded. A careful walker with a good guidebook can read the layers of history in the same landscape: a prehistoric shelter, a Roman farmstead, an Arab watchtower, a Christian chapel.

Weather decides the quality of the ride. From April to June the hills are green and the roads fairly empty. July and August are hot and crowded around the canyoning spots, and in November the fog can lie in the lower valley, while the heights above stay bright. The surface on the main road is dependable but patched, and the connecting tracks are not for loaded road bikes. Trust the maps and be ready to turn around.

If you are running low on fuel, the nearest sizeable town is Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres away, with fuel stations on the approach roads and a wide choice of lunch places, from fast bars to restaurants where lamb and mushrooms are cooked over vine cuttings. Alquézar has coffee and little else in the way of services. Carry water, and leave the shelter as you find it.
t.chimiachas e@42.2,0.0:
The cliffs above the Vero are the property of vultures. On most days you will see griffon vultures, great brown birds with a wingspan close to three metres, spiralling on warm air above the rim, and with luck an Egyptian vulture, smaller and white with a yellow face. The Sierra de Guara is also one of the places where the rare bearded vulture, the lammergeier, has been seen. The shelter called Chimiachas E lies almost four kilometres from Alquézar, in the middle of that airspace, and the painted rock shelters of this valley are all within sight of those cliffs.

Chimiachas is a small place name, and the E is a catalogue letter, so the shelter is one of a series studied and numbered by archaeologists. The paintings in this region belong to what is called Levantine art, small naturalistic figures usually in red, and the whole group has been protected by UNESCO since 1998. In truth, you will not be riding up to the paintings. They are a walk away, and some are closed off or unmarked to protect them, and you should check with the local tourist office before you set out.

What makes the area worth a long day is the rhythm of the ride. The road from Barbastro enters the foothills in a long gentle climb, then drops towards the river, then climbs again to Alquézar through a sequence of bends that start tight and open as you rise. The rock walls have an orange-grey colour, and at certain bends the whole canyon opens to the north with a view of the Sierra's high ridge. Wild boar tracks cross the road near dusk, and roe deer and foxes are common enough to make evening riding a gamble.

For fuel and a proper meal you will need Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres away. Alquézar has bars, a small shop in summer and a habit of putting bread, oil and tomato on the table without being asked. Take water if you plan to walk, and a pair of binoculars if you have one, because the vultures are most active mid-morning.
t.vinamala ii@42.2,0.0:
Viñamala is a name that sounds more dramatic than the quiet slope it marks, and the shelter catalogued as Viñamala II sits four and a half kilometres from Alquézar on a stony shoulder above the Vero. As in the rest of the valley, the numbering tells you that archaeologists found several shelters in the same area, a cluster that formed part of a prehistoric landscape, and that this one belongs to the Levantine rock art of the Mediterranean side of Spain, recognised by UNESCO in 1998.

The Sierra de Guara has a second life as one of the great canyoning destinations in Europe. Since the 1980s people have come from all over the continent to descend its ravines on ropes, jumping into pools and swimming through narrow slots, and villages like Rodellar, Bierge and Alquézar depend on them. For a rider the effect is simple: in summer the roads carry minibuses and vans with trailers full of wetsuits, mostly at the start and end of the day, and cafés open early. If you can, schedule your riding for the middle of the day, when the canyoners are underground and the roads are free.

The road itself rewards a careful rider. Beyond Alquézar the A-1232 continues deeper into the sierra, with sections where the carriageway narrows and the bends tighten to near hairpins. Sheer rock walls line one side and a steep drop the other, and there is little in the way of barriers, so lean smoothly and keep a margin. The road surface is patched but sound. In summer thunderstorms appear in the afternoon, and flash floods in the gorges are real, so if the sky over the sierra turns black, stay on the road and out of the gullies.

Fuel and shops are down on the plain at Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres from the pin, where the Somontano wine cooperatives and a good cathedral add something to the errand. In Alquézar you will find coffee, simple meals and a handful of rooms for the night, and the pace of life is gentle outside the main season.
t.gallinero iii b@42.2,0.0:
The old olive groves of the Somontano are the quiet backdrop to the shelter called Gallinero III B, which lies five kilometres from Alquézar among the terraces and scrub on the margin of the Sierra de Guara. The B in its name suggests a neighbour, A, which turns up in another list, and these letters and numbers are the archaeologist's way of dividing a large area of broken rock into manageable pieces. The paintings in this area belong to the Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO in 1998 and are small, red and often faded.

Olive oil is the better story at ground level. Aragon produces oil in its dry foothills, and in the Somontano the old mills still press the fruit between November and January. Some of the trees you pass are many centuries old, with trunks twisted into shapes that look like rope, and the local variety, the empeltre, gives a mild, fruity oil. Stop at any cooperative shop in the villages around Barbastro and you can buy a bottle straight from the press, a better souvenir than most.

Riding in this area has a gentle, undulating character. After Barbastro the road threads through low hills lined with almond trees, which flower pale pink in February, then climbs gradually toward the Vero. There is little traffic on weekdays, though tractors sometimes appear, and the road surface varies from fresh asphalt to rough patches where the frost has lifted it. The safest speed is the one that lets you stop within your own sight line, because blind corners are common and gravel collects on the inside.

Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres away, is the place for petrol and supplies. It has a covered market, a cathedral and a long main street that fills with locals every evening for the paseo. In Alquézar you can eat well, though prices climb in July and August. Take a bottle of water for the shelter walk and, in autumn, a layer for the evening, because the temperature drops quickly after sunset.
t.covacho de palluala@42.2,0.0:
Covacho is the Aragonese word for a small cave or overhang, and Palluala is one of the hillside patches near Alquézar that carry the old farming names of the valley. The shelter, a mere kilometre and a bit from the village, is probably the nearest to it of all the painted rocks on this list, which means you can leave the motorbike in the village and walk instead of making a project of it. As with its neighbours it belongs to the Levantine rock art of the Spanish Mediterranean, listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Alquézar is where the day should be spent. It lies on a spur of rock above a bend in the Vero, a huddle of stone houses with brown tiles around the collegiate church, which was built on the site of a Muslim fortress, and which the Aragonese king took in the eleventh century. A series of wooden walkways, the pasarelas, hang from the cliff on the far side of the village and lead you in a loop above the river and down to a viewpoint. Allow two hours and take a hat. It gets very hot in the narrow part of the gorge.

The ride from Barbastro up the A-1232 has a quality that many riders overlook, because it is not especially fast. It twists, drops and rises through a landscape of oak, almond and scrub, with the Sierra de Guara looming larger at each bend. In spring the fields are bright with poppies and the stream is full. In summer the villages are busy with weekenders and in winter many bars close, so check opening before you plan a long lunch.

Because Alquézar has only about three hundred residents, the pumps are down in Barbastro, nineteen kilometres away. The town is the commercial heart of the district, with a late Gothic cathedral, a market and a long tradition of wine making, and it is a good place to buy bread, cheese and cured meat for a picnic before heading up the valley. Bring water for the shelter, and remember that the paintings cannot be touched.
t.the amphitheatre@41.1,1.3:
Seen from the sea, Tarragona seems to be built on a cliff, and the Roman amphitheatre was put where the cliff meets the beach, so that spectators could look out over the water. It lies less than a kilometre from the city's centre, between the old town and the sand of Miracle beach, and it is one of the best-preserved Roman arenas in Spain. Tàrraco was the capital of a vast province, Hispania Tarraconensis, and the empire's governors, soldiers and tax officials spent years here, so the buildings were meant to be impressive.

In AD 259, according to the early Christian accounts, the bishop Fructuosus and his deacons Augurius and Eulogius were burned alive in this arena during the persecutions of Valerian. Later a basilica was raised on the spot, and in the twelfth century a Romanesque church, Santa Maria del Miracle, rose over its remains. You can still see the church's foundations in the middle of the oval. That layering, gladiators and martyrs and monks, gives the place a weight which the simple stone terraces do not.

The riding on this side of Catalonia is a mixed bag. The coast road is busy and urban, and you will want to leave the motorway for the lesser roads of the Camp de Tarragona, which wind through vineyards and hazelnut orchards. A good day in the hills behind the city takes you towards Prades and the Priorat, whose slate slopes produce some of Spain's most sought-after reds. The Mediterranean light is bright, and the best months for riding are May, June and October.

Tarragona itself is easy for motorbikes, with parking bays along the seafront and a ring of garages on the edges, and the main hazards are one-way streets and tram-like traffic in the old centre. A late afternoon walk along the Rambla Nova ends at the Balcó del Mediterrani, a viewpoint above the sea, and the old town has restaurants specialising in rice with seafood and a sauce called romesco, made with peppers and almonds. The city is also known for the castells, human towers built by teams of local people, which you can catch at festivals in summer and autumn.
t.muriecho e2@42.2,0.1:
There is a corner of the Vero valley where the road begins to remind you of Pyrenean country, and Muriecho, five kilometres from Alquézar and a little to the east, is on the edge of it. The shelter listed as Muriecho E2 is the second in its series in this area, and belongs with the painted rocks of the Vero that UNESCO placed on its World Heritage list in 1998. The village of Muriecho itself is one of the many small settlements in this part of Huesca that lost most of their people in the twentieth century, as the young moved to Zaragoza, Barcelona or abroad.

Depopulation is the quiet story of the high Aragonese countryside. Houses that once held large farming families stand locked and shuttered, terraces that once grew wheat and vines have returned to oak, and the old paths that tied the hamlets to each other are slowly disappearing. In recent decades newcomers, walkers and a growing number of summer visitors have brought some life back, and people are rebuilding houses. A rider is a witness to this change, in the shape of a handsome stone church with no village around it, or a mule track that stops at a pile of rubble.

On the road, expect modest challenges. The connecting roads from Alquézar are narrow and unlined, rising and dropping across the grain of the land, and the bends have a way of tightening just when you think you can relax. Cattle sometimes wander over the road, and in autumn the surface can be slippery with fallen leaves and acorns. If it has rained, give extra distance to anything that looks green.

Fuel is available at Barbastro, nearly twenty kilometres away, and you pass a handful of small villages on the way with bars that open sporadically. Barbastro has the cathedral, the Somontano wine cooperatives and a long arcaded square. Carry water, and do not trust a phone map to know which tracks are open to vehicles.
t.mallata iii@42.2,0.0:
Few place names sound as folded into the landscape as Mallata, and the shelter called Mallata III sits in a patch of oak and rock about four and a half kilometres from Alquézar. I take mallata to be a local word for a sheepfold, which would make sense, because the rock overhangs of the Vero valley served for thousands of years as natural barns, and shepherds put up a stone wall across the mouth and kept their flocks there overnight. Before the shepherds came, hunters used the same overhangs, and some of them painted on the walls. Those paintings are part of the Levantine tradition recognised by UNESCO in 1998.

The shepherds have a story to tell as well. Transhumance, the seasonal move of flocks between lowland winter pastures and high summer grass, shaped the paths and the economy of this country for centuries. In the Sierra de Guara it meant a slow walk up from the Somontano plain to the Pyrenean meadows in June and a return in October, along tracks that are still marked on maps as cañadas. A handful of flocks still make the trip, mostly by truck these days.

Riding here is a matter of picking the hour. In midsummer the pass of the A-1232 above Alquézar is a snail's pace of cars and minibuses at ten in the morning and nearly empty at seven. In the shoulder seasons you meet a few other bikes and an occasional group of cyclists in bright shirts. The surface is mostly good, though a few patches are rough, and the bends are best taken a little slower than you think necessary.

Barbastro is twenty-one kilometres from the pin, and a good place for a final coffee before heading up into the hills. A packed lunch from a baker, with ham and cheese and a piece of fruit, will be far better than anything you can find along the way, and water is essential if you walk.
t.cueva palomera@42.2,0.0:
Barely five hundred metres from the centre of Alquézar, the Cueva Palomera takes its name from the doves that nested in it, a palomera being a dovecote. That makes it the closest of all the painted shelters on this list to a village, and the easiest to fit into a day of riding. The cave is among the sites catalogued in the Vero valley and falls within the UNESCO listing of the Mediterranean rock art of the Iberian Peninsula. Whether any paintings are visible, and whether the cave is open to visitors, you should check locally, because access rules change.

Alquézar is the better reason to come, and a short walk from the cave takes you back into the village. It hangs on a rock above the river, with a plaza of arcaded houses, a collegiate church whose cloister has capitals carved with biblical scenes, and a castle that was a Muslim stronghold before the Christians took it in the eleventh century. From the church terrace you look over the Vero canyon, with its cliffs of cream and rust-red stone, and on a clear day you can see the Pyrenean ridge on the horizon.

The best approach by bike is from Barbastro, a road of about twenty kilometres that has all the elements of a good motorcycle ride in a short space. It climbs, drops and twists through almond and oak, crosses a stream or two, and finishes with a short, sharp rise to the village car park. Park there rather than trying the streets, which are steep and cobbled, and walk. Bikes are welcome in the lower square, and the walk gives you a chance to stretch before the next leg.

Fuel is a problem only if you forget it. There are no pumps in Alquézar and the next ones are in Barbastro, eighteen kilometres away, so fill the tank before you come. Food in the village is dependable, and the bars that cater to canyoners open early. Summer weekends are busy, and you may find it hard to get a table at midday without booking.
To the north of Alcalà de Xivert, in the hills that carry the Maestrat toward the Ports, the Coves del Civil, also called Ribasals, are a group of overhangs in a limestone gorge close to the village of Albocàsser. Abric III is the third in the series, a bit under six kilometres from the village, which has about fourteen hundred people. The paintings of the region belong to the northern extension of the Levantine art of the Spanish Mediterranean, protected by UNESCO since 1998, and the nearby Valltorta ravine is one of the most celebrated sites.

Valltorta, a few kilometres away, deserves a mention. This deep, dry gorge was recognised in the early twentieth century as one of the great concentrations of prehistoric art in Europe, with scenes of hunters, archers and animals in motion that are said to be among the liveliest of their kind. A museum in the nearby village of Tírig explains the site, and it is the proper starting point for anyone who wants to understand what the Maestrat shelters are about.

For a rider, the interest is in the roads. The country between Albocàsser, Catí and Cuevas de Vinromá is a little-visited tangle of lanes through almond groves, olive terraces and rock, with steep drops into ravines and unexpected views of a distant sea. Catí is known for its goat cheese, and if you see a shop in the village with cheeses on display, it is worth buying one for the evening. Winters are cold, summers hot and dry, and spring is the best time, when the ground is green and the roads are quiet.

The nearest sizeable town for fuel is Alcalà de Xivert, nineteen kilometres away towards the coast. Albocàsser and Catí have bars and a few shops, and if you are riding in the middle of a weekday you will often have the place to yourself. Take plenty of water, because summer walks in the gorges can be hot and unshaded, and leave the shelters as you find them.
t.barfaluy i@42.2,0.0:
There is more than one reason to come to the Barfaluy ravine, but the clearest is the sudden change in the land. From Alquézar the road runs along a plateau of fields and scrub, and then the ground simply drops away into a deep, narrow gorge where the walls rise sheer on either side and sunlight reaches the floor only briefly. Barfaluy I, one of the shelters in the series catalogued along it, lies five kilometres from the village, and as with others in the Vero valley it forms part of the Levantine rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998.

Barfaluy is also a place where you notice how the geology works. The rock is a pale limestone laid down in a warm sea, tilted and cracked by the rise of the Pyrenees, and the water that runs off the Sierra de Guara has cut through it like a saw. Hollows and overhangs form where softer layers are undercut, and swifts and choughs nest in the cracks. A good pair of binoculars will show you most of the birds in an hour, and the noise of the swifts at dusk is a joy.

If you are riding, the ravine itself is for walkers and canyoners, and you stay on the road above. The road from Alquézar along the Vero has a roughness that suits its character: not smooth, not fast, but full of little turns and drops. Expect to be passed by vans loaded with ropes and wetsuits, and slow down for walkers on the verge. In winter the cold can be sharp at the bottom of the valley, so wear a layer you do not need at midday.

Petrol is a short ride away in Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres from the pin. Alquézar has coffee and some simple meals, and gets crowded on summer weekends. A lunch of grilled lamb or local sausage and a glass of Somontano wine makes a good break, and nobody minds if you take your time over it. Carry water if you walk, and watch the weather, because flash floods in narrow gorges are not a joke.
t.gallinero iii a@42.2,0.0:
At this end of the Vero valley, the logic of the place names starts to feel familiar, and Gallinero III A is the first half of a pair whose sibling, III B, lies close by. Both sit about five kilometres from Alquézar among the dry terraces and oak scrub on the edge of the Sierra de Guara. The paintings belong to the Levantine rock art recognised by UNESCO in 1998, and in the shelters you may find red stick-like figures and traces of animals, usually faded by weather and time.

A different thought is worth having here. People often imagine prehistoric painters as isolated geniuses, but the numbering scheme itself is a reminder that the rock art of the Vero is a collective creation, with dozens of shelters in a small area, some with a single figure and some with several. The groups seem to have been used over very long periods, and later people sometimes painted over earlier work. It is more like a village noticeboard than a gallery.

Ride this area when the weather is kind. In April the almond trees have finished flowering and the fields are green, with poppies in the margins, and the road from Barbastro rewards a slow pace. The tarmac is a little uneven but sound, the corners are tight in places, and the view opens at every crest. In high summer the heat is intense, and the best moment for a ride is an hour after sunrise. October is excellent for colour.

Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres away, has pumps along the approach and a good choice of supermarkets. Alquézar itself has simple lunches and good coffee, and the walk down from the village to the river is a pleasant way to spend the cooler end of the afternoon, with swifts screaming around the church tower in summer and the stone turning gold. Take a bottle of water if you plan to walk to the shelter, and tread lightly.
t.fajana de pera superior@42.2,0.0:
Fajana is an old word for a strip of cultivated ground on a slope, a terrace in effect, and the Fajana de Pera Superior is presumably the upper strip of a farm called Pera. The shelter lies about five kilometres from Alquézar in the foothills of the Sierra de Guara, among old field boundaries that have been taken back by oak and box. It belongs to the rock art of the Vero, listed by UNESCO in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean arc, and carries the usual faint red marks of hunters and animals.

It tells you something that the shelters are named after terraces and farms, not mountains or heroes. The people who named them were farmers who lived in the valley until the middle of the twentieth century, working fields that now look inaccessible. Every bit of flat land was used, and walls of dry stone held the soil on slopes that seem too steep for a goat. The effort that went into those terraces rivalled that of the painters, and in many ways it was an art form.

Riding the Vero valley gives you a close view of what is left. Beyond Alquézar the road winds through country with abandoned farms, stone barns with caved-in roofs and olive trees gone wild. The road itself is good, with bends that tighten as the valley narrows and some sections of rough surface. Traffic is light during the week and heavier on weekends. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and you should be prepared to stop under the trees or in a village while a downpour passes.

Fuel is down on the plain. Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres away, is the place to fill the tank and buy supplies, and has a covered market worth visiting if you are there in the morning. Alquézar offers coffee, simple food and a handful of rooms. A little care will be needed on the walk to the shelter, because the paths are rough and the slopes loose.
t.els gascons@41.0,0.2:
The Matarraña, or Matarranya in Catalan, is a river that runs from the high ground of the Ports de Beseit through southern Teruel and down toward the Ebro, and its valley is one of the most appealing corners of inland Spain. Els Gascons lies nine kilometres from Valderrobres and seven from Calaceite, in a country of olive groves, almond terraces and low stone walls. The painted shelters here are among the eastern outliers of the Levantine art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and the catalogue includes names such as Valcomuna and Albi, which turn up in this route.

Calaceite is a handsome small town with arcaded streets, and it has a link with the earlier Iberians: the nearby site of the Tossal Redó, a fortified settlement from the first millennium BC, shows how long this country has been inhabited. Valderrobres is the show-off of the district, with a medieval stone bridge, a fortified gate and a castle-church ensemble reflected in the river, and every visitor who passes through takes a photograph of it. The valley is sometimes called the Spanish Tuscany, a comparison that works only in part, but the ochre light and rows of olive trees give it a similar feel.

For riders, the Matarraña is the surprise of the north-east. The roads are narrow and tightly wound, with gentle gradients and long views, and in the Ports de Beseit they rise into limestone mountains where griffon vultures soar above the road. Olive oil of excellent quality is produced in the area, and many farms sell it directly. The best time is spring or autumn, and you should avoid the hot hours in July.

Fuel is not a problem if you plan a little, because Alcañiz, twenty-eight kilometres away, is a sizeable town. It is also home to Motorland Aragón, a racing circuit that holds a round of the MotoGP world championship, so the town is used to motorcyclists and the pumps are numerous. Calaceite and Valderrobres have bars and restaurants, and a good lunch of lamb, local vegetables and a glass of the strong local oil on bread is cheap by European standards.
t.mallata b 2@42.2,0.0:
Here is a different angle on Mallata: the B 2 in the name is a scrap of archaeological bookkeeping, showing that a second subgroup was recorded in the neighbourhood of the original shelters. It lies a little under five kilometres from Alquézar, among the oak scrub and limestone outcrops of the Vero valley. As with other sites in the district, it is part of the Levantine rock art of the Spanish Mediterranean, protected by UNESCO since 1998, and what you see there, if anything, is likely to be small, red and weathered.

Think about how the valley's reputation has changed. A hundred years ago the Sierra de Guara was a poor, remote, depopulated district, with villages losing their young to the cities. Today it is a magnet for adventure sports: canyoning, climbing, mountain biking and walking, and a modest network of rural guesthouses has appeared. The paintings are now part of a strategy to attract visitors, and a cultural park along the Vero has been created to interpret them, with an information centre in the village of Colungo.

Riding here is best in the quiet shoulder seasons. The road beyond Alquézar threads along the canyon, climbing to give you views of the sierra's high ridge and dropping to cross the river. The tarmac is decent but narrow, and in places the verge is crumbling. Look out for cyclists, who flock here in early summer, and for livestock on the road. In winter, the north wind and morning frost call for warm gloves.
