It also has the best shops and the most varied places to eat. Alquézar itself serves good coffee and lunches, though service can be slow when the canyoning groups come in. If you walk to the shelter, take water, a hat and sturdy shoes.
t.huerto raso ii@42.2,0.0:
Huerto Raso is the name of a small clearing, literally a flat garden, in the stony hills above the Vero, and the shelter marked Huerto Raso II lies about five kilometres from Alquézar. It is the second in a numbered pair, and, like the others near it, it belongs to the Levantine painted rocks that UNESCO listed in 1998. The flat patch of ground after which it is named is a rarity in this tilted country, and you can see why someone planted vegetables there.

The soil of the valley deserves a mention. Over most of the Sierra de Guara the earth is thin, stony and pale, a product of limestone that dissolves slowly in rain, and every patch of deeper soil has been used for crops. The pockets of red clay that you see in the fields are the insoluble residue of the rock, and they hold water better than the surrounding stone. Farmers here developed a system of dry-stone terraces to trap that soil and keep it from washing away in the violent storms of late summer.

The road to the shelter is slow, careful riding. From Alquézar you take a minor road that rises through oak and juniper, past a few abandoned farms, and the tarmac gets narrower and more broken as you go. There are no barriers, and the edges are often soft, so keep to the centre and slow down for blind corners. The reward is a feeling of being a long way from anywhere, with the Pyrenean ridge hazy in the north and griffon vultures soaring overhead.

Supplies are all in Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres away, and the pumps are on the roads into town. Alquézar offers simple meals, good coffee and a view, and the nearby walkways above the river make a fine short walk in the evening when the day-trippers have gone. In spring and autumn the light is excellent for photography, and the nights are cool enough to make you glad of a jumper.
t.coves del civil o ribasals abric ii@40.4:
Think of the Coves del Civil, also called Ribasals, as a series of upturned bowls in a limestone wall. Abric II is the second shelter in the sequence, a little under six kilometres from the village of Albocàsser, tucked into a rocky ravine of the Maestrat. The wall above is pale and weathered, and the shelter faces east, so that it gets the early light. Its paintings are part of the Levantine art of the Spanish Mediterranean, protected by UNESCO since 1998, and are a short drive from the great Valltorta gorge.

Albocàsser is a small town with a Gothic church, and Catí, about eight kilometres off, is bigger and more handsome, with a medieval centre of stone arcades and a reputation for its cheese. The Maestrat itself is named for the Order of Montesa, a military order that held much of the district after the thirteenth century, and its old castles and fortified churches are scattered across hills that look much as they must have done in the Middle Ages. Stone-walled terraces step down the slopes, and on many hillsides you can see the ruins of masos, the isolated farmhouses of the region.

The ride here is a slow-burn affair. Bends are tight but short, with little distance between them, and the road surface varies from smooth modern asphalt to ancient patchwork. The light, especially in the early morning, is wonderful, picking out the lines of terraces and the shapes of the ridges. Sheep and goats still graze on the hillsides, and you may share a corner with a shepherd and his flock. Spring brings a profusion of wild flowers, and autumn a thin, clean air.

For fuel and a bigger shop, go to Alcalà de Xivert, nineteen kilometres away. Albocàsser and Catí have bars and small supermarkets, and a plate of grilled lamb or a wedge of cheese with honey is a satisfying lunch. Take water and a hat, since the sun reflects off the limestone, and do not expect any phone coverage in the ravine.
t.park guell@41.4,2.2:
Few people arrive at Park Güell without a sense of anticipation, and the first view is rarely a disappointment. The park lies on a hill called Carmel in the north of Barcelona, a short distance from the dense streets of Gràcia, and it was conceived at the beginning of the twentieth century by the industrialist Eusebi Güell as a garden suburb for the wealthy. He hired Antoni Gaudí to design it, and between 1900 and 1914 the architect laid out roads on stone viaducts, a great hall of Doric columns, a serpentine bench covered in colourful broken tile and a lizard fountain at the entrance. Very few plots were ever sold, and in 1926 the city bought the grounds and opened them as a public park.

The entrance fee is the first thing to understand. The central monumental zone, with the dragon, the hall and the bench, requires a timed ticket and is often sold out in high season, so book ahead. The outer areas of the park are free, with paths through Mediterranean pine and carob and views over the city to the sea, and the Carmel viewpoint above offers one of the best panoramas of Barcelona. Gaudí lived for twenty years in one of the show houses, which is now a small museum.

Riding in Barcelona is a different matter from the rural roads of the rest of this list. The streets around the park are steep, narrow and crowded, with one-way systems that confuse the visitor, and the nearest parking for motorbikes is on the pavement bays that the city designates. Scooters are everywhere. The ring road, the Ronda de Dalt, passes close and offers a fast way around the hill, and the Collserola range above the city has a handful of good twisting roads, much loved by local bikers on Sunday mornings.

Fuel is no problem in a city of this size, and the neighbourhood of Gràcia, just below the park, is full of cafés and small restaurants. The hill is busy at all times, but the best moment is first thing in the morning, before the tour buses arrive, or in the hour before the park closes, when the light turns the mosaics orange.
t.abric de la baridana ii@41.3,1.1:
Montblanc is the kind of small walled town that Catalonia does so well, and the story it tells about itself is the legend of Saint George, Sant Jordi, who is said to have killed the dragon here before rescuing the princess. Every Catalan knows the tale, and on 23 April, when people exchange roses and books, Montblanc is the place where the legend is celebrated with most conviction. Its medieval walls, with thirty-odd towers, still circle the old centre, and the town sits in the Conca de Barberà, a basin of vineyards between the coast and the hills of Prades. The Abric de la Baridana II lies eight kilometres away in the broken country of the Serra de Prades.

The shelter is one of the Catalan group of Levantine paintings, a family of rock art which UNESCO listed in 1998, and whose figures turn up in the dry mountain country that runs from the Ebro delta to the Pyrenean foothills. Its neighbours on the route, the Barranc de Sant Jaume and Esquarterades, are in the same area. The ravines that run down toward the Francolí river are steep and wooded, with holm oak, pine and juniper, and Mediterranean birds are numerous.

A short ride east brings you to Poblet, the great Cistercian monastery near Vimbodí, founded in the twelfth century and for a long time the burial place of the kings of Aragon. Its walls, cloisters and church, now a World Heritage site, are among the finest monastic buildings in Europe, and the monks who live there still welcome visitors. The road from Montblanc toward Poblet is easy and pleasant, with gentle bends through vineyards and almond orchards, and the rise toward the Prades mountains offers a more demanding ride of tighter bends and short climbs.

Montblanc has about six and a half thousand people, with fuel stations on its edges, a good number of bars and restaurants and a lively medieval quarter. Alcover, ten kilometres away, is another useful stop. Local wines from the Conca de Barberà, notably those from the trepat grape, make a fine accompaniment to a lunch of grilled meat and vegetables. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and the Prades hills can be very cold in winter.
t.muriecho e3@42.2,0.1:
Barbastro is the place that gives the whole district its sense of order, and it is worth a few minutes of history before you ride on. The town, twenty kilometres from the pin, was a Muslim city on the frontier of the kingdom of Aragon, and in 1064 it was the target of a multinational Christian expedition, a kind of precursor to the Crusades, which captured it after a siege and then lost it again the next year. Aragon finally took the town for good in the early twelfth century. Much later, in 1902, Josemaría Escrivá, the founder of Opus Dei, was born here, which has brought a steady stream of pilgrims.

The shelter marked Muriecho E3 lies about five kilometres from Alquézar and ten from Salas Altas, on the eastern side of the Vero valley. It is one of three or four in the Muriecho series, and it belongs to the Levantine rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, with figures that are typically small and red. The countryside around it is a patchwork of dry fields and oak scrub, and the view to the north takes in the first snowy ridges of the Pyrenees on clear days.

The road from Barbastro to Alquézar is the reason you are here. It is the A-1232, and it climbs gently from the plain through a landscape of vines and olives, with a surface that varies from excellent to patchy. The bends are generally moderate, and the road is best enjoyed at a relaxed pace, with stops to look at the view. On weekdays it is quiet, and on summer weekends you will share it with canyoners' minibuses and cyclists. Winter brings cold, and in the shade ice can last until the afternoon.

Barbastro is large enough, with about seventeen thousand inhabitants, to have all the fuel and food you could want, and the old town around the cathedral is worth an hour. In the Somontano wine bars you can taste the local reds and whites by the glass. Alquézar, in contrast, has few services, so fill the tank before you leave town.
t.huerto raso i@42.2,0.0:
The most common name for a cave in the Spanish countryside is not the name of a saint or a landowner but the Cueva de los Moros, the Moors' Cave, and the Vero valley is full of them. When people did not know who had painted an overhang or dug a hollow in the rock, they said it was the work of the Moors, who left the peninsula in the fifteenth century but whose memory remained as a catch-all for the mysterious past. Buried treasures, enchanted princesses and secret passages feature in the tales, and several caves on these routes carry the name. Huerto Raso I, five kilometres from Alquézar, belongs to the real painted tradition, though, and not the legendary one.

The paintings are of the Levantine type recognised by UNESCO in 1998, made at least six thousand years ago and perhaps more, by hunters and early farmers who lived long before the Moors or the Romans. It tells you something about the human mind that, when confronted with a faded red archer, we need to invent a story about it. Modern archaeologists study pigments, superimpositions and styles to build a chronology, but the human impulse behind the images remains out of reach.

The ride in is an easy pleasure from Barbastro, climbing up the A-1232 through country of vines, olives and oak, and the Sierra de Guara grows in the windshield. The bends are not severe, but there are a lot of them, and they come in groups of three or four. Traffic is light except on summer weekends, when cyclists and canyoners are out in force. In winter the road can be icy in shaded corners, and fog sometimes settles in the lower valley.

For lunch, there are small restaurants in Alquézar with terraces looking over the valley, and the local specialities are grilled lamb, mushrooms and cured meats. A glass of Somontano wine is a good accompaniment. If you go to the shelter on foot, bring water and wear walking shoes.
t.the circus@41.1,1.3:
Chariots in Tarragona raced beneath the walls of the upper city, and the great circus where they ran is still there, though it is hard to see as a whole, because the medieval and modern town grew over it. The Circus was built in the late first century AD, and it was well over three hundred metres long, with room for many thousands of spectators. Today you find its vaulted corridors under the Plaça de la Font and its curved stands incorporated into the buildings around it, with a tower, the Torre del Pretori, rising over one end. The legend says that Pontius Pilate was born here, or at least lived in the tower, a story with no historical basis but which the Tarragonans like to repeat.

The circus was part of the Roman capital's panoply, and it is on the list of Tarraco monuments that UNESCO protected in 2000, together with the amphitheatre, the forums, the walls and the necropolis. Tàrraco was founded in the third century BC as a military base during the war with Carthage, and under Augustus it became the capital of a province that covered much of the peninsula. Its remains are scattered across the city, stitched into modern streets.

Riding to Tarragona from the north brings you down off the hills of the Camp, through a landscape of vines, hazelnut and almond. A short climb takes you through the pass at the Coll de Lilla, with a view of the coast, and then the road drops to the city. The AP-7 motorway is fast but dull, and the older N-340 along the coast is more fun but busier. Inland, the Prades mountains offer twisty roads and a good day's ride.

In the city itself, fuel stations ring the centre, and the old upper town is walkable, with plenty of bars and restaurants. Fish and seafood are the strength, notably the romesco sauce made with roasted peppers and almonds, and a glass of local white. The best moment to visit is early evening, when the heat has gone out of the stone and the lights come on. Parking for bikes is possible in marked bays, and the old town streets are best explored on foot.
t.the roman theatre@41.1,1.2:
Wherever you sit in the Roman theatre of Tarragona, you face the sea. The builders carved the seating into the slope of a hill that runs down to the shore, so that the audience looked past the stage toward open water, and the effect on a clear evening is of a stage set whose back wall is the Mediterranean. Only part of the structure survives, its curved terraces partly rebuilt and its stage area cluttered with the foundations of the later buildings that stood on it, and yet the shape of the whole is easy to read. It lies in the lower town, a few hundred metres from the harbour, and is one of the monuments of the Tàrraco ensemble listed by UNESCO in 2000.

The Romans built the theatre in the first years of the empire, when Tàrraco was a thriving capital, and it served for centuries as the setting for plays and festivals. When the empire declined, the building was abandoned and used as a quarry, and in late antiquity a Christian basilica was put up on the stage, with burials and a later medieval church on top. The accumulation of centuries gives the site a layered quality that archaeologists enjoy and which makes the visit more interesting than a plain ruin.

By motorbike, you come to Tarragona from the north through the wine and hazelnut country of the Camp, with the Prades mountains to the west and the Gaià river valley cutting through. The roads here are a mix of fast main routes and gentle back lanes, and the best riding is in the hills behind the city, where you can find twisty, empty roads that lead to Poblet and the Priorat. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, with light of a fine, clear quality.

The city has about a hundred and forty thousand people, so fuel and food are no problem. Park the bike in the lower town in one of the marked bays and walk. The Serrallo, the old fishermen's quarter by the port, is the place for a plate of fresh fish, and the evening paseo along the Rambla Nova ends at a balcony over the sea. If you visit in August, expect heat and crowds, and bring a hat and water to the theatre because shade is limited.
t.malfora ii@42.2,0.0:
Honey is the quiet product of the Sierra de Guara, and if you ride through the Vero valley in spring you will smell why. Thyme, rosemary, lavender and wild sage cover the dry slopes, and the bees that visit them produce a thick, aromatic honey that is sold in the villages by the jar. Malforá II lies four kilometres from Alquézar, among the scrub and oak woods on the northern slopes of the valley, and it is the second of three shelters of that name in the catalogue. Like the others it belongs to the Levantine rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and it may carry the usual red figures of hunters and animals.

There is an old link between bees and rock art in Spain, famous from the Cueva de la Araña at Bicorp, in Valencia, where a painted figure climbs a rope to reach a hive. The Vero shelters are not known for such scenes, but they remind you that honey was one of the few sweet things available to prehistoric people and that collecting it was a risky, valuable job. Beekeeping is still a living tradition here, and if you see white hive boxes at the edge of a field, keep your visor down and your distance.

The ride along the Vero is a fine thing in May and June, when the verges are filled with flowers and the air is warm but not hot. The A-1232 beyond Alquézar passes through low oak woods and small clearings, with a few tight bends and short straights. Traffic is light and the surface is decent, though you should watch for loose gravel on the inside of corners and for the farm vehicles that use the road. In the heat of July and August it can be unpleasant in the middle of the day.

Barbastro is also the place to buy honey, cheese and cured ham from the market stalls. A walk down to the river from Alquézar, on the paths that lead to the footbridges, is a good way to cool off, and you can carry a picnic. Take a bottle of water with you to the shelter and tread softly.
t.lecina superior@42.2,0.0:
It is a curious thing, but the shelters of the Vero valley are mostly found not in the canyon itself but on its upper edges, on the open hillside above the cliffs, where the early painters could look across a wide landscape. Lecina Superior, the upper Lecina, lies five kilometres from Alquézar on such a slope, and its name implies a lower twin. The paintings there belong to the Levantine rock art that UNESCO listed in 1998, and the habit of having a view seems to run through the whole tradition.

Farther west the Sierra de Guara has its own legend, the Salto de Roldán, a narrow gap in the cliffs near Nueno where the knight Roland, pursued by Moors, is said to have leapt across the chasm on his horse. The tale belongs to the cycle of stories that grew up after the defeat of Charlemagne's rearguard in the Pyrenees in 778, and which gave rise to the Song of Roland, an epic poem of the eleventh century. In reality the battle took place at Roncesvalles, and the enemy were Basques rather than Moors, but legends do not bother with such details. The rock is worth a visit if you are riding toward Huesca.

Riding from Alquézar toward Colungo along the Vero is the best of this district. The valley narrows, the walls climb, and the road squeezes between rock and river in a series of short bends and little rises. It is not a high-speed road, but its rhythm is quite hypnotic, and you will find yourself slowing down to look at the cliffs. Griffon vultures soar above, and swifts scream around the crags. In the afternoon the sun lights the western wall and turns the stone a rich honey colour.

Fuel is a long way off, and Barbastro is twenty-two kilometres from the shelter. It would be wise to fill the tank there and to carry some food and water, since the valley villages have few shops. A lunch in Alquézar, with its views of the canyon, is a pleasant stop, and you can walk down to the river on the paths below the town. Be ready for sudden storms in summer afternoons.
t.vinamala iii@42.2,0.0:
Few Pyrenean views are as satisfying as the one that opens at a certain bend above the Vero in early morning, when the cold air has cleared and the snow-covered ridge stands up on the northern horizon like a row of white teeth. The shelter named Viñamala III lies four and a half kilometres from Alquézar, on the sunny side of the valley, and is the third in a series that includes Viñamala II nearby. It belongs to the Levantine art of the Spanish Mediterranean, protected by UNESCO since 1998, and sits in the sort of position that the painters seem to have liked: a dry, sheltered ledge with an open outlook.

If you carry a camera, the light is worth thinking about. In the valley, the cliffs face in different directions, so each part of the canyon has its own best hour. East-facing walls glow in the first light, west-facing walls catch the late afternoon, and the bottom of the gorge is in shade for most of the day. The golden hour is brief but intense in a country with dry air, and clouds roll in from the north at unpredictable times. A polarising filter helps with the blue of the sky and the glare on the water.

The road from Barbastro is a good one for a photographic ride, since you can stop at several lay-bys and gateways. It climbs in gentle stages, passes through the village of Alquézar and then enters the narrower part of the valley, where it winds above the river. Be careful with stopping, because the verges are narrow and there are blind bends. Traffic is light, but the road is shared with local farm vehicles, cyclists and the occasional camper van.

Fuel and food are in Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres from the pin, and in Alquézar you can buy coffee and a sandwich. Plan your day around the light, and take water if you intend to walk to the shelter. Autumn is the best season for clear air, and spring for flowers, though winter brings the sharpest views of the snow.
t.works of antoni gaudi@41.4,2.2:
Antoni Gaudí died on 10 June 1926, after being struck by a tram on the Gran Via, and since this year marks the centenary of his death, Barcelona has been in a mood of homage. The seven works of his that UNESCO lists as a group, among them the crypt of the Colònia Güell, a few kilometres outside the city, form one of the most distinctive bodies of architecture in Europe. They include the Sagrada Família, which he began to direct in 1883 and which is still being completed, the Casa Batlló and Casa Milà with their rippling façades, the Palau Güell on a narrow street off the Rambla, Casa Vicens in Gràcia, and Park Güell.

What links them is a fascination with nature. Gaudí studied plants, bones and rock formations, and he turned them into structure: columns that branch like trees, vaults that follow the curve of a hanging chain turned upside down, roofs that ripple like waves. He worked with ceramicists, ironsmiths and glassmakers to cover surfaces with colour, and he used a technique called trencadís, which makes mosaics from broken tile. The result looks playful, but it rests on rigorous geometry.

The ride to the city from the south or north is fairly unglamorous, since the coastal road and motorways are busy. What improves it is the hinterland. Montserrat, the serrated mountain to the north-west, has a famous monastery and some twisting approach roads, and the Garraf coast to the south has a winding cliff road with sea views. Inside Barcelona, motorbikes are a normal sight, and parking is allowed on the pavement in designated areas, though thefts are a risk and a good lock is essential.

Fuel is available all over, and the area near Park Güell, in the Gràcia district, is full of cafés. The most popular buildings are often sold out, so book timed tickets in advance, and pay attention to the weather: the mosaics and ironwork are slippery in the rain. Evenings are the nicest time for walking, when the buildings are lit and the heat has gone out of the day.
t.the colonial forum@41.1,1.2:
The colonial forum of Tàrraco was the heart of the lower city, the place where citizens did their business, gossiped and worshipped, and its remains lie in the middle of the modern grid of streets, a few hundred metres from the sea. You see a patch of excavated stone, a few columns, some paving and the base of a temple, surrounded by apartment blocks and cafés. It is an unassuming sight that becomes more interesting when you realise that this was the commercial and civic centre of a Roman city of tens of thousands, with law courts, a basilica and shops.

Tàrraco had two forums, a distinction that tells you about its status. The Provincial Forum, on the hill, was the stage for the imperial cult and the provincial assembly, while the Colonial Forum, down below, belonged to the ordinary citizens of the colony. Both are part of the ensemble of Roman monuments that UNESCO listed in 2000. Archaeologists have found traces of a public notice board, a place where decrees and announcements were displayed, and the idea of Romans standing in this square to read the latest edict is surprisingly human.

Tarragona is a city for walking, and a motorbike is better left parked. Come in from the north by the N-340 or from the west through the wine country of the Camp, then leave the bike in a garage or at a marked bay. The Rambla Nova, the main boulevard, runs from the sea balcony to the upper town, and cafés line its length. If you want to ride after lunch, the Costa Daurada has a string of beaches to the south, and the roads inland toward Prades are twisty and quiet.

Fuel and services are everywhere, with several stations on the outskirts of a city of a hundred and forty thousand people. For food, the market hall in the lower town is worth a visit, and a plate of rice with seafood or a dish of salt cod with romesco sauce makes a satisfying lunch. In August the heat is heavy, and a siesta is not an affectation.
t.argantin i@42.2,0.0:
The Argantín shelter, the first in its series, lies five kilometres from Alquézar and nearly twelve from Salas Altas, in a quiet corner of the Vero valley where oak scrub mixes with fields and old stone walls. It belongs to the painted shelters of the Aragonese pre-Pyrenees, a group that UNESCO listed in 1998 as part of the Mediterranean rock art, and as with the others in the Vero it is probably small and faded. The point of coming is the valley, and in particular the way it changes at different times of year.

In January the valley is cold and clear, the oaks are bare and the snowline is low on the Pyrenean ridge. In April it is green and loud with birdsong, with cuckoos calling from the woods and the first swifts arriving over Alquézar. In July the heat drives life into the shade, and the cicadas sing all day. In October the mornings are misty and the oaks turn rust and gold, and wild mushrooms appear in the damp hollows. Each season has its character, and the valley rewards a rider who visits more than once.

Practically, the road from Barbastro is the main approach, and it is easy to enjoy at moderate speed. The A-1232 passes through a landscape of almond groves, olives and low hills, then climbs to the village and the canyon beyond. The tarmac is decent, the bends are varied, and there are plenty of places to stop for a photograph. Be careful with gravel in the corners, with cyclists, and with sudden changes of weather, as afternoon storms are common in late summer.

Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres away, has several stations and a range of shops, and Salas Altas is a small village with a bar or two. A good lunch can be had in Alquézar itself, with terraces overlooking the canyon, and in the shoulder seasons you can often get a table without booking. Take water for the walk, and keep to the paths.
t.malfora iii@42.2,0.0:
Malforá III is the third in a trio of shelters that share a name, and the neighbouring village of Alquézar, four kilometres away, is the base for all of them. The shelters lie among the dry terraces and oak scrub on the northern side of the valley, and they are part of the Levantine rock art of the Spanish Mediterranean, protected by UNESCO since 1998. If you have already seen the first two, you may wonder why the early painters kept returning to the same patch of rock. The answer is probably the position: sheltered from the north wind, facing the midday sun and looking over a wide stretch of country.

Standing on that hillside you can see the shape of the Somontano, the foot of the mountain. The Pyrenees are the high wall to the north, the Sierra de Guara is the first broken step in front of them, and the plain of the Ebro opens to the south, patched with vines and cereals. The land was a natural crossing place between the mountain and the plain, with seasonal routes for people and animals, and it still is. Today the paths have become roads, and the roads are a pleasure to ride.

The best of them, from Barbastro to Alquézar and beyond to Colungo, runs for about forty kilometres of continuous interest. It begins with smooth, flowing bends in the wine country, then tightens as the valley closes, then relaxes again toward the head of the gorge. Many riders pair it with a day on the Guara's southern roads, around Bierge and Rodellar, which add climbs and canyons. Late April and October are the sweetest months.

Barbastro, twenty-one kilometres from the pin, is where you find fuel, supermarkets and a good range of food. It also has several cooperative wineries that sell by the bottle, and the local Somontano wines are reasonably priced and approachable. In Alquézar you can find simple meals and coffee, and the village is a good place to watch the sunset over the canyon. Bring water if you plan to walk, and watch the sky if clouds are building.
t.provincial forum@41.1,1.3:
The Provincial Forum of Tàrraco stood on the highest ground of the Roman city, on a series of terraces that rose above the lower town and the harbour, and it was the place where the province itself, not just the city, was on display. Delegates from towns across Hispania Citerior met here to organise the cult of the emperor and to send their petitions to Rome. A large temple of Augustus stood in the upper part, and what remains of the forum is incorporated into the medieval centre, with a tower, the Torre del Pretori, and sections of wall visible among the later houses. The site is part of the UNESCO ensemble of 2000.

Tarragona's cathedral stands on the same hill, on what was probably the site of the main temple, and the combination of Roman stone, Romanesque apse and Gothic cloister gives the upper town its character. The cathedral cloister has a small garden and a doorway carved with a procession of animals, a mock funeral of a hunter attended by cats and rabbits. The streets around are narrow, and the walls of the old town carry traces of enormous Roman blocks, laid without mortar, which have survived two thousand years.

For a rider, the old upper town is best left to walkers, though the roads around it have fine views of the sea. Take the road along the walls, the Passeig Arqueològic, which circles part of the Roman and medieval fortifications, and the sea balcony at the end of the Rambla Nova. From there, a day in the Camp de Tarragona is easy. The hills behind the city, with the monastery of Poblet and the slate slopes of the Priorat, give much better riding than the coast.

Fuel and food are plentiful in a city of this size. In the upper town the restaurants tend to be pricier, so walk down to the Serrallo or the market for a more local meal. In summer, the sun on the stone can be intense, and the best light for photographs is in the late afternoon, when the walls turn honey-coloured. Parking a bike near the walls is possible in marked bays, but luggage should not be left on it.
t.barfaluy iv@42.2,0.0:
There is a moment on the way up the Vero when the road leaves the last cultivated terraces and enters a more enclosed landscape, with oak and box on both sides and the sound of water somewhere below. The ravine of Barfaluy is on that stretch, five kilometres from Alquézar, and Barfaluy IV is the fourth shelter in its series. It belongs to the Levantine rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and like the others it is a small painted panel on a wall of weathered limestone, probably of red figures. The ravine is the real interest, as one of the most popular short walks in the Guara.

The landscape here is a lesson in how water shapes rock. During heavy rain the streams of the sierra turn into torrents that carry stones and gravel, scouring the beds and polishing the walls into smooth, curved shapes. Between storms the same channels are dry, and you can walk in them, but the walls above show the line of the highest flood. Walkers are warned to leave the ravine if the weather turns, and local guides check the sky before they set out.

If you are on two wheels, keep to the road and enjoy the unfussy qualities of the Vero valley. The surface is moderate, the bends are sharp in places, and the traffic is light on weekdays. The road is also a favourite of cyclists, who climb it in groups, so ride with care on blind corners. In July and August afternoon heat can be draining, and a morning start is best. In autumn the early mist gives the valley a soft, hushed look.

For petrol you need Barbastro, twenty-two kilometres away. Alquézar has coffee, simple meals and a grocery that opens when it feels like it. A bottle of water and a hat are essential for a walk, and you should wear shoes with grip. In winter the ravine is cold and slippery, and in summer it can be crowded, so go early.
t.cova de la taruga@40.4,0.1:
The Cova de la Taruga sits in the same part of the Maestrat as the Coves del Civil, six kilometres from Albocàsser and ten from Cuevas de Vinromá, in a landscape of low limestone hills, dry-stone walls and scattered almond and olive trees. The name probably refers to a tortoise or a rounded boulder, since taruga is a local word of that kind, and I would not push the etymology further. The cave belongs to the painted shelters of the Valencian Maestrat, which are part of the Mediterranean rock art listed by UNESCO in 1998, and the nearby sites of Abric de la Tenalla and Cabra Feixet are on the same route.

The interest of this piece of Spain is its emptiness. Castellón's interior has lost much of its population since the nineteenth century, and the abandoned farmhouses, called masos, sit in the fields with their roofs falling in. The stone walls that divide the fields are some of the finest in Europe, built without mortar and often five or six hundred years old, and they snake over the hills in elegant patterns. Rosemary, thyme and wild lavender grow between them, and in spring the air is full of scent.

The roads are a real find. Narrow lanes with little traffic link the villages of Albocàsser, Tírig, Catí and Cuevas de Vinromá, and the main roads in the district, such as the CV-10 or the road toward Morella, have good surfaces and open bends. The ride feels remote, though the sea is only an hour away. In summer the heat is dry and intense, and in winter cold winds from the north can be fierce. Spring and autumn are comfortable.

Alcalà de Xivert, seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full set of services, including fuel. Albocàsser has a couple of bars and small shops, and Catí is known for its cheese. A plate of grilled lamb, bread with olive oil and a glass of local wine is a good lunch. Take plenty of water for the walk, because there is no shade on the slopes, and avoid the middle of the day in summer.
t.arpan l@42.2,0.0:
Arpán is the closest of the Vero shelters to Alquézar in distance but one of the farthest in feel, and the letter L is part of the archaeologists' labelling of several shelters in the same area. The shelter lies three kilometres from the village, on the dry slopes of the valley, and it forms part of the rock art of the Mediterranean arc that UNESCO listed in 1998. The numbers and letters give a hint of the work that archaeologists have done to record every panel.

Alquézar rewards a closer look than it usually gets from visitors who race through to the walkways. The collegiate church, built in the twelfth century and extended later, has a Romanesque cloister whose carved capitals show scenes from the Bible in a lively, rough style. The castle was part of a chain of Muslim strongholds guarding the approaches to the Pyrenees, and it fell to the Aragonese king in the eleventh century. From the church terrace the view up the canyon, with the village roofs below, is the one every postcard shows, and it is still worth the climb.

On the road, the stretch from Barbastro is a pleasant introduction to Aragonese riding. It begins in vineyards and fields, climbs gently, and then offers a series of curves as the valley narrows. Surface quality is good in most places, with a few rough patches. Traffic is moderate at weekends and light on weekdays. Take your time, since the scenery is the point, and avoid the middle of the day in July and August, when the heat can be harsh.

Fuel is only available in Barbastro, twenty kilometres away. Alquézar has coffee, snacks and several restaurants, and if you can stay for an evening the village is quiet and its lights over the canyon are lovely. Take water to the shelter, wear good shoes, and treat the paintings as you would a museum exhibit.
t.artica de campo@42.2,0.0:
Artica is the kind of small place name that appears on only the most detailed maps, and Artica de Campo, one and a half kilometres from Alquézar, is a field or small farm on the slope above the village. Its shelter is the closest after Cueva Palomera to the centre of Alquézar, and it belongs to the rock art of the Vero listed by UNESCO in 1998. The ride that features it also links to Navarra's beech forests at Aztaparreta, a long way to the west in the Pyrenees, which are a lovely place in October.

What makes the neighbourhood of Alquézar unique is how close the main sights are. In a single morning you can walk the footbridges over the gorge, climb to the collegiate church, look at a painted shelter and have a coffee in the square, without a car or a bike. It is a village built for walking, and the surrounding paths link it to the hamlets and ravines around it. A guidebook from the tourist office in the village gives route descriptions and tells you where the shelters are, and some paths are waymarked.

The ride from Barbastro is best taken slowly, and in early morning when the light picks out the folds in the hills. The road climbs through almond and olive country, with views to the Sierra de Guara, and enters the village with a final steep ramp. There is a car park at the entrance, and the village streets are too steep and narrow to ride. Cobbles can be slippery, especially when wet, so walk with care in riding boots.

Fuel and shops are in Barbastro, nineteen kilometres away, and you should arrive with a full tank. In Alquézar there are several places to eat, and on a weekday in spring or autumn you can usually find a table with a view. Water is available from the fountains in the village, and you should carry a bottle for walks. The nights are cool, and a jacket is useful after sunset.
t.theatre antique@44.1,4.8:
The Théâtre antique d'Orange is one of the best-preserved Roman theatres anywhere, and the thing that surprises people is the wall. The stage wall at the back, known as the scaenae frons, still stands to its full height of around thirty-six metres, a huge, sun-bleached cliff of stone that Louis XIV is supposed to have called the finest wall in his kingdom. Built in the early first century AD when Orange was the Roman colony of Arausio, the theatre could seat several thousand, and the acoustics are so good that it hosts the Chorégies d'Orange opera festival every summer, as it has for generations.

Orange is a town of thirty thousand people on the Rhône plain in northern Provence, and the theatre sits right in the middle of it, a hundred steps from the cafés and the pedestrianised streets. A few hundred metres away stands the Arc de Triomphe, one of the oldest surviving Roman triumphal arches in Gaul, set on a roundabout on the old Via Agrippa. Together they earned a UNESCO listing, and an hour on foot covers both.

As for the riding, this is a town stop, but what a town stop. The surrounding country is flat vineyards of the southern Rhône, with Châteauneuf-du-Pape just to the south and the dry limestone ridges of the Dentelles de Montmirail to the east, and the mistral can blow hard enough to push a loaded bike across the lane. If a forecast says mistral, be ready for sharp gusts on open stretches and bridges, especially on the Rhône valley highway. In summer the heat is fierce by midday, so the best hours are early morning and evening, when the stone glows warm gold.

Fuel, food and coffee are all easy in Orange, with supermarkets on the edge of town and plenty of cafés around the Place aux Herbes. The local specialities are what you would expect from the southern Rhône: olives, tapenade, lavender honey, and the wines of Côtes du Rhône, though the bike limits you to a sip. A morning market in the town fills the streets on Thursdays, which is worth knowing both for the pleasure and for the parking.

Go early, before the tour buses arrive, and take the hour to sit in the stone seats and look at that wall. It is the kind of place that makes a ride feel older than it is.
t.barcelona catalonia@42.0,2.1:
Osona is the plain around Vic, a high, cool basin ringed by hills, and the Lluçanès, to its north-west, is a quiet plateau of farmhouses, woods and cornfields that few visitors ever see. These coordinates fall close to Olost, a village of about twelve hundred people, and the land around it is a patchwork of stone-walled fields and isolated masías, the big, fortified farmhouses that are the backbone of rural Catalonia. It is a place to slow down, and the roads reward it.

Catalonia's reputation rests on its cooking, and Osona is where much of it comes from. The area is famous for its cured meats, including the fuet, a thin, dry sausage that goes into every picnic, and the botifarra, a fresh sausage grilled over coals. Pigs are raised in large numbers, and in winter the villages hold traditional slaughter days, when families gather to make sausages and hams. Cheese, honey and mushrooms from the hills round out the table, and a meal in a farmhouse restaurant is an experience that justifies a long ride.

The roads here are narrow and winding, with tight bends, short climbs and frequent junctions. The surface is mostly good, though some of the lanes are patched and gravelly at the edges, and tractors and cyclists are common. Views across the plain to the Pyrenees, a white line of snow on the horizon in winter, are splendid on a clear day. Autumn brings mist in the valleys, and the colours of the woods in October are superb. In summer the heat can be fierce, and the best time to ride is the early morning.

Olost and Oristà are tiny and have little more than a bar and a shop. Vic, a fine old market town of nearly forty thousand people, lies about fifteen kilometres away, and has stations, supermarkets and a cluster of good restaurants. Gurb, a village near it, has a few more facilities. The nearest large town with every service is Vic, and it is also a pleasure to visit, with a Roman temple, a cathedral decorated with murals by Josep Maria Sert and a big Saturday market. Fill up before you go, and bring layers, because the weather on the plateau can change in an hour.
t.pyrenees n 260 weekend@41.8,1.6:
Calaf, Súria and Fonollosa sit on the long, dry plateau that links the Anoia valley to the Bages, in the middle of Catalonia, and these coordinates fall among them, in a landscape of wheat fields, almond groves and low scrub-covered hills. The countryside is open and wide, with long views to the Pyrenees in the north and the great grey bulk of Montserrat in the south, and the light, in the evening, is warm and golden.

Súria is known for its salt. Under the town lie deposits of potash and rock salt, which have been mined for decades, and a huge white heap of waste salt stands beside the town like a snow-capped hill. The mines have given the place an industrial character, but the old centre, with its castle on the hill, is pleasant, and the museum tells the story of the mines. Calaf, with just over three thousand people, is a country market town with an arcaded square and a handful of good bars and restaurants.

The road that gives the ride its name, the N-260, is the long, winding highway that runs across the Pyrenees from the Mediterranean to Aragón, following the line of the mountains and crossing passes and valleys as it goes. It is one of the most scenic roads in Spain, and one of the most testing, with hundreds of bends, tight climbs and steep descents, and a surface that varies from silk to rubble. The stretch near Calaf is gentler, running along a ridge with open views, and it makes a fine warm-up for the mountains.

Fonollosa and Rajadell are small villages with a bar and a shop, so fuel and a substantial meal are best found in Calaf or Súria, which has about six thousand people. The Catalan lunch is the great institution, with the menú del día usually served from half past one, and a good one includes a first course, a main dish, dessert and wine. Order the grilled meat, the stewed beans and the crema catalana, and linger over the coffee. In winter, the plateau can be bitterly cold, with wind and frost, and in summer it is fierce, so choose your season with care.
t.pyrenees n 260 weekend high point@41.0,2:
Look at these coordinates on a map and you will find open sea, about thirty kilometres south-east of Barcelona, in the lanes of the busiest shipping in the western Mediterranean. Container ships, ferries and tankers pass in a steady procession, heading to and from the port of Barcelona, one of the largest in Europe, and the water is crisscrossed by routes that connect Spain to Italy, North Africa and the islands of the Balearics. It is not a place for motorcyclists, but it is the horizon that Barcelona looks across.

The Pyrenees ride that begins and ends in the city is a long weekend in the mountains, a journey along the N-260 that is one of the great roads of Europe. The high point of the ride, in the literal sense, lies far from here, among the passes of the Catalan Pyrenees, where the road climbs to well over a thousand metres and snow lies on the verges into May. But the sea is the starting point, and the contrast between the hot, humid coast and the cool, thin air of the high valleys is part of the adventure.

The Mediterranean here is warmer than the Atlantic, with a summer temperature around twenty-five degrees, and the winds are local and changeable. The tramontana blows from the north in winter, clear and cold, and the garbí, a south-westerly, brings squalls in autumn. Fishing boats still work out of the harbours along the coast, bringing in sardines, anchovies and prawns, and the restaurants of the old fishing quarters serve them grilled with sea salt.

On land, Barcelona has fuel stations on the ring roads and in the suburbs, but few in the dense city centre, so fill up before you enter. Motorcycles are everywhere in the city, and drivers are used to them, but the traffic is fast and aggressive, and theft is a real risk, so lock the bike and never leave luggage on it. In the morning, with the sun rising over the water and the port waking up, it is a fine place to begin a ride.
t.pyrenees n 260 weekend scenic road@41.1,:
The finish of a long Pyrenean weekend is rarely graceful, and Barcelona does not pretend otherwise. These coordinates sit offshore, in the water south-east of the city, so the last part of the ride is a matter of picking a way through the metropolis: down off the hills on the motorway, round the ring road, then into the grid of the Eixample, where the streets are wide and the corners are chamfered, and the traffic moves in surges. Motorbikes are the city's favourite vehicle, thousands of scooters stand parked at every kerb, and the other drivers know exactly where you are, which is some comfort.

What awaits at the end is the old waterfront. La Barceloneta, the fishermen's quarter built in the eighteenth century on a spit of reclaimed land, is a grid of narrow, tall, laundry-draped streets that runs down to the beach, and the arguments over which of its restaurants serves the best paella are conducted with passion. The Olympic Games of 1992 changed the seafront, with the old industrial zone replaced by a marina, beaches and a pair of towers, and the city has been turned toward the sea ever since. A late afternoon walk along the promenade, with the sun low and the sand full of volleyball players, is the right antidote to hours in the saddle.

The Mediterranean on this coast is a gentle sea, tideless and warm in late summer, and the beaches, though artificial, are clean and wide. Swimming is easy from June to October, and a dip at the end of a hot ride is one of the great pleasures. The wind often rises in the afternoon, bringing a cool, salty breeze into the city, and in winter the air is mild and the sky a clear blue. In summer the nights are hot, noisy and long, and dinner is rarely before nine.

Practical questions in a big city are mostly about parking and theft. Use a secure garage if your hotel has one, lock the bike to a fixed post and take your helmet and luggage with you. Fuel stations are less common in the centre than on the ring roads, so fill up before you come in. Barcelona has about one and a half million people and every kind of food, but a cold vermouth with olives and potato chips, taken at a bar counter at one in the afternoon, is a local ritual worth following.
t.priorat vineyard curves photo pull off@4:
Between Tarragona and the Penedès, the low country of the Baix Penedès is a patchwork of vineyards, almond orchards and small towns, and these coordinates fall near Bonastre, Salomó and Vilabella, about ten kilometres from El Vendrell. The land is rolling, with red soil and pale limestone, and the vines run in neat rows to the edge of the village. The Penedès is the home of cava, the Spanish sparkling wine, and though the main producers are further north, around Sant Sadurní, vines are grown here as well.

El Vendrell is the birthplace of Pau Casals, the great cellist, who was born in 1876 and became one of the finest musicians of the twentieth century. He left Spain after the civil war and never returned to live there, but his house at the seaside village of Sant Salvador, now a museum, preserves his cello and his letters. The town is also a centre of castells, the human towers that Catalans build at festivals, in which teams climb on each other's shoulders to form pillars up to ten levels high. The tradition was recognised by UNESCO in 2010, and a performance is thrilling to watch.

The ride is the Priorat Vineyard Curves, and this is the quiet approach to it, the plain before the hills. The roads are narrow and straight at first, running between vineyards, with a few tight turns through villages and a surface that is mostly good. Ahead, the land rises to the Montsant and Prades ranges, and the road begins to climb and twist. Spring brings green leaves and wild flowers, summer is hot and dry, and the harvest in September fills the air with the smell of crushed grapes.

Bonastre and Salomó are tiny, with a bar and not much else. Fuel and a proper lunch are better found at El Vendrell, a town of nearly thirty-six thousand, which has stations, supermarkets and many restaurants, and a long, sandy beach close by. Eat the local specialities, such as the calçots, spring onions grilled over a fire and dipped in romesco sauce, a feast of the winter and early spring, or a plate of rice with seafood. In the afternoon heat, a long, slow lunch is wise, and the ride resumes when the sun is lower.
t.priorat vineyard curves scenic road@41.0:
The Llobregat Delta spreads out to the south-west of Barcelona, a wide plain of reeds, fields and wetlands where the river meets the sea, and these coordinates fall in the water just off its shore. Castelldefels, a seaside town of sixty thousand people, stands at the southern end, with a long beach, a hilltop castle of tenth-century origin and a mix of apartment blocks and villas. In summer the beach is crowded with families from the city, and in winter it is a long, empty strip of sand where dog-walkers and joggers have the run of the shore.

The delta itself is a surprise, because it lies in the shadow of Barcelona's airport, and yet it is a haven for wildlife. Lagoons and reedbeds at El Remolar and Cal Tet shelter flamingos, herons and many ducks, and bird-watchers come from all over Europe to watch the migrations in spring and autumn. Farmers grow artichokes, peaches and vegetables on the fertile plain, and the sight of a field of green leaves with the roar of an aircraft above has a surreal charm.

This is the starting area for the Priorat ride, which heads west and south into the hills of Tarragona province. The way out is along the coast on the C-31 and the motorway, a fast and busy route, with the Garraf hills rising to the west. These limestone hills, crowded with scrub, cliffs and caves, form a rocky barrier between the delta and the Penedès, and the road that threads them has tunnels and high viaducts, and a view of the sea from the top. Allow plenty of time at weekends, when the beaches draw traffic.

Castelldefels has fuel stations and supermarkets on the main road, and Gavà and Viladecans, close by, have many more. If you are leaving early, a coffee and a pastry from a bakery make a good start, and you can fill the tank before the motorway. Sea breezes cool the air in the summer, but the humidity is high, and the nights are warm. In winter, the weather is mild and the sunlight clear, and it is easy to see why so many people choose this coast.
t.priorat vineyard curves high point@40.9,:
The Garraf massif is the rugged block of limestone that rises between Barcelona and Sitges, and these coordinates sit out at sea, off its southern coast. There is nothing to ride here, only a long view over a calm, blue Mediterranean. The nearest land, the cliffs and coves of the Garraf coast, is wild and sparsely settled, a place of pines, rosemary and thyme, and the smell on a warm day is intoxicating.

The park behind the coast protects some of the driest and most rugged hills in Catalonia, a karst landscape of caves, sinkholes and bare rock. The highest point, La Morella, rises to a little under six hundred metres, and the view from the top takes in the sea, the Llobregat Delta and the peaks of Montserrat. Bonelli's eagles nest on the cliffs, and the scrub is home to genets, wild boar and the dwarf fan palm, the only palm native to continental Europe. At Garraf village, a cluster of white houses beside a small harbour, stands the wine cellar designed by one of Gaudí's disciples, Francesc Berenguer, a fantasy in rough stone with parabolic arches.

For a rider, the road that matters is the C-31, the old coast road from Castelldefels to Sitges, which runs through a series of tunnels and cuttings above the sea. It is fast and well surfaced, but busy, with trucks and holiday traffic. Inland, the lanes through the park are narrower, with tight hairpins, steep climbs and a view of the sea at every turn, and cyclists swarm them at weekends. The ride is the Priorat Vineyard Curves, and these hills are a sweet, short prelude to it.

There are no stations in the park, so fill up in Castelldefels, Gavà or Sitges. Summer is hot and the fire risk is high, so access to the park is sometimes restricted, and the autumn and spring are the best seasons for riding. A visit to Sitges, with its beaches and its old town, makes a pleasant end to the day, and the sea is warm enough for a swim until October.
t.costa brava and tossa de mar@41.5,2.4:
Argentona is a small town in the hills behind the Maresme, about thirty kilometres north-east of Barcelona, and these coordinates sit right beside it, among the pines and holm oaks of the Serralada Litoral. The place has the look of a prosperous commuter village, with a handsome old centre, a plane-shaded square and a number of grand villas built by wealthy Barcelona families in the early twentieth century. The architect Josep Puig i Cadafalch, one of the leading figures of Catalan Modernisme and a native of neighbouring Mataró, designed several buildings here, and his work is one of the town's sights.

The town is also known for pottery, and its museum of the càntir, the traditional Catalan drinking jug with its two spouts, holds hundreds of examples. The jug is designed to be held high, so that a thin stream of water pours into the mouth without touching the lips, a skill that is harder than it looks and entertaining to watch. Nearby Cabrils and Òrrius are quiet villages, with views over the sea and the hills, and the area is a favourite with walkers and mountain bikers.

The ride goes north along the Costa Brava to Tossa de Mar, a walled town on the coast, where the old fortifications, built in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries, still enclose a tangle of narrow streets above the bay. The road from Tossa to Sant Feliu de Guíxols, the GI-682, is a legend among riders, a narrow ribbon of tight curves cut into the cliffs high above the sea. The surface is good, the views are spectacular and the traffic can be heavy in summer, so it is best ridden early in the morning or in the shoulder seasons of spring and autumn.

For fuel and food, Argentona has stations, supermarkets and several good restaurants, and Cabrils, a few minutes away, has more. Òrrius is small and quiet. Top up here before the coast, because the road from Blanes to Tossa has few stations and prices are higher. A coffee and a croissant at a village café, eaten at an outdoor table in the early sun, is a pleasant way to begin, and the bends ahead promise a long and memorable day.
The Segarra is a high, open plain of wheat, almonds and olives in the west of Catalonia, and these coordinates fall in the middle of it, near Guimerà, Cervera and Verdú. It is a dry, windswept country, a long way from the sea, and the summers are hot and the winters bitter. The sky is large, the villages are built of golden stone and the roads run straight for kilometres between fields. It is the Catalonia that most visitors miss, and it has a quiet and austere beauty.

Cervera, a town of about nine thousand people, is the centre. In 1717, after the War of the Spanish Succession, King Philip V closed all the universities in Catalonia and set up a single one here, as a reward for the town's loyalty, and its great baroque building, with its courtyard and stone staircase, still dominates the old town. Verdú, a smaller place nearby, is the birthplace of Saint Peter Claver, the Jesuit who worked among enslaved Africans in Cartagena, in what is now Colombia, in the seventeenth century. Guimerà, a village of fewer than four hundred people, clings to a cliff above a ravine, a medieval jumble of stone houses and narrow lanes that seems barely to have changed in five hundred years.

The ride is named for the Montseny Natural Park, a high massif to the east of Barcelona that rises to about seventeen hundred metres, and the road there lies a long way across the country. The Montseny is a cool, wooded range of beech, oak and heath, and its summit gives long views towards the Pyrenees on a clear day. Its roads climb in a series of bends, with fog often covering the upper slopes, and they are a delight for riders.

Here, the pleasure is of space and silence. Cervera has fuel stations, supermarkets and good restaurants, so fill up here, because services are sparse in the villages. Verdú has a bar and a shop, and Guimerà has little more. Lunch in Cervera is a fine thing, with local lamb, grilled vegetables and almond cakes. Carry a windproof layer, for the breeze across the plain can be cutting even in spring, and in winter the temperature often falls below freezing.
t.barcelona catalonia@42.0,2.9:
Girona sits where the Onyar River meets the Ter, and its old town is one of the best-preserved in Spain. These coordinates fall in the countryside to the east, near Bordils, Celrà and Foixà, in the flat, fertile plain of the Gironès, a landscape of poplars, maize and orchards. The town of Girona, about ten kilometres away, has nearly a hundred thousand people and is the main city of the northern part of Catalonia.

The old quarter climbs a hill above the river, with a cathedral at the top that is approached by a monumental staircase of ninety steps, which was used as a location in a famous television fantasy series. Below it lies the Call, the medieval Jewish quarter, a tangle of lanes and stairways that was home to a thriving community until its expulsion in 1492. Along the Onyar, rows of houses painted in yellow, ochre and red hang over the water, and the iron footbridge that crosses it was built in a workshop run by Gustave Eiffel's company. A walk along the city walls gives a view over the red roofs to the mountains.

The ride finishes or starts here, as part of a loop that runs from Barcelona to the Pyrenees and back. The roads east of Girona are flat and straight, with a good surface and light traffic, and in spring the fields are green and the poppies bloom. A short ride to the north leads to the Albera hills and the border, while to the east, the Empordà coast, with Begur, Pals and Cadaqués, is some of the finest in Spain. Autumn is the best season, when the heat has eased and the crowds have gone.

Foixà has a castle and little else, and Bordils and Celrà are small towns with the basic services. Girona has all the fuel and food you could need, from supermarkets to Michelin-starred restaurants, and the Roca brothers' famous restaurant is one of the best in the world. For a simpler meal, try a menu del día in the old town, with rice, fish and a glass of wine. Park outside the centre, because the old quarter is a maze of steps.
t.tibidabo dawn short loop@41.2,1.9:
Castelldefels is a long beach town south-west of Barcelona, and these coordinates fall on the hills behind it, in the northern edge of the Garraf massif near the village of Begues. The road up from the coast climbs through pine woods and scrub, with views over the sea and the plain of the Llobregat, and in the early morning, when the sky is pink and the air is still, it is a lovely place to start a ride. This is the starting point for a dawn loop to Tibidabo, the hill that looks over Barcelona from the north-west.

Tibidabo, rising to about five hundred and twelve metres, is the highest point of the Collserola range. On its summit stands the Temple of the Sacred Heart, a large church topped by a statue of Christ, and beside it a funfair that opened in 1901 and is one of the oldest in the world. Its old rides, including a Ferris wheel and a small aeroplane that swings out over the city, retain a wonderful, faded charm. A short way down, the old Tramvia Blau, the Blue Tram, climbs the hill, though its service has been intermittent in recent years.

The road to the summit is called the Carretera de l'Arrabassada, and it has a long motoring history. It hosted a famous hill climb as early as 1908, and rally cars and motorcycles have raced on it since. Its bends are fast and open, with a good surface and wide views, and at dawn on a weekday, with the city asleep, it is among the best rides in the region. Weekends bring cyclists in huge numbers, and the police watch the speed limits.

Fuel is the thing to settle first. Castelldefels, about five kilometres away, has several stations and cafés open early, and Gavà and Begues have more. In the hills, there is nothing, so fill up before you start. A coffee and a croissant in a village bar, taken standing at the counter among the workmen, is the proper beginning to a dawn ride. Pack a windproof layer, because it is chilly before the sun rises, and the summit can be breezy even in summer.
t.tibidabo dawn short loop high point@41.2:
Where the Garraf massif meets the sea, limestone cliffs, scrub and a few small coves are all that stand between the Mediterranean and the plain of the Penedès, and these coordinates fall in the heart of it, near Sant Pere de Ribes and Sitges. This is a dry, bright, aromatic country, covered in rosemary, thyme, juniper and a low, spiky palm called palmito, the only palm native to continental Europe, and the air smells sweet and resinous in the sun.

The village of Sant Pere de Ribes has a medieval castle and a pleasant old centre, and Vilanova i la Geltrú, a bigger town on the coast, has a fine railway museum, with steam locomotives from the nineteenth century, and a museum of the writer and politician Víctor Balaguer, who founded a library there. Sitges, a few kilometres away, is the stylish seaside town where artists and filmmakers have always gathered. The three towns together make up one of the best-known stretches of coast in Spain, and in summer it is crowded.

The ride is a short dawn run from the city to the Tibidabo hill, and the high point is a gentle rise on the way, a turn of the road from which you can look back over the sea. Garraf's lanes are narrow and winding, with tight bends and steep gradients, and rock falls and gravel are common. The best time is early on a weekday in spring or autumn, when the air is cool and the roads are empty. In summer, the heat in the afternoon can reach thirty-five degrees, and fires are a real danger, so take care with sparks and cigarettes.

Sitges and Vilanova have stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafés, and Sant Pere de Ribes has the basics. Fill up before you go into the hills, where stations are few. Eat a simple breakfast of toast rubbed with tomato and drizzled with olive oil, called pa amb tomàquet, with a strong coffee, and you will be set for the morning.
Caldes de Montbui is a town in the Vallès, about thirty kilometres north of Barcelona, and it has been famous since Roman times for its hot springs. The water emerges from the ground at about seventy-four degrees, one of the hottest springs in Europe, and it feeds a fountain in the main square where locals fill bottles and cook eggs. The Romans built baths here, and the remains of their pools can still be seen. Today the water supplies a modern spa and a number of old bathing houses, which makes a rewarding stop after a morning's ride.

The countryside around it is a mix of low hills, pine woods and farmland, with the ragged outline of Sant Llorenç del Munt rising to the west. This is a rugged massif of pink conglomerate, whose rocky towers and cliffs are popular with climbers and walkers, and a road climbs from Matadepera to a visitor centre on its flank. Sentmenat has a handsome castle that has been in the same family for centuries, and Castellar del Vallès is a bigger, newer town with a long industrial past.

The ride is the Tibidabo Dawn Short Loop, a quick morning circuit from the city, and the roads in the Vallès are the second half of it. They wind through woods and hills in easy bends, with a good surface, and are fast and enjoyable, but also popular with cyclists and other riders, so watch for blind corners. The morning light slants through the pines, and the smell of resin and warm earth is strong. In spring, the hills are green and the wildflowers bloom, and in autumn the oaks turn golden.

Caldes de Montbui has about seventeen thousand people and a good range of stations, shops and restaurants, and Sentmenat and Castellar del Vallès have more. Fuel is easy to find on the main roads, and a coffee at a village bar is a good way to start the day. If you want to try the thermal water, bring a swimsuit and a towel. Many of the old bathing houses are small and charming, and the warm water feels very good after hours on the bike.
t.vic@41.9,2.3:
Vic is the capital of Osona, a prosperous market town of nearly forty thousand people in a high, fertile basin about seventy kilometres north of Barcelona, and it is the natural stopping point on the way to the Pyrenees. The main square, the Plaça Major, is a huge cobbled space ringed by arcades and old houses, and on Tuesdays and Saturdays it fills with stalls selling vegetables, cheese and cured meats. The Saturday market has been a fixture for centuries, and it is a good place to buy a sausage for the road.

The town has a Roman temple, whose columns stand in the middle of a medieval street, a cathedral with striking twentieth-century murals by the Catalan painter Josep Maria Sert and a museum with one of the finest collections of Romanesque and Gothic art in Europe. Vic is also the capital of Catalan charcuterie, famous for its fuet, its botifarra and its llonganissa, the long, thin, dry sausage that hangs in every shop window. During Holy Week, the town hosts the Mercat del Ram, a big fair that sells palm leaves, crafts and farm produce.

North of Vic, the road climbs towards the Collada de Toses, a pass at about eighteen hundred metres on the N-152, the old road from Barcelona to Puigcerdà. The ride is a long run up through Ripoll and the valley of the Freser, a series of climbing bends through forest and meadow, with the peaks of the Pyrenees ahead. In winter, the pass can be icy, and snow chains are sometimes required, so check the conditions before you set out. The destination, La Molina, is a ski resort, and an overnight stay there is a good break.

Vic has fuel stations, supermarkets and a wide choice of restaurants, so it is the best place to fill up before the mountains, because the stations thin out beyond Ripoll. Gurb and Santa Eugènia de Berga have a few services. Start early in summer, when the heat can be fierce, and carry warm clothing, because the temperature on the pass can be ten degrees colder than in the town. A sausage sandwich from the market, eaten on a bench in the sun, is a fine way to start.
t.sort@42.4,1.1:
Sort sits in the heart of the Catalan Pyrenees, in the Pallars Sobirà valley, where the Noguera Pallaresa river runs fast and green between steep mountains. It is a small town of about two thousand people, with a few streets of old stone houses, a tidy square and a surprising claim to fame: the lottery. A shop here has sold so many winning tickets over the years that Spaniards drive for hours to buy a ticket from it, and the name, which means luck in Catalan, adds to the legend.

The river is the real draw. The Noguera Pallaresa is one of the best white-water rivers in Europe, and Sort is its rafting capital, with outfitters offering trips down the rapids from spring to early autumn. The valley itself is beautiful, with terraced fields, small villages and steep forested slopes, and the high peaks of the Pyrenees rising to the north. Espot, eighteen kilometres to the east, is the gateway to the Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park, a mountain wilderness of granite peaks and glacial lakes.

The road here is the N-260, the long Pyrenean road that follows the mountains from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic side, and the section through Sort is one of its best. It winds up and down through gorges and over passes, with tight bends, blind corners and wonderful views. South-west of Sort, the road climbs to the Port del Cantó, at about 1,700 metres, and then drops through a spectacular, twisty descent towards La Seu d'Urgell. The surface is generally good, though rockfalls and patching are common, and snow can close the pass in winter.

Sort has fuel, a few restaurants and hotels, and it is a good place to stop for the night. The food is mountain fare, with grilled lamb, local cheeses, and a stew of beans and sausage called escudella. A visit to the nearby villages gives a glimpse of the Pyrenees as they were: stone, slate and smoke, with the occasional Romanesque church. Early summer is lovely, with flowers on the meadows, while autumn brings gold to the beech woods.
t.besalu@42.2,2.7:
Besalú arrives suddenly. You come round a bend on the N260 and there it is, a fortified stone bridge with a tower in the middle, seven arches crossing the Fluvià river, and behind it a cluster of tawny roofs and church towers that has hardly changed since the twelfth century. It is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Catalonia and it is small enough, with only a couple of thousand residents, that you can walk across it in ten minutes. The bridge itself is for walkers only, so you leave the bike on the edge of town and cross on foot, which is how you should see it.

The town was once the capital of a county that was independent for several centuries, until its line died out in 1111 and its lands passed to Barcelona. A monastery, a Romanesque church and a very old Jewish quarter survive from those days. The quarter has a mikveh, a ritual bath fed by spring water, which is one of only a handful found in Europe and came to light only in the 1960s. A small museum explains it, and the local guides are good at telling the story without making it feel like a lecture.

For riding, Besalú sits at an interesting junction. To the north the Pyrenees are rising, with the road bending into valleys, and to the south-west is the Garrotxa, a volcanic landscape of forested cones and lava flows around Olot. Roads in that area have good surfaces and many tight bends in beech and oak woodland, particularly in autumn when the leaves are gold. The N260 runs along the foot of the mountains and it is a long, enjoyable road with many changes of rhythm, though in July and August it can be busy with holiday traffic.

Come early to avoid the midday crowds and heat, because by noon the narrow lanes can be crowded with tour groups and the cobbles hold the heat. Cafés around the main square sell coffee and local pastries, and the restaurants serve the hearty food of this region: grilled meats, sausages, mushrooms in autumn and beans. Fuel is available in towns nearby, with Olot, to the west, the nearest large one. Beside the river there are shady spots to rest.
t.ripoll@42.2,2.2:
The Catalan nation, if you believe the story, begins at Ripoll. In the year 879 Count Wilfred the Hairy, called Guifré el Pelós, founded a monastery here at the meeting of two rivers, the Ter and the Freser, and later it became the burial place of the counts of Barcelona. The monastery of Santa Maria still stands in the middle of town, and what draws visitors is its west portal, a huge Romanesque doorway covered in carved stone scenes from the Bible, so detailed that it is often compared to a stone book. Inside the cloister there is a quiet courtyard with two storeys of columns, each with its own carved capital, and you can walk around it in about half an hour.

Ripoll is a real town with about eleven thousand people, not a museum, and that is a good thing at the end of a ride. It has fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of bars. Historically it was known as a centre of ironwork, with forges that used the rivers' power and made weapons and tools, and the traces of that trade are visible in the old working quarter along the water. Neighbouring Campdevànol and Sant Joan de les Abadesses, with its own beautiful Romanesque monastery, are within easy reach and worth a short detour.

The riding around Ripoll is a pleasure because the mountains begin right at the edge of town. To the north the road climbs the Freser valley toward the high Pyrenees and the border, through steep green country with villages perched on the hillsides, and to the east the road through Sant Joan and Camprodon winds up into forest and meadows. The roads here are generally well surfaced, and there are enough hairpins to keep you busy without being exhausting. In winter some of the high stretches can see snow and ice, and in summer the afternoons can bring thunderstorms that blow up over the ridges.

As a finish, it works well. You can park near the monastery, eat dinner in one of the town restaurants, and sleep in a hostal within walking distance. The air is cooler than on the coast, and in the evening the rivers are loud.
t.cap de creus coastal ride scenic road@41:
The coordinates land near Ullastrell and Abrera, in the corridor where the Llobregat river leaves the hills and heads for the sea, and Montserrat's serrated skyline rises over the valley to the north-west. It is a very good view, even if the label says Cap de Creus, which lies far off on the French border.

Martorell, a few kilometres south, has an old stone bridge known as the Pont del Diable, the Devil's Bridge, whose medieval arches and Roman-looking triumphal arch have given rise to the usual legends about the devil building it in a night. The bridge sat on the Via Augusta, the Roman road that ran from the Pyrenees to southern Spain, and the local story tells you how much travel passed through here. Today the valley carries a large car factory, motorways and railway lines, so industrial and rural scenes sit beside each other.

For riders, the road network here is a tangle of motorways and fast regional roads, with quieter lanes that climb into the low hills of the Penedès to the south or toward Montserrat to the north. Abrera is the closest sizeable town, with around eleven thousand people, so fuel and coffee are easy. Surfaces vary, with heavy truck wear on the main routes, and the light can be harsh in summer, when the stone seems to bleach and the valley fills with a haze.

What makes the place worth noting is the view toward Montserrat. At dawn, with the first sun on the pinnacles, the mountain looks like a row of organ pipes or a broken saw, depending on your mood. It is easy to see why monks chose it for a monastery and why Catalans treat it as a symbol of their country. Stopping to look is no hardship.

Lay out your day with that in mind. If you want to ride up, do it early, before the tour buses arrive, and take the cooler hours for the climb. Later in the afternoon the valley is hot and traffic builds, so it is best to be somewhere else.
t.cap de creus coastal ride photo pull off:
The point sits near Castellar del Vallès, in the Vallès Occidental, just north of Terrassa and Sabadell, on the edge of the Sant Llorenç del Munt i l'Obac natural park. Cap de Creus, which the label names, is far off on the French border; here the landscape is a different sort of drama, rust-red conglomerate cliffs, pine forest and the flat farmland of the Vallès spread out below.

The park is easy to recognise because of La Mola, a flat-topped massif crowned by a Romanesque monastery that has stood on the summit for nearly a thousand years. The rocks around it are an extraordinary red, layered and eroded into rounded pillars and gullies, a little like a smaller cousin of Montserrat. If you enjoy walking, the paths are good, and the monastery has a restaurant that is a popular goal for Sunday lunch.

Castellar del Vallès has about twenty-three thousand people, which means fuel, bakeries and bars are all near at hand. It is a good place to break a ride in the morning or afternoon, and the town is quieter and more local than the nearby cities. The roads that climb into the hills are narrow and twisty, with patchy surface in places and a lot of cyclists at weekends, so be generous with space.

Traffic on the approach roads can be heavy at rush hour, since this is a commuter belt for Barcelona, and on holiday weekends the park's car parks fill early.
