If you want the hills to yourself, ride on a weekday or start at dawn. In winter the air is cold and clear, and you can see the Pyrenees on good days; in summer it gets hot, and fire restrictions can close some of the tracks.

It is a place that rewards a small amount of curiosity. Pull over, look at the rocks and think about the monks who carried stone up there. A short walk, a cold drink and the smell of warm pine make a good break from the road.
t.montserrat mountain roads@41.6,2.2:
Montmeló is a name that means something to anyone who follows motorsport. The Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya sits right beside the town, hosting Formula 1 testing and the Catalan MotoGP round, and on race weekends the whole district fills with fans, noise and the smell of hot rubber. For a rider, filling up here feels vaguely like visiting a cathedral.

The town itself is small, with fewer than nine thousand people, and lies in the Vallès Oriental, about twenty kilometres north-east of Barcelona. The Besòs river valley runs close by, flanked by industrial estates and the motorway to Girona. The hills of the Serralada de Marina are to the south-east, and the pre-Pyrenean ranges rise in the distance on the north. It is a busy, working landscape, with modern roads and little charm, but it is a good place to organise yourself.

Fuel is readily available, with stations along the main road and at the motorway junction. The circuit has its own roads and car parks, and on non-event days you can often see the grandstands from the road. If you like, ride past and imagine the sound of a pack of bikes at full throttle. Cafes in the town serve a decent coffee and a pastry, and the little bakeries do a fine ensaïmada, a spiral pastry that is a Catalan and Balearic favourite.

The riding north of here is where the day gets interesting. The roads into the Montseny and the Vallès hills offer long curves and forest, but they start only after you have cleared the ring of industry and traffic. Weekday mornings are slow, and at weekends there is a steady stream of other riders. Be aware of heavy trucks on the main road, and keep an eye out for the occasional speed camera.

It is a place to take a deep breath, check the map and enjoy the fact that you are about to leave the city. Come back in the evening and the same road can feel like a victory lap.
t.montserrat mountain roads scenic road@41:
The coordinates fall on Vilassar de Mar, about twenty-five kilometres north-east of Barcelona on the Maresme coast, and they are on or very near the town's old centre. Behind it rises the Serralada de Marina, a low wooded range that separates the coastal strip from the inland Vallès, and the roads across it are some of the best riding on this side of Barcelona.

The town has about nineteen thousand people and a seafaring past, with houses built by merchants who made money in the Americas. The railway line that runs along the beach dates from the middle of the nineteenth century, and the old station is still in use. Vilassar is known for its carnations and its cut flowers, and the fields on the edge of town are a reminder of the horticulture that has long been part of the Maresme.

Heading inland, the road climbs from the coast through pine forest with wide, steady bends and views back over the sea. The surface is mostly good, but sections have been patched, and leaf litter collects on the shaded corners. Traffic is light on weekdays and heavier on Sundays, when cyclists and families head to the hills. The air smells of resin and, on cool mornings, of damp earth.

Fuel is no trouble, with stations in town and along the coast road. There are bakeries opening early, and a coffee and a croissant make a good beginning. If you need a bigger centre, Mataró is not far to the north-east, and has everything from motorcycle shops to hospitals.

The best moment is a clear morning in spring or autumn, when the air is cool, the sea is sharp blue and the hills are quiet. You can see the Montseny massif on the horizon on a good day, snow on its top in winter. Afterward, return to the coast, find a seat on the front and watch the fishing boats come in. The scenic road here earns its name, and it does so without fuss.
t.montserrat mountain roads@41.2,1.8:
Sitges is a place that likes being looked at. Perched on the Garraf coast about forty kilometres south-west of Barcelona, it has a long line of golden beaches, a baroque church standing on a promontory, and a seafront promenade lined with palms. With nearly twenty-eight thousand residents, it has the facilities of a proper town, which makes it a good lunch stop for riders.

The town has been a magnet for artists since the late nineteenth century, when the painter Santiago Rusiñol bought a house here, now a museum, and made Sitges a centre of Catalan modernism. In modern times, it has become known for its carnival, its film festival devoted to fantasy and horror, and a lively and open atmosphere that has long made it popular with visitors. The sweet Malvasia wine of Sitges is a local speciality that you will find on many menus.

The road in from the north is the C-32 and the older C-31, which cut through the Garraf hills in a series of tunnels and cliffside curves. The corners are open and the surface is usually good, but the traffic is dense on weekends, particularly in summer. Early starts are rewarded with quiet roads and a clear sea. Sea breezes can be strong in the afternoon, and you will feel them on exposed sections.

For fuel, there are stations on the main road at the edge of town. For lunch, the old centre has narrow streets with places serving rice dishes, grilled fish and tapas, often with a table outside. The best seat is one in the shade with a view of the sea. A simple plate of grilled sardines and a glass of cold white wine is hard to beat.

In summer, parking in the centre is a challenge, so aim for the edges and walk in. In winter, the town is quieter and the light is lovely. It is a place for a long, slow lunch, and a reminder that a ride is not always about the corners.
t.montserrat mountain road@41.6,1.8:
Collbató sits at the foot of Montserrat's southern flank, and the road from here to the monastery is one of the classic mountain rides of Catalonia. The village is small, with about three thousand people, and old enough that its streets feel more like a Mediterranean hill town than a suburb. Above it, the rock rises in a wall of towers and fingers, some of them with names that locals use to point them out.

The mountain is composed of conglomerate, a rock made of pebbles cemented together over millions of years, which weathers into rounded shapes that can look like faces or animals. Walkers and climbers know the area well, and Collbató has caves with stalactites that were known since medieval times. In the winter, mist often fills the valley, leaving the summits floating above the cloud.

The road is twisty, with hairpins and good views, and it is well surfaced because of the heavy tourist traffic. At the weekend it can feel crowded, and the best time to ride is on a weekday or early in the morning. The air is cool, the light is clear, and the road belongs to those who start early. Be wary of cyclists and tour buses on the narrower stretches, and take care on the hairpins, where gravel can collect.

Fuel is in the valley, not on the mountain. Esparreguera, the nearest large town, has more than twenty thousand people and plenty of stations, and Collbató has a few services. If you need food, the bakeries and bars in the village serve strong coffee and pastries, and the restaurants a bit further up the road offer traditional Catalan cooking, with plenty of grilled meat and vegetables. Local honey and cheese are sold near the monastery.

As the road climbs, the air changes, and the sounds of the valley fall away. The silence near the top is striking, broken only by bells and the hum of a distant engine. It is an ideal start for a day of riding, and one of the most memorable.
t.siurana cliff village@41.3,0.9:
Siurana is the kind of place that makes you slow down on the approach. The village sits on top of a sheer cliff in the Priorat, above a reservoir, with a few stone houses and a Romanesque church crowded on a narrow rock. From the road, you see it from far off, a little crown of buildings above an abyss.

It has a legend, as such places do. The last Moorish stronghold in Catalonia, it fell to the Christians in 1153, and the story goes that the Moorish queen, Abdelazia, rode her horse off the cliff rather than surrender, leaving a hoofprint in the rock. Whether or not that happened, the cliff is real, and the view over the valley is huge. Siurana is also one of the best-known sport climbing destinations in the world, with pale limestone walls that draw climbers from many countries.

The road is the draw for riders. The approach from Cornudella climbs in a series of bends with wide views of the Montsant range, and the surface is narrow but decent. It is very quiet on weekdays, and the village has a few cafes that serve coffee and simple food. Parking is limited, and the final stretch is tight, so take care when meeting cars.

Alforja and Riudoms, the nearest towns, have stations, and you should fill before you climb. The terrain is dry, with rosemary, thyme and wild olive on the slopes, and in summer the heat can be fierce. Carry water, and go early or late for the best light.

In autumn, the vines in the valley turn red and gold, and the air smells of woodsmoke and ripe fruit. In spring, the almond trees flower. It is a fine place to sit with a coffee and watch the clouds move across the hills.
t.priorat@41.1,0.8:
Falset is the capital of the Priorat, a wine country that Catalans talk about with a certain hush. The town is small, under three thousand people, and sits in a hollow between the Montsant ridge and the stony hills toward the coast, with a castle on a rise above the old centre and a maze of narrow lanes below. For a food stop it is perfect: modest, local and quite serious about what it puts on the table.

What makes the Priorat special is the soil. The vines here grow in llicorella, a dark, flaky slate that holds heat and forces roots deep, and the wines that come from it, based on Garnacha and Carinyena, are dense, mineral and expensive enough to have put the region on the world map in the 1990s. Wine has been made here since Carthusian monks founded the priory of Scala Dei in the twelfth century, which is where the name Priorat comes from. Terraces climb the hillsides, and in autumn they blaze red and gold.

For a rider, the roads around Falset are narrow, quiet and rewarding. Tight bends climb through vineyards and olive groves, with long views across the valley and few cars. The surface can be rough where it has not been renewed, and tractors appear around corners, especially during harvest in September. It is not a place for speed, but for steady, attentive riding.

Food in Falset is the reason to stop. Look for places that serve grilled lamb, rabbit with snails, calçots in season, and plates of cured meats and local cheese. Olive oil here is first-rate, and the bread comes with it. If you plan to drink wine, remember you are on a bike; ask for a small glass and take the rest home, as plenty of shops will sell you a bottle. Fuel is available in the town, and Mont-roig del Camp, about thirteen kilometres away, is a larger place with a connection to the painter Joan Miró, who spent summers at the family farm there.

Aim for mid-afternoon in spring or autumn, when the sun is mild. Summer can be fiercely hot, and the wine terraces offer little shade.
t.ripoll mountain@42.2,2.2:
Ripoll is where Catalonia, in a sense, began. In 879 Guifré el Pelós, Wilfred the Hairy, the count credited with founding the Catalan dynasty, established the monastery of Santa Maria de Ripoll, and he is buried there. The carved Romanesque doorway, with its crowded scenes from the Bible and the lives of kings, is among the finest in Spain. Even if you only have time for a coffee, walk over and look at it.

The town lies in a valley where the Ter and Freser rivers meet, ringed by the foothills of the Pyrenees, with about eleven thousand people. It was once known for its forges and, later, for making firearms and ironwork, and a few old factories still stand along the rivers. Today it is a pleasant place with a market, arcaded streets and a good selection of bakeries, bars and small shops.

For a rider, Ripoll is an important gateway. The road north, the N-152, climbs steadily through the valley of the Freser toward the Collada de Toses and on to Puigcerdà, while the road east leads to Olot and the volcanic country of La Garrotxa. Fuel is easy, with stations at the edge of town, and it makes sense to fill up here before the mountains. The temperature drops as you climb, so a spare layer is worth carrying.

There is more to eat here than most travellers expect. Catalan mountain cooking runs to stews, grilled sausages, wild mushrooms in autumn and trinxat, a fried mixture of potatoes and cabbage. Cheese from nearby farms is excellent, and the local bakeries sell a variety of pastries. Lunch with a view of the square, under an arcade, is a good way to spend an hour.

In winter, snow can reach the town, and the roads above can be icy. In summer, the valley is warm and the evenings pleasant. Ripoll is a quiet place, but it carries a great weight of history, and you can sense it in the stone.
t.collada de toses@42.3,2.0:
The Collada de Toses is a Pyrenean pass at about 1,800 metres, on the road between Ripoll and Puigcerdà, and it is one of those places where you feel the landscape change as you cross it. On the south side, the valley of the Freser is green and wooded. On the north, the high basin of the Cerdanya opens out, broad and bright, with snow-covered peaks to the horizon in winter and spring.

The road is old, and it has been a route between the Catalan lowlands and the Cerdanya for centuries. The village of Toses lies just below the summit, a cluster of stone houses with a Romanesque church, and used to be a stopping place for muleteers and merchants. Nowadays the road mostly carries holiday traffic to the ski resorts of La Molina and Masella, with trucks using the tunnel under the Cadí for through traffic. That makes the pass itself comparatively quiet, which is a bonus.

For a rider, the Collada de Toses offers a sequence of bends and hairpins that climb through beech and pine, then open up to alpine meadow near the top. The surface is generally good, but in spring there can be gravel and potholes after the winter frost. In the cold months, ice and snow are real concerns, and the pass may need chains or be closed briefly after heavy snowfall. Check conditions before you go.

Ripoll, on the south side, is the main town for supplies, and Puigcerdà, about fourteen kilometres on the other side, is larger and has everything. A small bar or restaurant near the top sometimes serves coffee, but hours vary, so do not count on it.

The air is thin and clean, and in summer the meadows are full of wildflowers and cattle. Late afternoon light on the peaks is wonderful, and the view over the Cerdanya is worth a stop at any time of year. Pull over, let the engine cool and listen to the cowbells.
t.jinshan coast@25.2,121.6:
Jinshan sits on the north coast of Taiwan, a short ride from Taipei, and it has the look and feel of a place with several identities. It is a hot-spring town, with sulphur water that bubbles up from the volcanic hills of Yangmingshan behind it. It is a beach town, with a long strip of dark sand that fills with swimmers in summer. And it is a food town, where the local specialities are sweet potatoes, duck, and the street snacks sold along the old street, from fried dough to taro balls.

The coast itself is a mixture of rock and sand. To the east, the shoreline is cut by headlands and bays, with rock platforms washed by the sea, and to the west it is a long, gentle curve of beach, with the green hills rising directly behind. The Yangmingshan massif, a group of dormant volcanoes, is a national park above the town, with steaming vents, sulphur deposits and, in winter, a regular veil of mist. The weather on the north coast is changeable: in winter, the northeast monsoon brings grey skies, cold wind and drizzle, while in summer it is hot and humid, with typhoons from July to October.

The coastal road, Provincial Highway 2, is a pleasure to ride when the weather is good. It follows the shore with curves and short climbs, passing fishing harbours, rocky capes and small temples, and the sea is visible for much of the way. Traffic is a hazard, particularly at weekends when Taipei empties onto the coast, and the roads are crowded with scooters, buses and tour groups. The surface is generally good, but salt air and rain mean damp patches and loose grit, so be careful on the bends. In the early morning, the road is quiet and the light is lovely.

The swimming beaches have lifeguards in summer, and the sea can have strong currents, so respect the flags. Fuel and food are easy, with stations and shops in the town and along the coast, and Keelung, fourteen kilometres to the east, is a large port city with everything you could want. Autumn, from October to December, is the best season, with clear skies and a warm sea, though winter weekdays have a quiet charm of their own.
t.keelung food@25.1,121.7:
Keelung is a port that rains. It is the northernmost big city in Taiwan, a harbour town squeezed between steep green hills and a dark sea, and the damp climate is so reliable that the local joke is about carrying an umbrella as a matter of course. The harbour is busy, with container ships, ferries and fishing boats, and the old streets rise in steps up the hillsides, lined with shophouses, temples and the odd Japanese-era building.

It is also, to a Taiwanese, a place to eat. The night market that runs along the streets beside Dianji Temple, known as Miaokou, is one of the best-known in the country, with its stalls arranged in long, brightly lit rows, selling fried seafood, fish soups, noodles, sweet and savoury pastries, and a famous cold dessert of shaved ice. The speciality of the port is fresh fish and shellfish, cooked simply, often in a broth or fried with garlic, and you queue with everyone else at the stall that has the longest line. Stand at a counter with a bowl in your hand, as the locals do, and you have eaten as well as in any restaurant.

Riding in and out of Keelung is a lesson in Taiwanese traffic. The roads are crowded with scooters, which move in swarms and filter through every gap, and the city is a maze of one-way streets, tunnels and flyovers. Take it easy, keep your distance and watch for scooters coming from the side. Parking for motorcycles is plentiful, but you may need to find a marked space. Wet roads are slippery, especially painted lines and manhole covers, and the rain falls often, so a waterproof layer is not optional.

Above the city, the hills climb toward Jiufen, an old gold-mining town with narrow stairways and tea houses overlooking the sea, which is about eleven kilometres away along a winding mountain road. It is lovely and extremely crowded at weekends. Fuel is available everywhere in Keelung, and the roads to the north coast and to Taipei are straightforward. The driest months are October and November, though no month is reliably dry.
t.montpellier@43.6,3.9:
Montpellier is a young city in an old shell. More than a quarter of its population is made up of students, and its university, whose medical faculty dates back to the thirteenth century, is among the oldest in Europe. The centre is the Place de la Comédie, a huge oval square paved in stone, with the opera house at one end and the fountain of the Three Graces in the middle, and from there the old town of tight, shaded lanes spreads out, with elegant stone houses and hidden courtyards.

A short walk to the west brings you to the Promenade du Peyrou, a raised terrace laid out in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries with a triumphal arch and an equestrian statue of Louis XIV. At the far end you can see the long arches of the Saint-Clément aqueduct, built in the eighteenth century to bring water to the city. In the evening, locals gather here to watch the sunset.

For riders, Montpellier is a good base. To the north the garrigue, the scrubland of holm oak, thyme and rosemary, rises into the hills toward the Pic Saint-Loup and the Cévennes, with roads that wind through vineyards and small villages. To the south and east lie the beaches, the lagoons with flamingos and the Camargue marshes. In summer the heat is intense, and the wind, the tramontane, can be strong, so start early. Spring and autumn offer clear light and quiet roads.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of a quarter of a million. Parking a motorbike is generally easy, with many spaces reserved for two wheels. In the evenings, the bars and restaurants around the old town fill up, and the local specialities include seafood from the Thau lagoon, Sète-style fish stews and wines from the Languedoc, such as the red of Pic Saint-Loup. The tram lines, with their bright designs, are easy to follow but need respect on wet days.
t.roc de saint cirq@44.9,1.0:
The Vézère is the river of prehistory, and the valley around Les Eyzies is so crowded with caves, shelters and decorated walls that archaeologists have been working here since the nineteenth century. The limestone cliffs form a long, golden wall above the water, full of overhangs where people lived and painted for tens of thousands of years, and the whole group of sites is on the UNESCO list. The Roc de Saint-Cirq is one of those places, a cliff and shelter close to the small village of Saint-Cirq, set on a bend of the river.

The roads in this part of the Périgord Noir, the black Périgord named for its dark oak forests, are a delight. They follow the Vézère through meadows and past walnut groves, with the cliffs on one side and the river on the other, and every few kilometres there is a village of honey-coloured stone, a château or a troglodyte house tucked beneath a rock. Corners are gentle, surfaces generally good, and the traffic light except in July and August, when the tourist coaches arrive.

Le Bugue, about three kilometres away, is a small town with about three thousand people, and it has fuel, supermarkets and several restaurants. The region is famous for its food: duck and goose, confit and foie gras, walnuts, strawberries and truffles in winter. A plate of confit with sautéed potatoes is the standard order. Prices in the busy villages can be high, so look for the market days, when local producers sell straight from the table.

Come in spring or autumn if you can. The valley is green and soft in May, and in October the oaks turn rust and the mist lies on the river in the morning. Summer evenings are lovely, and the cliffs hold the warmth long after the sun has gone. Be aware that the shelters and caves are protected, with timed entry, so check opening times in advance, and be ready for cool air inside, even on a hot day.
t.le grand roc@44.9,1.0:
Le Grand Roc is a cliff above the Vézère, near Les Eyzies, with a cave that is famous not for paintings but for rock formations. Inside are stalactites, stalagmites and delicate crystal growths called eccentrics, which twist in every direction as if they had ignored gravity. Visitors walk through the cave along a lit path, and on the way out there is a terrace cut into the cliff, with a view over the valley, the river and the roofs of Les Eyzies. It is one of the best places to understand the geography of the valley.

Les Eyzies, a short way along, calls itself the capital of prehistory, and with good reason. The national museum of prehistory sits in the cliff above the village, and nearby, in 1868, workers found the remains of several people in a rock shelter, who became known as Cro-Magnon man, the first anatomically modern humans to be recognised in Europe. A statue of a Neanderthal man, a little too happy, stands at the side of the road.

The riding in the area is among the loveliest in south-west France. The D706 follows the Vézère in a gentle line, with the cliffs on one side and the river on the other, and the roads that climb out of the valley through oak and chestnut woods give views across the plateau. Surfaces are good, and corners are mostly gentle, so it is a relaxed ride. Be careful with tractors, cyclists and campervans in summer, and with the shade of the cliffs, where damp patches stay on the tarmac after rain.

Le Bugue, a few kilometres downstream, has fuel and shops, and Les Eyzies has bars, restaurants and a bakery. Try the walnut cake and the local strawberries in June, and in autumn, the chestnuts and the mushrooms. The caves are cool, around thirteen degrees, so a light jacket is useful even on a summer day. Book tickets in advance in summer, because the number of visitors is limited to protect the formations.
t.perpignan@42.7,2.9:
Perpignan feels more Catalan than French on a good day, and most locals would not argue. The city was the mainland capital of the Kingdom of Majorca in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and the Palais des Rois de Majorque still sits on its hill, a fortress-palace of pink brick with a double-storey courtyard. In the old centre the Castillet, a squat brick gate with crenellated towers, guards the entrance to the lanes, and street signs often come in two languages. In 1963 Salvador Dalí declared the railway station to be the centre of the universe, and the city has never quite let go of the joke.

For a rider it is a very good launch pad. To the south-west the Pyrenees begin, with Mount Canigou, a sacred peak for Catalans, standing at nearly 2,800 metres above the plain. To the north the Corbières hills roll off into dry limestone country, with the ruined Cathar castles of Peyrepertuse and Quéribus perched on crags, which is where the afternoon ride heads. These roads climb through garrigue and vineyard, with sudden drops, hairpins and long straight runs, and on a clear day you can see the sea. The wind in these parts, the tramontane, can blow for days and has a way of pushing bikes off the line, so brace yourself on exposed ridges.

The plain around the city is an orchard, and in early summer the stalls sell apricots, peaches and cherries picked that morning. Further along the coast, Collioure and Banyuls produce sweet red wine, and anchovies are a point of pride. A simple lunch is a plate of Catalan sausage with white beans, finished with a crema catalana. Perpignan itself, with about a hundred and ten thousand people, has plenty of fuel and bike parking, and the ring roads are straightforward.

Go early in summer. By afternoon the heat is considerable, and the castle walls hold it, so water and a light jacket are the right kit, and leave time to be on the ridge when the light turns amber.
t.abri du poisson@44.9,1.0:
There is a fish in the cliff. It is about a metre long, carved into the ceiling of a small rock shelter in the Gorge d'Enfer, a short, steep-sided valley that opens onto the Vézère near Les Eyzies, and it has been there for roughly twenty-five thousand years. The carver made use of the natural shape of the rock, shaping the outline of a salmon in relief, with the head, an open mouth with its hooked jaw, and the gills. The fish was found in the early twentieth century, and it remains one of the oldest known sculptures of its kind in Europe.

Look at the setting, and you can see why the salmon matters. The river below still runs cold and clean, and the cliff walls give shelter from the wind and rain. For Stone Age people, a seasonal run of fish was a gift, and the fish on the ceiling is a kind of calendar. The shelter is protected, and a barrier keeps visitors at a distance, so the carving is seen from below with some guidance. Check visiting times before you set out, and expect a short walk.

The gorge is cool and shaded, with moss on the rock, and smells of wet stone and walnut leaf. The roads around Les Eyzies are narrow and winding, and the stretch along the river to Le Bugue is a pleasure at a gentle pace. In July and August it is busy, with campervans and coaches, and the early morning is better. In spring, the cliffs are green with box and ivy, and in autumn the walnut orchards turn yellow.

Le Bugue, with about three thousand people, has fuel and shops, and Les Eyzies has restaurants and a bakery. The ride that starts here heads west toward Bordeaux, following the Dordogne valley through Bergerac and the vineyards of Saint-Émilion, so the day moves from ancient stone to some of the most famous wine country in the world. Take your time, and pack a wind layer for the slower miles.
t.priorat vineyard@41.3,2.6:
Look at the coordinates for this one and you find open water, a little way off the Maresme coast northeast of Barcelona, so the nearest real places are the beach towns of Vilassar de Mar, Premià de Mar and Cabrera de Mar. They are old fishing and seafaring villages strung along the railway line, with tall townhouses, a stony beach and market gardens in the hills behind, and this is where the ride begins and ends. Sailors from here took part in the Atlantic trade in past centuries, and some of the houses were built with money brought home from Cuba.

Priorat is another world, well over a hundred kilometres to the southwest, a small mountain region of steep terraced vineyards, slate slopes and tiny villages. The wine has become famous, with deep, mineral reds made from old Garnacha and Carignan vines grown in a soil of dark, flaky slate called llicorella, and the area has the highest classification in Spanish wine. The vines are planted on slopes so steep that they are worked by hand, and yields are tiny, which is why the bottles are expensive. Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Scala Dei here in the twelfth century, and the name of the region comes from the priory.

The road in Priorat is a pleasure for riders. It winds in tight bends between the villages, with views of terraces and the rocky ridge of Montsant, and it climbs to Siurana, a village on a cliff top with a medieval castle ruin and a reservoir below. Traffic is light. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and farm vehicles and cyclists are common in harvest time. Autumn, in September and October, when the vines turn red and gold, is the most beautiful season, while summer is hot and dry.

Back on the coast, fuel and food are easy, with stations at Vilassar and Premià and plenty of cafes and fish restaurants by the beach. In Priorat, Falset is the main town, with stations and shops, and the villages beyond are small, so fill the tank there before climbing.

Pack a light layer for the mountains, where it is cooler, and take care with tasting, as most cellars welcome visitors but riding does not mix with wine.
t.talayotic menorca@40.0,3.9:
Menorca's prehistory is stranger and more abundant than its tourist image suggests. From around 1000 BC, the island's people built huge monuments of unmortared stone, and the big circular towers called talaiots, which probably served as lookout posts, houses or meeting places, dot the island by the hundred. The culture that built them is called Talayotic, and the sites were listed by UNESCO in 2023 as a group of outstanding prehistoric settlements and sanctuaries. This stretch of land, west of Ciutadella, is not far from some of the best examples, among them the Naveta d'es Tudons, one of the oldest roofed buildings in Europe.

The naveta is a burial chamber shaped like an upturned boat, built of massive limestone blocks without any binding material, and the remains of more than a hundred people were found inside. It stands in a field of low walls and olive trees, and from a distance it looks like an overturned ship dragged from the sea. The name naveta simply means little ship. A short drive away other sites show the T-shaped monoliths, called taulas, that stood at the centre of Talayotic sanctuaries and whose purpose is still debated. They may have been altars, or supports for a roof.

Riding here is peaceful and flat. The roads across western Menorca are narrow, bordered by stone walls and fields, with gentle curves and few vehicles outside the summer months. The island is small, so every road seems to end at the sea, and the light on the stone is warm and bright. The wind can blow hard from the north, called the Tramuntana, and bring salt and a chill even in spring. Avoid riding on gravel tracks without enough grip, since many access roads to the sites are unpaved.

Ciutadella, with nearly thirty thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and a handsome harbour of white houses and fish restaurants. Ferreries and Mercadal are smaller, but have stations too. Ciutadella was the capital of the island until 1722, and every June it holds a festival of horses, the Sant Joan, in which riders in black and white costumes rear their mounts in the narrow streets as crowds press in. The smell of the area is of thyme, dry stone and sea air, and the cicadas sing all afternoon.
t.c1 plains of ciutadella@40.0,3.9:
West Menorca is a low, open plateau of limestone, and the plains around Ciutadella are the island at its most pastoral. The land is divided into small fields by dry-stone walls, thousands of kilometres of them, built over centuries by hand without mortar, and the walls give the whole landscape a stitched, patchwork look. Cows graze in the meadows, and farmhouses called llocs, painted white, sit among clusters of pines and wild olive trees. The soil is red in places, grey in others, and the sea shows at the end of almost every lane.

The island's cows are the basis of the local cheese, and Menorcan butter and ice cream are good enough that it is worth stopping for. The western plains also have the fierce wind that shapes everything: the trees along the coast grow bent and flat, tilted away from the Tramuntana, and in winter the gusts can be strong enough to move a loaded motorcycle. This is a place where you check the forecast before you ride, and it pays to keep a firm grip in exposed spots. In summer, the wind is a friend, cooling the afternoon.

The roads are quiet, narrow and well surfaced, and they are best for slow, undemanding riding. A network of small lanes links farms and hamlets, with lots of junctions and few signs, so a map or a navigation app is handy. The Camí de Cavalls, the old horse path that circles the island, is for walkers and horses, not motorbikes, but it crosses the lanes in many places, and you may see hikers. Take care at blind bends in the walls, where tractors may be coming the other way.

Ciutadella is about six kilometres away and has everything you need, while Ferreries and Mercadal lie to the east along the main road. Fuel is available in all three, but stations are sparse between them. In the evening the sun sinks behind the western horizon, the walls throw long shadows, and the smell of grass and sea drifts across the fields. It is a landscape of repetition, in the best possible sense, and one in which time seems to slow without any fuss.
t.canal du midi@43.6,1.4:
The Canal du Midi has a reputation for being slow, and the stretch within Toulouse is no exception. The canal was dug in the seventeenth century by Pierre-Paul Riquet, a tax collector turned engineer, who spent most of his fortune and the last years of his life on a waterway that joined the Atlantic to the Mediterranean through the pass at Naurouze. He died in 1680, a few months before the water finally flowed all the way through. Today the canal is a UNESCO World Heritage site, its banks lined with plane trees whose branches meet overhead.

You meet it here in a city of more than 430,000 people, near the railway station and the canal's basins, where towpaths host joggers and cyclists and old barges are moored under the trees. Fuel is close by, in any direction, and the narrow streets around the canal are full of small cafés. The quiet stands out against the busy streets: you can walk down the stone steps to the water and be alone with ducks within a minute.

For a rider, this is more start than destination. From here the roads lead southeast along the canal toward the Lauragais hills, a country of rolling wheat fields and sunflowers, where the Black Mountain rises in the distance and the corners start to flow. The towpath itself is not for motorcycles, and signs make that plain, but the parallel roads often run within sight of the water and allow glimpses of locks, bridges and old keepers' houses.

Toulouse is hot in summer, with afternoon temperatures that make helmets uncomfortable, and in the cooler months fog and drizzle can come off the Garonne. Spring and autumn are best. The pink brick of the city glows warm in the evening, and the canal reflects it. After a day on the road, an evening here, with a table by the water and a glass of local red, is a very French way to finish.
t.toulouse@43.6,1.4:
Toulouse has two characters, and they sit on the same streets. One is the pink city, built from handmade brick that glows rose and orange in evening light, with a square, a basilica and a long river of old merchants' houses. The other is the aerospace city, home to Airbus and a museum of flight, whose engineers have shaped the modern aviation of Europe. The two live side by side, and they give the city a pleasing mix of old stone and ambitious young people.

The Basilica of Saint-Sernin is the monument to see. Built in the eleventh and twelfth centuries on the grave of the city's first bishop, it is the largest surviving Romanesque church in Europe, with a tall tower of tiered arches and a vast interior of stone. Nearby, the Capitole, the city hall, stands on its great square with a long, pink façade, and the Garonne flows beneath the old bridge. The city's food is no less impressive: cassoulet, a stew of beans and duck or sausage, is the local passion, and violets, candied and scented, are the odd local sweet.

As a start and finish for a ride, Toulouse is a large and easy place. With over 430,000 people, it has fuel at every corner, and the ring road gives quick access to the countryside. From here you can head east into the Lauragais, a gentle farming region, or south toward the Pyrenees, whose white summits are visible from the city on a clear day. The traffic is heavy at rush hour, and the narrow streets in the centre are best left to scooters and bicycles. The tram and metro are good, and many riders park outside and take them in.

Toulouse can be fierce in July and August, with temperatures well above thirty degrees, and a spring or autumn visit is far more comfortable. When the evening comes and the bricks glow, find a café on a square and watch the city light up.
t.portbou@42.4,3.2:
Portbou is a border town in the most literal sense. It is wedged into a steep, rocky cove at the very end of the Costa Brava, a few hundred metres from France, with houses stacked up the hillside and a railway station so oversized that it looks like a cathedral beached by mistake. The station once handled all the rail traffic between Spain and France, where the track gauge changed, and passengers and goods were transferred between trains. Today the town has just fourteen hundred people and feels half-asleep, hushed by the wind and the sea.

The Tramontana, the cold north wind that whips down from the Pyrenees, can blow here with startling force, scouring the sky to a hard blue and making a loaded bike twitch on the exposed road. It is part of the character of the coast. Sheltered coves and stone-walled terraces of old vines run up the slope, and the sea below is a deep clear green. Across the border, Cerbère in France is only a few minutes away, and the two places share a long and sometimes dramatic history of smugglers and refugees.

Portbou has a haunting place in twentieth-century history. In September 1940, the German philosopher and critic Walter Benjamin, fleeing the Nazis and hoping to cross Spain to Portugal, died here, apparently by suicide, after being told he would be turned back. A memorial by the Israeli sculptor Dani Karavan, called Passages, descends in a steel tunnel through the cemetery cliff to a glass pane facing the sea, and it is a quietly moving place to stand for ten minutes. In 1939, thousands of Spanish Republican refugees streamed through the pass toward exile.

From here, the N-260 heads west along the southern foot of the Pyrenees, a long and unusually varied road that threads through the Empordà plain, the volcanic landscape of Garrotxa, the medieval town of Besalú, and over a number of passes in the Catalan Pyrenees. The first part is steep and winding, with views of the sea fading behind. Surfaces are generally good, but traffic and tight bends demand attention.

For fuel, Portbou is thin, so plan to fill up in Llançà or Figueres, and carry some cash. There are small bars and restaurants by the sea, where grilled fish, anchovies from nearby L'Escala and a glass of cold white wine are the standard order. Early morning has the best light on the water.
t.montserrat@41.6,2.2:
Montmeló is a small town of about nine thousand north of Barcelona, and for anyone who loves motorcycles it has a particular fame. The Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya lies right beside it, a purpose-built track that opened in 1991 and has hosted both the Formula One Spanish Grand Prix and the MotoGP Catalan round, and a lot of testing. On a race weekend the whole town fills with fans, flags and the whine of engines, and on quiet days you can sometimes hear a test bike through the trees. It is an unlikely place for an agricultural village to end up.

The surrounding country is the Vallès Oriental, a plain with low hills between the Serralada Litoral and the Montseny massif, dotted with towns like Mollet del Vallès and Parets. Montmeló itself has an older face, with a Roman villa site nearby and a few farmhouses, called masies, that survived the housing. A stream runs along the edge of town, and in spring the poppies and wild fennel grow along the verges.

For riding, the area is built around motorways and ring roads. The C-33 and the AP-7 carry heavy traffic between Barcelona and Girona, and the junctions are fast and complicated. The reward lies north and east, where roads lead up into the Montseny and the Serralada de Marina. Weekends bring many motorcyclists, and the roads near the circuit fill with riders on sport bikes, so ride with awareness. Police patrol the area, and speed cameras are common. In summer, the heat on the plain is intense, and the best time is early in the morning.

Fuel is easy, with several stations between Montmeló and Mollet, and supermarkets and bakeries in each town. The circuit has a shop and cafe open on event days, and there are bars in the village centre that serve coffee and bocadillos. If you have time, consider visiting the circuit museum or a track day, when you can ride the circuit itself. Parking is easy in the village except on race weekends, when streets close.
t.cardona castle sight@41.9,1.7:
Cardona castle looks down on a town built on salt. The fortress sits on a ridge above the Cardener river, a hilltop of towers and walls that dates back to the ninth century, and it served as the seat of the Dukes of Cardona, one of the most powerful noble families in medieval Catalonia. Today much of the castle has become a Parador hotel, and its Romanesque church of Sant Vicenç, consecrated in the eleventh century, is a gem of early Catalan architecture. The town below has about five thousand people and a quiet, cobbled centre.

The salt is the thing. Beside the town rises the Muntanya de Sal, a mountain of rock salt that has been mined for centuries, and a section of the mine is now a museum, where guides lead you underground through glittering tunnels. In the old days, salt was one of the sources of Cardona's wealth, and the colour of the mountain varies with the minerals, with streaks of red, grey and white after rain. Potash mining in nearby Súria shaped the area's economy in the twentieth century, and the landscape bears the marks.

The roads here are interesting. The route from Manresa winds through low hills, vineyards and forests, with gentle bends and good views, and it carries on toward Solsona and the Pre-Pyrenees. The surface is generally decent, but the narrow roads in the villages can be rough and gravelly. Traffic is light on weekdays, and weekends bring visitors to the castle. Summers are hot and dry, with wildfires a risk, and winters can be foggy. Spring is lovely, with green fields and blossom.

Practically, Cardona has fuel and small supermarkets, along with bars and restaurants serving Catalan food, including grilled meat, snails in season and local cheeses. The Parador has a restaurant with views over the valley. Parking near the castle is possible, though the final approach is steep and cobbled, so you may prefer to walk up from the town. Súria is the next large settlement, and Manresa, a bigger city, offers every service. Take a jacket for the cool underground mine.
t.montserrat@41.6,1.8:
A mountain that has been eaten by a thousand tourist buses still manages to be impressive. The Montserrat massif, with its serrated skyline of rounded stone pinnacles, rises just a few kilometres from this pin, which lies between Collbató and Monistrol de Montserrat. The rock is conglomerate, a gravelly stone of ancient river deposits, which erodes into towers and needles, and which makes the mountain a favourite of rock climbers. The name means serrated mountain, and from the plain the outline looks like the teeth of a saw.

On the face of the cliff, a Benedictine monastery stands where monks first settled in the eleventh century. Pilgrims come to see La Moreneta, the dark-skinned wooden statue of the Virgin, and to hear the boys' choir, the Escolania, one of the oldest choirs in Europe. During periods of repression under Franco, the monastery quietly kept Catalan language and culture alive, which is why Catalans regard it with deep affection. Hermits' cells dot the hills, and walking paths lead to chapels and viewpoints.

The roads around the mountain are a pleasure to ride. From Monistrol, the climb to the monastery runs in long bends with wonderful views, and from Collbató a smaller road winds through pine forest on the south side. Surfaces are generally good, but the narrow stretches can have gravel, and the cliff edges have little protection. On weekends and in the holiday season, traffic is heavy, with tour buses and cars queuing on the access road. Fog and cloud sometimes cover the top, and the temperature drops, so layers are useful. Autumn and spring are best, when the air is clear and the light lights up the pinnacles.

For services, Collbató has fuel and a few bars, but Esparreguera, about seven kilometres away, has more shops and fuel stations. At the top, a cafeteria and a restaurant serve simple Catalan food, and a shop sells mató cheese with honey, a traditional dessert. Parking for motorbikes is separate from cars, which makes life easier. If you want a short walk, the path to the Sant Joan chapel gives a fine view. Allow extra time on Sundays.
t.la molina overnight option@42.3,1.9:
La Molina is the old ski village at the Catalan end of the Cerdanya, a high, sunny valley that the Pyrenees split between Spain and France. At roughly 1,400 metres, it is one of the early ski stations in Spain, with lifts that go back to the middle of the twentieth century, and today the slopes above it reach beyond 2,500 metres. The pin falls nearby, about ten kilometres from Puigcerdà, which has a lake and a fine old centre, and from the French villages of Osséja and La Guingueta d'Ix.

The Cerdanya is an odd piece of geography. It is a broad glacial valley, wide and flat in the middle, with snowy peaks all round, and the border runs through it in a way that leaves Llívia, a Spanish town, entirely surrounded by France. The sun shines here for most of the year, and the air is thin and bright. In summer, the ski slopes turn into walking terrain, with wildflowers and marmots, and in autumn, the larch and beech woods turn gold.

For riders, a night in La Molina means the road is on your doorstep. The Collada de Toses, at about 1,800 metres, is the pass on the N-152 that climbs from Ripoll through woods and open pasture, with wide bends and long views. It is well surfaced and popular with riders, and the descent into Cerdanya is a favourite. Ice and snow can close or restrict the road from late autumn to spring, so check before you go. Fog is common in the valleys, and the mountain air is cold even in summer, especially after dark. The Cadí tunnel to the south and the roads into France offer more variety.

Practically, La Molina has hotels and apartments, many shut outside the ski and summer seasons, so book ahead. Fuel is in Puigcerdà, which has nearly nine thousand people and several stations, and in Alp, below La Molina. Restaurants serve mountain food, such as stews, grilled meat and local cheese, and a hot chocolate after a cold ride is a good idea. Carry warm clothes, even in July, and put gloves in the top box.
t.cap de formentor@40.0,3.2:
Everything in the Serra de Tramuntana, the mountain wall that runs along Mallorca's northwest coast for about ninety kilometres, comes to a head at Formentor. After all the terraced olive groves, stone villages and hairpin passes, the range pushes out into the sea as a narrow, jagged peninsula, with cliffs dropping vertically for several hundred metres on both sides. The Tramuntana was listed by UNESCO in 2011 as a cultural landscape, in recognition of the dry-stone terraces and water systems that generations of farmers built into the slopes, and this is the wildest end of it.

The road that gets you here is a masterpiece in its own right. It was built in the late 1920s under the Italian engineer Antonio Parietti, who chose a line hugging the cliffs, with bridges, tunnels and viewpoints, and the road is still essentially unchanged. At the Mirador des Colomer, a stone terrace on the edge, you look down some two hundred metres to the water and across to a pinnacle of rock sticking out of the sea. The gradient is gentle, the bends are many, and the surface is generally good, though it can be rough in places. Do not look at the scenery while you ride, because the drop is real.

In July and August, traffic on the Formentor road is heavy, with coaches, rental cars and cyclists in every corner, so go early, before nine, when the light is clear and the road is almost empty. You may meet wild goats on the road, standing still and unbothered, and see raptors circling over the cliffs. Eleonora's falcons nest on the cliffs in summer and hunt migrating birds in the autumn. The sea below is an astonishing turquoise, and the pine forest smells of resin.

The bay of Formentor, with its long pale beach, is a short stop on the way, and a famous old hotel above it hosted writers, artists and politicians in the twentieth century. Wind at the end of the cape can be strong, and a sudden gust on a cliff road is not to be underestimated. Late September is a good time, when the summer crowds are gone and the sea is still warm.
t.cap de formentor lighthouse@40.0,3.2:
The lighthouse at Formentor stands on the very end of the cape, some two hundred metres above the sea, in a spot that feels like the edge of everything. It was built in 1863, a squat white tower and keeper's house on bare rock, with only grass, thyme and a few twisted pines to soften the scene. On a clear day, you can see across the sea to Menorca on the horizon, and below your boots the cliffs fall in sheer walls to water so blue it looks artificial. The wind is almost always blowing, sometimes hard enough to rock a parked bike on its stand.

The road to the lighthouse is the last section of the Formentor ride, and it is a quiet, narrow strip of tarmac with a short tunnel and a couple of tight bends. On the way, a small bar with a terrace sells coffee and sandwiches, which makes a fine reward after a long ride. The road is a dead end, so everyone has to turn and come back, which means there is traffic in both directions, and in July and August the car park can be full by late morning. Come in the early evening, when the buses have gone and the light turns gold.

Nature around the lighthouse is hardy. Wild goats graze on the slopes, and you can often see them picking their way across rocks that would terrify a human. Birds of prey ride the updrafts, including Eleonora's falcons in the summer, and the sea below holds shoals of fish and, if you are lucky, a passing dolphin. The air smells of salt and rosemary. A path leads along the cliff for walkers, but take care near the edge, since there are few barriers.

Bring water in summer, since the sun on the exposed rock is hot, and a windproof layer in winter, when the wind can be bitter. Sunset is the best moment, though you will want to leave soon after to avoid riding the cliff road in the dark. The return is just as good as the way out, with the Bay of Pollença opening ahead of you.
t.stateline@39.0,-119.9:
Stateline is a town that exists because of a line on a map. On the southeast corner of Lake Tahoe, the border between California and Nevada runs straight through the street, and a cluster of casino towers stands on the Nevada side, a few steps from the motels, cafes and gas stations of South Lake Tahoe. When California tightened its rules on gambling, the casinos took their chance on the other side of the line, and the glitter has been there ever since. It looks odd against the pines and the mountains behind, and that is part of the joke.

As the end of a lake loop, it works well. After a day in the saddle, tourist-heavy but lovely, you roll onto the long, busy strip of Highway 50 and find all the practicalities in a row: fuel, groceries, bars, big buffet restaurants that are cheap and satisfying after a long ride, and an unending supply of rooms. Casino car parks are free and handy for a bike, and the food is dependable, if not subtle. Weekends are loud, and summer evenings are busy, but you do not have to gamble to enjoy the show.

Behind the casinos, the ski area of Heavenly climbs the slope, with a gondola from town and views from the top across the whole basin: a vast, blue lake ringed by granite peaks. In summer, the gondola carries walkers and sightseers, and on the lake itself there are paddle-wheel boats and beaches. The east shore of Tahoe is quieter, with the Nevada side's pine-covered state park and a few secluded sandy coves, and it is worth a detour if you have time.

Weather in the Sierra changes fast. Summer evenings are cool even after a hot day, thunderstorms can build over the crest in the afternoon, and early snow can arrive from October. Altitude, at roughly 1,900 metres, means the sun is strong and you will feel the air is thinner if you have just come from the coast. Lock your bike, stay hydrated and make time for sunset on the beach before you collapse into bed.
t.tioga road point 4@37.9,-119.4:
Tuolumne Meadows is the largest subalpine meadow in the Sierra Nevada, a long, flat sweep of grass at 8,600 feet with the Tuolumne River winding through it and a ring of granite domes and peaks around the edge. Lembert Dome rises on one side like a bald head, and the spires of Cathedral Peak stand on the south, with snow lingering in their gullies into July. The meadow is lovely in the evening, when the alpenglow touches the peaks and the river is silver.

John Muir, who spent summers in these mountains in the 1870s and 1880s, camped here often, and the Sierra Club, which he founded in 1892, held its first outings in the meadows. Muir's campaign to protect the high country led to the creation of Yosemite National Park in 1890. The meadow was also an old trade route for the Mono Paiute, who crossed the Sierra here to trade with the people of the western slope, carrying obsidian and pinon nuts.

For a rider, the stretch from Tenaya Lake to the meadow is a joy. The road is open and smooth, with long, easy bends and views across the meadow, and the air is cool and fresh. Traffic is steady in summer, but the road is wide enough that you can find space. Watch for deer, which graze near the road at dusk, and for cyclists. A few corners have gravel, especially in early summer after snowplough operations, so take care.

Tuolumne has a store, a grill and a visitor centre, along with a campground and a lodge with tent cabins that book out early. Fuel has traditionally been sold at a seasonal station here during summer, though availability changes from year to year, so fill up at Crane Flat or Lee Vining if you are unsure. The snow melts late, and the road may not open until June. The meadows are at their best from July to September, when wildflowers bloom.

The weather at this altitude is changeable, with sudden afternoon thunderstorms that can bring hail and lightning. If you hear thunder, get off exposed areas. Nights are cold, and frost is possible even in August. Mosquitoes can be a nuisance in early summer, especially near the water. Bring insect repellent and a warm sleeping bag if you plan to camp.

Walk out onto the meadow at dusk and listen. The silence is deep, broken only by the river.
t.tioga road point 5@37.9,-119.3:
Tioga Pass, at 9,943 feet, is the highest highway pass in California and the eastern gate of Yosemite. The entrance station sits just below the top, in a high alpine landscape of granite, scattered pines and small lakes, with the snow-streaked ridges of the Sierra crest rising on every side. Beyond the pass, the road plunges down the eastern escarpment in a series of long, steep descents toward Mono Lake, losing nearly 3,200 feet in 12 miles.

The pass has a history older than the road. Paiute traders crossed here for centuries, and in the 1860s miners staked claims on the eastern slope, finding silver ore at Bennettville, a short way below the top. The Great Sierra Mining Company built a road in 1883 to haul supplies to the mine, and it was a costly failure, since the ore proved poor and the company collapsed. The road, however, remained, and in 1915 it was purchased and given to the federal government, becoming the basis for the modern Tioga Road.

The ride to the pass is magnificent. From Tuolumne Meadows, the road climbs gently through meadows and rock, then passes the Dana Meadows, with views of Mount Dana and Mount Gibbs. The surface is generally good, though frost heaves are common. Just beyond the entrance station, a small resort, the Tioga Pass Resort, serves a famous slice of pie to riders and hikers, and has a few cabins. It opens only in summer, and the dates depend on the snow.

The pass is closed in winter, usually from November to late May or June, when snow can be twenty feet deep. Check the status online, since it varies each year. Lee Vining, about twelve miles down the east side, is the nearest, with several stations and cafes. Fill up there if you are heading west, or at Crane Flat if you come from the other direction.

Be careful of the altitude. Even a few hours at nearly 10,000 feet can cause headaches and tiredness, so drink water and take it easy. Wind and cold are common, and storms can arrive within minutes. Dress in layers and carry rain gear.

On the east side, Ellery Lake and Tioga Lake are small, cold alpine lakes beside the road, with brilliant blue water. They are good places for a break, with picnic tables and views.

The road from Tioga Pass drops into Lee Vining in a headlong rush, and the first thing you see is Mono Lake spread out below like a pool of molten silver. It sits in a basin at 6,400 feet, with no outlet, so the water that flows in from the Sierra streams leaves only by evaporation, and the lake has become strange. It is two and a half times as salty as the ocean and highly alkaline, with a texture that feels slippery on the skin, and it supports no fish, but trillions of brine shrimp and alkali flies.

Rising from the water are the tufa towers, pale spires and knobs of limestone formed when calcium-rich springs bubble up through the alkaline water. They were built underwater and exposed when the lake level fell. The level fell because, from 1941, Los Angeles diverted most of the streams that fed the lake into its aqueduct, and the lake dropped by about forty-five feet. Local people fought a long campaign to save it, and in 1994 the state ordered the diversions reduced, and the lake has been slowly recovering since. The shrimp and flies feed huge flocks of migrating birds, including California gulls and phalaropes, and the lake is one of the key bird sites of the West.

For a rider, Lee Vining is the practical place after the long descent from Tioga Pass. The town is small, a strip of cafes, motels and gas stations along US 395, but it is the best place on this side for fuel and food. A gas station here has a restaurant attached, called the Whoa Nellie Deli, which is famous for its fish tacos and the view of the lake from the picnic tables. It is a favourite among riders, and the parking lot is often full of bikes.

The riding north and south on US 395 is excellent, with wide, flowing highway through volcanic and high-desert country. South leads toward Mammoth Lakes and the Owens Valley, and north to Bridgeport and the road to Bodie, a well preserved ghost town. The weather on the east side is dry and often windy, with strong gusts in the afternoon, and thunderstorms in summer. Winters are cold, and the pass may be closed.

Visit the lakeshore at the South Tufa area at sunset, when the towers glow and the water turns pink. The air smells of sage and salt, and the quiet is deep.

Osona is the plain around Vic, a high, cool basin ringed by hills, and the Lluçanès, to its north-west, is a quiet plateau of farmhouses, woods and cornfields that few visitors ever see. These coordinates fall close to Olost, a village of about twelve hundred people, and the land around it is a patchwork of stone-walled fields and isolated masías, the big, fortified farmhouses that are the backbone of rural Catalonia. It is a place to slow down, and the roads reward it.

Catalonia's reputation rests on its cooking, and Osona is where much of it comes from. The area is famous for its cured meats, including the fuet, a thin, dry sausage that goes into every picnic, and the botifarra, a fresh sausage grilled over coals. Pigs are raised in large numbers, and in winter the villages hold traditional slaughter days, when families gather to make sausages and hams. Cheese, honey and mushrooms from the hills round out the table, and a meal in a farmhouse restaurant is an experience that justifies a long ride.

The roads here are narrow and winding, with tight bends, short climbs and frequent junctions. The surface is mostly good, though some of the lanes are patched and gravelly at the edges, and tractors and cyclists are common. Views across the plain to the Pyrenees, a white line of snow on the horizon in winter, are splendid on a clear day. Autumn brings mist in the valleys, and the colours of the woods in October are superb. In summer the heat can be fierce, and the best time to ride is the early morning.

Olost and Oristà are tiny and have little more than a bar and a shop. Vic, a fine old market town of nearly forty thousand people, lies about fifteen kilometres away, and has stations, supermarkets and a cluster of good restaurants. Gurb, a village near it, has a few more facilities. The nearest large town with every service is Vic, and it is also a pleasure to visit, with a Roman temple, a cathedral decorated with murals by Josep Maria Sert and a big Saturday market. Fill up before you go, and bring layers, because the weather on the plateau can change in an hour.

Girona sits where the Onyar River meets the Ter, and its old town is one of the best-preserved in Spain. These coordinates fall in the countryside to the east, near Bordils, Celrà and Foixà, in the flat, fertile plain of the Gironès, a landscape of poplars, maize and orchards. The town of Girona, about ten kilometres away, has nearly a hundred thousand people and is the main city of the northern part of Catalonia.

The old quarter climbs a hill above the river, with a cathedral at the top that is approached by a monumental staircase of ninety steps, which was used as a location in a famous television fantasy series. Below it lies the Call, the medieval Jewish quarter, a tangle of lanes and stairways that was home to a thriving community until its expulsion in 1492. Along the Onyar, rows of houses painted in yellow, ochre and red hang over the water, and the iron footbridge that crosses it was built in a workshop run by Gustave Eiffel's company. A walk along the city walls gives a view over the red roofs to the mountains.

The ride finishes or starts here, as part of a loop that runs from Barcelona to the Pyrenees and back. The roads east of Girona are flat and straight, with a good surface and light traffic, and in spring the fields are green and the poppies bloom. A short ride to the north leads to the Albera hills and the border, while to the east, the Empordà coast, with Begur, Pals and Cadaqués, is some of the finest in Spain. Autumn is the best season, when the heat has eased and the crowds have gone.

Foixà has a castle and little else, and Bordils and Celrà are small towns with the basic services. Girona has all the fuel and food you could need, from supermarkets to Michelin-starred restaurants, and the Roca brothers' famous restaurant is one of the best in the world. For a simpler meal, try a menu del día in the old town, with rice, fish and a glass of wine. Park outside the centre, because the old quarter is a maze of steps.
